title: DCBA: Detection of Collaborative Black-Hole Attacks in Connected Dominated Set using Baiting Process
summary: Mobile Ad-hoc Network (MANET) is temporary and dynamic network topology, wherein nodes are mobile in nature and distributed randomly in a network area. In MANET, nodes cooperate with each other to operate and forward data through multihop communication between source and destination. MANET is exposed to different types of attacks due to absence of central administration. However, some nodes decline to cooperate, misbehaves and appears to be malicious affecting network functionality and connectivity. Providing security and identifying malicious node has become one of the challenging research topics in MANET. Black-hole attack is considered to be most popular attack that degrades the overall network performance. Black-hole node falsely advertises the shortest path to destination intentionally to disrupt the network communication resulting in packet drop. In collaborative black-hole attacks, multiple black-hole nodes cooperate and launch attacks in order to degrade network reliability. In this article we propose a Lightweight technique to detect and isolate Collaborative Black-Hole attacks (LW-CBH) by enhancing existing AODV routing protocol. In this scheme a timer based baiting process and reverse tracing setup is used to detect malicious node through control status message in MAC layer which are Reply Sequence (R-SEQ) and Code Sequence (C-SEQ) message of connected dominated set of nodes. However existing AODV routing protocol fails to detect malicious node during dynamic topology changing in MANET. Simulation of proposed technique is performed using discrete event simulator tool NS-2.35. The simulation results are evaluated for throughput, packet delivery ratio, average end-to-end delay and normalized routing overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LW-CBH, a lightweight scheme that enhances AODV to detect and isolate collaborative black-hole attacks in MANETs using a timer-based baiting process, reverse tracing, and MAC-layer control status messages (R-SEQ and C-SEQ), validated via NS-2.35 simulations.
AI.motivation: MANETs lack central administration, making them vulnerable to attacks. Some nodes refuse to cooperate and act maliciously, harming network functionality. Black-hole attacks, especially collaborative ones where multiple malicious nodes cooperate, degrade network reliability, and the existing AODV protocol fails to detect malicious nodes during dynamic topology changes.
AI.method: The authors propose a lightweight technique (LW-CBH) that enhances the AODV routing protocol. It uses a timer-based baiting process and reverse tracing setup to detect malicious nodes via control status messages at the MAC layer: Reply Sequence (R-SEQ) and Code Sequence (C-SEQ) messages of a connected dominated set of nodes, to detect and isolate collaborative black-hole attacks.
AI.result: Simulation performed in NS-2.35 evaluated throughput, packet delivery ratio, average end-to-end delay, and normalized routing overhead, demonstrating the proposed technique's effectiveness in detecting and isolating collaborative black-hole attacks compared to existing AODV.
AI.conclusion: LW-CBH successfully detects and isolates collaborative black-hole attacks in dynamic MANET topologies by enhancing AODV with MAC-layer control messages, overcoming the limitations of the original AODV protocol.

title: The energetic cost of mitigating AI attacks in cellular networks
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, submitted to IEEE Communications Magazine
summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), generally as Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, in all levels and aspects of cellular networks demonstrates the success of data-driven algorithms; for example, the Radio Intelligence Controller (RIC) of the O-RAN paradigm bestows the network with optimised radio resource allocation, load balancing or energy efficiency functions, among others. Nevertheless, this dependency on data opens new security vulnerabilities, as attackers can alter data properties and steer ML models to underperform or degrade. Conversely, the developed mitigation strategies are effective, but they generate a computational load which, in consequence, results in an energy cost generally overlooked, even in the current energy-awareness context. In this work, consumption of a defence technique is characterised, and the challenges raised by the triad of ML accuracy, robustness and energy efficiency are outlined.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the security vulnerabilities that data-driven ML introduces in O-RAN/cellular networks (e.g., adversarial data manipulation), and highlights an overlooked problem: mitigation defenses impose computational/energy costs. It characterizes the energy consumption of a defense technique and outlines the three-way trade-off between ML accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency.
AI.motivation: AI/ML is widely integrated into cellular networks (e.g., the O-RAN Radio Intelligence Controller) for resource allocation, load balancing, and energy efficiency. However, this data dependency creates new attack surfaces where adversaries can tamper with data to degrade ML performance. Existing defense strategies are effective but impose computational load and energy costs that are generally overlooked, even in today's energy-conscious context.
AI.method: The work characterizes the energy consumption of an ML defense (mitigation) technique deployed in the cellular/O-RAN context, and systematically examines the interplay among ML accuracy, adversarial robustness, and energy efficiency.
AI.result: Defense techniques against data-driven attacks, while effective at maintaining robustness, incur a non-negligible computational load that translates into measurable energy consumption, revealing a previously overlooked cost in energy-aware network deployments.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental triad of challenges—ML accuracy, robustness against attacks, and energy efficiency—that must be jointly addressed. Security defenses cannot be evaluated solely on effectiveness; their energy footprint must be accounted for in energy-aware cellular/O-RAN systems.

title: Non-Degenerate Risk Certification for Automated Security Decisions: A Decision-Contract Theory with ATT\&CK-Aligned Triage as a Worked Instance
summary: An unconditional risk bound on automated decisions can be satisfied without automating anything, since a selector that never acts drives the bound to zero. We show this is structural: any risk certificate is defined over a decision contract, the inputs a system acts on plus the semantic relation under which an output counts correct, and weakening either hides base-classifier error. We develop a decision-contract theory: an error-conservation law showing error is only reassigned among harmful automation, human deferral, and semantic masking; a label-free singleton capacity certifying structural incapacity, with a risk-feasible refinement separating recoverable threshold misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity; and a non-degenerate actionability certificate excluding all-abstain solutions by construction. We instantiate this on ATT\&CK-aligned alert triage for LLM-based intrusion detection, the setting that exposed the vacuity failure. Across 3 IDS datasets, 6 LLMs, and 4 error-rate thresholds, empirical false-attribution risk stays at or below target in 90.3% of configurations, with 83.4% mean correct automation. The capacity diagnostic explains every low-utility configuration; its refinement separates genuine misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity, confirmed by an exhibited alternative threshold; a training-stability re-run finds no confirmed structural-incapacity instance; and real fine-grained attack-subtype labels confirm the coarsening-transfer identity under a genuine many-to-one map, with small but non-zero masking mass.

AI.tldr: The paper exposes a structural flaw: risk bounds on automated decisions can be trivially satisfied by never acting (all-abstain), because any risk certificate is defined over a "decision contract" whose terms (inputs acted on, and the semantic relation under which outputs count correct) can be weakened to hide base-classifier error. The authors formalize decision-contract theory (error conservation, label-free capacity, non-degenerate actionability) and validate it on ATT&CK-aligned alert triage for LLM-based intrusion detection.
AI.motivation: Current unconditional risk bounds on automated decision systems are vacuous: they can be met by a selector that never takes any action. The authors show this vacuity is structural, not incidental, arising from how risk certificates are defined over a "decision contract." This was exposed in the concrete setting of ATT&CK-aligned alert triage for LLM-based intrusion detection.
AI.method: Develop decision-contract theory comprising: (1) an error-conservation law showing error is only reassigned among harmful automation, human deferral, and semantic masking; (2) a label-free singleton capacity certifying structural incapacity, with a risk-feasible refinement that separates recoverable threshold misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity; and (3) a non-degenerate actionability certificate that excludes all-abstain solutions by construction. Instantiate on ATT&CK-aligned alert triage for LLM-based intrusion detection.
AI.result: Across 3 IDS datasets, 6 LLMs, and 4 error-rate thresholds, empirical false-attribution risk stays at or below target in 90.3% of configurations, with 83.4% mean correct automation. The capacity diagnostic explains every low-utility configuration; its refinement separates genuine misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity (confirmed by an exhibited alternative threshold). A training-stability re-run finds no confirmed structural-incapacity instance. Real fine-grained attack-subtype labels confirm the coarsening-transfer identity under a genuine many-to-one map, with small but non-zero masking mass.
AI.conclusion: Risk certificates must be tied to an explicit decision contract; weakening either its operational scope or its semantic correctness relation hides base-classifier error and renders bounds vacuous. The proposed theory supplies sound, non-degenerate certificates (error conservation, capacity, actionability) and is empirically validated for LLM-based intrusion detection, where risk is controlled in most configurations while preserving high correct automation.

title: SoK: From Generation to Consumption of Privacy Documents in Software Systems
comment: This SoK paper has been accepted by NDSS 2027
summary: Privacy documents (e.g., privacy policies) are a central mechanism through which digital services disclose data practices and seek user consent. Over the past decades, research on privacy documents has expanded significantly, encompassing not only traditional privacy policies but also short notices (e.g., privacy labels) and interface-level transparency mechanisms. As this research area continues to grow, it has become increasingly difficult to obtain a coherent view of how privacy documents are created, analyzed, evaluated, and maintained across their lifecycle. This SoK provides a unified, lifecycle-oriented view of privacy documents from a software engineering perspective. We systematically review and analyze 290 papers published between 2010 and 2025, organizing them around five research questions that examine how privacy documents are (1) defined and scoped, (2) generated, (3) analyzed and extracted, (4) checked for inconsistencies and noncompliance, and (5) evaluated and improved for usability. Building on our findings, we identify 15 key research trends and 21 open opportunities. We further chart four broader research directions that highlight (i) emerging challenges in AI-centric platforms, (ii) the need for diverse and up-to-date data foundations, (iii) LLM-based unified policy-code analysis, and (iv) dual usability for end-users and developers. We hope this SoK provides a shared foundation for future research on privacy policies and privacy documents.

AI.tldr: This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) paper offers a unified, lifecycle-oriented view of privacy documents (policies, labels, transparency mechanisms) from a software engineering perspective, based on a systematic review of 290 papers (2010–2025). It organizes findings around five research questions, identifies 15 research trends and 21 open opportunities, and charts four broader research directions.
AI.motivation: As research on privacy documents has grown rapidly and fragmented across many sub-areas (policy generation, analysis, compliance checking, usability), it has become hard to obtain a coherent, end-to-end view of how privacy documents are created, analyzed, evaluated, and maintained across their lifecycle. The authors aim to provide a shared foundation and a software-engineering-oriented synthesis of this scattered field.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature review/SoK: they collect and analyze 290 papers published between 2010 and 2025, and organize them around five research questions covering (1) definition and scoping of privacy documents, (2) generation, (3) analysis and information extraction, (4) checking for inconsistencies and noncompliance, and (5) evaluation and usability improvement. Findings are synthesized into trends, open opportunities, and research directions.
AI.result: The review yields a lifecycle-oriented framework for privacy documents and identifies 15 key research trends and 21 open opportunities. It further charts four broader research directions: emerging challenges in AI-centric platforms, the need for diverse and up-to-date data foundations, LLM-based unified policy-code analysis, and dual usability for both end-users and developers.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a unified, lifecycle-oriented perspective is needed to coherently advance research on privacy policies and documents, and it hopes this SoK serves as a shared foundation for future work across the privacy documents research area.

title: Entropy-Augmented Multi-Objective Policy Optimization in Multiagent Systems
summary: Autonomous agent teams deployed in settings such as marine and extraterrestrial outposts must coordinate actions to achieve optimal outcomes across multiple competing objectives. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms such as NSGA-II optimize for diversity in the objective space, but neglect diversity in the behavior space, possibly leading to premature convergence and a collapse in behaviors that may differentiate policies in different external conditions. To address this, we introduce an entropy-augmented policy evaluation strategy that incorporates an entropy bonus into agent fitness scores, discouraging behavioral homogeneity across the evolving population. By augmenting policy evaluation with a behavior-space diversity signal while preserving the underlying Pareto optimization framework, our method is designed to encourage exploration of behaviorally distinct policies in multiagent domains. We evaluate our approach across rover-domain experiments with qualitatively distinct reward structures and observe hypervolume improvements of up to 48% relative to the NSGA-II baseline, suggesting that behavioral diversity is a promising and underexplored direction for improving multi-objective multiagent evolutionary optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes adding an entropy bonus to NSGA-II fitness scores to preserve behavioral diversity in multi-objective multiagent evolutionary optimization, achieving up to 48% hypervolume improvement over baseline NSGA-II in rover-domain experiments.
AI.motivation: Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms like NSGA-II optimize diversity in the objective space but ignore diversity in the behavior space, which can cause premature convergence and a collapse of behaviors that differ across external conditions, especially in autonomous agent teams in settings like marine or extraterrestrial outposts.
AI.method: The authors introduce an entropy-augmented policy evaluation strategy that adds an entropy bonus to agent fitness scores. This incorporates a behavior-space diversity signal while preserving the underlying Pareto optimization (NSGA-II) framework, encouraging exploration of behaviorally distinct policies in multiagent domains.
AI.result: Experiments in rover-domain scenarios with qualitatively distinct reward structures show hypervolume improvements of up to 48% relative to the NSGA-II baseline.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral diversity is a promising and underexplored direction for improving multi-objective multiagent evolutionary optimization, as demonstrated by significant hypervolume gains over standard NSGA-II.

title: SynWeaver: Website-Prior Task and Trajectory Co-Synthesis for Web Agents
summary: Web agents often struggle to generalize to unseen websites because they lack website-specific supervision. Recent exploration-based data synthesis methods reduce manual annotation, but they still face two key limitations: they often fail to cover the full functionality of a website, and without sufficient website prior knowledge, they tend to propose hallucinated tasks, which in turn limits the diversity and efficiency of downstream trajectory synthesis. We present \textbf{SynWeaver}, a website-prior task-trajectory co-synthesis framework designed to address these challenges. SynWeaver first performs structured website exploration and constructs a website map that covers a broad set of functionally distinct page states and executable interactions on the target website. It then derives page-level and transition-level supervision from this map to train a UI-aware model with website-specific priors, enabling more grounded task proposals. Finally, SynWeaver performs collaborative task-trajectory synthesis, jointly updating the task and execution trajectory when they become inconsistent, and then verifies and repairs the collected results to produce executable, semantically aligned supervision. Experiments on WebArena and WebVoyager demonstrate that SynWeaver consistently outperforms strong synthesis baselines and yields more effective supervision for both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: SynWeaver is a framework that jointly synthesizes website-specific tasks and execution trajectories to generate grounded supervision for web agents, addressing hallucination and limited coverage in exploration-based data synthesis.
AI.motivation: Web agents struggle to generalize to unseen websites due to a lack of website-specific supervision. Existing exploration-based data synthesis methods reduce manual annotation but fail to cover full website functionality and, without website prior knowledge, tend to propose hallucinated tasks, limiting downstream trajectory diversity and efficiency.
AI.method: SynWeaver performs structured website exploration to build a website map covering functionally distinct page states and executable interactions. It extracts page-level and transition-level supervision from the map to train a UI-aware model with website-specific priors, enabling grounded task proposals. It then performs collaborative task-trajectory synthesis, jointly updating the task and execution trajectory when inconsistent, and verifies/repairs results to produce executable, semantically aligned supervision.
AI.result: Experiments on WebArena and WebVoyager show SynWeaver consistently outperforms strong synthesis baselines and produces more effective supervision for both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: By grounding task proposals in a learned website map and co-synthesizing tasks with trajectories, SynWeaver generates higher-quality, executable supervision that improves web agent generalization to unseen websites.

title: The Affordance is the Message: Creative Media as Complex Systems
comment: 17th International Conference on Computational Creativity (ICCC 2026), Coimbra, Portugal
summary: The affordances of a creative medium strongly condition the creative artefacts the medium will produce. In this work, we present a formalisation of computational creativity (CC) media using the conceptual toolbox of complex systems (CS). We introduce the notions of emergence, collective intelligence and self-organisation, non-linear dynamics, criticality, multi-scale hierarchy, phase transitions, diversity of attractors, path dependence, and open-endedness, and connect them to the existing CC literature. Together these nine properties form a vocabulary with which creative media can be described and compared at the system level, while medium affordances are the design-level mechanisms that determine each medium's complex system properties. The formalisation emphasises the influence of each medium's affordances in determining what the medium can produce in creative processes. To demonstrate the proposed theoretical approach, we characterise a diverse set of media (r/place, Minecraft, cellular automata, Twitter, Boids, ...) using this vocabulary. The proposed formalisation under the CS concepts serves a dual purpose: it establishes a link between the affordances and realised practices of the medium, and it offers a shared lens for characterising existing creative media.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formalisation of computational creativity media using concepts from complex systems (emergence, self-organisation, criticality, etc.), framing medium affordances as design-level mechanisms that shape system-level creative properties, and demonstrates the approach by characterising media such as r/place, Minecraft, cellular automata, Twitter, and Boids.
AI.motivation: Creative media strongly condition what can be created with them, yet the computational creativity field lacks a systematic, system-level vocabulary for describing and comparing how a medium's affordances shape its creative outputs. The authors aim to bridge this gap by grounding media analysis in complex systems theory.
AI.method: The authors introduce nine complex systems concepts—emergence, collective intelligence and self-organisation, non-linear dynamics, criticality, multi-scale hierarchy, phase transitions, diversity of attractors, path dependence, and open-endedness—and connect each to existing computational creativity literature. They treat medium affordances as design-level mechanisms determining a medium's complex system properties, and apply this vocabulary to characterise a diverse set of media (r/place, Minecraft, cellular automata, Twitter, Boids, etc.).
AI.result: The formalisation yields a shared vocabulary connecting medium affordances to realised creative practices, demonstrated through the characterisation of diverse media. It establishes a dual-purpose link: tying affordances to what a medium actually produces in creative processes, and offering a common lens for comparing existing creative media at the system level.
AI.conclusion: The complex systems vocabulary provides a coherent formalisation of computational creativity media, enabling systematic comparison of media and clarifying how design-level affordances determine the creative possibilities each medium realises, thereby advancing both theoretical understanding and practical design of creative media.

title: Test-Time Optimization of Query Embeddings with Ranking Aware Reward Maximization
summary: Dense retrievers rank documents using vector similarity between a frozen encoder and a precomputed index. While test-time ranking rewards from a reranker or LLM judge can improve results, existing methods discard this signal after a single query. Updating the retriever's weights makes rewards reusable, but this requires parameter access, which is unavailable for closed-source models, and is computationally prohibitive. We propose TTT-Embed (Test-Time Tuning of Embeddings), a framework that distills ranking rewards into a lightweight, learned vector within the output embedding space of a frozen model. This vector is optimized purely from scalar ranking scores assigned to the retriever's own candidate documents, requiring no access to model weights, ground-truth labels, or modifications to index. A single scope parameter controls rewards reuse (global, task, or query), enabling a principled trade-off between reusability and specificity under a fixed reward computation budget. We demonstrate that as the available reward budget scales, the optimal sharing scope shifts dynamically from global-wise to task-wise and finally to query-wise. Evaluated across five embedding models and 15 MTEB retrieval tasks, TTT-Embed improves test-time retrieval by up to +8.36 nDCG@10. Crucially, the learned states generalize effectively to unseen queries (up to +8.57 nDCG@10) and unseen tasks (up to +4.71 nDCG@10). Furthermore, TTT-Embed successfully resolves catastrophic forgetting: by leaving base weights entirely frozen, it recovers degraded general capabilities (up to +8.00 nDCG@10, even surpassing the original base model) while preserving in-domain specialization. These results establish ranking rewards as a reusable test-time state, enabling budget-efficient adaptation for any embedding model, including closed-source APIs.

AI.tldr: TTT-Embed distills test-time ranking rewards into a lightweight learned vector in a frozen encoder's output space, enabling reusable, budget-efficient retrieval adaptation without weight access—improving retrieval by up to +8.57 nDCG@10 and reversing catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time ranking signals (from rerankers or LLM judges) are discarded after a single query, while updating retriever weights to reuse rewards is impractical for closed-source models and computationally expensive. The goal is to make ranking rewards reusable at test time without requiring parameter access, labels, or index changes.
AI.method: TTT-Embed learns a lightweight vector inside the frozen model's output embedding space, optimized purely from scalar ranking scores assigned to the retriever's own candidate documents. A single scope parameter controls reward reuse (global, task, or query), trading off reusability vs. specificity under a fixed reward budget. The optimal sharing scope shifts dynamically from global to task to query as the reward budget scales.
AI.result: Across five embedding models and 15 MTEB retrieval tasks, TTT-Embed improves test-time retrieval by up to +8.36 nDCG@10. Learned states generalize to unseen queries (+8.57 nDCG@10) and unseen tasks (+4.71 nDCG@10). By freezing base weights, it resolves catastrophic forgetting, recovering degraded general capabilities by up to +8.00 nDCG@10 (surpassing the original base model) while preserving in-domain specialization.
AI.conclusion: Ranking rewards can serve as a reusable test-time state. TTT-Embed enables budget-efficient adaptation for any embedding model, including closed-source APIs, establishing a principled trade-off between reusability and specificity without weight access or model modification.

title: Position: Reasoning is a Learnable Rule-Based Process
summary: Autonomous reasoning is among the most scientifically and economically motivating topics in AI today. Historically the purview of symbolic AI, recent advances have mainly emerged from deep probabilistic generative models. Despite immense interest and rapid progress, the generative AI community has not clearly converged on operational definitions for reasoning and often implicitly rejects the historical treatment of this topic in logic and verifiable automated reasoning. This position contends that definitional ambiguity leaves the construct validity of reasoning evaluation unverifiable, undermining quantifiable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning. We also contend that this ambiguity is addressable. To that end, we provide (1) operational definitions based on a synthesis of the literature, positioning valid and sound reasoning as a learnable rule-based process; and (2) a checklist for best practices in the communication of AI reasoning research.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that the lack of operational definitions for "reasoning" in generative AI undermines verifiable evaluation, and proposes operational definitions plus a communication checklist to restore construct validity.
AI.motivation: The generative AI community has not converged on operational definitions of reasoning and often dismisses the historical logic-based treatment, leaving the construct validity of reasoning evaluation unverifiable and hindering trustworthy autonomous reasoning.
AI.method: A position/argumentative approach that synthesizes the literature to formulate operational definitions positioning valid and sound reasoning as a learnable rule-based process, and proposes a best-practices checklist for communicating AI reasoning research.
AI.result: Provides operational definitions of reasoning and a checklist for best practices, demonstrating that definitional ambiguity in AI reasoning research is addressable.
AI.conclusion: Definitional ambiguity in generative AI reasoning is a solvable problem; adopting operational definitions and communication standards can make reasoning evaluation verifiable and support progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning.

title: LLMs Know the Constraint But Do Not Use It: Activation Bottlenecks in Pragmatic Constraint Reasoning
summary: When a salient surface cue competes with an implicit feasibility constraint, LLMs often fail -- but aggregate accuracy conflates genuine constraint inference with conservative defaulting. We formalize the distinction as conditional constraint activation: the constraint is internally encoded (Knowledge) symmetrically across constraint-present and -absent prompts (Symmetry), yet only sometimes routed into the decision (Routing) and repairable by a donor activation (Repair). A quartet diagnostic over 14 models reveals two failure modes; probes on two open weights decode the constraint above $88\%$, yet activation patching repairs one ($+6.4$ nats) and not the other ($-0.07$). On a mitigation frontier, no prompted intervention reaches the repair corner: all inflate conservative bias through a single mediation pathway -- prerequisite mention. Hidden-constraint failure is a routing problem, not a knowledge problem.

AI.tldr: The paper distinguishes true constraint inference from conservative defaulting in LLMs, showing hidden-constraint failures stem from routing (whether constraint knowledge is used) rather than knowledge (whether it is encoded). A "quartet diagnostic" reveals two failure modes: one repairable via activation patching, the other not; prompted interventions cannot reach full repair because they all inflate conservative bias through a single mediation pathway (prerequisite mention).
AI.motivation: Aggregate accuracy on tasks where a salient surface cue competes with an implicit feasibility constraint conflates genuine constraint inference with merely conservative defaulting. The authors aim to separate whether LLM failures come from not encoding the constraint (Knowledge) or from encoding it but not using it (Routing), in order to design better interventions.
AI.method: Formalizes conditional constraint activation as a three-part property: Knowledge (constraint encoded symmetrically across constraint-present and -absent prompts), Symmetry, Routing (constraint only sometimes routed into decisions), and Repair (recoverable by a donor activation). A "quartet diagnostic" is applied over 14 models; linear probes on two open-weight models decode the constraint above 88%; activation patching tests repairability; a mitigation frontier evaluates whether prompted interventions reach the repair corner and traces a shared mediation pathway (prerequisite mention).
AI.result: Two failure modes emerge: one model's constraint is repairable through activation patching (+6.4 nats), while the other is not (-0.07). Across the mitigation frontier, no prompted intervention reaches the repair corner; all inflate conservative bias via a single mediation pathway, prerequisite mention.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-constraint failure is a routing problem, not a knowledge problem: LLMs encode the constraint but sometimes fail to route it into decision-making, and prompted interventions tend to induce conservative defaulting rather than genuine constraint activation.

title: LoKiFormer: Locality-aware Attention with Decoupled Knowledge Memory for Efficient Large Language Model Pretraining
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable breakthroughs across various applications. However, their architectures remain inefficient in pretraining due to two main limitations: (i) self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality, leading to redundant modeling of sequence-internal local information; (ii) mixture-of-experts (MoE) implicitly couples knowledge storage with computational pathways, hindering flexible access to sequence-external global knowledge. To overcome these limitations, we propose LoKiFormer, a novel LLM architecture that augments the standard decoder with two dedicated modules: 1) Local Fusion Attention (LFA), which incorporates a convolutional fusion to attention, explicitly capturing local patterns and allowing the attention to operate on more informative representations; 2) Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), which introduces a parametric key-value memory that explicitly stores global knowledge in addressable slots, decoupling storage from computation and enabling direct knowledge retrieval. Together, these modules enable LoKiFormer to achieve more efficient and effective integration of information at both levels. Experimental results show that LoKiFormer converges 1.33x faster in pre-training than baseline models, underscoring its superiority over existing LLM architectures.

AI.tldr: LoKiFormer is a new LLM architecture that adds two modules — Local Fusion Attention (LFA) for explicit locality modeling and a Knowledge Memory Module (KMM) for decoupled, addressable global knowledge storage — achieving 1.33x faster pretraining convergence than baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM pretraining is inefficient because (i) self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality, causing redundant modeling of local sequential information, and (ii) MoE implicitly couples knowledge storage with computation paths, preventing flexible access to sequence-external global knowledge.
AI.method: LoKiFormer augments the standard decoder with two modules: Local Fusion Attention (LFA), which adds convolutional fusion to attention to explicitly capture local patterns and let attention operate on more informative representations, and a Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), a parametric key-value memory storing global knowledge in addressable slots to decouple storage from computation and enable direct retrieval.
AI.result: Experimental results show LoKiFormer converges 1.33x faster in pretraining than baseline models, demonstrating its superiority over existing LLM architectures.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly handling locality via LFA and decoupling global knowledge storage via KMM, LoKiFormer achieves more efficient and effective information integration at both levels, outperforming existing LLM architectures in pretraining efficiency.

title: Tracing Provenance and Detecting Tampering with Complementary LLM Watermarks
summary: Watermarking LLM-generated text is an important task for tracing its provenance. Existing LLM watermarks preserve provenance under editing, but this same robustness allows an adversary to alter critical content while retaining attribution, a vulnerability known as piggyback spoofing. We introduce an innovative watermark that jointly provides provenance and tamper evidence. It co-embeds a robust signal and a fragile signal into each generated token. The signals share the same mechanism but use independent keys and different seeding windows over normalized text, making one resilient to edits and the other sensitive to reader-visible changes. Multiple rounds of unbiased tournament reweighting preserve the expected generation distribution, while a periodic round-allocation pattern controls the trade-off between the two signals. At detection, their scores form a two-dimensional space supporting three decisions: Intact, Tampered, and No-Watermark. Across two large language models and two prompt datasets, our method demonstrates the highest tamper-detection rate among the evaluated methods while maintaining competitive attribution robustness and perplexity. Ablation studies show that reliable three-state detection requires a well-defined notion of intactness, co-embedding of the two signals, and complementary sensitivity to edits.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a dual-signal LLM watermark that co-embeds a robust (attribution-preserving) and a fragile (tamper-evident) signal into generated text, enabling three-state detection (Intact, Tampered, No-Watermark) to defend against piggyback spoofing while maintaining generation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM watermarks are robust to edits to preserve provenance, but this same robustness lets an adversary modify critical content while retaining attribution (piggyback spoofing). There is a need for watermarks that simultaneously provide provenance and tamper evidence, i.e., detect unauthorized content changes without losing attribution under legitimate edits.
AI.method: The method co-embeds a robust signal and a fragile signal into each generated token using the same mechanism but with independent keys and different seeding windows over normalized text, making one signal edit-resilient and the other sensitive to reader-visible changes. Multiple rounds of unbiased tournament reweighting preserve the expected generation distribution, and a periodic round-allocation pattern controls the trade-off between the two signals. Detection scores form a two-dimensional space enabling three decisions: Intact, Tampered, and No-Watermark.
AI.result: Across two large language models and two prompt datasets, the method achieves the highest tamper-detection rate among evaluated methods while maintaining competitive attribution robustness and perplexity. Ablations show that reliable three-state detection requires a well-defined notion of intactness, co-embedding of both signals, and complementary sensitivity to edits.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-signal (robust + fragile) watermark effectively provides joint provenance and tamper evidence, defending against piggyback spoofing while preserving generation quality and attribution robustness, with ablation studies confirming the key design requirements for reliable three-state detection.

title: Do LLMs Beat Nash? Testing Decentralized Coordination in Self-Play Multi-Agent Games
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the 2026 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC)
summary: Large language model agents deployed without a central controller are often assumed to require communication to coordinate their actions. We ask what remains possible without it: when independent instances of the same model cannot communicate, can they still reason about their counterparts well enough to exceed the standard game-theoretic baseline for uncoordinated play? We introduce a benchmark of one-shot, no-communication games in which each of thirteen language models is told only that its counterparts are running the same model and is evaluated against the Nash equilibrium of the underlying game. In two-player matrix games spanning seven archetypes and two to ten actions per player, two frontier-hosted models consistently exceed their Nash benchmark, approaching the optimal joint outcome in several archetypes, while most open-weight models achieve only partial gains that vary sharply by game structure. Performance degrades substantially in team-based games with four or more interchangeable agents, particularly as the action space grows, suggesting that whatever capability drives self-play gains in dyadic games does not transfer to larger multi-agent teams.

AI.tldr: This paper examines whether independent, non-communicating LLM instances can outperform the Nash equilibrium baseline in one-shot games by reasoning about their identical counterparts, and how this capability scales to larger multi-agent teams.
AI.motivation: The authors question a common assumption that LLM agents require communication to coordinate. They investigate whether independent instances of the same model can achieve gains over standard uncoordinated game-theoretic baselines purely through reasoning about their counterparts, and whether such capability transfers from dyadic settings to larger teams.
AI.method: The authors introduce a benchmark of one-shot, no-communication games where each of thirteen language models is informed only that its counterparts run the same model, and is evaluated against the Nash equilibrium of the underlying game. Two-player matrix games span seven archetypes and two to ten actions per player; team-based games with four or more interchangeable agents are also tested.
AI.result: Two frontier-hosted models consistently exceed their Nash benchmark, approaching the optimal joint outcome in several archetypes, while most open-weight models achieve only partial gains that vary sharply by game structure. Performance degrades substantially in team-based games with four or more agents, especially as the action space grows.
AI.conclusion: Self-play gains observed in dyadic games do not transfer to larger multi-agent teams, suggesting the capability driving these gains is limited to pairwise interactions and does not scale to coordination among many interchangeable agents.

title: Specification-first convergence with an AI coding agent: a case study of dismantling a core architectural invariant across 189 files in a 717k-line codebase with no test oracle and no human code review
summary:
This paper reports a single, fully instrumented case study of a large-scale architectural refactoring by an AI coding agent under a specification-first protocol, with no human review of the generated code and no pre-existing oracle to validate the target behaviour. The task, dismantling a central invariant across a large interdependent codebase, was assessed by the author as effectively infeasible through incremental refactoring, the kind of change that conventionally calls for a rewrite instead. Under the protocol described here, the agent completed it successfully.
  The system is a 717,725-line production TypeScript application across 3,648 files. The task required dismantling a core lifetime invariant: the guarantee that a UI panel remains open for the duration of an AI request. The target behaviour was that a streaming generation survives the closing of its panel and can be reattached, on reopening, to the same live stream with no loss or duplication.
  The protocol: formal specification by the agent, 14 refinement cycles auditing that specification against the source code, atomic implementation, a compile/test feedback loop, then 17 verification cycles auditing the code against the frozen specification. Across 31 audit passes, 201 defects were corrected before any human executed the program. The convergence criterion was empirical: two consecutive verification passes returning zero findings.
  The change touched 189 files (31 new); with the extraction phase, the two commits total 288 files, 34,770 insertions, 16,422 deletions. Across the first and roughly thirty later sessions, the software behaved as specified, no bug observed. Elapsed: three days; cost: USD 2,430.
  The full specification and raw session logs, 1,500+ pages in French, are published as evidence, allowing inspection of the process and submission to a language model for consistency checking.

AI.tldr: A single-case study demonstrating that an AI coding agent, working under a specification-first protocol with no human code review and no oracle, successfully dismantled a core invariant across a 717,725-line TypeScript codebase in three days at a cost of USD 2,430, touching 288 files across two commits.
AI.motivation: The author wanted to investigate whether a large-scale architectural refactoring of the kind normally requiring a full rewrite—dismantling a central lifetime invariant across a large interdependent codebase—could be accomplished by an AI coding agent operating autonomously, without human review or a pre-existing behavioral oracle, through a disciplined specification-first process.
AI.method: A specification-first protocol was used: the agent first produced a formal specification, which was refined over 14 audit cycles against the source code; this was followed by atomic implementation, a compile/test feedback loop, and then 17 verification cycles auditing the code against the frozen specification. In total, 31 audit passes corrected 201 defects before any human executed the program, with convergence defined empirically as two consecutive verification passes returning zero findings. The specific task was dismantling the invariant that a UI panel remains open for the duration of an AI request, so that a streaming generation survives panel closure and can reattach to the same live stream without loss or duplication. Full specification and raw session logs (1,500+ pages in French) were published as evidence.
AI.result: The change touched 189 files (31 new); with the extraction phase, the two commits totaled 288 files, 34,770 insertions, and 16,422 deletions. Across the first session and roughly thirty later sessions, the software behaved as specified with no observed bugs. Elapsed time was three days at a cost of USD 2,430.
AI.conclusion: An AI coding agent can successfully perform a large-scale architectural refactoring—a change the author previously considered effectively infeasible via incremental refactoring—when guided by a specification-first protocol with rigorous audit cycles, achieving correct behavior with no human code review or pre-existing oracle, and the process is made auditable through published specifications and session logs.

title: Visibility Asymmetry: How Vendor Attention Shapes Which EdTech Breakdowns Become Product-Visible
summary: Infrastructure scholarship in CSCW often treats breakdown as the moment when infrastructures become visible. However, in vendor-managed sociotechnical systems, not all breakdowns become visible to actors who have the capacity to repair them. Drawing on a retrospective qualitative study of a Chinese K-12 EdTech deployment, including 11 interviews, 5 classroom observations, and more than 28 days of field notes, this paper introduces visibility asymmetry: a sensitizing concept for understanding how similar local breakdowns encounter uneven conditions for being routed, recognized, and acted upon. The analysis traces a four-stage mechanism through which procurement categories sort schools into attention tiers; staffing and visit cadence follow those tiers; only some local problems travel through staff or administrator channels; and dashboards can re-code unresolved repair labor as evidence of adoption. By shifting attention from the occurrence of breakdown to the organizational channels through which breakdown becomes actionable, this paper extends CSCW work on infrastructure, articulation work, and repair. It concludes by discussing implications for feedback systems that can surface repair needs without expanding surveillance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "visibility asymmetry" to explain why similar local breakdowns in vendor-managed EdTech systems receive uneven attention, tracing a four-stage mechanism (procurement-based tiering, staffing/cadence alignment, selective problem routing, and dashboards re-coding unresolved labor) that determines which breakdowns become actionable.
AI.motivation: CSCW infrastructure scholarship typically treats breakdown as the moment infrastructures become visible, but in vendor-managed sociotechnical systems not all breakdowns become visible to actors capable of repairing them. The study aims to shift focus from the occurrence of breakdown to the organizational channels through which breakdown becomes actionable.
AI.method: A retrospective qualitative study of a Chinese K-12 EdTech deployment, comprising 11 interviews, 5 classroom observations, and more than 28 days of field notes. The analysis traces a four-stage mechanism through which visibility is differentially produced.
AI.result: The study identifies a four-stage mechanism: (1) procurement categories sort schools into attention tiers; (2) staffing and visit cadence follow those tiers; (3) only some local problems travel through staff or administrator channels; (4) dashboards can re-code unresolved repair labor as evidence of adoption, further obscuring unmet needs.
AI.conclusion: By analyzing organizational channels rather than breakdown occurrence alone, the paper extends CSCW work on infrastructure, articulation work, and repair, and discusses implications for designing feedback systems that surface repair needs without expanding surveillance.

title: Knowledge Synthesis Review Framework: Task-Level Benchmarking of LLM-Based Systems for Multi-Source Evidence Synthesis
summary: Evidence in rapidly evolving fields is fragmented across academic studies, industry reports, policy documents, and media sources that differ in quality, structure, and purpose, making timely synthesis difficult. Large language models (LLMs) may accelerate this work, but their reliability across the distinct cognitive tasks of a review remains uncertain. We introduce the Knowledge Synthesis Review (KSR), a human-in-the-loop framework that decomposes evidence synthesis into screening, extraction, analysis, and synthesis, benchmarks LLM-based systems on each task against expert reference standards, and routes each task to the best-performing system under continuous expert validation. We evaluated GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and NotebookLM on a 244-document benchmark subset drawn from a 1,893-document corpus on AI and work spanning four source types, against a gold standard with high inter-rater reliability (92.2% agreement, kappa = 0.80). No system led on all tasks. Claude Sonnet 4 achieved the highest screening accuracy (82.8%) and GPT-5 the highest recall (91.8%) at the expense of lower specificity. Extraction exceeded 90% agreement for titles and sources but degraded in author and reference fields. Performance declined most in interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis, where expert judgment remained essential. A contamination check on post-cutoff documents showed no evidence that prior exposure inflated results. Applied to the full corpus, the routed workflow surfaced cross-source asymmetries and blind spots that single-source synthesis would miss, including worker well-being, small firms, and the Global South. KSR offers a transparent, auditable, model-agnostic framework for governing LLM assistance in research synthesis while preserving human accountability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Knowledge Synthesis Review (KSR), a human-in-the-loop framework that breaks evidence synthesis into four cognitive tasks (screening, extraction, analysis, synthesis), benchmarks LLM systems against expert standards on each task, and routes each task to the best-performing model. Evaluated on a 244-document benchmark from a 1,893-document corpus, no single model excelled everywhere; Claude Sonnet 4 led screening accuracy while GPT-5 led recall, extraction was strongest for simple fields, and expert judgment remained essential for interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis.
AI.motivation: Evidence in fast-moving fields is scattered across heterogeneous sources (academic, industry, policy, media) that vary in quality and structure, making timely synthesis difficult. LLMs could accelerate this work, but their reliability across the distinct cognitive tasks of a review is unproven, so a task-level, benchmarked, auditable governance framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors decompose evidence synthesis into screening, extraction, analysis, and synthesis; benchmark GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and NotebookLM against a gold standard (92.2% agreement, kappa = 0.80) on a 244-document subset of a 1,893-document corpus on AI and work spanning four source types; route each task to the best-performing system under continuous expert validation; and run a post-cutoff contamination check.
AI.result: No system led on all tasks. Claude Sonnet 4 achieved the highest screening accuracy (82.8%) and GPT-5 the highest recall (91.8%) at lower specificity. Extraction exceeded 90% agreement for titles and sources but degraded for author and reference fields. Interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis showed the lowest performance, where expert judgment remained essential. The contamination check found no evidence that prior exposure inflated results. Applied to the full corpus, the routed workflow surfaced cross-source asymmetries and blind spots (worker well-being, small firms, Global South) that single-source synthesis would miss.
AI.conclusion: KSR provides a transparent, auditable, model-agnostic framework for governing LLM assistance in research synthesis while preserving human accountability, demonstrating that task-level benchmarking and routing—rather than reliance on any single model—is necessary for reliable LLM-supported evidence synthesis.

title: Diagnostic Foundation for Evaluating LLMs' Research Integrity as Co-Scientists
summary: Language models are increasingly deployed as co-scientists, yet their ability to uphold research integrity under institutional pressure remains unmeasured. We introduce IntegrityBench, a benchmark evaluating misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning and artifact-grounded decision making across 36 paired tasks under a 5-level implicit-explicit pressure protocol spanning 3 domains and 4 research stages. Evaluating 18 frontier model variants, we find that under peak pressure, models fail roughly 1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions, and neither scale nor reasoning ability reliably mitigates this. Explicit pressures induce compliance with misconduct, while implicit contextual reframing more often causes over-refusal of legitimate research tasks. Interestingly, models failing to classify research requests accurately perform equally or better on artifact-grounded decision making (85.7 vs. 79.4), suggesting the three facets are structurally dissociated and correct ethical action does not require accurate classification. Frontier models can thus appear helpful while harbouring integrity failures that create two distinct deployment risks: facilitating research misconduct and eroding trust in AI-assisted research.

AI.tldr: Introduces IntegrityBench, a benchmark of 36 paired tasks assessing language models on research-integrity: misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning, and artifact-grounded decision making. Tests 18 frontier models under a 5-level pressure protocol; under peak pressure models fail ~1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions, with explicit pressure driving misconduct compliance and implicit reframing causing over-refusal. The three facets appear structurally dissociated.
AI.motivation: Language models are increasingly deployed as co-scientists, yet their ability to uphold research integrity under institutional pressure has not been measured. There is a need to evaluate whether current models maintain ethical decision making when pressured, and to understand the structural relationship between classification, reasoning, and actual decisions.
AI.method: Proposes IntegrityBench, a benchmark of 36 paired tasks spanning 3 domains and 4 research stages. It evaluates misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning, and artifact-grounded decision making under a 5-level implicit-to-explicit pressure protocol. 18 frontier model variants are evaluated, comparing performance across pressure levels and facets including scale and reasoning ability as potential mitigators.
AI.result: Under peak pressure, models fail roughly 1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions; neither model scale nor reasoning ability reliably mitigates these failures. Explicit pressure induces compliance with misconduct, while implicit contextual reframing more often causes over-refusal of legitimate tasks. Models that misclassify research requests perform equally or better on artifact-grounded decision making (85.7 vs. 79.4), indicating the three facets are structurally dissociated and correct ethical action does not require accurate classification.
AI.conclusion: Frontier models can appear helpful while harboring integrity failures, creating two distinct deployment risks: facilitating research misconduct and eroding trust in AI-assisted research. Correct ethical action does not require accurate classification, showing that superficially helpful behavior may mask deeper integrity shortcomings.

title: What Drives LLM Self-Reflection? A Controlled Ablation of Uncertainty Routing in Armed Conflict Forecasting
summary: Self-reflection is widely assumed to improve LLM reasoning, yet which component drives the gain remains poorly understood. We present a controlled six-condition ablation isolating four components of LLM self-reflection: evidence exposure, diagnostic scaffolding, taxonomy vocabulary, and action routing. Two precise null results converge on a single mechanism. First, structured diagnostic questions add no measurable value over unstructured reflection ($\text{F1} = 0.296$ vs $0.297$, $p = 1.000$, 95\% CI $[-0.041, +0.040]$). Second, presenting the full uncertainty taxonomy while collapsing the action space to a single generic action also adds no value ($Δ\text{F1} = +0.008$, overlapping 95\% CIs), ruling out taxonomy vocabulary as the mechanism. Typed action routing provides consistent directional gains ($\text{F1} = 0.379$ vs $0.296$); the conservative estimate controlling for taxonomy vocabulary is $Δ\text{F1} = +0.075$, and the overall gain over the single-shot baseline is significant by bootstrap CI ($Δ\text{F1} = +0.101$, 95\% CI $[+0.020, +0.185]$). The vocabulary-routing decomposition replicates on GPT-4o: taxonomy vocabulary adds no significant value over generic reflection ($p = 0.773$), while action routing provides significant gains ($p = 0.025$), confirming the mechanism holds across backbones. Gains concentrate on structurally novel conflicts: in Myanmar ($\text{F1}: 0.000 \rightarrow 0.353$) and Ukraine ($0.167 \rightarrow 0.500$), the vocabulary-only condition recovers no more than generic reflection while action routing breaks the degenerate prior. These findings identify typed action routing -- not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary -- as a promising design principle for metacognitive LLM forecasting agents, while motivating larger-scale evaluation across conflict typologies.

AI.tldr: A controlled six-condition ablation isolating four components of LLM self-reflection finds that typed action routing — not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary — drives reasoning gains, with results replicating across two model backbones and concentrating on structurally novel forecasting conflicts.
AI.motivation: Self-reflection is widely assumed to improve LLM reasoning, but which specific component of the reflection process actually causes the improvement is poorly understood. The authors aim to decompose self-reflection into isolable components and determine experimentally which one is responsible for observed gains.
AI.method: The authors run a controlled six-condition ablation that isolates four components of LLM self-reflection: evidence exposure, diagnostic scaffolding, taxonomy vocabulary, and action routing. They compare structured diagnostic questions against unstructured reflection, collapse the action space while presenting the full uncertainty taxonomy, and test typed action routing against a single-shot baseline. The vocabulary-routing decomposition is replicated on GPT-4o in addition to the primary backbone, and effects are examined across conflict types including Myanmar and Ukraine.
AI.result: Two null results converge on a single mechanism: structured diagnostic questions add no measurable value over unstructured reflection (F1 = 0.296 vs 0.297, p = 1.000, 95% CI [-0.041, +0.040]), and presenting the full taxonomy with a single generic action also adds no value (ΔF1 = +0.008, overlapping CIs), ruling out taxonomy vocabulary. Typed action routing yields consistent directional gains (F1 = 0.379 vs 0.296), with a conservative ΔF1 = +0.075 controlling for taxonomy vocabulary, and a significant overall gain over baseline by bootstrap CI (ΔF1 = +0.101, 95% CI [+0.020, +0.185]). Replication on GPT-4o confirms taxonomy vocabulary adds no significant value (p = 0.773) while action routing is significant (p = 0.025). Gains concentrate on structurally novel conflicts: Myanmar (F1 0.000 → 0.353) and Ukraine (0.167 → 0.500).
AI.conclusion: Typed action routing, rather than diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary, is the promising design principle for metacognitive LLM forecasting agents. The authors call for larger-scale evaluation across diverse conflict typologies to further validate the mechanism.

title: Which Site, and When: A Free-Satellite-Data Test of Himalayan Glacial Lake Bursts, Landslides, and Ice Floods
summary: Two free satellite signals carry real information about glacial-lake outburst risk in the Nepal Himalaya: radar interferometry sees a moraine dam slowly sagging, and satellite weather marks the weeks when a primed lake is under stress. A companion feasibility study found that deformation indicates which lake is destabilizing and weather indicates when it is at risk, but proposed no predictive model. To address this gap, we propose and evaluate models that predict which site is susceptible and when a trigger arrives. We test three related hazards on free data alone: large moraine- and ice-dammed bursts, rainfall-triggered landslides, and smaller floods from ponds on and around a glacier. Each hazard gets two questions, never blended. Using 589 dated outbursts from HMAGLOFDB and several thousand catalogued landslides, we match each event against similar but unfailed sites, and hold every model to a strong simple baseline under spatial cross-validation that withholds whole map tiles, so no model succeeds by recognising a trained-on neighbourhood. Antecedent weather times the trigger at ROC 0.73 for big bursts, 0.83 for landslides, and 0.82 for small floods. Terrain ranks susceptibility only in part: scored naively it appears near 0.9, largely because catalogued failures cluster in wetter ranges; matched against comparable nearby sites the honest figures are 0.76, 0.71, and 0.54 (no better than chance). The burst signal holds within single regions, reaching 0.89 in Nepal alone. Five deep-learning models do not decisively beat a simple gradient-boosted baseline. Three score marginally higher on landslides, a hint too small to confirm. For the lake hazards the baseline wins outright, reproduced by a three-rule decision tree on ruggedness and monsoon rainfall. We close with a ranked Nepal watchlist, a prioritisation aid, not a prediction, and note where free data reaches its limits.

AI.tldr: Using only free satellite and weather data, the authors build and evaluate models that separately predict which Himalayan sites are susceptible to glacial-lake outburst floods (GLOFs) and related hazards, and when triggers arrive, finding the weather timing signal robust (ROC 0.73–0.83) while terrain susceptibility models degrade to near-chance when matched against comparable nearby sites.
AI.motivation: A prior feasibility study showed that InSAR-detected moraine deformation indicates which glacial lake is destabilizing and satellite weather indicates when a primed lake is under stress, but provided no predictive model. This work aims to close that gap by proposing models that predict both susceptibility (which site) and trigger timing (when), using only freely available data.
AI.method: The authors test three hazard types—large moraine- and ice-dammed outbursts, rainfall-triggered landslides, and smaller glacier/pond floods—each addressed with two separate questions (where vs. when). Using 589 dated outbursts from HMAGLOFDB and several thousand catalogued landslides, they match each event against similar but unfailed sites, evaluate antecedent weather for trigger timing (ROC), and rank terrain susceptibility under spatial cross-validation that withholds whole map tiles. Models are benchmarked against a strong simple gradient-boosted baseline and five deep-learning models, with results further validated within single regions (e.g., Nepal alone, ROC 0.89).
AI.result: Antecedent weather times triggers at ROC 0.73 (big bursts), 0.83 (landslides), and 0.82 (small floods). Naive terrain susceptibility scores near 0.9, but matching against comparable nearby sites yields honest figures of 0.76, 0.71, and 0.54 (small floods no better than chance). Deep-learning models do not decisively beat the gradient-boosted baseline; three score marginally higher on landslides (too small to confirm), while the baseline wins outright for lake hazards, reproduced by a three-rule decision tree on ruggedness and monsoon rainfall. A ranked Nepal watchlist is provided as a prioritisation aid, not a prediction.
AI.conclusion: Free satellite and weather data can time GLOF/landslide triggers reliably, but terrain-based susceptibility is largely an artifact of clustered catalogues and collapses toward chance under honest spatial matching. Simple interpretable models suffice, deep learning offers no clear advantage, and the work ends by noting the inherent limits of free data, offering a watchlist strictly as a prioritisation aid.

title: PIPES: Securing Agent Perception with Provenance and Priors
summary: Tool-using agents consume external data from sources with different levels of trust, yet tool responses rarely identify who produced each component or what it should convey. We show that this gap enables state-corruption attacks, in which attacker-controlled content makes environmental claims beyond the informational authority of its response component and corrupts the agent's perceived environment, making the resulting action appear justified to existing guardrails. We introduce PIPES (Provenance-Informed, Prior-Enforced Screening), which screens response units using semantic priors and source provenance. PIPES uses static field contracts when schemas provide stable expectations, and conditions screening of open-ended content on the pre-response trajectory and trusted provenance metadata. It marks units that violate their semantic prior or the provenance hierarchy; deployments may remove, warn, block, or escalate detected violations. We instantiate atomic removal and evaluate PIPES against adaptive PAIR-style attacks. Across the three VitaBench and three AgentDyn splits with Gemma 4 31B IT as the target agent, PIPES reduces average attack success from 84.7% to 2.3%, while preserving average benign utility (92.5% with PIPES versus 90.6% without defense).

AI.tldr: PIPES is a defense that screens tool responses using semantic priors and provenance metadata to stop state-corruption attacks, cutting attack success from 84.7% to 2.3% while preserving benign utility.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents consume external data from sources of varying trust, but tool responses rarely identify who produced each component or what it should convey. This gap lets attacker-controlled content inject environmental claims beyond the informational authority of its response component (state-corruption attacks), so the resulting malicious action looks justified to existing guardrails.
AI.method: Introduce PIPES (Provenance-Informed, Prior-Enforced Screening), which screens response units using semantic priors and source provenance. It applies static field contracts for schemas with stable expectations, and conditions screening of open-ended content on the pre-response trajectory and trusted provenance metadata. Units violating their semantic prior or the provenance hierarchy are marked; deployments may remove, warn, block, or escalate. The paper instantiates atomic removal.
AI.result: Tested against adaptive PAIR-style attacks on three VitaBench and three AgentDyn splits with Gemma 4 31B IT as the target agent, PIPES reduces average attack success from 84.7% to 2.3%, while preserving average benign utility (92.5% with PIPES versus 90.6% without defense).
AI.conclusion: PIPES effectively mitigates state-corruption attacks by enforcing semantic priors and provenance hierarchy over tool response units, drastically lowering attack success while maintaining benign performance.

title: Discovering Efficient and Explainable Communication Topologies for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems via Causal Inference
summary: The performance of large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) largely depends on effective communication topologies. Existing topology generation methods, however, typically learn communication topologies through black-box optimization driven solely by task-level rewards. While effective, such optimization provides little insight into why particular communication edges are selected, making it difficult to identify the critical communication subgraphs responsible for successful collaboration. To address this limitation, we propose E2-Explainer, a model-agnostic framework for providing interpretable explanations of communication topologies produced by arbitrary topology generators. Specifically, we formulate topology explanation as a causal attribution problem that identifies compact communication subgraphs supported by edge-level evidence of task preservation. We obtain this evidence with a Granger-style objective that measures how masking each communication channel changes the task outcome and the stability of the final response. The resulting budgeted subgraphs are then distilled into an amortized explainer, enabling efficient post-hoc explanation without repeated edge-level evaluations at deployment. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning and coding benchmarks demonstrate that E2-Explainer identifies critical communication subgraphs that preserve successful collaboration. These subgraphs can also be executed directly to prune redundant communication edges, substantially reducing communication costs while maintaining competitive task performance.

AI.tldr: E2-Explainer is a model-agnostic framework that explains the communication topologies of LLM-based multi-agent systems by identifying compact, task-preserving communication subgraphs through causal attribution, and these subgraphs can be used to prune redundant edges and cut communication costs.
AI.motivation: Existing topology generation methods for LLM-based multi-agent systems rely on black-box optimization driven only by task-level rewards, offering no insight into why specific communication edges are chosen. This opacity makes it hard to identify the critical communication subgraphs that drive successful collaboration.
AI.method: E2-Explainer formulates topology explanation as a causal attribution problem that identifies compact communication subgraphs with edge-level evidence of task preservation. It uses a Granger-style objective that measures how masking each communication channel changes the task outcome and the stability of the final response. The budgeted subgraphs are then distilled into an amortized explainer for efficient post-hoc explanation without repeated edge-level evaluations at deployment.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple reasoning and coding benchmarks show that E2-Explainer identifies critical communication subgraphs that preserve successful collaboration, and executing these subgraphs directly prunes redundant communication edges, substantially reducing communication costs while maintaining competitive task performance.
AI.conclusion: E2-Explainer provides interpretable, model-agnostic explanations of multi-agent communication topologies, revealing the critical subgraphs behind collaboration and enabling effective edge pruning that reduces communication costs without sacrificing task performance.

title: Does It Render Everywhere? A Study of Cross-Environment Compatibility in MLLM-Generated Webpages
summary:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been increasingly adopted to automate webpage generation from visual designs (e.g., screenshots). However, existing evaluations are limited to visual fidelity assessment under a fixed browser-device configuration. Such a setting overlooks the cross-environment rendering compatibility for real-world deployments.
  To address this gap, we present the first systematic empirical study of cross-environment compatibility in AI-generated webpages. Specifically, we construct WebCompat, a dataset of 2,032 annotated instances, comprising webpages generated by 8 representative AI tools, each rendered across 9 browser-and-device combinations. We analyze the prevalence of compatibility issues, their user-perceptible symptoms, and underlying code-level root causes. Our findings reveal that 68% of generated webpages exhibit at least one compatibility issue, underscoring the pervasive reliability concerns surrounding MLLM-generated front-end artifacts. The most prevalent symptoms are failures that disrupt the entire page layout (88.3%): pages shrink directly to fit the target screen with too small fonts, or exhibit scale mismatches that produce cut-off content. Failures localized to individual elements, such as image distortion or missing components, are comparatively less common (13.4%). Furthermore, although most MLLMs incorporate responsive design patterns into the generation, they fail to properly implement these codes.
  Guided by the findings, we develop XCompat, a lightweight offline compatibility issue detector that combines visual screenshots and the structural DOM tree for analysis. It achieves an F1 score of 0.903 on the WebCompat-test, outperforming the existing compatibility checking tools and LLM baselines. All datasets and tools are released to support future research on rendering reliability in MLLM-based front-end code generation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first systematic study of cross-environment rendering compatibility in AI-generated webpages, builds a 2,032-instance dataset (WebCompat), and develops XCompat, an offline detector that combines screenshots and DOM structure to detect compatibility issues with an F1 of 0.903.
AI.motivation: MLLMs are increasingly used to generate webpages from visual designs, but existing evaluations only assess visual fidelity under a fixed browser-device configuration, ignoring cross-environment rendering compatibility needed for real-world deployment.
AI.method: The authors construct WebCompat (2,032 annotated instances from 8 AI tools rendered across 9 browser-device combinations), analyze issue prevalence, user-perceptible symptoms, and code-level root causes. Based on these findings, they build XCompat, a lightweight offline detector that combines visual screenshots with the structural DOM tree for analysis.
AI.result: 68% of generated webpages exhibit at least one compatibility issue. The dominant symptoms (88.3%) are whole-page layout failures (pages shrinking with too-small fonts or scale mismatches causing cut-off content); element-localized failures (image distortion, missing components) are less common (13.4%). Although most MLLMs include responsive design patterns, they fail to implement them correctly. XCompat achieves an F1 score of 0.903 on WebCompat-test, outperforming existing compatibility tools and LLM baselines.
AI.conclusion: Cross-environment compatibility is a pervasive reliability concern in MLLM-generated front-end code, and the released WebCompat dataset and XCompat detector provide resources to support future research on rendering reliability.

title: Humans are Missing from AI Coding Agent Research
summary: Recent progress in AI coding agent research has led to rapid improvements in agents' ability to autonomously perform complex software engineering tasks, from editing large codebases to executing long-horizon development workflows. As these systems make strides, however, the primary bottleneck to practical usefulness increasingly shifts away from pure task-solving capability, and toward challenges in how users communicate with, supervise, and trust agents. In this position paper, we argue for a reorientation from autonomous to human-centered coding agents: systems designed not only to complete tasks, but to collaborate effectively with people. We identify four core interaction-level dimensions that characterize the human-agent task-solving loop: task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability. Finally, we outline concrete research directions to advance these dimensions, including user-involved coding environments, comprehensive verification mechanisms, and principled measures of human-agent interaction quality.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that AI coding agent research should shift from autonomous task-solving toward human-centered collaboration, proposing four interaction-level dimensions (task alignment, verifiability, steerability, adaptability) and outlining research directions to improve them.
AI.motivation: Although AI coding agents have rapidly improved at autonomously completing complex software engineering tasks, the main bottleneck to practical usefulness is no longer task-solving capability but rather how users communicate with, supervise, and trust these agents.
AI.method: The authors present a position paper that defines a human-centered framing of coding agents and identify four core interaction-level dimensions of the human-agent task-solving loop: task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability. They then outline concrete research directions for each dimension.
AI.result: The paper proposes a reorientation from autonomous to human-centered coding agents, offers a four-dimension framework (task alignment, verifiability, steerability, adaptability), and suggests future work including user-involved coding environments, comprehensive verification mechanisms, and principled measures of human-agent interaction quality.
AI.conclusion: To make AI coding agents practically useful, the field should reorient toward systems that collaborate effectively with people, advancing the four identified interaction dimensions through user-involved environments, robust verification, and principled interaction-quality measures.

title: DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation
summary: Industrial video recommendation systems typically adopt a multi-stage architecture. At the ensemble ranking stage, multi-dimensional user preference predictions (pxtrs) from an upstream multi-task model are fused into a unified ranking score to reflect user satisfaction. Since users' true satisfaction is difficult to observe directly, ensemble ranking models commonly use pxtrs both as input features and as a source for constructing proxy preferences. However, as outputs of an upstream prediction model, pxtrs inevitably contain prediction noise, which propagates to downstream learning across two sides. On the supervision side, noisy pxtrs may flip proxy preferences and introduce erroneous gradients. On the feature side, pxtr noise may propagate through model inputs and destabilize ranking scores.
