Across four host systems, prompting, commit-untangling, and minimality-aware baselines reduce patch size only by sacrificing 49 to 217 resolved instances. In contrast, RECAP achieves a substantially better size-correctness tradeoff, cutting average total changes from +242.14% to +4.24% and net changes from +348.24% to -39.75% relative to developer patches while preserving or improving resolution by up to 42 instances. Our results indicate that minimality cannot be simply reduced to syntactic compression, and that decoupling minimization from generation offers a practical path to more reviewable repairs.

AI.tldr: LLM-based program repair patches are overly verbose. The paper proposes RECAP, a post-generation refinement adapter that drastically reduces patch size (to near or below developer-patch levels) while preserving or improving resolution, unlike prompting/untangling baselines that shrink patches only at the cost of many solved instances.
AI.motivation: Although LLM-based APR systems increasingly solve real-world repository-level issues, the quality of patches is judged mainly by whether they pass tests. The authors identify patch verbosity—patches being much larger and more complex than human developer patches—as an overlooked problem that hurts reviewability and maintainability, and investigate its root causes.
AI.method: Characterize 28 state-of-the-art approaches on SWE-bench Verified, measuring total changes, net changes, and cyclomatic complexity versus developer patches. Attribute verbosity to design choices (iterative refinement, broad context) rather than surface-level settings. Formulate post-generation patch refinement and build RECAP, a plug-and-play adapter applied after generation. RECAP's refiner is trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) with distilled reasoning traces on a self-constructed dataset of patch pairs from multiple sources. Compare against four host systems and prompting, commit-untangling, and minimality-aware baselines.
AI.result: Median SOTA approach produces 121.78% more total changes, 80.91% more net changes, and 43.99% higher cyclomatic complexity than developer patches. Surface controls (output format, minimality prompts) barely reduce verbosity. Prompting, commit-untangling, and minimality-aware baselines reduce patch size only by sacrificing 49–217 resolved instances. RECAP cuts average total changes from +242.14% to +4.24% and net changes from +348.24% to -39.75% relative to developer patches while preserving or improving resolution by up to 42 instances.
AI.conclusion: Patch minimality cannot be reduced to syntactic compression. Decoupling minimization from patch generation via a post-generation adapter (RECAP) achieves a substantially better size–correctness tradeoff, offering a practical route to more reviewable, maintainable repairs.

title: Legally Mandated, but Still Inaccessible: Digital Tensions in Older Adults' Use of Norwegian Web Services
summary: Norway is among the most digitalized countries in the world, where access to essential services increasingly depends on digital systems. Although universal design of ICT is legally required across public and private sectors, ensuring cognitive accessibility for older adults involves more than technical compliance. We analyzed responses from 294 participants aged 55 to 90 to examine the barriers they encounter when using digital services. Our findings identify four tensions, namely navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal, which reveal how accessibility barriers emerge through misalignments between service design, system assumptions, and older adults' capabilities. Together, these tensions show that checklist-based compliance does not necessarily translate into lived accessibility when engaging with mandatory or near-mandatory digital services. We discuss the need to move beyond minimum compliance frameworks toward accessibility approaches that better support older adults' independent participation in digital society.

AI.tldr: A survey of 294 Norwegian adults aged 55–90 reveals that cognitive accessibility of digital services relies on more than legal/checklist compliance, identifying four tensions (navigational, semantic, procedural, temporal) between service design and older adults' capabilities.
AI.motivation: Norway is highly digitalized and legally mandates universal ICT design, yet older adults still face cognitive barriers when using essential digital services. The authors argue that technical/checklist compliance does not guarantee lived accessibility for this population.
AI.method: Analyzed survey responses from 294 participants aged 55 to 90 to examine the barriers they encounter when using digital services, and synthesized the findings into four categories of tension.
AI.result: Four tensions were identified: navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal. These reveal that accessibility barriers arise from misalignments between service design, system assumptions, and older adults' capabilities, showing that checklist-based compliance does not translate into lived accessibility in mandatory or near-mandatory services.
AI.conclusion: There is a need to move beyond minimum compliance frameworks toward accessibility approaches that better support older adults' independent participation in a digital society.

title: When Should Multi-Round RAG Stop? Structured Stopping Judgments and Retrieval Reduction in Search-R1
summary: Multi-round retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must decide when to stop searching as evidence accumulates. Because the deployed policy is determined by the first STOP on each trajectory, this is a sequential selection problem rather than an independent state-classification task. We adapt S2G-RAG's structured sufficiency-and-gap judgment to a frozen Search-R1 pipeline and train a Qwen3.5-2B judge on 3,009 states from 900 disjoint HotpotQA questions. Search-R1's reasoner, retriever, corpus, prompt, and search budget remain unchanged, while the judge checkpoint and stopping threshold are selected on grouped validation and frozen before confirmatory evaluation. On the confirmatory test set, the resulting policy reduces retrieval calls by 77 (3.70\%) relative to Native Search-R1, while Official Exact Match decreases by 0.625 percentage points. Thus, the trained S2G-style structured judge reduces retrieval while broadly preserving answer accuracy. The result does not imply unchanged or improved accuracy, safe stopping, or lower total inference cost.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts a structured sufficiency-and-gap (S2G) judge to a frozen Search-R1 pipeline, training a 2B-parameter judge on 3,009 states to learn when to stop retrieval. The resulting policy cuts retrieval calls by 77 (3.70%) with only a 0.625 percentage-point drop in Official Exact Match, showing retrieval can be reduced while roughly preserving answer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multi-round retrieval-augmented generation must decide when to stop searching as evidence accumulates. Since the deployed policy depends on the first STOP action along each trajectory, stopping is a sequential selection problem, not an independent state-classification task. The work seeks a principled stopping policy that reduces redundant retrieval calls without meaningfully harming answer accuracy.
AI.method: The authors adapt S2G-RAG's structured sufficiency-and-gap judgment framework to a frozen Search-R1 pipeline. They train a Qwen3.5-2B judge on 3,009 states sampled from 900 disjoint HotpotQA questions. Search-R1's reasoner, retriever, corpus, prompt, and search budget are left unchanged; only the judge checkpoint and stopping threshold are tuned on grouped validation and then frozen before confirmatory evaluation.
AI.result: On the confirmatory test set, the S2G-style policy reduces retrieval calls by 77 (3.70%) relative to Native Search-R1, while Official Exact Match decreases by only 0.625 percentage points. The authors stress this does not imply unchanged or improved accuracy, safe stopping, or lower total inference cost.
AI.conclusion: A trained S2G-style structured judge can reduce retrieval usage while broadly preserving answer accuracy in a frozen Search-R1 pipeline. However, the modest gains are framed cautiously: the result does not establish improved accuracy, safe stopping, or reduced total inference cost.

title: Learning to Adapt Cross-Domain Preferences via Meta-LoRA for LLM Personalization
summary: Cross-domain zero- or few-shot personalization aims to generate user-preferred responses in unseen conversational domains from only a handful of target-domain interactions. Existing adaptation methods struggle to calibrate update magnitude under sparse evidence and thus overfit, whereas history-transfer methods often entangle user preferences with source-domain artifacts, yielding unreliable personalization priors and negative transfer. To calibrate adaptation to evidence quality, we propose PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA, which uses a meta-learned LoRA initialization as both the adaptation start and prior center, while adjusting update strength according to support-set size and predictive uncertainty. This limits overfitting under sparse or ambiguous evidence while permitting stronger personalization as evidence grows. Controlled adaptation alone does not determine which preferences should transfer across domains or how they should be expressed. We therefore functionally decompose personalization priors into user and domain components, using a human-readable prompt for stable preferences and topology-preserving soft tokens for domain-specific hidden-space conditioning. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and personalization tasks show consistent gains over strong baselines. On HiCUPID, our method reduces cross-domain win-rate degradation by 47.9% relative to the best competing baseline and improves win rate by 110.2% under unseen-user cold start.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA for cross-domain zero-/few-shot personalization, combining evidence-calibrated adaptation with functionally decomposed personalization priors to reduce negative transfer and overfitting.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-domain personalization methods either overfit from sparse target-domain evidence (poor calibration of update magnitude) or transfer source-domain artifacts that entangle user preferences, causing unreliable priors and negative transfer. The goal is to adapt reliably under very limited evidence while preserving stable user preferences across domains.
AI.method: The method has two parts: (1) PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA uses a meta-learned LoRA initialization as both the adaptation starting point and prior center, adjusting update strength according to support-set size and predictive uncertainty to limit overfitting under sparse/ambiguous evidence and allow stronger personalization as evidence grows. (2) Personalization priors are functionally decomposed into user and domain components: a human-readable prompt encodes stable preferences, while topology-preserving soft tokens carry domain-specific hidden-space conditioning.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks and personalization tasks show consistent gains over strong baselines. On HiCUPID, the method reduces cross-domain win-rate degradation by 47.9% relative to the best competing baseline and improves win rate by 110.2% under unseen-user cold start.
AI.conclusion: Combining evidence-calibrated PAC-Bayesian LoRA adaptation with decomposed user/domain personalization priors yields robust cross-domain zero-/few-shot personalization, mitigating overfitting and negative transfer while achieving substantial performance improvements.

title: Thought-Aware KV Cache Compaction for Reasoning via Adaptive Attention Matching
summary: Reasoning language models generate lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences whose key-value (KV) cache grows linearly and becomes a memory bottleneck during decoding. Existing compaction methods treat reasoning trajectories as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring the hierarchical structure of CoT reasoning where different steps vary drastically in importance. We propose \textbf{Thought-Aware Attention Matching (TAM)}, which exploits this structure through three mechanisms: (i)~thought segmentation that decomposes the trajectory into reasoning blocks, (ii)~adaptive budget allocation that assigns compression budget based on each segment's importance and size, and (iii)~pivotal token protection that preserves high-attention reasoning anchors. We prove that the allocation rule is optimal under a convex error model and that cumulative error under sequential compaction remains bounded. Experiments on AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B show that TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory footprint, with periodic compaction bounding peak memory to 3.1--3.2\,GB (a 65\% reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: TAM improves KV-cache compaction for reasoning LLMs by exploiting the hierarchical structure of chain-of-thought, using thought segmentation, adaptive budget allocation, and pivotal token protection to reduce memory while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Reasoning language models produce long chain-of-thought sequences whose KV cache grows linearly, creating a memory bottleneck during decoding. Existing compaction methods treat these trajectories as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring that different reasoning steps vary greatly in importance.
AI.method: The paper proposes Thought-Aware Attention Matching (TAM) with three mechanisms: (i) thought segmentation to decompose the trajectory into reasoning blocks, (ii) adaptive budget allocation that assigns compression budget according to each segment's importance and size, and (iii) pivotal token protection that preserves high-attention reasoning anchors. It proves the allocation rule is optimal under a convex error model and that cumulative error under sequential compaction remains bounded.
AI.result: Experiments on AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B show TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory footprint. Periodic compaction bounds peak memory to 3.1-3.2 GB (a 65% reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the hierarchical structure of chain-of-thought reasoning enables more effective KV-cache compaction, achieving significant memory reduction without sacrificing accuracy compared to uniform compression methods.

title: Exemplar-based objective classification of gust-induced loads across multiple flight conditions
summary: Is it possible to find an objective classification criterion that organizes the complexity of gust-induced loads across many flight conditions? And one that remains as interpretable as a labelling based on coarse parameters, such as the flight attitude? Our approach encodes a large number of experimental observations through a machine-learned representation and applies a summarization procedure to select a minimal subset of highly significant exemplars. The exemplars provide a similarity-based objective classification criterion of all the observations, they can be more conveniently inspected by experts and can become subject of more refined experiments. We demonstrate the approach on a database of 3480 pressure-load measurements induced by random gusts on a flying-wing model across six flight attitudes. We find nine fundamental response types that recur across multiple attitudes; analysis of a type's transient response enables physical intuition into the underlying fluid mechanics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a machine-learning approach that encodes experimental gust-load data into a learned representation, then selects a minimal set of exemplars to provide an objective, similarity-based classification of response types across many flight conditions.
AI.motivation: To find an objective classification criterion for the complexity of gust-induced loads across many flight conditions that is also as interpretable as coarse parameter labels (e.g., flight attitude), rather than relying on subjective or parameter-based labelling.
AI.method: A machine-learned representation encodes a large number of experimental observations, and a summarization procedure selects a minimal subset of highly significant exemplars. These exemplars define a similarity-based objective classification criterion for all observations, enabling expert inspection and guiding refined experiments. Demonstrated on 3480 pressure-load measurements from random gusts on a flying-wing model across six flight attitudes.
AI.result: The method identifies nine fundamental response types that recur across multiple flight attitudes. Analyzing a type's transient response provides physical intuition into the underlying fluid mechanics.
AI.conclusion: An objective, interpretable classification via minimal exemplars is feasible; the exemplar-based criterion organizes gust-induced loads across flight conditions and yields physically meaningful insights into transient response and fluid mechanics.

title: ATOBench: Tracing How Autonomous Penetration-Testing Agents Verify Vulnerabilities When Target Evidence Lies
summary: Autonomous penetration-testing agents rely on target responses. These responses guide both subsequent actions and the final report. A deceptive response can therefore redirect both the attack trajectory and the agent's verification process. However, final reports reveal little about how an agent interprets conflicting evidence, changes course, decides to stop, or turns observations into a vulnerability claim. We introduce ATOBench, an evaluation framework that makes this verification process observable. ATOBench injects registered response transformations at runtime and pairs each transformed episode with a native episode under the same environment. Each pair is aligned at the first affected response. A source-linked reconstruction then follows later actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and report support. Three frozen observation contracts cover exploit proof, resource ownership, and reusable artifacts. We evaluate five model routes over 450 episodes. The analysis shows that increased activity can mask a broken verification chain, while successful recovery depends on finding usable evidence and preserving it through reporting. ATOBench turns deceptive target observations into a reproducible probe of evidence handling in autonomous penetration testing. This process-level view extends offensive pentest agent evaluation beyond final outcomes by revealing how untrusted observations shape actions, verification, and reporting.

AI.tldr: ATOBench is an evaluation framework that makes the verification process of autonomous penetration-testing agents observable by injecting deceptive target responses at runtime, pairing them with native episodes to trace how agents recover evidence and support their reports.
AI.motivation: Final reports reveal little about how an agent interprets conflicting evidence, changes course, decides to stop, or turns observations into a vulnerability claim. Deceptive target responses can silently redirect both the attack trajectory and the verification process, so outcome-only evaluation misses critical flaws in evidence handling.
AI.method: ATOBench injects registered response transformations at runtime and pairs each transformed episode with a native episode under the same environment, aligning each pair at the first affected response. A source-linked reconstruction then tracks later actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and report support. Three frozen observation contracts cover exploit proof, resource ownership, and reusable artifacts.
AI.result: Across five model routes and 450 episodes, increased activity can mask a broken verification chain, while successful recovery depends on finding usable evidence and preserving it through reporting.
AI.conclusion: ATOBench turns deceptive target observations into a reproducible probe of evidence handling, extending offensive pentest agent evaluation beyond final outcomes to reveal how untrusted observations shape actions, verification, and reporting.

title: LigBench: A Unified and Human-Aligned Benchmark for LLM-based Research Idea Generation
summary: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), research idea generation has attracted increasing attention. Existing approaches enable LLMs to retrieve relevant literature and propose novel ideas for research areas. However, current evaluation practices for idea generation remain fragmented and lack objective standards, often relying on direct LLM scoring, which limits their ability to provide unified and reliable assessments across a coherent distribution of generated ideas. To address this challenge, we propose LigBench, an automated evaluation benchmark that enables fine-grained and reliable evaluation of AI research ideas, consistently applicable across different generation distributions. In addition, we introduce PAIR-IQ, a dataset tailored for training pairwise idea judgment models and serving as an auxiliary reference to support more objective comparative evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LigBench achieves stable and interpretable evaluations, significantly improving alignment with expert judgments. Furthermore, models trained on PAIR-IQ exhibit enhanced ranking accuracy and robustness, establishing a principled standard for scalable and objective research idea assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LigBench, an automated benchmark for fine-grained, distribution-agnostic evaluation of AI-generated research ideas, plus PAIR-IQ, a pairwise judgment training dataset. Together they improve alignment with expert judgments and ranking robustness.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of LLM-generated research ideas is fragmented, lacks objective standards, and relies heavily on direct LLM scoring, which cannot provide unified or reliable assessments across the varied distributions of generated ideas.
AI.method: The authors propose LigBench, an automated benchmark supporting fine-grained and reliable evaluation of research ideas applicable across different generation distributions, and PAIR-IQ, a dataset designed to train pairwise idea judgment models that serve as an auxiliary reference for objective comparative evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show LigBench yields stable, interpretable evaluations with significantly improved alignment to expert judgments, while PAIR-IQ-trained models achieve enhanced ranking accuracy and robustness.
AI.conclusion: LigBench and PAIR-IQ establish a principled standard for scalable and objective assessment of research ideas, addressing the lack of unified, reliable evaluation in AI idea generation.

title: Integration-First Structural Coverage for Embedded Software:Trace-Based Evidence, Hybrid Runtime Analysis, and Cross-Variant Consolidation
summary: Structural coverage is widely used as evidence that testing is complete, yet in embedded projects it is predominantly collected at unit level, simply because that is where instrumentation and observability are inexpensive. This produces a mismatch. The most representative completeness signal would come from integration and system tests executed on the device under test, but classical instrumentation perturbs timing, memory footprint and concurrency behaviour, while purely trace-reconstructed coverage loses reliability for decisions and conditions as soon as the compiler optimizes aggressively. We address this mismatch from both ends. On the process side we describe an integrationfirst coverage strategy that treats integration and system tests as the baseline measurement and drives the residual gaps through an explicit closure loop, so that completeness is established as covered or justified rather than as covered alone. On the technical side we use embedded trace as the observation path and add hybrid runtime analysis (hRA): a minimal, semantics-preserving observability scaffolding that keeps decision and condition boundaries distinguishable in the trace stream of an optimized (-O3) build, while all coverage state and counting remain off-target. This converts object-to-source mapping from a heuristic reconstruction into reviewable evidence and makes branch, condition and MC/DC measurement practical on release-like binaries. Finally we describe Hyper Coverage, a consolidation layer that merges evidence across test levels, test runs, variants and build configurations, and that exposes source lines which remain untested in every relevant variant.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles the mismatch between where structural coverage is collected (unit level) and where it matters (integration/system tests on the device), proposing an integration-first coverage strategy plus hybrid runtime analysis (hRA) using embedded trace to reliably measure branch, condition, and MC/DC coverage on optimized binaries, consolidated via a Hyper Coverage layer.
AI.motivation: Structural coverage is mainly collected at unit level because instrumentation is cheap there, but the most representative completeness signal comes from integration and system tests on the device under test. Classical instrumentation perturbs timing, memory, and concurrency, while trace-reconstructed coverage is unreliable for decisions and conditions under aggressive compiler optimization. This creates a mismatch the authors aim to resolve.
AI.method: On the process side, an integration-first coverage strategy treats integration/system tests as the baseline and drives residual gaps through an explicit closure loop so completeness is "covered or justified." On the technical side, embedded trace serves as the observation path, extended with hybrid runtime analysis (hRA): a minimal, semantics-preserving observability scaffolding that keeps decision/condition boundaries distinguishable in the trace of an -O3 build, with coverage state and counting kept off-target. A Hyper Coverage consolidation layer merges evidence across test levels, runs, variants, and build configurations and exposes source lines untested in every relevant variant.
AI.result: Object-to-source mapping becomes reviewable evidence rather than heuristic reconstruction, making branch, condition, and MC/DC measurement practical on release-like binaries. The Hyper Coverage layer identifies source lines that remain untested across all relevant variants.
AI.conclusion: Combining an integration-first process with hRA-based trace reconstruction and the Hyper Coverage consolidation layer addresses the coverage mismatch, enabling reliable, reviewable structural coverage on optimized embedded binaries and establishing completeness as covered-or-justified.

title: InvisIto: Weaving Unobtrusive Infrared Markers for Ubiquitous Textile Interaction
comment: 11 pages. To appear in the Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST 2026)
summary: Textiles are increasingly explored as media for interacting with digital information. However, many of the existing approaches rely on visible tags, printed overlays, or electronic modules that compromise the fabric's aesthetic and tactile qualities. To address this, we present InvisIto, a method for weaving visually unobtrusive yet machine-readable infrared markers directly into fabrics using near-infrared (NIR)-absorbing yarns. Although these yarns look similar to standard fibers in ambient light, they produce strong contrast in NIR imaging. Our method includes: (1) a design tool that helps users easily embed infrared markers into weaving drafts, (2) five disguising strategies that further reduce marker visibility under ambient light, and (3) a camera-based detection pipeline for decoding and tracking the woven markers. InvisIto supports both woven QR codes for data encoding and woven ArUco markers for binary input and deformation tracking. We demonstrate applications across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial fabrication, showing that InvisIto supports scalable interaction and fabrication from bespoke artifacts to mass production.

AI.tldr: InvisIto weaves machine-readable infrared markers into fabrics using near-infrared-absorbing yarns that look like normal thread in ambient light but show high contrast under NIR imaging, preserving textile aesthetics while enabling encoded data and deformation tracking.
AI.motivation: Existing textile interaction methods rely on visible tags, printed overlays, or electronic modules that compromise the fabric's aesthetic and tactile qualities, so there is a need for unobtrusive yet machine-readable markers woven directly into fabric.
AI.method: Uses near-infrared (NIR)-absorbing yarns that resemble standard fibers under ambient light but produce strong contrast in NIR imaging. The system comprises: (1) a design tool to embed infrared markers into weaving drafts, (2) five disguising strategies to reduce marker visibility under ambient light, and (3) a camera-based detection pipeline for decoding and tracking woven markers. It supports woven QR codes for data encoding and woven ArUco markers for binary input and deformation tracking.
AI.result: InvisIto supports woven QR codes and ArUco markers and is demonstrated across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial fabrication, showing scalable interaction and fabrication from bespoke artifacts to mass production.
AI.conclusion: Infrared-absorbing yarns enable visually unobtrusive woven markers, offering a scalable, aesthetic-preserving approach to textile-computer interaction that spans hand-crafted to industrial production contexts.

title: Structure then Query: Enabling Precise Analytical Queries over Unstructured Documents
summary: Unstructured documents constitute the majority of enterprise and web data. With the rapid development of large language models(LLMs), researchers have started to build data systems that analyze unstructured textual documents like operating on databases. However, because mainstream retrieval methods still relies on fuzzy matching based on vector similarity, accurately obtaining information and performing structured analysis and reasoning remains a major challenge. To address these limitations, AnnoIndex introduces two core fundamental components. The first is Annotation Index. The system uses a module called SchemaLoop to automatically create hierarchical annotation schemas from the raw corpus, and then uses lightweight language model to extract specific values. It turns scattered unstructured text into a materialized, structured index that enables low-cost filtering and querying. The annotation index avoids the black-box matching of vector similarity and amortizes attribute extraction costs from online queries to a one-time build. The second innovation is a Structured Query Engine. It compiles user questions into execution plans based on SQL extension. It first uses the Annotation Index for precise documents filtering, then gradually applies extraction operations in ascending order of cost, resorting to LLMs only for the remaining minimal fraction of the corpus that require deep semantic understanding. The extracted attributions are merged into the annotation index, reducing the cost of future queries. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AnnoIndex consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the highest average F1 score (0.87) while maintaining robust performance on complex multi-hop join and progressive reasoning queries.

AI.tldr: AnnoIndex is a document-analysis data system that converts unstructured text into a structured "annotation index" via automatically generated hierarchical schemas, then answers queries through a cost-aware SQL-extension query engine, outperforming baselines with an average F1 of 0.87.
AI.motivation: Unstructured documents dominate enterprise and web data, but mainstream retrieval still relies on vector-similarity fuzzy matching, making it hard to accurately extract information and perform structured analysis/reasoning. The authors aim to move beyond black-box vector matching and reduce the cost of expensive LLM extraction on entire corpora.
AI.method: AnnoIndex has two core components: (1) Annotation Index, where a SchemaLoop module automatically builds hierarchical annotation schemas from the raw corpus and a lightweight language model extracts specific attribute values, materializing a structured index for low-cost filtering/querying; (2) a Structured Query Engine that compiles user questions into SQL-extension execution plans, first filtering documents via the Annotation Index, then applying extraction operations in ascending cost order, invoking LLMs only on the minimal remaining fraction, and merging newly extracted attributes back into the index to benefit future queries.
AI.result: On three real-world datasets, AnnoIndex consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the highest average F1 score of 0.87 while remaining robust on complex multi-hop join and progressive reasoning queries.
AI.conclusion: By coupling an annotation index with a cost-aware structured query engine, AnnoIndex improves both accuracy and efficiency in analyzing unstructured text, demonstrating that materialized, schema-based annotation and incremental LLM use can effectively replace fuzzy vector matching for structured analysis and reasoning over documents.

title: Research Assistant: AstraZeneca's Agentic System for R&D
summary: We describe Research Assistant, an internal LLM-based system developed at AstraZeneca to help scientists and clinicians explore biomedical questions across a broad range of data sources. The system provides a chat-style interface that brings together evidence from scientific literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety resources, expression data, and internal experimental systems. It supports both a fast mode for direct question answering and a multi-step mode for more complex research tasks. Responses are grounded in retrieved evidence and linked back to the original sources, allowing users to review and further explore the underlying data. In this technical note, we outline the system architecture, the main design choices behind the product, and lessons learned from deploying it at scale to support day-to-day R&D workflows across AstraZeneca.

AI.tldr: AstraZeneca developed Research Assistant, an internal LLM chat system that helps scientists answer biomedical questions by integrating evidence from literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety data, expression data, and internal experimental systems, offering both fast and multi-step modes with source-grounded responses.
AI.motivation: To help scientists and clinicians explore complex biomedical questions across many disparate data sources, supporting day-to-day R&D workflows at scale within AstraZeneca.
AI.method: Built an internal LLM-based system with a chat-style interface that aggregates evidence from scientific literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety resources, expression data, and internal experimental systems. It provides a fast mode for direct question answering and a multi-step mode for complex tasks, grounding all responses in retrieved evidence with links back to original sources.
AI.result: The system was successfully deployed at scale across AstraZeneca to support day-to-day R&D workflows, producing grounded, source-linked answers.
AI.conclusion: The technical note outlines the system architecture, key design choices, and lessons learned from large-scale deployment, demonstrating the practical value of an LLM-based assistant for pharmaceutical R&D.

title: Can Spectral-Clipping Enable Better Learning While Forgetting Less for Low-Rank Adaptation?
summary: In recent years, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a significant paradigm that freezes pre-trained weights and introduces small, learnable adapters instead of fine-tuning the full set of parameters. In this work, we uncover several key insights regarding the singular components of network parameters based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Firstly, the principal singular components with large singular values in pre-trained network parameters can be effectively reused during fine-tuning, whereas the minor components with smaller singular values are more task-specific and require substantial adaptation. Secondly, we first establish the theoretical connection that the uncontrolled growth of singular values in LoRA adapters leads to the forgetting of pre-trained knowledge -- a well-known issue referred to as catastrophic forgetting. Building on these observations, we propose SCLoRA, which injects parameterized singular components with spectral clipping into the pre-trained model in a way that is aware of the spectral distribution of the pre-trained model. SCLoRA effectively adapts to new tasks by focusing updates on components that require adaptation, while simultaneously alleviating catastrophic forgetting. We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate that SCLoRA not only improves downstream performance but also effectively retains pre-trained knowledge.

AI.tldr: SCLoRA is a low-rank adaptation method that leverages SVD of pre-trained weights to intelligently update only task-specific minor singular components while clipping singular-value growth, thereby improving downstream performance and reducing catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: LoRA freezes pre-trained weights and adds small adapters, but lacks guidance on which singular components should be adapted. The authors observe that principal (large singular value) components can be reused while minor (small singular value) components are task-specific and need adaptation. They also establish that uncontrolled growth of singular values in LoRA adapters causes forgetting of pre-trained knowledge (catastrophic forgetting). These insights motivate a spectrally-aware adaptation scheme.
AI.method: SCLoRA injects parameterized singular components into the pre-trained model using the model's spectral (SVD) distribution, applying spectral clipping to constrain singular values. It focuses adaptation on components that require change (minor components) while reusing principal components, and clips singular value growth to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show SCLoRA improves downstream task performance compared to standard LoRA while effectively retaining pre-trained knowledge, alleviating catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: By aligning updates with the spectral structure of pre-trained weights and clipping singular values, SCLoRA achieves better adaptation to new tasks while preserving pre-trained knowledge, offering a principled improvement over standard LoRA.

title: Learning Under Treatment-Induced Label Indeterminacy with Expert Annotations of Counterfactual Outcomes: A Case Study in Neurological Prognostication
summary: Clinical prediction models are often developed as if the outcome of interest were cleanly observed for every patient. This assumption fails when treatment decisions make the clinically relevant outcome permanently unobservable. As a case study of this problem, we consider post-cardiac-arrest neurological prognostication using a cohort of 2,497 patients, including 1,429 patients whose outcomes were rendered indeterminate by treatment decisions. These patients with indeterminate outcomes were reviewed by independent clinical experts, who provided their guesses of counterfactual outcomes about what would have happened to the patients. We refer to these patients as uncertain cases. We also have patients for whom we observe their clinically relevant outcomes; we refer to these patients as certain cases. We propose a framework for evaluating prediction models that explicitly splits the evaluation between certain and uncertain cases. Here, we cannot easily evaluate both types of cases in a uniform manner as the available target labels differ. We then propose a simple prediction model that uses target labels from both certain and uncertain cases in a manner that allows us to trade off between them. Across the proposed neural model and a collection of tabular baselines, models with similar certain-case AUROC can nevertheless differ substantially in both certain-case Brier score and their probability estimates for uncertain cases. Improving alignment with target labels of uncertain cases for our proposed model generally comes at the cost of worse accuracy on certain cases, highlighting an explicit tradeoff that standard evaluation conceals. These results show that when treatment decisions determine whether clinically meaningful outcomes remain observable, conventional evaluation metrics can miss important failure modes in the very patients for whom prognostic support matters most.

AI.tldr: Standard clinical prediction model evaluation assumes outcomes are observable for all patients, but this fails when treatment decisions cause the clinically relevant outcome to be permanently unobservable. Using post-cardiac-arrest neurological prognostication (2,497 patients; 1,429 with indeterminate outcomes), the authors propose an evaluation framework that separately handles "certain" (observed outcome) and "uncertain" (indeterminate, expert-guessed counterfactual) cases, show that models with similar AUROC differ substantially on Brier score and uncertain-case probabilities, and demonstrate an explicit tradeoff between certain-case accuracy and uncertain-case alignment that conventional metrics conceal.
AI.motivation: Clinical prediction models are typically developed under the assumption that the outcome is cleanly observed for every patient. This assumption breaks down when treatment decisions render the clinically relevant outcome permanently unobservable, as in post-cardiac-arrest neurological prognostication where withdrawal-of-care decisions make many outcomes indeterminate. Standard evaluation conceals important failure modes precisely for the patients for whom prognostic support matters most.
AI.method: The authors use a cohort of 2,497 post-cardiac-arrest patients, of whom 1,429 had outcomes rendered indeterminate by treatment decisions ("uncertain cases," reviewed by independent clinical experts providing counterfactual outcome guesses) and the remainder had observed clinically relevant outcomes ("certain cases"). They propose an evaluation framework that explicitly splits evaluation between certain and uncertain cases, and a simple prediction model that incorporates target labels from both certain and uncertain cases, enabling an explicit tradeoff between the two. The approach is compared against a proposed neural model and a collection of tabular baselines.
AI.result: Models with similar certain-case AUROC can differ substantially in both certain-case Brier score and their probability estimates for uncertain cases. For the proposed model, improved alignment with uncertain-case target labels generally comes at the cost of worse accuracy on certain cases, revealing an explicit tradeoff that standard evaluation conceals.
AI.conclusion: When treatment decisions determine whether clinically meaningful outcomes remain observable, conventional evaluation metrics can miss important failure modes in the very patients for whom prognostic support matters most. Explicitly separating evaluation between certain and uncertain cases is necessary to surface these otherwise-hidden tradeoffs.

title: OmniSphinx: Active Mix Networks (Extended Version)
summary: Mix networks are an important tool to implement anonymous communication, which protects not just the content but also the metadata of messages. Over time, various packet formats for mix networks have been proposed, usually with single, specific goals in mind. These formats are incompatible with each other, requiring separate software and infrastructure to be set up. In this paper, we propose a new format, OmniSphinx, which solves this issue. In OmniSphinx, senders embed code in their packets that determines how they must be processed. The resulting active mix network can emulate any other mix format within a single deployment. Our empirical evaluation shows that emulation in OmniSphinx incurs reasonable overhead compared to native execution for typical mix network use cases: For Sphinx, the most compact format, computation time increases by around 90μs, while headers increase by 33% in size.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OmniSphinx, a new active mix network packet format that lets senders embed processing instructions in packets, enabling a single deployment to emulate any existing mix format (e.g., Sphinx) with modest overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing mix network packet formats are designed for specific goals and are mutually incompatible, forcing separate software and infrastructure per format. The authors aim to unify these formats within a single, flexible deployment.
AI.method: OmniSphinx introduces an active mix format where senders embed code in their packets that determines how the mix network processes them. This turning-complete/active design allows one deployment to emulate arbitrary other mix formats. The proposal is evaluated empirically against native execution.
AI.result: Emulation incurs reasonable overhead for typical use cases: for Sphinx (the most compact format), computation time increases by roughly 90μs and header size grows by about 33%.
AI.conclusion: OmniSphinx successfully consolidates incompatible mix formats into one active mix network, enabling format emulation within a single deployment at acceptable computational and bandwidth cost.

title: Does Fixing Break Security? An Empirical Study of Security Degradation in Iterative LLM-Driven Infrastructure-as-Code Repair
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 20th International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM 2026). To appear in LIPIcs Vol. 394
summary: Background: Iterative feedback loops are the dominant paradigm for improving LLM-generated Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC): validators such as Checkov and terraform validate feed error signals back for successive repair attempts. Prior work reports cumulative-best metrics, which are non-decreasing by construction, so the raw per-iteration security trajectory has never been examined for IaC. Aims: We study security regression (a previously-passing CIS Benchmark check that fails after a repair iteration) to determine whether and how often iterative LLM repair degrades security while fixing other issues. Method: We analyze 5,968 scenario timelines from the IaC-Eval benchmark, each one scenario run through one configuration for up to 5 repair iterations. The 15 configurations (six model-specific RAG, nine model-aggregated non-RAG, three temperatures each) yield 4,440 iteration transitions with Checkov data on both sides. We track 30 individual CIS check IDs and classify root causes from code diffs, under two detection modes: standard (inclusive) and strict (exclusive check failures only). Results: Under standard detection, 13.8% of scenarios (24.8% of transitions) exhibit at least one regression. Under strict detection the rate falls to 3.3% of scenarios (5.2% of transitions), indicating most apparent regressions are multi-resource measurement artifacts. Resource restructuring (79.0%) is the dominant root cause. Regression transitions show 2.6x more code churn (Cohen's d=0.90) and 4.9x higher strict-mode check volatility (d=1.49). Of standard-mode regressions, 36.6% self-correct within an average of 1.2 iterations; iteration 3 is the optimal stopping point. Conclusions: Iterative IaC repair does introduce security regressions, but the conservative, defensible rate is about 3.3% of scenarios. Our findings motivate security-aware feedback-loop design and actionable iteration-budget guidance.

AI.tldr: Iterative LLM repair of Infrastructure-as-Code can break previously-passing security checks. Examining 5,968 IaC-Eval scenario timelines (4,440 iteration transitions across 15 configurations), the paper finds that while 13.8% of scenarios show some regression under standard detection, only 3.3% do under strict detection—most apparent regressions are multi-resource measurement artifacts, with resource restructuring (79.0%) the dominant root cause.
AI.motivation: Prior work reports cumulative-best metrics, which are non-decreasing by construction, so the raw per-iteration security trajectory of LLM-generated IaC has never been examined. The authors aim to determine whether and how often iterative repair degrades security (regresses previously-passing CIS checks) while fixing other issues, and to characterize root causes and mitigation/stopping guidance.
AI.method: The study analyzes 5,968 scenario timelines from IaC-Eval, each run through one configuration for up to 5 repair iterations. Fifteen configurations (six model-specific RAG, nine model-aggregated non-RAG, at three temperatures each) yield 4,440 iteration transitions with Checkov data on both sides. They track 30 CIS check IDs, classify root causes from code diffs, and use two detection modes: standard (inclusive) and strict (exclusive check failures only).
AI.result: Under standard detection, 13.8% of scenarios (24.8% of transitions) exhibit at least one regression; under strict detection the rate drops to 3.3% of scenarios (5.2% of transitions). Resource restructuring accounts for 79.0% of root causes. Regression transitions show 2.6x more code churn (Cohen's d=0.90) and 4.9x higher strict-mode check volatility (d=1.49). 36.6% of standard-mode regressions self-correct within an average of 1.2 iterations, and iteration 3 is the optimal stopping point.
AI.conclusion: Iterative IaC repair does introduce security regressions, but the conservative, defensible rate is about 3.3% of scenarios. The findings motivate security-aware feedback-loop design and provide actionable iteration-budget guidance (stop at iteration 3).

title: Not All Nudges Land: Behavioral Controllability and Elaboration Quality in AI-Supported Journaling
summary: AI journaling tools can tailor prompts to a person's own sensed behavior, but it is unclear which behaviors respond to them. We analyzed 369 journal entries from an eight-week passive sensing study. An LLM labeled each entry as expressing an intention to change a behavior or not, and we measured follow-through against 26 sensor features with a 3-day before/after comparison. Responsiveness depended most on whether a behavior involves other people. Behaviors that depend on others improved in only 15 to 22% of cases, while behaviors a person can act on alone improved more often, up to 50 to 63%, though unevenly. How users wrote mattered less. No single text feature separated improved from unimproved entries; writing carried signal only within specific behaviors, most clearly for text messaging and for longer, more personal intention entries. The sample is small, so we treat these as exploratory patterns that point to where AI journaling nudges are most likely to work.

AI.tldr: An eight-week passive sensing study of AI-assisted journaling (369 entries) found that follow-through on self-reported behavior-change intentions depends mainly on whether the behavior involves other people: social behaviors improved only 15–22% of the time versus 50–63% for solo behaviors, while text features carried little general signal.
AI.motivation: AI journaling tools can tailor prompts to a person's sensed behavior, but it is unknown which behaviors actually respond to such personalized nudges. The study aims to identify what makes a journaled intention more likely to lead to actual behavior change.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 369 journal entries from an eight-week passive sensing study. An LLM labeled each entry as expressing an intention to change a behavior or not. Follow-through was measured by comparing 26 sensor features in a 3-day before/after window. They also examined whether the way users wrote the entries predicted improvement.
AI.result: Responsiveness depended most on whether a behavior involves other people. Behaviors that depend on others improved in only 15–22% of cases, while behaviors a person can act on alone improved more often (50–63%), though unevenly. Writing style mattered less: no single text feature separated improved from unimproved entries. Writing carried signal only within specific behaviors, most clearly for text messaging and for longer, more personal intention entries.
AI.conclusion: The sample is small, so findings are treated as exploratory patterns indicating where AI journaling nudges are most likely to work—specifically, solo behaviors that a person can act on independently, rather than behaviors dependent on others.

title: MindMemOS: A Portable and Self-Evolving Memory Operating Layer for AI Agents
summary: Memory is a core component of AI agents, enabling them to accumulate experience, maintain personalization, and adapt over long-term interactions. However, existing memory systems often remain fixed after development, limiting their ability to adapt their memory models, organization strategies, and procedural knowledge through continued use. We present MindMemOS, a portable and self-evolving memory operating layer that organizes open-world information using a unified entity property timestructure. MindMemOS supports scenario-adaptive memory modeling, higher-order pattern discovery, autonomous memory refinement, and continuous skill evolution. Its MindMemEvolve algorithm employs validation-driven evolutionary search to optimize memory schemas for target scenarios, whiledreaming consolidates accumulated memories by merging redundant records and resolving conflicts. In addition, implicit corrective feedback serves as a human-in-the-loop signal for identifying and revising potentially inaccurate or misaligned memories. Its MindSkillEvolve algorithm further transforms agent execution trajectories into reusable and progressively refined skills. MindMemOS achieves 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO and 70.63% on PersonaMem. MindSkillEvolve improves SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 percentage points over the initial-skill baseline.

AI.tldr: MindMemOS is a portable, self-evolving memory operating layer for AI agents that unifies memory modeling, organization, and skill evolution. It attains 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO, 70.63% on PersonaMem, and improves SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems are largely static after development and cannot adapt memory models, organization strategies, or procedural knowledge through continued use. The authors aim to build a self-evolving memory layer that continuously improves in real-world, open-world scenarios.
AI.method: MindMemOS organizes open-world information using a unified entity-property-time structure and supports scenario-adaptive memory modeling, higher-order pattern discovery, autonomous memory refinement, and continuous skill evolution. Its MindMemEvolve algorithm uses validation-driven evolutionary search to optimize memory schemas for target scenarios. Dreaming consolidates memories by merging redundant records and resolving conflicts, while implicit corrective feedback provides human-in-the-loop signals to identify and revise inaccurate memories. MindSkillEvolve transforms agent execution trajectories into reusable, progressively refined skills.
AI.result: MindMemOS reaches 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO and 70.63% on PersonaMem. MindSkillEvolve improves SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 percentage points over the initial-skill baseline.
AI.conclusion: A portable, self-evolving memory operating layer can substantially improve long-term memory accuracy and skill reuse for AI agents, enabling them to adapt memory schemas and skills autonomously over time through evolutionary search, memory consolidation, human feedback, and trajectory-driven skill refinement.

title: Large Language Models Can Follow Instructions, But Not Many at Once: Phase Transitions in Compositional Constraint Satisfaction
comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, 13 tables. Reviewed in the ARR May 2026 cycle
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed in settings that require simultaneous adherence to multiple explicit constraints - reasoning structure, safety boundaries, output schemas. Individual constraints are handled proficiently, but the compositional regime, where many must hold jointly, remains poorly characterized: how rapidly does performance degrade, what governs the degradation, and can the collapse be mitigated? We introduce Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark that systematically varies the number of simultaneous constraints (k), with every constraint scored by a deterministic, rule-based verifier and zero LLM-judge involvement: 15 models, 36 constraint types, 369,753 checks at k=1-12. Three findings emerge. First, per-constraint pass rate decays gradually and predictably, while the chance of satisfying all k constraints collapses - a model passing individual constraints at ~41% at k=8 succeeds on all eight just 5.7% of the time. Second, constraints do not degrade equally: structural constraints lose 2x more baseline capability per added constraint than lexical ones, ordered by a comprehension-maintenance gap that separates constraints requiring sustained tracking from binary decisions immune to composition. Third, failures are nearly independent, which is what makes the accumulation multiplicative; the residual coupling that does exist tracks shared output features rather than pairwise interference - a wrong sentence count fails every constraint that reads it. Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints: probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model, and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark varying the number of simultaneous constraints (k=1-12) across 15 models, 36 constraint types, and 369,753 rule-verified checks. It finds that while per-constraint pass rates decay gradually, joint satisfaction collapses multiplicatively, driven by nearly independent failures and constraint-type-specific degradation, with reliable instruction following breaking down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly required to satisfy multiple explicit constraints simultaneously (reasoning structure, safety, output schema). While individual constraints are handled well, the compositional regime where many constraints must hold jointly remains poorly characterized: how fast performance degrades, what governs the degradation, and whether the collapse can be mitigated.
AI.method: The authors introduce Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark that systematically varies the number of simultaneous constraints k (from 1 to 12). Every constraint is scored by a deterministic, rule-based verifier with zero LLM-judge involvement. The evaluation spans 15 models, 36 constraint types, and 369,753 checks.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) Per-constraint pass rate decays gradually and predictably, but the chance of satisfying all k constraints collapses - a model passing individual constraints at ~41% at k=8 succeeds on all eight only 5.7% of the time. (2) Constraints degrade unequally: structural constraints lose 2x more baseline capability per added constraint than lexical ones, ordered by a comprehension-maintenance gap separating constraints requiring sustained tracking from binary decisions immune to composition. (3) Failures are nearly independent, making accumulation multiplicative; residual coupling tracks shared output features rather than pairwise interference (e.g., a wrong sentence count fails every constraint reading it). Probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model, and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15 models.
AI.conclusion: Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints. The multiplicative nature of near-independent failures underlies the collapse, and constraint-type-specific degradation (structural vs. lexical) is governed by a comprehension-maintenance gap, suggesting the compositional constraint regime is a distinct and underexplored failure mode for LLMs.

title: Vision-Language Models are Fragile Multilingual Associators
summary: Vision-language models must associate visual entities with textual attributes. Whether these associations or concept bindings remain stable when the language of the input changes is unexplored. We introduce M$^2$BIND, a benchmark varying the language of the context and query across multiple languages. We evaluate binding both extrinsically through task performance metrics and intrinsically through causal interventions. We find that binding is not language-invariant: cross-family and cross-script settings trigger significant binding collapse, with the model's internal binding computation shifting to later layers and losing causal strength. Closely related languages preserve associations comparatively better. In a broader sense, our findings indicate how VLMs deployed globally in multilingual settings cannot be assumed to maintain the same association quality observed in monolingual evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents M²BIND, a multilingual benchmark showing that vision-language models' concept bindings (associations between visual entities and textual attributes) are not language-invariant; cross-family and cross-script language settings cause notable binding collapse, with binding computation shifting to later layers and weakening causally, while closely related languages preserve associations better.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models must associate visual entities with textual attributes, but whether these conceptual bindings remain stable when input language changes has been unexplored. This matters for deploying VLMs in global multilingual settings where association quality observed in monolingual evaluation cannot be assumed to hold.
AI.method: The authors introduce M²BIND, a benchmark that varies the language of both context and query across multiple languages. Binding is evaluated through two complementary lenses: extrinsically using task performance metrics, and intrinsically via causal interventions on the model's internal computation.
AI.result: Binding is not language-invariant. Cross-family and cross-script settings trigger significant binding collapse, where the model's internal binding computation shifts to later layers and loses causal strength. Closely related languages preserve associations comparatively better.
AI.conclusion: VLMs deployed globally in multilingual settings cannot be assumed to maintain the same association quality observed in monolingual evaluation, cautioning against relying on monolingual results for multilingual deployment.

title: When Can You Trust Offline Evaluation of Equal-Cost Top-k Allocation? A Controlled, Reproducible Benchmark and Practitioner's Guide
summary: Organizations decide whom to treat under a budget and want to know what a targeting rule would have earned before deploying it. Off-policy evaluation promises this from logged data, but the deployable rule is a deterministic top-k policy: it removes all averaging over actions, so weak overlap hits the estimate directly. We benchmark six estimators across five datasets and two known-effect sweeps, and validate the mechanisms against a non-simulated paired reference. First, weak overlap is governed by logger-target action alignment, not by logging sharpness alone: what governs support is the logger's probability of the target's actions. Sharpening a logger built from the target's own score barely moves overlap over the tested range; action-level disagreement collapses it. Effective sample size ranks this risk across logging environments, but is weak at ranking candidates within the single log a practitioner holds, and its cut point does not transfer. Second, the optimizer's curse is not fixed by cross-fitting the outcome nuisance. When the rule is fit on the data used to evaluate it, cross-fitting the nuisance alone leaves the reuse bias in place and makes it worse. Honest policy-level splitting avoids the reuse by targeting the learning procedure's value -- a change of estimand, not a de-biasing of the full-sample policy. Third, propensity-estimation error is the largest degradation we measure: an out-of-fold estimate hurts IPS more than any other stress we apply, leaves doubly-robust estimation almost unchanged, and can invert the overlap diagnostic itself. Logging is synthesized and propensities floored at 0.02, so every failure occurs with bounded weights; the floor also reduces the two tuned hybrids to their untuned parents, leaving four practically distinct estimators, and all exact-value surfaces are synthetic or semi-synthetic. We release the benchmark; public data only.

AI.tldr: A benchmark of six off-policy estimators for deterministic top-k targeting under a budget reveals that weak overlap is governed by logger-target action alignment (not logging sharpness), cross-fitting the outcome nuisance does not fix the optimizer's curse, and propensity-estimation error is the largest degradation source.
AI.motivation: Organizations deploying a budget-constrained targeting rule need to estimate its value from logged data, but the deployable rule is a deterministic top-k policy with no averaging over actions, so limited overlap between the logging distribution and the target policy's actions directly degrades off-policy estimates. Practitioners need to know which failure mechanisms matter and which estimators remain robust.
AI.method: Benchmark six off-policy estimators across five datasets and two known-effect sweeps, validated against a non-simulated paired reference. They analyze (1) overlap/effective sample size diagnostics, (2) cross-fitting of the outcome nuisance, and (3) out-of-fold propensity estimation, using synthesized logging with propensities floored at 0.02.
AI.result: Weak overlap is driven by logger-target action alignment, not logging sharpness alone; sharpening a logger built from the target's own score barely moves overlap, while action-level disagreement collapses it. Effective sample size ranks risk across environments but is weak within a single log and its cut point does not transfer. The optimizer's curse is not fixed by cross-fitting the outcome nuisance; when the rule is fit on evaluation data, cross-fitting leaves reuse bias in place or worsens it, and only honest policy-level splitting (a change of estimand) avoids it. Propensity-estimation error is the largest degradation: an out-of-fold estimate hurts IPS most and can invert the overlap diagnostic, while doubly-robust estimation stays almost unchanged. The 0.02 floor reduces the two tuned hybrids to their untuned parents, leaving four practically distinct estimators.
AI.conclusion: For deterministic top-k targeting, practitioners should prioritize accurate action propensities (the dominant risk) and honest policy-level evaluation splitting, rather than relying on cross-fitted outcome nuisances or overlap cut points that do not transfer. The benchmark is released, with all exact-value surfaces synthetic or semi-synthetic and public data only.

title: LLM-Assisted Dynamic Threat Analysis for Attacker-Reachable Software Weaknesses in Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles depend on large safety-critical software stacks, where weaknesses reachable from adversarial inputs may affect steering, braking, or other control decisions. Static analysis can identify candidate sites, but dynamically confirming exploitability requires executable test artifacts that are difficult to construct manually. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can automate this process for Autoware, an open-source autonomous-driving stack. We perform compiler-precise static analysis across 185 packages, identifying 1,375 decision rules, 2,274 validation checks, and 482 input-to-safety-output flows, from which we derive a weakness taxonomy and sample 740 reachable sites. Two local open-weight LLMs, a no-static-context ablation, and a naive-template baseline generate 3,700 artifact sets, which are compiled against the real build under sanitizers, repaired through compiler-in-the-loop feedback, and fuzzed when executable. The main result is a build-integration failure taxonomy showing that 80% of first-shot compilation failures arise from dependency wiring rather than program logic. The reasoning model compiled 64% of harnesses on the first attempt, compared with 6% for the code-specialized model. Repair achieved full object-compileability for the reasoning model only through extensive stubbing; fewer than half of its harnesses reached the fuzzer, and all 37 observed crashes originated in stubbed code rather than Autoware. No candidate weakness was dynamically confirmed within budget. These results show that build integration, not candidate generation or fuzzing, is the primary barrier to reliable LLM-assisted dynamic analysis of full autonomous-vehicle software stacks.

AI.tldr: LLMs can generate executable test harnesses for Autoware safety-critical code, but build integration—not candidate generation or fuzzing—is the dominant failure mode, with no weaknesses dynamically confirmed within budget.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles rely on large safety-critical software stacks where adversarial inputs could impact control decisions. Static analysis finds candidate dangerous sites, but dynamically confirming exploitability needs executable test artifacts that are hard to build manually. The authors investigate whether LLMs can automate this harness construction for the open-source Autoware autonomous-driving stack.
AI.method: Compiler-precise static analysis across 185 Autoware packages identifies 1,375 decision rules, 2,274 validation checks, and 482 input-to-safety-output flows, yielding a weakness taxonomy and 740 sampled reachable sites. Two local open-weight LLMs (a reasoning model and a code-specialized model), a no-static-context ablation, and a naive-template baseline produce 3,700 artifact sets. These are compiled against the real build under sanitizers, repaired via compiler-in-the-loop feedback, and fuzzed when executable.
AI.result: A build-integration failure taxonomy shows 80% of first-shot compilation failures stem from dependency wiring, not program logic. The reasoning model compiled 64% of harnesses on the first attempt versus 6% for the code-specialized model. Full object-compileability was achieved only with extensive stubbing; fewer than half of the reasoning model's harnesses reached the fuzzer, and all 37 observed crashes originated in stubbed code rather than Autoware. No candidate weakness was dynamically confirmed within budget.
AI.conclusion: Build integration is the primary barrier to reliable LLM-assisted dynamic analysis of full autonomous-vehicle software stacks, rather than candidate generation or fuzzing. The results suggest future work should focus on automating dependency resolution and build wiring to enable effective LLM-driven dynamic vulnerability confirmation.

title: Surprise2Refine: Axis-Centered Exploration-To-Refinement for Agent-Assisted Creative Scaffolding
summary: Designers require different design spaces across creative stages: broad during exploration, and targeted during refinement. Yet existing agent-driven tools assume a fixed or continuously expanding space, leaving designers to manage and navigate it themselves. Informed by a formative study with five designers, we propose an axis-centered workflow that adaptively broadens and narrows the design space to support structured exploration and refinement. We implemented this workflow in Surprise2Refine, a prototype that allows users to build and reshape an nxn design space through a set of axis-centered interactions as their creative intent evolves. A within-subjects study with 14 designers shows that Surprise2Refine enhances users' sense of control, supports tracking of scaffolding paths, and improves the perceived creativity of design outcomes. We further distill design insights to guide future agent-assisted tools for creative scaffolding.

AI.tldr: Surprise2Refine is an agent-assisted creative tool that lets designers adaptively broaden and narrow their design space via an axis-centered workflow, improving control, scaffolding-path tracking, and perceived outcome creativity.
AI.motivation: Designers need different design-space sizes at different creative stages (broad during exploration, targeted during refinement), but existing agent-driven tools assume a fixed or continuously expanding space, forcing designers to manage and navigate it manually. A formative study with five designers informed the need for a tool that adaptively reshapes the design space as creative intent evolves.
AI.method: The authors proposed an axis-centered workflow that adaptively broadens and narrows the design space, and implemented it in a prototype called Surprise2Refine. The prototype lets users build and reshape an n×n design space through axis-centered interactions. Evaluation used a within-subjects study with 14 designers.
AI.result: The within-subjects study with 14 designers showed that Surprise2Refine enhances users' sense of control, supports tracking of scaffolding paths, and improves the perceived creativity of design outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The work distills design insights to guide future agent-assisted tools for creative scaffolding, contributing a workflow and prototype that adaptively reshape design spaces across exploration and refinement stages.

title: CRAFT: LLM-Based Iterative Refinement for Temporal Reasoning over Clinical Narratives
summary: Understanding the temporal progression of symptoms in clinical narratives is critical for disease monitoring, safety surveillance, and causality assessment. Clinical narratives, however, rarely provide explicit temporal anchors. Current approaches to temporal information reasoning focus predominantly on pairwise relation classification across multi-visit and timestamp-rich records, leaving the reconstruction of structured symptom trajectories from individual anchor-sparse reports largely unaddressed. We propose CRAFT, an LLM framework that pairs a generator with a constraint-based verifier to iteratively produce and refine stage-wise symptom timelines through targeted feedback. We conduct evaluation on MedTempo, a new benchmark of 5,347 vaccine adverse-event narratives spanning three COVID-19 vaccine types, with expert-validated temporal stage annotations for 3,166 reports. Experiments across four LLM backbones demonstrate that CRAFT consistently improves temporal ordering accuracy, with ablation analysis isolating the contribution of generator and verifier components across model capability levels.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CRAFT, an LLM framework combining a generator and a constraint-based verifier to iteratively reconstruct stage-wise symptom timelines from anchor-sparse clinical narratives, and introduces MedTempo, a benchmark of vaccine adverse-event reports for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Clinical narratives rarely contain explicit temporal anchors, and existing temporal reasoning methods focus on pairwise relation classification in timestamp-rich, multi-visit records, leaving the reconstruction of structured symptom trajectories from single, anchor-sparse reports largely unaddressed.
AI.method: CRAFT pairs a generator with a constraint-based verifier in an iterative loop that produces and refines stage-wise symptom timelines using targeted feedback. Evaluation uses MedTempo, a new benchmark of 5,347 vaccine adverse-event narratives across three COVID-19 vaccine types, with expert-validated temporal stage annotations for 3,166 reports.
AI.result: Across four LLM backbones, CRAFT consistently improves temporal ordering accuracy. Ablation analysis isolates the individual contributions of the generator and verifier components at different model capability levels.
AI.conclusion: CRAFT effectively addresses the underexplored task of reconstructing structured symptom timelines from anchor-sparse clinical narratives, and the MedTempo benchmark provides a validated resource for evaluating temporal reasoning in this setting.

title: Steering the Language Axis: From Linear Decodability to Causal Control
summary:
Despite the impressive multilingual capabilities of Large Language Models, the latent dynamics dictating language selection remain poorly understood. In this work, we ask whether language identity is merely linearly decodable from hidden states, or if it can be causally controlled by a compact activation direction. We conduct an exhaustive causal intervention analysis across multiple model families, including Qwen 3.5-2B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, isolating PCA-derived "language axes" to perform steering and ablation experiments across 1.26 million generations on the FLORES-200 dataset.
  Steering along these geometric directions reliably forces language switching in both cross-script (English to Chinese) and same-script (English to Spanish) settings, whereas equal-magnitude random perturbations yield virtually no effect. Our layerwise analysis reveals that language commitment is highly localized and explicitly language-pair-dependent. While English to Chinese switching resists early intervention and steers easily in the later layers, the English-Spanish transition shifts earlier, displaying a distinct, bimodal sensitivity. Furthermore, targeted ablation uncovers a fundamental reversion to English: once the language signal is removed, the model falls back to English regardless of the input prompt. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that language decision boundaries function during inference as causally active features that are direction-dependent and layer-specific.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether language identity in multilingual LLMs can be causally controlled via compact, PCA-derived activation directions, finding that steering along these "language axes" reliably triggers language switching, with effects that are layer-localized and language-pair-dependent.
AI.motivation: To determine whether language selection in Large Language Models is merely linearly decodable from hidden states ("readable") or whether it can be causally manipulated through targeted activation directions, moving beyond correlational analysis to establish causal control over language identity.
AI.method: An exhaustive causal intervention analysis across multiple model families (Qwen 3.5-2B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct), isolating PCA-derived "language axes" to perform steering and ablation experiments over 1.26 million generations on the FLORES-200 dataset, testing both cross-script (English-Chinese) and same-script (English-Spanish) transitions with layerwise analysis.
AI.result: Steering along language axes reliably forces language switching in both cross-script and same-script settings, while equal-magnitude random perturbations have virtually no effect. Language commitment is highly localized and language-pair-dependent: English-Chinese switching resists early intervention and steers easily in later layers, whereas English-Spanish shifts earlier with distinct bimodal sensitivity. Targeted ablation causes a fundamental reversion to English regardless of input prompt.
