AI.conclusion: Language decision boundaries function during inference as causally active features that are direction-dependent and layer-specific, demonstrating that language identity in LLMs is not merely decodable but causally controllable via compact geometric directions.

title: Exploring Oversmoothing with Householder Matrices
summary: Deep graph neural networks(GNNs) suffer from oversmoothing- a progressive collapse of node representation towards a low information subspace as network depth increases because the normalized graph propagation operator is repeatedly applied directly to the hidden representations. In this work we study Householder Graph Neural Network (HouseGNN). Rather than updating the hidden state like standard GCN, HouseGNN uses the aggregated neighbourhood message solely to estimate a reflection direction; the node embedding is then updated by a Householder reflector followed by GroupSort, yielding a piecewise orthogonal layer that preserves Euclidean norm at every node and at every depth. We prove three core properties: (i) every internal layer preserves the node-wise Euclidean norm; (ii) the Householder reflector is scale scale and sign-invariant in the message; and (iii) pairwise distance between nodes can change through mismatch between node-wise orthogonal operators.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Householder Graph Neural Network (HouseGNN), which replaces standard GCN hidden-state updates with a norm-preserving piecewise orthogonal transformation (Householder reflector + GroupSort) driven by neighborhood messages, to combat oversmoothing in deep GNNs.
AI.motivation: Deep GNNs suffer from oversmoothing: node representations progressively collapse toward a low-information subspace as depth increases because the normalized graph propagation operator is repeatedly applied directly to hidden representations. The goal is to design a layer that propagates information without this representation collapse.
AI.method: HouseGNN uses the aggregated neighborhood message only to estimate a reflection direction (rather than directly updating the hidden state as in GCN). The node embedding is then updated via a Householder reflector followed by GroupSort, producing a piecewise orthogonal layer that preserves the Euclidean norm at every node and every depth.
AI.result: The paper proves three core properties: (i) every internal layer preserves the node-wise Euclidean norm; (ii) the Householder reflector is scale- and sign-invariant in the message; and (iii) pairwise distances between nodes can change through mismatch between node-wise orthogonal operators.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling message-based direction estimation from norm-preserving embedding updates, HouseGNN provides a principled mechanism to avoid oversmoothing in deep architectures, with norm preservation and invariance guarantees that distinguish it from standard GCN-style updates.

title: InSPECtor: Improving SLEIGH Processor Specification Veracity via Proxy
comment: Extended version published at USENIX Security (USENIX Security'2026). Code available at: https://github.com/Sleigh-InSPECtor/
summary:
Processor specifications underpin critical security and program- analysis tools such as disassemblers, decompilers, and emulators, yet, their correctness is rarely examined. Errors in specifications distort program behaviour, obscure vulnerabilities, and enable analysis-evasion techniques. Validating processor specifications is a non-trivial task. Our study is a significant undertaking to enable, for the first time, the systematic validation of open-source SLEIGH language specifications, predominantly used by Ghidra. We design and implement a testing framework based on an automated oracle validation strategy by proxy. Our approach leverages the structure encoded in a specification itself to enumerate decodable instruction forms and generate targeted initial states. Then differentially test the successful decoding and emulation of those instructions by comparing emulators exercising the processor specification against hardware references.
  Applying InSPECtor across diverse, open-source specifications---x86-64, AArch64, ARM/Thumb, RISC-V, MSP430---embedding differences in specification styles, author preferences, and instruction set architecture designs, we uncovered over 38,920 discrepancies that led to 125 unique bugs with proposed fixes, identifying decoding and semantic defects as well as cross-vendor inconsistencies. We distill our findings into 8 concrete recommendations to drive future improvements. Our work underscores the importance of specification correctness and provides a practical tool to substantially improve the fidelity of SLEIGH processor specifications, strengthening the reliability of downstream security and analysis tools.

AI.tldr: InSPECtor is a testing framework that systematically validates open-source SLEIGH processor specifications (used by Ghidra) via oracle-by-proxy differential testing, comparing emulators against hardware references; it found over 38,920 discrepancies and 125 unique bugs across five ISAs.
AI.motivation: Processor specifications underpin security and program-analysis tools (disassemblers, decompilers, emulators) but their correctness is rarely examined. Errors distort program behavior, hide vulnerabilities, and enable analysis-evasion techniques, yet validating specifications is non-trivial.
AI.method: The authors designed InSPECtor, an automated oracle-validation-by-proxy testing framework. It leverages the structure encoded in a specification to enumerate decodable instruction forms and generate targeted initial states, then differentially tests successful decoding and emulation by comparing emulators that exercise the processor specification against hardware references. It was applied to x86-64, AArch64, ARM/Thumb, RISC-V, and MSP430 specifications.
AI.result: InSPECtor uncovered over 38,920 discrepancies leading to 125 unique bugs with proposed fixes, spanning decoding defects, semantic defects, and cross-vendor inconsistencies. The findings were distilled into 8 concrete recommendations for future improvements.
AI.conclusion: Processor specification correctness is critically important, and InSPECtor offers a practical tool to substantially improve SLEIGH specification fidelity, thereby strengthening the reliability of downstream security and analysis tools.

title: CAPRI: Contract-Aware Proof Repair for Isabelle
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Submitted to SBMF 2026. Reproducibility artefact available on Zenodo
summary: We address the use of large language models (LLMs) to help discover Isabelle proofs. An Isabelle build establishes that the submitted theory is accepted, but not that an LLM changed only what the developer authorised. We present CAPRI, a contract-aware repair workflow in which Isabelle checks the proof and an independent checker enforces a machine-readable edit contract. Prompts, proposals, candidate repositories, diagnostics, verdicts, and hashes are retained for audit. We evaluate five workflows on twelve failed proofs from four developments, with three replicates per task and condition, giving 180 runs and 138 valid repairs. Of 144 terminal candidates accepted by Isabelle, six had modified protected text; all arose in iterative workflows that could edit a complete theory. A proof-body-only interface produced 29/36 valid repairs and no contract violations, compared with 31/36 for the corresponding full-theory workflow. One-shot repair produced 22/36, while a later prospectively frozen iterative workflow produced 32/36; these figures compare complete workflows rather than individual mechanisms. A separate post hoc OpenRouter campaign found no improvement in the designated Luna comparisons. A Sol configuration with matched demonstrations produced 33/36 repairs, compared with 29/36 in the frozen OpenAI Responses condition, but the difference was not statistically significant in a one-sided exact McNemar test ($p=0.0625$).

AI.tldr: CAPRI is a contract-aware Isabelle proof-repair workflow that lets Isabelle verify proofs while an independent checker enforces an edit contract, ensuring LLMs only modify developer-authorized text. Across 180 runs on twelve failed proofs, contract enforcement prevented unauthorized edits, with proof-body-only and contract-aware iterative workflows achieving strong repair rates without violations.
AI.motivation: Large language models can help find Isabelle proofs, but Isabelle's build only confirms that the submitted theory is accepted—it does not verify that the LLM modified only what the developer authorized. There is a need to guarantee that LLM-assisted proof repair respects developer-intended edit boundaries while retaining auditability.
AI.method: The authors propose CAPRI, a contract-aware repair workflow combining Isabelle proof checking with an independent checker that enforces a machine-readable edit contract. Prompts, proposals, candidate repositories, diagnostics, verdicts, and hashes are retained for audit. They evaluate five workflows (including proof-body-only, full-theory, one-shot, iterative, and a prospectively frozen iterative variant) on twelve failed proofs from four developments, with three replicates per task and condition. They also run a post hoc OpenRouter campaign and a Sol configuration with matched demonstrations, comparing workflows via a one-sided exact McNemar test.
AI.result: The 180 runs yielded 138 valid repairs. Of 144 terminal candidates accepted by Isabelle, six had modified protected text, all arising in iterative workflows that could edit a complete theory. The proof-body-only interface produced 29/36 valid repairs with zero contract violations, versus 31/36 for the full-theory workflow. One-shot repair produced 22/36, while the prospectively frozen iterative workflow produced 32/36. A post hoc OpenRouter campaign showed no improvement in the designated Luna comparisons. A Sol configuration with matched demonstrations produced 33/36 repairs versus 29/36 for the frozen OpenAI Responses condition, but the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.0625).
AI.conclusion: Contract-aware, proof-body-only repair workflows can achieve repair rates comparable to full-theory editing while eliminating contract violations by restricting LLM edits to authorized regions. The audit trail and independent contract checker provide accountability, and no statistically significant advantage was found for the alternative model configurations tested.

title: NavSight in the Wild: Understanding Real-World Use of a Mobile Augmented Reality Application for People with Low Vision in Outdoor Navigation
summary: The ability to navigate outdoors safely and independently is crucial yet challenging for people with low vision (PLV). While various augmented reality (AR) systems for low vision have been designed and evaluated in ideal lab environments, no research has investigated their real-world feasibility and challenges. We present NavSight, a mobile AR application that assists PLV in outdoor navigation by recognizing important outdoor objects (e.g., curb, vehicle) and rendering real-time visual augmentations. Through a seven-day diary study with 12 PLV in real-world settings, we characterize the impact of NavSight on scene perception, users' configuration strategies on what objects to augment and how to augment them across scenarios, how users made sense of and responded to recognition errors, and the social acceptability of using NavSight in public. We further identify environmental factors affecting recognition, such as weather conditions, lighting and shadows, and nonstandard road markings and textures, as well as usability issues in daily use. We discuss these real-world challenges and derive design implications for future AI-powered assistive AR systems for outdoor use.

AI.tldr: NavSight is a mobile AR app that helps people with low vision navigate outdoors by detecting objects and showing visual augmentations. A seven-day real-world diary study with 12 participants revealed its impact on perception, user configuration preferences, error handling, and social acceptance, while uncovering environmental and usability challenges that inform future assistive AR design.
AI.motivation: Outdoor navigation is critical but difficult for people with low vision. Existing AR assistive systems have only been tested in controlled lab settings, leaving a gap in understanding how these systems perform and what challenges arise in real-world everyday use.
AI.method: The authors developed NavSight, a mobile AR application that recognizes important outdoor objects (e.g., curbs, vehicles) and renders real-time visual augmentations. They then conducted a seven-day diary study with 12 people with low vision who used NavSight in real-world settings, capturing qualitative data on scene perception, configuration strategies, recognition-error handling, and social acceptability.
AI.result: NavSight improved scene perception. Users developed varied strategies for configuring which objects to augment and how, depending on the scenario. They adapted to recognition errors in individualized ways, and social acceptability was a notable concern in public use. The study also identified environmental factors affecting recognition (weather, lighting/shadows, nonstandard road markings/textures) and daily-use usability issues.
AI.conclusion: Real-world deployment reveals challenges that lab studies miss, including environmental robustness and social factors. The paper derives design implications for future AI-powered assistive AR systems intended for outdoor use by people with low vision.

title: HybridRAG-BN: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework with Fine-Tuned Verification for Bangla KBQA
comment: Developed for the IEEE Computer Society CUET Student Branch
summary: Knowledge-base question answering (KBQA) systems rely on effective retrieval and reasoning mechanisms to generate accurate answers from external knowledge sources. However, developing reliable KBQA systems for low-resource languages such as Bangla remains challenging due to limited retrieval-focused research, scarce language resources, and difficulties in grounding generated responses in external knowledge. In this work, we propose HybridRAG-BN, a retrieval-augmented framework for Bangla KBQA that integrates hybrid retrieval using BM25 and BGE-M3, answer generation using the GGUF version of Gemma-4-31B-Instruct, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma-4-31B-Instruct model for answer verification and refinement. To further improve robustness, the framework incorporates a post-processing stage that addresses unresolved cases through fallback answer replacement and DuckDuckGo-assisted retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving token-level F1 scores of 0.71654 and 0.72912 on the public and private leaderboards, respectively, securing first place in the competition.

AI.tldr: HybridRAG-BN is a retrieval-augmented framework for Bangla knowledge-base question answering that combines hybrid retrieval (BM25 + BGE-M3), Gemma-4-31B-Instruct answer generation, a LoRA-fine-tuned verifier, and post-processing with fallback/DuckDuckGo retrieval, achieving first place with token-level F1 of 0.71654 (public) and 0.72912 (private).
AI.motivation: Developing reliable KBQA systems for low-resource languages such as Bangla is challenging because of limited retrieval-focused research, scarce language resources, and difficulty in grounding generated answers in external knowledge.
AI.method: Proposes HybridRAG-BN, which integrates: (1) hybrid retrieval using BM25 and BGE-M3; (2) answer generation via the GGUF version of Gemma-4-31B-Instruct; (3) a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma-4-31B-Instruct model for answer verification and refinement; and (4) a post-processing stage handling unresolved cases through fallback answer replacement and DuckDuckGo-assisted retrieval.
AI.result: Achieved token-level F1 scores of 0.71654 on the public leaderboard and 0.72912 on the private leaderboard, securing first place in the competition.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HybridRAG-BN framework effectively addresses retrieval and generation challenges in Bangla KBQA, demonstrating robust performance and state-of-the-art results as evidenced by its first-place ranking.

title: Governed Persistent Memory: Source-Bound State Semantics and Fail-Closed Release for Long-Horizon Agents
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 11 tables. Includes a sealed end-to-end governed-memory service evaluation with an ungoverned local Qwen2.5-7B comparison
summary:
Long-term agent memory is usually treated as select--store--retrieve, but retrieval does not decide whether contradictory, superseded, retracted, deleted, or stale records may support an outgoing claim. We introduce Governed Persistent Memory (GPM), an auditable bitemporal state-transition model with source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release. Five executable clauses cover ledger integrity, source binding, conflict isolation, non-revival after retraction or deletion, and exact claim closure over a fresh view at one verified head.
  On a prespecified hash-frozen 3,600-case GPM-ReleaseBench, GPM matches all complete outcomes; the strongest of three intentionally simple complete policies matches 1,800/3,600 and makes unmatched releases on 50% of violation cases. A separate sealed end-to-end service evaluation exercises real ingestion and release across eight query families. In its publicly disclosed V3 arm, the governed lane is correct on 2,400/2,400 clusters versus 600/2,400 for ungoverned local Qwen2.5-7B; it repairs all 1,800 baseline failures with no regression (one-sided 95% lower bounds 99.875% and 99.834%). A later V5 reseal over Chinese- and English-command arms, with generation-date pinning and no post-freeze reducer amendment, again obtains 2,400/2,400 per arm. A production-code-independent finite model explores 331,776 semantic and 1,990,656 query states without a full-contract counterexample, and a 100,000-trace three-engine differential yields zero mismatches.
  These are bounded contract and implementation results, not open-world model accuracy or evidence of world truth. Governed answers in the sealed service evaluation are deterministic service outputs; the 7B result is the ungoverned comparison, not a claim that a language model itself became perfectly accurate.

AI.tldr: Introduces Governed Persistent Memory (GPM), an auditable bitemporal memory model that enforces source-bound admission, lifecycle states, and fail-closed release so that only records valid at one verified head can support outgoing claims. Benchmarks and sealed evaluations show GPM achieves full correctness where simple baselines and an ungoverned 7B model fail.
AI.motivation: Standard select--store--retrieve memory lacks a retrieval-time decision about whether contradictory, superseded, retracted, deleted, or stale records are allowed to substantiate an outgoing claim. This gap permits unsupported or invalid claims to be released, motivating an auditable, governance-enforced memory model.
AI.method: Proposes GPM, a bitemporal state-transition model with source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release. Five executable clauses enforce ledger integrity, source binding, conflict isolation, non-revival after retraction/deletion, and exact claim closure over a fresh view at one verified head. Evaluated via a hash-frozen 3,600-case GPM-ReleaseBench, a sealed end-to-end service across eight query families, a later resealed V5 evaluation, finite-model checking (331,776 semantic and 1,990,656 query states), and a 100,000-trace three-engine differential test.
AI.result: On GPM-ReleaseBench, GPM matches all complete outcomes, while the strongest simple complete policy matches 1,800/3,600 and releases unmatched outputs on 50% of violation cases. In the sealed service V3 arm, the governed lane is correct on 2,400/2,400 clusters versus 600/2,400 for ungoverned Qwen2.5-7B, repairing all 1,800 baseline failures with no regression (one-sided 95% lower bounds 99.875% and 99.834%). The V5 reseal again yields 2,400/2,400 per language arm. Finite model checking finds no full-contract counterexample, and differential testing shows zero mismatches across 100,000 traces.
AI.conclusion: GPM provides bounded contract and implementation guarantees for governed memory release, not open-world model accuracy or evidence of world truth. Governed answers are deterministic service outputs, while the 7B scores serve only as ungoverned comparisons, not claims that a language model became perfectly accurate.

title: HC-RAG: Evidence-Centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Heterogeneous Financial Filings
summary: Financial question answering over annual reports requires more than retrieving semantically similar passages. It often involves identifying relevant companies and fiscal years, locating standardized filing sections, collecting textual and tabular evidence, and checking answers against the original documents. Existing RAG systems, however, usually flatten long filings into unordered chunks, pay limited attention to the typed structure of financial reports, and use fixed text-table fusion strategies without considering query intent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{HC-RAG}, a hierarchical cross-modal retrieval-augmented generation framework for evidence-centric financial QA. HC-RAG organizes filings into a typed financial evidence graph with documents, sections, text units, table units, and metadata nodes. It retrieves evidence through document-section-unit paths, aligns textual and tabular evidence in a shared retrieval space, and routes evidence according to four semantic intents: calculation, trend, fact, and comparison. We further introduce \textbf{Multi-Doc-2025}, a benchmark containing 2,327 expert-verified QA pairs from 179 SEC 10-K filings of 87 S\&P 500 companies across fiscal years 2022--2024, with labels for intent, difficulty, and structural evidence attributes. Experiments on public financial QA benchmarks and Multi-Doc-2025 show that HC-RAG improves both answer quality and evidence localization, especially in long-document, table-related, and cross-document settings. HC-RAG outperforms RAPTOR by 6.6 F1 points on DocFinQA and GraphRAG by 10.9 F1 points on Multi-Doc-2025. Evidence-level analysis and ablation studies show that the improvements mainly come from more accurate section localization, table grounding, cross-document evidence aggregation, and intent-aware text-table routing.

AI.tldr: HC-RAG is a hierarchical cross-modal retrieval-augmented generation framework that organizes financial filings into a typed evidence graph, retrieves evidence through structured paths, aligns text and tables, and routes evidence by query intent, achieving state-of-the-art financial QA results on public benchmarks and a new Multi-Doc-2025 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Financial QA over annual reports requires more than semantic similarity retrieval: it needs identifying companies/fiscal years, locating standardized filing sections, collecting textual and tabular evidence, and verifying answers against documents. Existing RAG systems flatten filings into unordered chunks, ignore typed report structure, and use fixed text-table fusion without considering query intent.
AI.method: HC-RAG organizes filings into a typed financial evidence graph (documents, sections, text units, table units, metadata nodes). It retrieves evidence via document-section-unit paths, aligns textual and tabular evidence in a shared retrieval space, and routes evidence according to four semantic intents: calculation, trend, fact, and comparison. A new benchmark, Multi-Doc-2025, contains 2,327 expert-verified QA pairs from 179 SEC 10-K filings of 87 S&P 500 companies (FY 2022–2024) with intent, difficulty, and structural evidence labels.
AI.result: HC-RAG improves answer quality and evidence localization, especially in long-document, table-related, and cross-document settings. It outperforms RAPTOR by 6.6 F1 on DocFinQA and GraphRAG by 10.9 F1 on Multi-Doc-2025. Gains come mainly from better section localization, table grounding, cross-document evidence aggregation, and intent-aware text-table routing.
AI.conclusion: By modeling the typed hierarchical structure of financial filings and aligning intent with text-table routing, HC-RAG substantially improves financial QA over RAG baselines, particularly for complex, long-document, and cross-document scenarios, and provides the Multi-Doc-2025 benchmark for future evaluation.

title: GENADA: efficient generative time series adversarial attack framework
summary: Deep learning models are widely used for time series analysis in domains such as healthcare, finance, energy systems, and environmental monitoring. However, these models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small input perturbations cause severe degradation in predictive performance. Commonly used gradient-based attacks, iterative first-order methods, are computationally burdensome, as they repeatedly backpropagate through the victim model to compute input gradients during a number of iterative refinement steps. We propose a GENerative ADversarial Attack (GENADA) that learns a generative model to produce deceptive perturbations directly in a single forward pass and a procedure to train it. Variants include single-step and iterative generative attack schemes. The validation considers attacks on several neural models and datasets in the time-series domain, a controlled, low-dimensional setting. Empirically, GENADA achieves comparable attack quality to strong baselines while requiring less time to generate perturbations during inference.

AI.tldr: GENADA is a generative adversarial attack that produces deceptive perturbations for time-series models in a single forward pass, matching strong white-box baselines in attack quality while being much faster at inference.
AI.motivation: Time-series deep learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, but standard gradient-based (iterative first-order) methods are computationally expensive because they repeatedly backpropagate to compute gradients over many refinement steps. The authors aim to reduce this computational burden while preserving attack effectiveness.
AI.method: The paper proposes GENADA (GENerative ADversarial Attack), which trains a generative model to directly output deceptive perturbations in one forward pass, together with a training procedure. It offers both single-step and iterative generative attack variants. Evaluation covers multiple neural models and datasets in the time-series domain using a controlled, low-dimensional setting.
AI.result: Empirically, GENADA achieves attack quality comparable to strong baseline (gradient-based) attacks while requiring significantly less time to generate perturbations during inference.
AI.conclusion: A learned generative attack can substitute for computationally costly iterative gradient-based methods, delivering comparable adversarial effectiveness with much faster perturbation generation for time-series models.

title: Operationalizing Cyber Threat Intelligence with GraphRAG
summary: When a security researcher publishes a report on a cyberattack, detection engineers are supposed to turn it into working detection rules. In practice, most automated attempts at this only extract the simplest clues from the report --- bad IP addresses, domain names, and file hashes --- and turn them into block lists. This is a weak strategy, because attackers can change these simple clues within hours or days, so the resulting detections stop working almost as soon as they are deployed. Security teams describe this idea with the Pyramid of Pain. This project asks whether feeding a report into a knowledge-graph retrieval system, Microsoft GraphRAG, rather than a standard vector-similarity retrieval system (Naive RAG), produces detection plans that rely more on these durable, top-of-pyramid clues. Both systems are given the same report, the same generation instructions, and the same language model to write the final plan; only the retrieval step differs. In a detailed case study of one APT28 report, the GraphRAG plan kept firing at 100\% of its detections after every IP address, domain, and file hash in the report was rotated, while the Naive RAG plan kept firing at only 29\%. Repeating the comparison across nine real CTI reports from four vendors confirms the same pattern: GraphRAG plans consistently reach higher, harder-to-evade levels of the pyramid, even when the two systems end up close on total score. The results support treating knowledge-graph-aware retrieval as the architecturally correct foundation for automatically generating SOC-deployable hunting plans, while showing that the wording of the generation prompt matters almost as much as the retrieval back-end itself.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether using a knowledge-graph retrieval system (Microsoft GraphRAG) instead of a standard vector-similarity retriever (Naive RAG) for generating detection plans from CTI reports produces detections based on more durable, top-of-pyramid clues that survive indicator rotation.
AI.motivation: Automated conversion of cyberattack reports into detection rules typically extracts only short-lived indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) that attackers can change quickly, causing detections to fail soon after deployment. The authors want to test whether a knowledge-graph-based retrieval backend promotes the use of durable, behavior-based clues higher on the Pyramid of Pain.
AI.method: Both a Naive RAG (vector-similarity) and Microsoft GraphRAG (knowledge-graph) system are given the same CTI report, identical generation instructions, and the same language model to write the final detection plan, with only the retrieval step differing. A case study on one APT28 report measures detection persistence after rotating all IPs, domains, and file hashes. The comparison is then repeated across nine real CTI reports from four vendors.
AI.result: In the APT28 case study, the GraphRAG plan kept firing at 100% of its detections after all indicators were rotated, versus only 29% for the Naive RAG plan. Across nine reports from four vendors, GraphRAG plans consistently reached higher, harder-to-evade pyramid levels, even when total scores were comparable. Prompt wording was found to matter almost as much as the retrieval backend.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-graph-aware retrieval is the architecturally correct foundation for automatically generating SOC-deployable hunting plans, yielding detections that rely on durable, top-of-pyramid clues. However, the wording of the generation prompt is nearly as influential as the retrieval backend itself and should not be overlooked.

title: Considering Contribution Statements in Visualization and HCI Research
summary: Contribution statements are an increasingly common way to make research labor visible, reduce academic malfeasance, and provide broader transparency. Despite this potential value, they remain uncommon in visualization and HCI. To explore this gap, we conducted an online study with (N=21) visualization and HCI researchers. We find a range of differing opinions about the utility of contribution statements, which are set against a background of tensions relating to contribution frameworks that inadequately fit contribution types in HCI and especially visualization, power dynamics between authors, bias in authorship perceptions, and the tedium of providing yet another form of documentation. From these factors, we offer a modest recommendation to authors: consider contribution statements. There are contexts when they may usefully explicate work, and others where they can cause author-team conflict or become a burdensome chore. Regardless of whether they are used by readers or not, we suggest that scaffolded mechanisms for reflecting on contribution roles are valuable both for public accountability and internal alignment. To institutions, we recommend that contribution statements be exempt from page or word limits, and that flexible templates and examples be provided to authors, but that they continue to not be required. By surfacing these perspectives, we seek to open a dialogue about what constitutes authorship, how our community might move toward more equitable and transparent attribution practices, and where the visualization and HCI communities might be uniquely equipped to help.

AI.tldr: Contribution statements are rare in visualization and HCI despite their benefits. An online study of 21 researchers reveals mixed opinions driven by ill-fitting contribution frameworks, author power dynamics, bias, and documentation fatigue. The authors recommend optional use of contribution statements, scaffolded reflection on roles, and institutional flexibility (no page limits, template guidance) while opening dialogue on equitable authorship attribution.
AI.motivation: Contribution statements can make research labor visible, reduce academic malfeasance, and improve transparency, yet they remain uncommon in visualization and HCI. The authors aim to understand this gap and its underlying reasons.
AI.method: An online study conducted with N=21 visualization and HCI researchers, gathering qualitative perspectives on contribution statements, authorship practices, and related tensions.
AI.result: Researchers hold differing opinions on contribution statement utility. Key tensions include contribution frameworks that poorly fit HCI/visualization contribution types, power dynamics among authors, bias in authorship perceptions, and the tedium of additional documentation.
AI.conclusion: The authors recommend authors consider (but not be forced to use) contribution statements, as they can help in some contexts but cause conflict or become burdensome in others. They suggest scaffolded mechanisms for reflecting on contribution roles for accountability and alignment. For institutions, they recommend exempting contribution statements from page/word limits, providing flexible templates and examples, while keeping them optional. This opens a dialogue on authorship, equitable attribution, and the communities' unique potential to contribute.

title: EviReform: Evidence-Guided Query Reformulation for Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval
summary: Multi-hop retrieval must recover passages that provide sufficient evidence together. An initial passage often resolves an entity or relation implicit in the question, making the missing evidence easier to describe only after retrieval begins. Graph retrieval improves access to related evidence through stored corpus structure, but its retrieval signal is commonly derived from the original question. Complementary evidence must then be reached through stored relations even when an observed passage provides a more direct semantic cue. We introduce EviReform, which separates revising the retrieval request from aggregating evidence in the graph. Retrieved source passages formulate residual queries for the unresolved information need. The original and residual retrieval signals are normalized separately, combined, and propagated between propositions that share entities. On 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, EviReform exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points. These results show that observed evidence can guide graph retrieval toward the part of a supporting chain left underspecified by the original question. Code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/EviReform.

AI.tldr: EviReform improves multi-hop graph retrieval by letting retrieved passages reformulate residual queries for missing evidence, combining original and residual signals before propagating them across entity-linked propositions. It achieves up to +5.59 Recall@5 and +4.50 F1 over the strongest baseline on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop questions often only become fully describable after an initial retrieval resolves an entity or relation; relying solely on the original question as the graph retrieval signal forces retrieval through stored relations, ignoring stronger semantic cues available in already-observed passages.
AI.method: EviReform decouples request revision from evidence aggregation. Retrieved source passages generate residual queries for the still-unresolved information need. The original and residual retrieval signals are normalized independently, combined, and propagated across propositions sharing entities in the graph.
AI.result: On 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, EviReform surpasses the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points.
AI.conclusion: Observed evidence can effectively steer graph retrieval toward the part of a supporting chain that the original question leaves underspecified; code is publicly available.

title: $\varepsilon$-MemEvo: Adaptive Cross-Task Memory Transfer for LLM Program Evolution
summary: LLM-based program evolution systems such as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve have shown strong ability to discover novel algorithms, but typically optimize each task in isolation, discarding search experience after completion. We introduce $\varepsilon$-MemEvo, a framework for cross-task knowledge transfer in LLM program evolution. $\varepsilon$-MemEvo stores prior experience as task-agnostic tactic memories: compact natural-language summaries of successful algorithmic strategies rather than raw code, enabling transfer across tasks with different APIs and evaluators. To avoid negative transfer from semantically mismatched memories, $\varepsilon$-MemEvo uses an adaptive injection gate that decides whether retrieved memories should be injected, and at what intensity. We evaluate $\varepsilon$-MemEvo on 8 diverse optimization benchmarks spanning mathematical optimization and systems engineering, using a content-level Leave-One-Out protocol that excludes target-task memory entries. On the primary GPT-5 backbone, $\varepsilon$-MemEvo improves AUCC over AdaEvolve on all 8 tasks, with a mean relative gain of +8.7%, and improves early-stage convergence by +9.4% on average. Ablations show that naive memory injection can fail catastrophically, while adaptive gating remains safe across all five ablation tasks. The data-updated posterior is interpretable in observed states: it favors skip during improving search and shifts from skip to hint across early and late plateaus. These gains incur less than 1% computational overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ε-MemEvo, a framework enabling cross-task knowledge transfer in LLM-based program evolution by storing past search experience as task-agnostic tactic memories (natural-language strategy summaries) with an adaptive injection gate that controls whether and how strongly retrieved memories are injected, achieving consistent improvements over baselines with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based program evolution systems (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve) optimize each task in isolation and discard search experience after completion. The authors aim to enable cross-task knowledge transfer, retaining reusable algorithmic insights without leaking task-specific code, while avoiding negative transfer from semantically mismatched memories.
AI.method: ε-MemEvo stores prior experience as task-agnostic tactic memories—compact natural-language summaries of successful algorithmic strategies rather than raw code, allowing transfer across tasks with different APIs and evaluators. It uses an adaptive injection gate to decide whether retrieved memories should be injected, and at what intensity, mitigating negative transfer. Evaluation uses 8 optimization benchmarks (mathematical optimization and systems engineering) under a content-level Leave-One-Out protocol that excludes target-task memory entries, with the primary GPT-5 backbone and AdaEvolve as baseline.
AI.result: On GPT-5, ε-MemEvo improves AUCC over AdaEvolve on all 8 tasks with a mean relative gain of +8.7% and improves early-stage convergence by +9.4% on average. Ablations show naive memory injection can fail catastrophically, while adaptive gating remains safe across all five ablation tasks. The data-updated posterior is interpretable: it favors skip during improving search and shifts from skip to hint across early and late plateaus. Overhead is less than 1%.
AI.conclusion: Cross-task knowledge transfer via task-agnostic tactic memories with adaptive gating is effective and safe for LLM program evolution, yielding consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks at negligible computational cost.

title: StorySpark: Module-wise Evolutionary Search for Story Premise Generation
summary: A story premise is the creative spark from which a full narrative can grow. Yet LLM-based story generation has mostly emphasized later-stage planning, controllability, coherence, and prose expansion, while premise-level ideation remains comparatively underexplored. We introduce StorySpark, a module-wise evolutionary search framework for story premise generation. StorySpark operates over interpretable narrative modules such as background, persona, event, ending, and twist, treating each active module not as a static field to fill once, but as a local search space conditioned on the partial premise built so far. For each module, it generates alternatives, evaluates them in context, refines them through feedback-driven mutation and recombination, preserves complementary strengths with Pareto-guided selection, and reallocates frontier capacity to balance branch coverage with promising directions. Multi-view automatic and human evaluations show that StorySpark produces stronger final premises than competitive baselines, with especially consistent gains in originality; when expanded with the same story writer, its premises also lead to higher-quality downstream stories while maintaining completeness, fascination, and diverse usable narrative directions.

AI.tldr: StorySpark is a module-wise evolutionary search framework for story premise generation that treats each narrative module (background, persona, event, ending, twist) as a local search space refined through feedback-driven mutation, Pareto selection, and frontier reallocation, outperforming baselines in originality and downstream story quality.
AI.motivation: LLM-based story generation has focused on later-stage planning, controllability, coherence, and prose expansion, while premise-level ideation—the creative spark that seeds a full narrative—remains underexplored.
AI.method: StorySpark operates over interpretable narrative modules (background, persona, event, ending, twist), treating each active module as a local search space conditioned on the partial premise. For each module it generates alternatives, evaluates them in context, refines them via feedback-driven mutation and recombination, preserves complementary strengths with Pareto-guided selection, and reallocates frontier capacity to balance branch coverage against promising directions.
AI.result: Multi-view automatic and human evaluations show StorySpark produces stronger final premises than competitive baselines, with especially consistent gains in originality; when expanded with the same story writer, its premises also yield higher-quality downstream stories while maintaining completeness, fascination, and diverse usable narrative directions.
AI.conclusion: StorySpark demonstrates that evolutionary search over interpretable narrative modules effectively improves story premise ideation, enhancing originality and downstream story quality while preserving completeness and narrative diversity.

title: Scaling Automatic Research Agents via World Models
summary: Automating empirical research is a long-standing direction of AI. Recent automatic research (AutoResearch) agents bring this goal within reach, as modern LLMs show the capability to independently implement solutions and learn from the execution outcomes. Behind these gains, post-training (especially RL) plays a central role. In this paper, we identify a fundamental tension when scaling RL for these agents: the two components of every AutoResearch trajectory (agent generation and environment execution) scale in very different manners, since all generation shares compute through batching, while each execution occupies its exclusive sandbox and real machine time. As a result, the environment execution dominates the training cost and becomes the bottleneck as trajectories grow. To resolve this tension, we propose World Model RL (WMRL), which replaces environment execution with a world model to remove this bottleneck. Additionally, the world model can be imperfect, as its rewards are corrupted by bias and noise. Therefore, we further equip WMRL with two mitigations, Online Debiasing and Inverse-Variance Denoising, which offset the bias and suppress the noise respectively. Theoretically, we prove that both mitigations of WMRL strictly improve the convergence guarantee. Empirically, WMRL accelerates training by 3-4x on various tasks at different agent scales, while exceeding the performance of standard RL baselines. Moreover, our post-trained 4B and 9B agents outperform much larger open-weight agents of 48B and 120B on held-out benchmarks. Beyond AutoResearch, WMRL also transfers to post-training embodied VLA policies, which demonstrates the generalizability of our method.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a cost bottleneck in post-training RL for automatic research (AutoResearch) agents—environment execution, not model generation, dominates compute and scales poorly because each execution needs an exclusive sandbox. The authors propose World Model RL (WMRL), which replaces real environment execution with a learned world model, plus Online Debiasing and Inverse-Variance Denoising to handle the world model's biased and noisy rewards. WMRL achieves 3–4x faster training, outperforms standard RL baselines, lets 4B/9B agents beat 48B/120B open-weight agents, and also transfers to embodied VLA policy post-training.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM-based AutoResearch agents can independently implement and learn from execution, with post-training (especially RL) playing a central role. However, scaling RL faces a fundamental tension: agent generation shares compute via batching, whereas each environment execution occupies an exclusive sandbox and real machine time. As trajectories grow, environment execution dominates training cost and becomes the bottleneck.
AI.method: WMRL replaces environment execution with a world model to remove the execution bottleneck. Since the world model can be imperfect, producing rewards corrupted by bias and noise, the authors add two mitigations: Online Debiasing (to offset bias) and Inverse-Variance Denoising (to suppress noise). They provide theoretical proofs that both mitigations strictly improve the convergence guarantee.
AI.result: WMRL accelerates training by 3–4x on various tasks at different agent scales while exceeding standard RL baselines. Post-trained 4B and 9B agents outperform much larger open-weight agents of 48B and 120B on held-out benchmarks. The method also transfers to post-training embodied VLA policies, demonstrating generalizability.
AI.conclusion: The environment-execution bottleneck in scaling RL for AutoResearch agents can be resolved by replacing execution with a world model. Online Debiasing and Inverse-Variance Denoising successfully mitigate the resulting bias and noise, improving convergence both theoretically and empirically. WMRL yields substantial speedups, strong performance gains, and generalizes beyond AutoResearch to embodied VLA policy post-training.

title: A Commitment-Based Hybrid Post-Quantum Cryptographic Model for Multi-File Cloud Storage
summary: Cloud storage clients increasingly require authentication that remains secure against future quantum-capable adversaries, motivating hybrid constructions that combine classical primitives with standardized post-quantum alternatives. Extended naively to multi-file upload, such constructions incur a per-file lattice signing cost that dominates authentication time and becomes prohibitive at realistic batch sizes. This paper presents a commitment-based hybrid post-quantum model that addresses this bottleneck. It comprises AES-256-GCM bulk encryption, a hybrid X25519 with ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation mechanism, and a hybrid Ed25519 with ML-DSA-65 dual signature, computed over a SHA3-256 batch commitment. The commitment binds all ciphertexts in a batch to a single fixed-size digest that is signed once, reducing the number of post-quantum signature invocations per batch from n to one, independent of batch size; the remaining encryption and hashing is bounded by fast symmetric throughput. On a commodity client platform, averaged over 20 repetitions, this holds signing-phase time near-constant as the batch grows while the per-file baseline scales linearly. At n = 1000, the model reduces signing-phase time by factors of 629, 606, and 725 for 100 KB, 1 MB, and 10 MB files respectively, against a per-file dual-signing baseline sharing every other primitive.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a commitment-based hybrid post-quantum authentication model for multi-file cloud uploads that signs a single batch digest instead of signing each file individually, slashing post-quantum signature overhead from n invocations to one per batch and achieving up to ~600–725× faster signing at n=1000 files.
AI.motivation: Cloud storage clients need authentication secure against future quantum adversaries, driving hybrid classical + post-quantum constructions. However, extending such constructions to multi-file upload naively imposes a per-file lattice signing cost that dominates authentication time and becomes prohibitive at realistic batch sizes.
AI.method: The system combines AES-256-GCM bulk encryption, a hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation mechanism, and a hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA-65 dual signature computed over a SHA3-256 batch commitment. The commitment binds all ciphertexts in a batch into one fixed-size digest signed a single time, reducing post-quantum signature invocations per batch from n to one independent of batch size, with remaining encryption and hashing bounded by fast symmetric throughput.
AI.result: On a commodity client platform averaged over 20 repetitions, signing-phase time stays near-constant as batch size grows, while the per-file baseline scales linearly. At n = 1000, the model reduces signing-phase time by factors of 629, 606, and 725 for 100 KB, 1 MB, and 10 MB files respectively, compared to a per-file dual-signing baseline sharing all other primitives.
AI.conclusion: Commitment-based batching effectively removes the post-quantum signature as the bottleneck in hybrid multi-file authentication, making hybrid post-quantum cloud uploads practical even at large batch sizes.

title: Smart Contract Invariants Protect Against Cybercriminals
summary: Blockchains are among the most adversarial environments in computing. Billions are stolen by cybercriminals who exploit vulnerabilities. This is an open problem and no concept or technique has proven to really make a difference. In this paper, we claim that the classical notion of program invariant is perhaps the most powerful solution to the problem. We devise anoriginal experimental protocol to 1) study how invariants would have protected against past real-world attacks and 2) whether state-of-the-art automated tools can find them. The experimental toolchain is sophisticated. It is based on INVARIANTEVAL, a benchmark of 28 real Ethereum exploits, each paired with a human-authored invariant that blocks the attack. We validate every invariant with PONDEREPLAY, a replay framework that re-executes transactions in order to prove the correctness and soundness of smart contract invariants. We demonstrate that smart contract invariants block all the cybercriminal attacks in INVARIANTEVAL, fully validated by replaying 108,637 historical transactions. Our large-scale experiments clearly demonstrate that smart contract invariants protect against cybercriminals.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that program invariants are a powerful defense against blockchain exploits, introducing INVARIANTEVAL (28 real Ethereum exploits with human-authored blocking invariants) and PONDEREPLAY (a replay framework). Invariants blocked all attacks in the benchmark, validated by replaying 108,637 historical transactions.
AI.motivation: Blockchains are highly adversarial environments where cybercriminals steal billions by exploiting vulnerabilities, yet no existing concept or technique has effectively solved this open problem. The authors seek a robust approach to protect smart contracts against real-world attacks.
AI.method: The authors claim the classical notion of program invariant is a powerful solution. They devise an experimental protocol and toolchain: (1) INVARIANTEVAL, a benchmark of 28 real Ethereum exploits each paired with a human-authored invariant that blocks the attack; and (2) PONDEREPLAY, a replay framework that re-executes transactions in order to prove the correctness and soundness of smart contract invariants. The study also examines whether state-of-the-art automated tools can find these invariants.
AI.result: Smart contract invariants blocked all cybercriminal attacks in INVARIANTEVAL, fully validated by replaying 108,637 historical transactions. Large-scale experiments demonstrate that smart contract invariants protect against cybercriminals.
AI.conclusion: Program invariants are an effective solution for protecting smart contracts against cybercriminal attacks, as evidenced by the benchmark results and validated historical transaction replays.

title: PolyPresentation: A Multimodal AI Platform for Slide-Aware Iterative Presentation Practice
summary: Presentations are essential for students, researchers, and professionals to communicate ideas persuasively, yet delivering them effectively requires repeated practice that coordinates content, delivery, visual materials, and audience interaction. Existing AI-assisted rehearsal tools provide scalable feedback, but they often treat presentations as single-run delivery performances, offering limited support for linking feedback to the slide deck or planning what to practice in the next iteration. To address this gap, we introduce PolyPresentation, a multimodal AI platform for slide-aware iterative presentation practice. PolyPresentation organizes slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsal, audience Q&A, and feedback into a unified practice loop, using slide-grounded evidence to help presenters diagnose performance issues and prepare for subsequent practice. We evaluate PolyPresentation through a rubric-based comparison with four baseline systems on 20 academic presentation rehearsals, and additionally assess its alignment with human ratings. Results suggest that PolyPresentation provides more actionable, context-aware, and practice-oriented support for improving presentations. The demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/MmWj9O_PJxw.

AI.tldr: PolyPresentation is a multimodal AI platform that links slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsals, Q&A, and feedback into a unified iterative loop, using slide-grounded evidence to help presenters diagnose issues and plan next practices; it outperforms four baselines and aligns with human ratings.
AI.motivation: Effective presentations require repeated practice coordinating content, delivery, visuals, and audience interaction. Existing AI rehearsal tools treat presentations as single-run performances, offering limited feedback tied to slides and weak guidance for planning the next practice iteration.
AI.method: A multimodal AI platform organizing slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsal, audience Q&A, and feedback into a unified practice loop, using slide-grounded evidence for diagnosis and next-practice preparation.
AI.result: In a rubric-based comparison with four baseline systems across 20 academic presentation rehearsals, PolyPresentation provided more actionable, context-aware, and practice-oriented support, and its assessments aligned well with human ratings.
AI.conclusion: PolyPresentation advances AI-assisted rehearsal by treating presentation practice as an iterative, slide-aware loop, demonstrating improved actionable and context-aware feedback that better supports presenters in improving over successive practices.

title: RAGSieve: Self-Referenced Local Contrast for Knowledge-Poison Detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation treats an external corpus as inference evidence, allowing injected documents to promote attacker-chosen claims. Existing detectors depend on trusted references, specific attack artifacts, or global thresholds sensitive to corpus topology. We present RAGSieve, a self-referenced detection framework that constructs its reference from the inspected system. RAGSieve-Query (RSQ) performs query-local contrast, scoring top-five candidates against ranks 6-20 of the same retrieval to detect answer-anchor concentration and carrier transitions. RAGSieve-Graph (RSG) performs corpus-local contrast, comparing each document's semantically similar but lexically distinct neighbors with its local baseline to detect coordinated density before queries arrive. Across three QA datasets and six poisoning constructions, RSQ achieves 95.2% AUROC and detects 82.2% of poison at 5% clean-document removal, versus 81.1%/52.5% for GMTP. RSG achieves 93.3%/79.8%, versus 79.4%/37.6% for CleanBase. Joint deployment reduces attack success from 67.4% to 14.0% while retaining 41.3% F1 on unpoisoned retrieval, demonstrating practical protection at both corpus ingestion and query time without poison labels or trusted corpora. Source code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/RAGSieve.

AI.tldr: RAGSieve is a self-referenced framework that detects poisoning attacks in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) without trusted corpora or poison labels. It combines query-time detection (RAGSieve-Query) and corpus-time detection (RAGSieve-Graph), reducing attack success from 67.4% to 14.0% while retaining 41.3% F1 on clean retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG poisoning detectors rely on trusted references, specific attack artifacts, or global thresholds that are sensitive to corpus topology. RAGSieve aims to remove these dependencies by constructing its reference directly from the inspected system itself, enabling detection both at query time and corpus ingestion time without poison labels or trusted corpora.
AI.method: RAGSieve comprises two self-referenced components. RAGSieve-Query (RSQ) performs query-local contrast by scoring top-5 retrieval candidates against ranks 6-20 of the same retrieval to detect answer-anchor concentration and carrier transitions. RAGSieve-Graph (RSG) performs corpus-local contrast by comparing each document's semantically similar but lexically distinct neighbors with its local baseline to detect coordinated density before queries arrive.
AI.result: Across three QA datasets and six poisoning constructions, RSQ achieves 95.2% AUROC and detects 82.2% of poison at 5% clean-document removal, versus 81.1%/52.5% for GMTP. RSG achieves 93.3%/79.8%, versus 79.4%/37.6% for CleanBase. Joint deployment reduces attack success rate from 67.4% to 14.0% while retaining 41.3% F1 on unpoisoned retrieval.
AI.conclusion: RAGSieve demonstrates practical protection against RAG poisoning at both corpus ingestion and query time, without requiring poison labels or trusted corpora, as shown by its substantial improvements over GMTP and CleanBase baselines and its effectiveness in joint deployment.

title: CAS: A Causal Attribution Score for Local and Global Explainable Artificial Intelligence
summary: Predictive explanation methods attribute a model output; they do not, by themselves, attribute an intervention effect on the real-world outcome. We introduce the Causal Attribution Score (CAS), a compact score architecture for causal explanation. CAS starts from an identified interventional coalition game, allocates the joint intervention contrast with causal Shapley contributions, and converts those raw outcome-scale effects into Local CAS, Signed Local CAS, and two complementary Global CAS summaries. The innovation is not a new Shapley formula, but a local-to-global causal reporting layer with an explicit intervention target. In the known-truth benchmark, eight repeated primary-interaction simulations (n = 2,200 each, three actions) gave mean Local CAS MAE of 0.107 for coalition-aware CAS, compared with 0.173 for one-at-a-time normalisation and 0.213 for a global normalised absolute ATE vector. The paired advantage over one-at-a-time normalisation increased from -0.003 under additivity to 0.091 under strong interactions. On both empirical DoubleML datasets, 401(k) eligibility/net financial assets (n = 9,915) and Pennsylvania reemployment bonus/unemployment duration (n = 5,099), predictive SHAP/TreeSHAP rankings differed materially from Feature-CAS rankings of treatment-effect modifiers. In Pennsylvania, dep1 (exactly one dependent) moved from predictive global rank 13 to Feature-CAS rank 2 and was the leading local Feature-CAS modifier. These results isolate the added value of separating what predicts the outcome from what explains heterogeneity in an estimated causal effect.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Causal Attribution Score (CAS), a causal explanation architecture that attributes intervention effects (not just model outputs) using causal Shapley contributions, with local-to-global reporting layers. Benchmarks show CAS outperforms one-at-a-time and ATE-based normalisations, and empirical DoubleML studies reveal causal modifiers differ substantially from predictive SHAP rankings.
AI.motivation: Predictive explanation methods attribute a model's output but fail to attribute the intervention effect on the real-world outcome. The paper seeks to separate "what predicts the outcome" from "what explains heterogeneity in an estimated causal effect," addressing the gap between predictive feature importance and causal treatment-effect modification.
AI.method: CAS starts from an identified interventional coalition game, allocates the joint intervention contrast using causal Shapley contributions, and converts raw outcome-scale effects into Local CAS, Signed Local CAS, and two complementary Global CAS summaries. The key addition is a local-to-global causal reporting layer with an explicit intervention target (not a new Shapley formula). Evaluation uses: (1) known-truth benchmark with eight repeated primary-interaction simulations (n=2,200 each, three actions), comparing coalition-aware CAS against one-at-a-time normalisation and a global normalised absolute ATE vector; and (2) two empirical DoubleML datasets — 401(k) eligibility/net financial assets (n=9,915) and Pennsylvania reemployment bonus/unemployment duration (n=5,099) — comparing predictive SHAP/TreeSHAP rankings against Feature-CAS rankings.
AI.result: In the benchmark, mean Local CAS MAE was 0.107 for coalition-aware CAS, versus 0.173 for one-at-a-time normalisation and 0.213 for the global normalised absolute ATE vector. The paired advantage over one-at-a-time normalisation rose from -0.003 under additivity to 0.091 under strong interactions. On empirical data, predictive SHAP/TreeSHAP rankings differed materially from Feature-CAS rankings of treatment-effect modifiers; in Pennsylvania, dep1 (exactly one dependent) moved from predictive global rank 13 to Feature-CAS rank 2 and was the leading local Feature-CAS modifier.
AI.conclusion: The results isolate the added value of separating outcome prediction from causal-effect heterogeneity explanation, showing CAS better recovers treatment-effect modifiers (particularly under interactions) than predictive or ATE-based normalisation approaches, and that predictive rankings should not be conflated with causal treatment-effect modifier rankings.

title: From Refuse to Richness: Rubric Rewards for Long-Form Hallucination Reinforcement Learning
summary: Rewards that penalize unsupported claims can improve grounding in long-form generation, but they can also teach models to answer less. We study this refusal-to-richness trade-off in long-form hallucination RL. Instead of using global richness proxies such as length, claim count, detail, or pairwise relevance, we represent each question with a key-point rubric that specifies the required and optional information a useful answer should cover. These rubrics define coverage directly and are used both for evaluation and as reward signals. Across grounding-only, proxy-based, rubric-only, and combined rewards, we find a stable trade-off: strict grounding rewards improve support but suppress coverage, while unconstrained rubric rewards improve coverage but weaken grounding. A soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance gives the best balance in our experiments, improving in-distribution support while transferring better to out-of-distribution checklist tasks than either grounding-only or rubric-only rewards.

AI.tldr: Strict grounding penalties reduce unsupported claims but cause models to answer less; replacing global richness proxies with per-question key-point rubrics reveals a stable refusal-to-richness trade-off, and a soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance rewards best balances support and coverage.
AI.motivation: Rewards that penalize unsupported claims improve grounding in long-form generation but can teach models to answer less (refusal). The authors aim to study and mitigate this refusal-to-richness trade-off in long-form hallucination reinforcement learning, moving beyond coarse/global richness proxies (length, claim count, detail, pairwise relevance).
AI.method: Represent each question with a key-point rubric specifying required and optional information a useful answer should cover. These rubrics define coverage directly and serve both as evaluation metrics and reward signals. Compare grounding-only, proxy-based, rubric-only, and combined rewards under RL.
AI.result: A stable trade-off emerges: strict grounding rewards improve support but suppress coverage, while unconstrained rubric rewards improve coverage but weaken grounding. A soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance yields the best balance, improving in-distribution support and transferring better to out-of-distribution checklist tasks than grounding-only or rubric-only rewards.
AI.conclusion: Direct coverage via key-point rubrics, combined softly with grounding and relevance rewards, best balances the refusal-to-richness trade-off, offering better grounding without sacrificing answer richness, including better out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Prof-K: Probabilistic One-Pass Filtering for Efficient Top-k Selection
summary: Top-k selection is a fundamental computational primitive with applications spanning databases, information retrieval, signal processing, and modern machine learning workloads, including sparse activations and attention pruning. As data sizes grow, existing approaches become inefficient: exact methods incur high memory and compute overhead, while approximate methods often rely on brittle heuristics that degrade under adversarial or heavy-tailed inputs. In this paper, we introduce Prof-K, a fast, scalable, and distribution-agnostic top-k algorithm with probabilistic correctness guarantees. Prof-K performs a single-pass filtering procedure: a small random sample estimates an adaptive threshold, the N input elements are streamed once into a compact buffer, and an exact top-k routine on this buffer recovers the true top-k elements with probability at least 1 - $ε$, where $ε$ > 0 is user specified. We derive high-probability guarantees for correctness and buffer size, together with an approximately optimal sample size that minimizes overhead as a function of N and k. Empirically, Prof-K achieves 1.5x-10x speedups over the highly optimized PyTorch topk and recent RadiK implementations, with the largest gains in the large-scale, small-to-moderate-k regime where prior methods struggle most. Unlike previous approaches, these guarantees hold independently of the input distribution, ensuring robustness to adversarial settings. By relaxing the recall target (e.g., recovering 95% of the true top-k values), Prof-K additionally provides a principled accuracy-speed trade-off. We further demonstrate its impact on training BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), where top-k selection constitutes a significant portion of the training cost.

AI.tldr: Prof-K is a single-pass, distribution-agnostic top-k selection algorithm that uses a small random sample to estimate an adaptive threshold, streams data into a compact buffer, and recovers the true top-k elements with a probabilistic correctness guarantee (probability ≥ 1-ε), achieving 1.5x-10x speedups over PyTorch topk and RadiK while supporting a principled accuracy-speed trade-off.
AI.motivation: Top-k selection is fundamental across databases, IR, signal processing, and ML workloads (e.g., sparse activations, attention pruning). Exact methods are too costly in memory/compute at scale, while approximate methods rely on brittle heuristics that fail under adversarial or heavy-tailed inputs. There is a need for a fast, scalable, distribution-agnostic algorithm with formal correctness guarantees.
AI.method: Prof-K performs a single-pass filtering procedure: (1) draw a small random sample to estimate an adaptive threshold; (2) stream all N input elements once into a compact buffer based on that threshold; (3) run an exact top-k routine on the small buffer to recover the true top-k. It derives high-probability bounds on correctness and buffer size, and computes an approximately optimal sample size minimizing overhead as a function of N and k. It also supports relaxing the recall target (e.g., 95% of true top-k) for a tunable accuracy-speed trade-off.
AI.result: Prof-K achieves 1.5x-10x speedups over highly optimized PyTorch topk and recent RadiK implementations, with the largest gains in the large-scale, small-to-moderate-k regime where prior methods struggle most. Its guarantees hold independently of the input distribution, ensuring robustness to adversarial settings. It is demonstrated to reduce cost in training BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders, where top-k selection is a significant cost component.
AI.conclusion: Prof-K provides a fast, scalable, distribution-agnostic top-k algorithm with probabilistic correctness guarantees and a principled accuracy-speed trade-off, outperforming exact and recent approximate baselines while remaining robust to adversarial inputs and applicable to real-world ML training workloads such as Sparse Autoencoders.

title: Vero: Can AI Agents Build Formally Verified Software Repositories?
summary: AI agents are increasingly used for programming, but do not provide any guarantee on the correctness of generated code. Verified code generation, in which an agent produces both an implementation and a machine-checked proof of its specification, offers a stronger path toward trustworthy AI-generated software. Existing benchmarks in this direction either focus on individual functions or only evaluate proof generation with provided implementations. It is still an open question whether agents can make coherent implementation and proof choices across real multi-module codebases. To bridge this gap, we introduce Vero, the first benchmark to evaluate joint implementation and proof synthesis at the repository level. Vero contains 43 multi-module instances sourced from real-world repositories spanning Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq, and covering diverse domains from cryptographic protocols to distributed systems. Each instance consists of a multi-module Lean 4 repository with predetermined API interfaces, manually curated formal specifications, and reference implementations, supporting both proof-only and code-and-proof evaluation modes. To improve benchmark reliability, Vero also includes an audit mechanism where agents are allowed to formally prove unsatisfiability of provided specification or incorrectness of reference code, which surfaces and corrects latent code and specification errors during curation. We evaluate frontier coding-agent configurations with Lean toolchain access. The strongest agent fully solves only 27 of 43 instances and closes no specifications on the hardest repositories. Vero provides a concrete testbed for measuring progress toward repository-scale verified software synthesis, where current agents still fall short. We release the benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/sunblaze-ucb/vero.

AI.tldr: Vero is the first benchmark for repository-level verified code generation, requiring agents to jointly synthesize both implementations and machine-checked proofs across 43 multi-module Lean 4 repositories. State-of-the-art agents only fully solve 27 of 43 instances, showing significant room for improvement.
AI.motivation: AI agents increasingly generate code but provide no correctness guarantees. Verified code generation—producing both an implementation and a machine-checked proof—offers a path to trustworthy AI software. However, existing benchmarks focus on single functions or only evaluate proof generation given implementations, leaving open whether agents can make coherent implementation and proof choices across real multi-module codebases.
AI.method: The authors introduce Vero, a benchmark of 43 multi-module instances sourced from real-world repositories in Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq, converted into multi-module Lean 4 repositories with predetermined API interfaces, manually curated formal specifications, and reference implementations. Vero supports two evaluation modes: proof-only and code-and-proof (joint synthesis). It includes an audit mechanism allowing agents to formally prove unsatisfiability of a specification or incorrectness of reference code, which surfaces and corrects latent errors during curation. Frontier coding-agent configurations with Lean toolchain access are evaluated on the benchmark.
AI.result: The strongest evaluated agent fully solves only 27 of 43 instances and closes no specifications on the hardest repositories, indicating that current agents fall short of repository-scale verified software synthesis.
AI.conclusion: Vero provides a concrete testbed for measuring progress toward repository-scale verified software synthesis and demonstrates that current state-of-the-art agents still fall short. The authors release the benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation harness publicly.

title: How LLMs Respond to Escalating Delusions: Four Longitudinal Trajectories of Model Behavior
summary: The widespread use of LLMs among psychiatric populations has raised concerns regarding their safety and potential iatrogenic impact in the context of AI psychosis. While growing literature conceptualizes AI psychosis and documents case studies, empirical evidence tracing AI-exacerbated psychotic processes remains scarce. We propose and test a longitudinal qualitative evaluation design, supported by automated metrics, to assess mainstream LLMs' potential to exacerbate psychosis. Fifteen widely used LLMs were prompted across 30 days using the same 30-message script, simulating progression from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation. Four trained evaluators independently rated 449 model-days, assessing (1) recognition stage (from naive engagement to stabilized clinical framing), (2) interpretative confidence, and (3) intervention profile (from education to treatment recommendation). Two computational metrics-entrainment and modality-were devised to increase evaluation reliability. Direct recommendations to disengage from the LLM were flagged and re-coded via adjudication using a strict two-level definition. Across model generations and vendors, we identified four response trajectories: (1) premature medicalization and disengagement (Claude Haiku 4.5); (2) recognition without safeguarding, marked by LLM self-sufficiency in offering help (GPT Instant/Thinking); (3) delayed and unstable recognition, marked by late, non-progressive conceptualization (Claude Opus 3/4/4.1, Claude Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 3.1 Pro); and (4) delusion co-construction through active engagement with delusional content (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4). Our findings indicate that LLMs' potential to exacerbate AI psychosis should be operationalized as a combination of recognition timing, stability, and intervention accuracy and evaluated longitudinally, focusing on temporal dynamics.

AI.tldr: A 30-day longitudinal study of 15 mainstream LLMs using a fixed escalating script found four response trajectories to simulated psychotic ideation, ranging from premature disengagement to active delusion co-construction, and argues LLM safety should be evaluated on recognition timing, stability, and intervention accuracy over time.
AI.motivation: LLMs are widely used by psychiatric populations, raising safety concerns about "AI psychosis," but empirical evidence tracing whether and how AI exacerbates psychotic processes is scarce. The authors seek to fill this gap with a testable, longitudinal evaluation framework rather than relying on conceptual discussion or isolated case studies.
AI.method: Fifteen widely used LLMs were prompted over 30 days with an identical 30-message script simulating progression from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation. Four trained evaluators independently rated 449 model-days on three dimensions: (1) recognition stage, (2) interpretative confidence, and (3) intervention profile. Two computational metrics (entrainment and modality) were devised to boost reliability. Direct LLM recommendations to disengage were flagged and re-coded via adjudication under a strict two-level definition.
AI.result: Four response trajectories were identified across model generations and vendors: (1) premature medicalization and disengagement (Claude Haiku 4.5); (2) recognition without safeguarding, marked by LLM self-sufficiency in offering help (GPT Instant/Thinking); (3) delayed and unstable recognition with late, non-progressive conceptualization (Claude Opus 3/4/4.1, Claude Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 3.1 Pro); and (4) delusion co-construction through active engagement with delusional content (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4).
AI.conclusion: An LLM's potential to exacerbate AI psychosis should be operationalized as a combination of recognition timing, stability, and intervention accuracy, and evaluated longitudinally with a focus on temporal dynamics rather than static, single-turn safety checks.

title: GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval
summary: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express complex and diverse information needs. However, conventional retrievers largely rely on surface-level matching between queries and documents, resulting in a growing gap between how users express their needs and how retrievers interpret them. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval through its own knowledge by explicitly reasoning about user intent and relevance criteria.
