GEM unifies generation and embedding within a single model: it first reasons over the query, then appends an embedding token to encode the enriched context for retrieval. \zhili{Evaluated on reasoning-intensive and instruction-following retrieval tasks, GEM demonstrates the effectiveness of its reasoning-augmented retrieval, outperforming its non-reasoning variant and matching baselines using substantially larger models.} Furthermore, GEM's generative nature allows test-time compute scaling via prompting to further enhance retrieval performance. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GEM.

AI.tldr: GEM is a generative embedding model that performs explicit reasoning over the query before producing an embedding, unifying generation and embedding in one model to close the gap between user-expressed information needs and surface-level matching retrievers.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs let users articulate complex, diverse information needs, but conventional retrievers rely on surface-level query-document matching. This creates a growing mismatch between how users express needs and how retrievers interpret them.
AI.method: GEM unifies generation and embedding in a single model: it first reasons over the query to infer user intent and relevance criteria, then appends a special embedding token that encodes the enriched context for retrieval. Its generative nature also enables test-time compute scaling via prompting to further boost retrieval.
AI.result: On reasoning-intensive and instruction-following retrieval tasks, GEM outperforms its non-reasoning variant and matches baselines that use substantially larger models. Test-time compute scaling via prompting further enhances retrieval performance.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting retrieval with explicit model reasoning is effective: a single unified generative embedding model narrows the expression-interpretation gap and achieves strong results even against much larger baselines, with additional gains available through test-time prompting.

title: Trie Automata for Constrained Decoding over Large Finite Sets
summary: Large language models increasingly need to generate structured outputs that conform to predefined schemas, with one common constraint being selection from a finite set of valid strings. Current constrained decoding systems handle this through general-purpose grammar compilation, which becomes prohibitively slow as the number of valid values grows into the thousands, a cardinality wall. We introduce the trie automaton, a specialized mechanism that exploits finite-set structure (shared prefixes, bounded depth, known cardinality) via Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching to precompute per-node token masks. The trie achieves 7X faster per-step valid-token computation (0.65 us vs. 5.8 us) compared to XGrammar, one of the primary backends in vLLM and SGLang, and 2--6.5X faster compilation at K >= 300. Because precomputed masks enable a stateless serving path that bypasses the guided decoding pipeline, this advantage compounds in batch serving: end-to-end vLLM throughput reaches 219 req/s vs. XGrammar's 7.5 req/s at batch size 256 (29X). The 29X combines the algorithmic speedup with integration-path savings that only precomputed masks can unlock. Across seven tokenizer families (32K--262K vocabulary), the trie maintains sub-100ms compilation up to K = 10,000 and flat per-step cost regardless of set size, while guaranteeing 100% output validity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a trie automaton using Aho-Corasick matching to precompute per-node token masks for constrained decoding over large finite string sets, overcoming the "cardinality wall" that makes grammar-based systems slow at thousands of valid values.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly must generate outputs restricted to a finite set of valid strings. Existing constrained decoding systems rely on general-purpose grammar compilation, whose cost becomes prohibitively slow as the number of valid values grows into the thousands, creating a cardinality wall that limits scalability for practical selection constraints.
AI.method: Introduces a specialized trie automaton that exploits finite-set structure (shared prefixes, bounded depth, known cardinality) using Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching to precompute per-node token masks. These precomputed masks enable a stateless serving path that bypasses the guided decoding pipeline during batch inference.
AI.result: The trie achieves 7X faster per-step valid-token computation (0.65 us vs. 5.8 us) and 2-6.5X faster compilation at K >= 300 compared to XGrammar. End-to-end vLLM throughput reaches 219 req/s vs. XGrammar's 7.5 req/s at batch size 256 (29X). Across seven tokenizer families (32K-262K vocab), compilation stays sub-100ms up to K = 10,000 with flat per-step cost, while guaranteeing 100% output validity.
AI.conclusion: A specialized trie automaton with precomputed masks eliminates the cardinality wall, providing fast compilation, flat per-step cost, and a stateless serving path that compounds into large end-to-end throughput gains (29X) over grammar-based systems like XGrammar.

title: SDAM: Structure-Difference-Aware Memory Evolution for Complex Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL aims to convert natural language questions into executable SQL queries. While memory-based agent system improves complex SQL generation, existing memory design neglect historical experience and suffer from weak structure analysis, shallow semantic understanding, and poor schema alignment. To address these challenges, we propose SDAM. Specifically, SDAM identifies potential errors via a structure-difference aware reasoning tree, extracts deep semantic rules through contradiction-aware reflection, and enhances structural consistency using a schema-grounded memory evolution mechanism to bind memory with database schemas. We integrate SDAM into a Text-to-SQL framework named SDAM-SQL. Experiment shows that SDAM-SQL achieves 2.0 and 0.4 improvement on BIRD-dev and Spider-test compared with mainstream Text-to-SQL methods, showing the effectiveness of SDAM-SQL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SDAM, a memory-based method that improves Text-to-SQL by addressing weak historical memory design through structure-difference error detection, contradiction-aware semantic rule extraction, and schema-grounded memory evolution. Integrated into SDAM-SQL, it achieves 2.0 and 0.4 gains on BIRD-dev and Spider-test over mainstream methods.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-based Text-to-SQL agent systems improve complex SQL generation but their memory design neglects historical experience and suffers from three weaknesses: weak structure analysis, shallow semantic understanding, and poor schema alignment. These limitations motivate the design of a more effective memory mechanism.
AI.method: SDAM uses three components: (1) a structure-difference aware reasoning tree to identify potential errors; (2) contradiction-aware reflection to extract deep semantic rules; and (3) a schema-grounded memory evolution mechanism that binds memory to database schemas to enhance structural consistency. SDAM is integrated into a Text-to-SQL framework called SDAM-SQL.
AI.result: SDAM-SQL achieves improvements of 2.0 on the BIRD-dev benchmark and 0.4 on the Spider-test benchmark compared with mainstream Text-to-SQL methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SDAM method effectively addresses the shortcomings of existing memory-based Text-to-SQL agents, and the SDAM-SQL framework demonstrates measurable performance gains on standard benchmarks, validating the value of schema-grounded, structurally and semantically aware memory evolution.

title: Represent, Then Generate: Multimodal-Conditioned Time-Series Generation under Irregular Missingness
summary: Continuous physiological time series underpin modern clinical monitoring, yet many of the most informative signals are invasive, expensive, or simply unavailable for a given patient. Conditional generation offers a remedy: an absent signal can be synthesized from co-recorded signals and routine clinical variables. Existing generators, however, are built around a single conditioning modality and degrade when forced to handle the heterogeneous, irregularly missing mix of time-variant signals and static covariates seen in practice. We propose ReCoGen (Represent Conditions, then Generate), a two-stage framework that decouples multimodal condition representation from target generation. Stage I trains one masked autoencoder per modality, distilling each time-variant condition into a compact and missingness-tolerant token sequence. Stage II trains a flow-matching generator that fuses these tokens with static conditions to synthesize the target signal. Across three physiological benchmarks, including continuous glucose monitoring on AI-READI and arterial blood pressure generation on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, ReCoGen attains the best downstream utility on all sixteen (dataset, task, metric) settings, surpassing six representative conditional generators; on thirteen of them its utility also reaches or exceeds the utility measured on the real signal, a reference we read as an approximate anchor rather than a ceiling. Ablations trace the gains to the conditioning path: learnable cross-attention over the frozen per-modality encoders, and a dual token-plus-AdaLN route for the static conditions. ReCoGen thus turns routinely collected signals into informative surrogates for invasive or unavailable ones, a step toward less invasive, lower-cost continuous clinical monitoring.

AI.tldr: ReCoGen is a two-stage conditional generation framework that synthesizes missing physiological signals from heterogeneous, irregularly missing multimodal conditions (time-series plus static covariates), achieving state-of-the-art downstream utility across 16 dataset/task/metric settings.
AI.motivation: Many clinically informative physiological signals are invasive, expensive, or unavailable for a given patient. Conditional generation could synthesize absent signals from co-recorded signals and routine clinical variables, but existing generators are built around a single conditioning modality and fail when handling the heterogeneous, irregularly missing mix of time-variant signals and static covariates encountered in practice.
AI.method: ReCoGen is a two-stage framework that decouples multimodal condition representation from target generation. Stage I trains one masked autoencoder per modality to distill each time-variant condition into a compact, missingness-tolerant token sequence. Stage II trains a flow-matching generator that fuses these tokens (via learnable cross-attention over frozen per-modality encoders) with static conditions (via a dual token-plus-AdaLN route) to synthesize the target signal.
AI.result: Across three physiological benchmarks—continuous glucose monitoring on AI-READI and arterial blood pressure generation on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV—ReCoGen attains the best downstream utility on all sixteen (dataset, task, metric) settings, surpassing six representative conditional generators. On thirteen of the sixteen settings, its utility also reaches or exceeds the utility measured on the real signal (treated as an approximate anchor rather than a ceiling). Ablations attribute the gains to learnable cross-attention over frozen per-modality encoders and the dual token-plus-AdaLN route for static conditions.
AI.conclusion: ReCoGen turns routinely collected signals into informative surrogates for invasive or unavailable ones, representing a step toward less invasive, lower-cost continuous clinical monitoring.

title: Slow and Steady: Preventing MEV with Verifiable Delays
comment: A revised version is accepted for publication at the 10th International Workshop on Cryptocurrencies and Blockchain Technology (CBT 2026)
summary: Our work presents a defense mechanism against Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) opportunities in distributed ledgers. The mechanism relies on the idea of enforcing a verifiable delay when generating transactions, such that a block creator cannot react to the appearance of a MEV opportunity without breaking liveness. We present positive results both in the Byzantine setting and in a game theoretic model of rational participants. We additionally present negative bounds that outline the limitations of this line of defense. Finally, we explore real-world implementation details of verifiable delays and show that, based on historical MEV data, our mechanism could realistically help prevent most existing MEV threats.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a defense against Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) in distributed ledgers by enforcing a verifiable delay on transaction generation, preventing block creators from reacting to MEV opportunities without sacrificing liveness. It provides positive results in both Byzantine and game-theoretic rational settings, establishes negative bounds, and analyzes practical implementations using historical MEV data.
AI.motivation: MEV creates fairness and security issues in distributed ledgers by allowing block creators to exploit and reorder transactions for profit. Existing defenses are limited, motivating a mechanism that prevents exploitation while preserving system liveness.
AI.method: The authors design a mechanism that enforces a verifiable delay when generating transactions. This delay prevents a block creator from reacting to newly appeared MEV opportunities without breaking liveness. Results are analyzed both in a Byzantine adversarial setting and in a game-theoretic model of rational participants, with negative bounds and real-world implementation considerations based on historical MEV data.
AI.result: The mechanism achieves positive security guarantees in both Byzantine and rational (game-theoretic) settings. Negative bounds identify theoretical limits of the delay-based defense. Analysis of historical MEV data suggests the mechanism could realistically prevent most existing MEV threats.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing verifiable delays on transaction generation is a practically viable defense against MEV: it offers provable guarantees against Byzantine and rational attackers and, based on real data, could prevent most current MEV threats despite some inherent limitations.

title: QuoteBench: How Matched Scores Can Hide Command-Path Failures
summary: LLM coding agents issue Bash commands through interfaces that may serialize, wrap, and reparse model output. Matched execution scores alone cannot distinguish command-generation errors from failures introduced after generation. QuoteBench measures this boundary with exact final-state validation on 56 one-shot tasks from 14 incident-derived families, crossing the generation contract with the execution transport around one deliberately unescaped added parser. Escaping at the interpolation point reproduces each replayed reply's raw-path outcome, so any recovery under a disclosed boundary must come from the model changing its generation. Across eight same-window configurations, replaying the same reply through the added parser lowers success by 55.4 to 73.2 percentage points; disclosure recovers 30.4 to 60.7 points for six configurations, and zero or slightly negative for the other two. Raw generation is nearly saturated at the frontier; boundary adaptation is what still separates models. GPT-5.6-sol's matched gap of -3.6 points hides -64.3 points of damage and +60.7 points of compensation. The deployment configuration reorders models: one reversal among 26 comparable pairs is unambiguous and four more sit on single-task margins. Evaluations of command-issuing agents should report the model configuration, generation contract, execution path, operating point, and final-state validator rather than treat a matched score as an intrinsic model property.

AI.tldr: QuoteBench isolates errors introduced by the execution transport (serialization/parsing of model-generated Bash commands) from errors in the model's own generation, using exact final-state validation on 56 one-shot tasks. Replaying replies through an added unescaped parser cuts success by 55.4–73.2 points; disclosing the boundary recovers 30.4–60.7 points for six of eight configs (zero/negative for two). A matched score can hide large damage plus compensatory recovery, so scores should be reported with full configuration details rather than treated as intrinsic model properties.
AI.motivation: Matched execution scores alone cannot distinguish command-generation errors from failures introduced after generation (during output serialization, wrapping, and reparsing). The paper seeks to measure this boundary and show how a benign transport layer can silently destroy or distort model performance.
AI.method: QuoteBench consists of 56 one-shot tasks across 14 incident-derived families. It deliberately adds one unescaped parser at the interpolation point and crosses two dimensions: the generation contract (raw vs. boundary-disclosed) and the execution transport. For each reply, escaping at the interpolation point reproduces the raw-path outcome, isolating transport-induced failures. Eight same-window configurations are evaluated; under a disclosed boundary, any recovery must come from the model changing its generation.
AI.result: Replaying the same reply through the added parser lowers success by 55.4 to 73.2 percentage points across eight configurations. Disclosure recovers 30.4 to 60.7 points in six configurations and zero or slightly negative in the other two. Raw generation is nearly saturated at the model frontier; boundary adaptation is what separates models. GPT-5.6-sol shows a matched gap of -3.6 points that hides -64.3 points of transport damage and +60.7 points of compensation. Deployment configuration reorders models: one reversal among 26 comparable pairs is unambiguous and four more sit on single-task margins.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations of command-issuing agents should report the model configuration, generation contract, execution path, operating point, and final-state validator, rather than treating a matched score as an intrinsic model property.

title: Tracing Methamphetamine abuse in under-treatment drivers: How biomechanical and oculomotor features help detect at-risk drivers?
summary: While the detrimental impacts of driving under the influence of stimulants such as methamphetamine are well-documented, the driving performance of individuals currently under-treatment has received considerably less attention. This study compared the behavior of individuals with a history of stimulant abuse (across two distinct treatment phases) with a control group of healthy drivers using a driving simulator. Oculomotor and biomechanical data were continuously collected via an eye-tracker and a Kinect sensor, respectively. These parameters were utilized to train a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification model designed to detect high-risk behavioral patterns in drivers undergoing methamphetamine rehabilitation. Through the evaluation of various feature combinations and neighborhood configurations, the optimized model successfully discriminated between normal drivers and those with a history of abuse with an accuracy of 90%. Detecting at-risk drivers through technologies embedded in Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) by continuously monitoring physiological and behavioral parameters, facilitates a proactive safety strategy. Issuing real-time alerts to the driver, passengers, and external monitoring networks can ultimately mitigate the risk of traffic collisions.

AI.tldr: Using a driving simulator with eye-tracking and Kinect sensors, this study trained a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) model to detect high-risk driving behaviors in individuals with stimulant (methamphetamine) abuse history during treatment, achieving 90% accuracy in distinguishing them from healthy controls. The goal is real-time detection via ADAS to prevent collisions.
AI.motivation: While methamphetamine-impaired driving is well-documented, the driving performance of individuals currently in treatment/rehabilitation for stimulant abuse is under-studied. There is a need to identify at-risk behavioral patterns in this population to enable proactive road-safety interventions.
AI.method: A comparative driving-simulator study was conducted across three groups: individuals with stimulant abuse history in two distinct treatment phases and a healthy control group. Oculomotor data (eye-tracker) and biomechanical data (Kinect) were continuously collected. These parameters were used to train a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier; multiple feature combinations and neighborhood configurations were evaluated to optimize performance.
AI.result: The optimized KNN model successfully discriminated between normal drivers and those with a history of stimulant abuse, achieving a classification accuracy of 90%.
AI.conclusion: Detecting at-risk drivers via technologies embedded in Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) through continuous monitoring of physiological and behavioral parameters enables a proactive safety strategy. Real-time alerts to drivers, passengers, and external monitoring networks could help mitigate traffic-collision risk.

title: Reasoning Jury: Multi-Model Consensus for Evaluating Reasoning Traces
summary: Improving reasoning LLMs requires the ability to judge the quality of long reasoning traces for effective reasoning data curation, strong training signals during reinforcement learning, and an in-depth understanding of reasoning behaviors during model performance evaluation. Additionally, surfacing reasoning mistakes that the model makes would enable improving the model's performance at runtime through providing feedback. Due to the difficulty of this complex task on long reasoning traces, single-model judges (even frontier models) do not do well at identifying reasoning defects. Additionally, leveraging frontier models during online training of reasoning LLMs is generally prohibited due to guardrails in terms of use. In this work, we introduce Reasoning Jury, a system that replaces the single judge with a jury of LLMs and a moderated consensus mechanism, to improve the fidelity of judgments for identifying reasoning defects. In reasoning jury, defects of a reasoning trace and their severity are surfaced through a deliberation where a moderator conducts a discussion amongst the jury where the jurors critique each other's judgments and get to modify their initial votes. The moderator derives a consensus through deliberation amongst jurors or consolidation of judgements. We show that Reasoning Jury with a jury of open-weight models (e.g., gpt-oss-120b) is able to significantly outperform frontier models (opus-4.6, sonnet-4.6, and gemini-3.1-pro) at correctly identifying reasoning defects. Besides accuracy performance improvements, the aggregated cost of the jury (initial verdicts, deliberations, consolidation, etc.) is a fraction (8 to 15%) of the cost of running frontier models in LLM-as-a-judge setup. We also show how these judgements can be leveraged to understand failure modes of reasoning LLMs on benchmarks, which allows much deeper understanding of a model's performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Reasoning Jury, a multi-LLM jury system with a moderated consensus mechanism that surpasses single frontier-model judges at identifying defects in long reasoning traces, at a fraction of the cost.
AI.motivation: Judging the quality of long reasoning traces is critical for reasoning data curation, providing training signals in RL, evaluating reasoning behavior, and surfacing runtime mistakes for feedback. Single-model judges (even frontier models) perform poorly at this task, and using frontier models during online training is often prohibited by usage guardrails.
AI.method: Reasoning Jury replaces a single judge with a jury of open-weight LLMs (e.g., gpt-oss-120b) and a moderated consensus mechanism. A moderator conducts deliberation among jurors, who critique each other's judgments and may revise their initial votes; the moderator then derives a consensus through deliberation or consolidation of judgments to surface defects and their severity.
AI.result: Reasoning Jury with open-weight models significantly outperforms frontier models (opus-4.6, sonnet-4.6, gemini-3.1-pro) at correctly identifying reasoning defects, while costing only 8-15% of the frontier LLM-as-a-judge setup. The judgments also enable deeper understanding of failure modes of reasoning LLMs on benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A moderated jury of open-weight LLMs provides higher-fidelity, lower-cost judgments of reasoning trace quality than single frontier-model judges, and supports richer analysis of model failure modes.

title: Mimicry without understanding: the origins of decision bias in large language models
summary: Large Language models (LLMs) were found to be susceptible to a host of social, affective, and cognitive biases. We examined two mechanisms through which such biases can be generated even when human preferences (in the training data) are not biased or when they are correctly categorized as being biased. The first is faulty mimicry of preferences based on human behavior: this involves LLMs inferring human preferences even when behaviors are logically unrelated to preferences. The second is mimicry of explicitly biased human behaviors. In four studies focusing on economic biases, we find that ChatGPT-4o and Qwen exhibited social proof biases even when prompted with reports of human behaviors that were clearly non-indicative of individuals' actual preferences. LLMs also displayed loss aversion when it was explicitly described as a bias. Indeed, when prompted with detailed scientific reports, the extent of the bias (i.e., loss aversion) in the scientific report predicted LLMs' own subsequent bias. Scientific papers of biases can thus become self-fulfilling prophecies, at least when it comes to LLMs' responses. The current study goes beyond fleshing out LLM biases and sheds light on the underlying component processes.

AI.tldr: The study demonstrates that LLMs can acquire and exhibit social, affective, and cognitive biases through two mimicry mechanisms—faulty inference of preferences from unrelated behaviors, and direct mimicry of explicitly described biased behaviors—even when the training data or the descriptions flag those behaviors as biased. Notably, reading scientific reports about a bias (e.g., loss aversion) causes LLMs to reproduce that bias proportionally, making scientific findings self-fulfilling prophecies in LLM responses.
AI.motivation: Prior work establishes that LLMs are susceptible to various biases, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. The authors aim to go beyond merely documenting biases by testing whether LLMs generate biases even when human preferences in training data are unbiased or correctly labeled as biased, and to illuminate the component processes that produce such biases.
AI.method: Four studies focused on economic biases using ChatGPT-4o and Qwen. The two mechanisms tested were: (1) faulty mimicry of preferences—inferring human preferences from behaviors logically unrelated to preferences (social proof), and (2) mimicry of explicitly biased human behaviors (loss aversion described as a bias). Detailed scientific reports were used as prompts, and the extent of bias stated in the reports was compared against the LLMs' subsequent biased outputs.
AI.result: Both ChatGPT-4o and Qwen exhibited social proof biases even when prompted with human behaviors that were clearly non-indicative of actual preferences. They also displayed loss aversion when it was explicitly described and labeled as a bias. The magnitude of loss aversion stated in detailed scientific reports predicted the LLMs' own subsequent bias, indicating that scientific descriptions of biases become self-fulfilling prophecies.
AI.conclusion: LLM biases can arise not only from biased training data but also from faulty mimicry of preference-indicative behaviors and from mimicry of explicitly labeled biased behaviors. Scientific papers documenting biases can causally induce those same biases in LLM responses, shedding light on the underlying component processes rather than merely cataloging bias prevalence.

title: Predicting When Random Low-Dimensional Reparameterizations Train Neural Networks
summary: Neural networks can often be trained or fine-tuned through random low-dimensional reparameterization, where a small latent vector is mapped into a full parameter update by a frozen random map. This raises a practical question: how large must the latent search space be to reach a low-loss region? We first express the known accessibility transition in an equivalent conic form, centered for compact convex targets at the statistical dimension of the polar cone. Our main theoretical contribution is an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula that predicts the random-slice residual from both the curvature spectrum and the reference-to-solution displacement profile. It yields a self-consistent isotropic-orientation predictor and, in a conservative radius-only specialization, recovers the earlier Gaussian-width quadratic bound. Building on this analysis, we introduce Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN), which instantiate the predicted latent dimension using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps. These constructions avoid the O(dP) storage of dense random maps and reduce optimizer-state memory from O(P) to O(d). We also develop matrix-free curvature approximations and sweep-free dimension selection. Across controlled quadratic and neural-curvature experiments, the orientation-resolved predictor closely tracks measured transition locations and outperforms orientation-agnostic approximations when displacement direction matters. End-to-end experiments further show sharp, protocol-dependent training transitions across image and language models.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large a random low-dimensional latent space must be for reparameterized neural network training to reach low-loss regions, derives a new orientation-resolved quadratic formula for the required dimension, and introduces Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN) that implement this efficiently with structured maps and memory savings.
AI.motivation: Neural networks can be trained through random low-dimensional reparameterization, but the practical minimum latent dimension needed to access low-loss regions is unknown. Efficiently predicting this dimension matters because dense random maps cost O(dP) storage and optimizer-state memory scales as O(P), which is expensive for large models.
AI.method: The authors reformulate the known accessibility transition in an equivalent conic form, centered for compact convex targets at the statistical dimension of the polar cone. Their main contribution is an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula predicting the random-slice residual from the curvature spectrum and the reference-to-solution displacement profile, yielding a self-consistent isotropic-orientation predictor and recovering the earlier Gaussian-width quadratic bound in a conservative radius-only specialization. They build Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN) using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps, plus matrix-free curvature approximations and sweep-free dimension selection.
AI.result: Across controlled quadratic and neural-curvature experiments, the orientation-resolved predictor closely tracks measured transition locations and outperforms orientation-agnostic approximations when displacement direction matters. End-to-end experiments show sharp, protocol-dependent training transitions across image and language models.
AI.conclusion: The orientation-resolved quadratic master formula accurately predicts the latent dimension at which random low-dimensional reparameterization reaches low-loss regions, and RaMaN provides a practical memory-efficient implementation. Using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps avoids dense-map storage and reduces optimizer-state memory from O(P) to O(d).

title: VR-Themis: A Scalable Framework for Virtual Reality Application Clone Detection
comment: 25 pages, 14 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 29th International Symposium on Research in Attacks, Intrusions and Defenses (RAID 2026)
summary: Repackaging of mobile applications (aka app cloning) not only threatens the security and privacy of mobile users but also infringes upon the copyright of the original app developers. However, existing detection methods that primarily focus on mobile platforms (such as Android) fail to capture the essential features of virtual reality (VR). Consequently, they are inadequate for effectively detecting cloned VR apps, which have often been targeted by illegal users in the VR market. Considering the unique features of VR apps, this paper proposes a two-stage app clone detection framework, namely VR-Themis, based on \emph{Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour} (HOB). Firstly, VR-Themis exploits the coarse-grained stage to cluster apps based on their retrievable statistical features, making this tool scalable to large-scale VR app datasets. Then, in the fine-grained stage, VR-Themis performs in-depth analysis of the suspicious apps (identified in the first stage) by calculating similarity using our defined \emph{HOB metrics}. Our extensive experiments indicate that VR-Themis successfully detects 307 suspected clone apps from the collected 4,277 VR apps without false positives, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability.

AI.tldr: VR-Themis is a two-stage framework that detects cloned (repackaged) VR apps using Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour (HOB) metrics, finding 307 suspected clones among 4,277 VR apps with no false positives.
AI.motivation: App repackaging threatens user security/privacy and developers' copyright. Existing clone-detection methods target mobile platforms like Android and fail to capture VR-specific essential features, making them inadequate for the VR market where cloning is prevalent.
AI.method: A two-stage framework, VR-Themis, built on Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour (HOB): (1) a coarse-grained stage clusters apps using retrievable statistical features for scalability to large datasets; (2) a fine-grained stage performs in-depth similarity analysis of suspicious apps using HOB metrics.
AI.result: VR-Themis detected 307 suspected clone apps from a collected dataset of 4,277 VR apps without any false positives, demonstrating both effectiveness and scalability.
AI.conclusion: By exploiting VR-specific features through HOB metrics and a scalable two-stage design, VR-Themis effectively and accurately identifies cloned VR apps, addressing a gap left by mobile-focused detection methods.

title: CogChat: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Conversational AI with Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Cognitive Grounding in Design Generation
summary: LLM-based chat systems have become valuable tools for design practice, enabling rapid ideation and flexible task support. Yet these systems process designer utterances as generic sequences, maintaining context through recency rather than through any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversation, this gap compounds as relational context decays between turns, identical words go unresolved across designers, and the conversation loops or restarts rather than deepens. We present CogChat, a real-time chat framework that grounds conversational AI in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph constructed from each designer's input. The system extracts typed entities and relations into a heterogeneous graph, then applies a HGT (Heterogeneous Graph Transformer) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to generate both intentional and exploratory probing questions. Technical evaluation shows that HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naive KG augmentation, which introduces noise that degrades response quality. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers indicates that grounding conversation in a relationally structured, designer-specific semantic context improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load. These findings suggest that structuring a designer's expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph can preserve relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

AI.tldr: CogChat grounds LLM chat in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph built from each designer's utterances, using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer to select context-relevant nodes for response generation and probing questions, thereby improving context retention, intent interpretation, and conversational depth.
AI.motivation: LLM-based chat systems treat designer utterances as generic sequences and maintain context only by recency, not by any model of the speaker's knowledge organization. In design conversations this causes relational context to decay between turns, identical words to remain unresolved across designers, and conversations to loop or restart instead of deepen.
AI.method: CogChat is a real-time chat framework that extracts typed entities and relations from each designer's input into a dynamic heterogeneous knowledge graph. It applies a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to produce both intentional and exploratory probing questions, grounding the LLM in a designer-specific semantic context.
AI.result: Technical evaluation shows HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naive KG augmentation (which introduces noise that degrades response quality). A within-subjects study with nine professional designers found that relationally structured, designer-specific grounding improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load.
AI.conclusion: Structuring a designer's expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph preserves relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

title: Auditable agentic AI for evidence-grounded thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting
summary: Thyroid ultrasound diagnosis requires coordinated lesion localization, measurement, risk stratification and reporting, yet most AI systems address these tasks in isolation and provide limited support for clinical review. We present ThyroidXAgent, a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that coordinates specialized diagnostic tools and stores their outputs as an auditable case-level evidence record. The system was developed using OpenThyroidDB, a multicentre, multitask resource integrating approximately 0.3 million ultrasound images and 24,000 paired reports, and was evaluated on 28,458 non-overlapping test cases, including 8,721 cases from 35 centres in the private NHC-MISD-TUS cohort. Across heterogeneous datasets, ThyroidXAgent achieved a mean Dice score of 87.21 percent for nodule segmentation and a mean AUROC of 0.9466 for benign-malignant classification. The same workflow supported lymph-node metastasis prediction and follicular versus papillary thyroid carcinoma classification, with AUROCs of 0.864 and 0.805, respectively. For report generation, evidence-grounded assembly outperformed multimodal language-model baselines across three cohorts. ThyClinScore, a lesion-level clinical semantic metric introduced here, showed the strongest correlation with a location-aware language-model judge. ThyroidXAgent improved physician classification accuracy, increased report diagnostic consistency from 70.3 percent to 86.2 percent, and reduced segmentation and reporting time by 35.9 percent and 27.4 percent, respectively. These findings support auditable, clinician-correctable agentic AI for thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting.

AI.tldr: ThyroidXAgent is a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that unifies nodule segmentation, classification, metastasis prediction, and evidence-grounded reporting for thyroid ultrasound, trained on ~0.3M images and evaluated on 28,458 test cases, improving physician accuracy, consistency, and workflow efficiency.
AI.motivation: Most thyroid ultrasound AI systems address individual tasks (localization, measurement, risk stratification, reporting) in isolation, providing limited support for clinical review and coordination. There is a need for an integrated, auditable, clinician-interactive system that coordinates multiple diagnostic tasks and supports the full diagnostic workflow.
AI.method: The authors developed ThyroidXAgent, a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that coordinates specialized diagnostic tools and stores their outputs as an auditable, case-level evidence record. It was developed using OpenThyroidDB, a multicentre multitask resource with ~0.3 million ultrasound images and 24,000 paired reports, and evaluated on 28,458 non-overlapping test cases (including 8,721 cases from 35 centres in the private NHC-MISD-TUS cohort). The system performs nodule segmentation, benign-malignant classification, lymph-node metastasis prediction, follicular vs. papillary carcinoma classification, and evidence-grounded report generation. A novel lesion-level clinical semantic metric, ThyClinScore, was introduced and correlated with a location-aware language-model judge.
AI.result: ThyroidXAgent achieved a mean Dice score of 87.21% for nodule segmentation and a mean AUROC of 0.9466 for benign-malignant classification. AUROCs were 0.864 for lymph-node metastasis prediction and 0.805 for follicular vs. papillary carcinoma classification. Evidence-grounded report assembly outperformed multimodal language-model baselines across three cohorts. ThyClinScore showed the strongest correlation with the location-aware language-model judge. Clinically, the system improved physician classification accuracy, raised report diagnostic consistency from 70.3% to 86.2%, and reduced segmentation and reporting time by 35.9% and 27.4%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The findings support auditable, clinician-correctable agentic AI as an effective approach for thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting, enhancing both diagnostic performance and clinical workflow efficiency.

title: Class-Structure Preservation Beats Diversity: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Text Augmentation Methods for Imbalanced Text Classification
summary: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), generative data augmentation has attracted considerable attention for imbalanced text classification in natural language processing. However, no empirical benchmark to date has compared LLM-based augmentation against the embedding-space SMOTE-style retrieval (EmbSMOTE), a strong classical reference for imbalanced classification. In this study, a controlled benchmark of 11 augmentation methods, spanning classical perturbation, embedding-space retrieval, and LLM-based generation, is newly constructed on seven public text classification datasets covering class counts $K=2$-$28$ and imbalance ratios of 1.1 to over 500, evaluated with five random seeds per cell using macro F1, Welch's $t$-tests, five distributional metrics, and an LLM-family sensitivity analysis based on Qwen3-8B. The experimental results reveal that all LLM-based methods are statistically equivalent or inferior to EmbSMOTE, with the performance gap widening monotonically as imbalance increases and reaching $Δ\text{F1}_\text{macro}\!\approx\!0.063$ on GoEmotions-28. Furthermore, it is observed that surface-level uniqueness has negligible correlation with downstream performance, whereas LLM-specific artifacts, such as text elongation and label-distribution uniformization, are negatively associated with classification accuracy. Compared with six LLM-based and four classical augmentation baselines, these results demonstrate that the effective variable is not surface-level diversity but class-conditional structural fidelity, namely the degree to which augmented samples preserve the class-conditioned geometry of the training distribution. Accordingly, retrieval-based oversampling should be adopted as the default for imbalanced multi-class classification, and a higher empirical bar should be required before LLM-based augmentation is deployed in practice.

AI.tldr: A controlled benchmark of 11 data augmentation methods (classical perturbation, embedding-space SMOTE retrieval [EmbSMOTE], and LLM-based generation) across seven imbalanced text classification datasets shows that LLM-based augmentation is statistically equivalent or inferior to EmbSMOTE, with the gap widening as imbalance grows. The findings attribute performance to class-conditional structural fidelity rather than surface-level diversity, recommending retrieval-based oversampling as the default.
AI.motivation: Despite growing interest in LLM-based generative data augmentation for imbalanced text classification, no empirical benchmark has compared it against EmbSMOTE—a strong classical reference—leaving practitioners without rigorous evidence on whether LLM generation actually outperforms retrieval-based oversampling.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled benchmark of 11 augmentation methods spanning classical perturbation, embedding-space retrieval (EmbSMOTE), and LLM-based generation. It is evaluated on seven public text classification datasets (K=2–28 classes, imbalance ratios 1.1 to >500) with five random seeds per cell, macro F1, Welch's t-tests, five distributional metrics, and an LLM-family sensitivity analysis based on Qwen3-8B.
AI.result: All LLM-based methods are statistically equivalent or inferior to EmbSMOTE, with the performance gap increasing monotonically as imbalance rises (reaching ΔF1_macro ≈ 0.063 on GoEmotions-28). Surface-level uniqueness shows negligible correlation with downstream performance, while LLM-specific artifacts (text elongation, label-distribution uniformization) correlate negatively with accuracy. The decisive factor is class-conditional structural fidelity—preserving the class-conditioned geometry of the training distribution—not surface-level diversity.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-based oversampling should be adopted as the default for imbalanced multi-class text classification, and a higher empirical bar should be required before deploying LLM-based augmentation in practice, since LLM methods do not outperform EmbSMOTE and the effective variable is class-conditional structural fidelity rather than surface-level diversity.

title: The Boolean Power of ReLU
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, comes with AI declaration
summary: We prove that, on finite simple undirected graphs equipped with a single Boolean node feature, the Boolean queries expressible in $Σ$-MPLang, for any collection $Σ$ of eventually constant activation functions and with arbitrary real coefficients, form a strict subclass of the Boolean queries expressible in ReLU-MPLang. We thereby settle a recently posed open problem: whether ReLU-MPLang is more powerful than trReLU-MPLang when it comes to Boolean queries. In particular, this implies that ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than {TrReLU,id}-GNNs with respect to Boolean queries on Boolean-featured graphs.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that for finite simple undirected graphs with a single Boolean node feature, Boolean queries computable by message-passing languages using eventually constant activation functions (Σ-MPLang) form a strict subclass of those computable with ReLU activations, settling an open problem and showing ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than truncated-ReLU-based GNNs on Boolean queries.
AI.motivation: To settle a recently posed open problem asking whether ReLU-MPLang is strictly more powerful than trReLU-MPLang for Boolean queries, i.e., whether ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than {TrReLU, id}-GNNs on Boolean-featured graphs.
AI.method: The authors analyze message-passing logic (MPLang) equipped with single Boolean node features and arbitrary real coefficients. They compare the class of Boolean queries expressible using ReLU activation functions against those expressible using any collection Σ of eventually constant activations, establishing a strict subclass (containment) relationship via a formal expressivity argument.
AI.result: The Boolean queries expressible in Σ-MPLang (for Σ a collection of eventually constant functions) form a strict subclass of the Boolean queries expressible in ReLU-MPLang. Consequently, ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than {TrReLU, id}-GNNs with respect to Boolean queries on Boolean-featured graphs.
AI.conclusion: ReLU-based message-passing is strictly more expressive than truncated-ReLU (and more generally eventually constant) activations for Boolean queries over Boolean-featured graphs, resolving the open question in the affirmative.

title: TeleGapper: On the (un)reliability of Privacy Policies in Telegram Mini apps
summary:
Telegram Mini Apps are Web applications embedded within the Telegram client, forming an ecosystem of third-party services within one of the world's most widely used messaging platforms. Despite their growing adoption and access to Telegram-provided context, their privacy properties remain largely unexplored. Unlike ecosystems such as WeChat, which rely on tightly controlled, proprietary execution frameworks, Telegram adopts a different model: Mini Apps run inside a WebView, combining platform-provided context with standard Web capabilities and unrestricted outbound networking. This enables applications to transmit sensitive information to analytics, advertising, tracking, or other third parties through ordinary Web requests, often with limited visibility.
  Privacy disclosures are therefore critical for transparency. Telegram allows Mini Apps either to define an application-specific privacy policy or to rely on a platform-provided default policy. While the latter reduces the developer's disclosure burden, it may lead to generic statements that do not accurately capture actual data practices of individual Mini Apps.
  In this paper, we present TeleGapper, a black-box dynamic analysis framework to assess the privacy posture of Mini Apps by capturing runtime network traffic, identifying third-party communications, and comparing observed data flows against disclosed privacy information. We evaluate 278 working Mini Apps collected from tApps Center, a community-driven catalogue for discovering third-party applications in Telegram. We find that 59.4% contact at least one undisclosed third party, 78.8% rely exclusively on Telegram's default privacy policy, and none provides a consent or opt-out mechanism. These findings expose a substantial transparency and compliance gap in a widely used yet understudied ecosystem.

AI.tldr: TeleGapper is a black-box dynamic analysis framework that measures the privacy posture of Telegram Mini Apps by capturing runtime network traffic, identifying third-party communications, and comparing observed data flows against disclosed privacy policies. Evaluating 278 working Mini Apps, the authors find that 59.4% contact undisclosed third parties, 78.8% rely solely on Telegram's default privacy policy, and none offer consent or opt-out mechanisms, revealing a substantial transparency and compliance gap.
AI.motivation: Telegram Mini Apps form a growing third-party ecosystem within a major messaging platform, yet their privacy properties are largely unexplored. Unlike WeChat's tightly controlled execution framework, Telegram Mini Apps run in a WebView with standard Web capabilities and unrestricted outbound networking, allowing them to leak sensitive context to analytics, advertising, and tracking third parties with limited visibility. Additionally, because Telegram permits reliance on a generic platform default privacy policy, disclosures may not accurately reflect actual data practices, motivating a systematic empirical assessment.
AI.method: The authors develop TeleGapper, a black-box dynamic analysis framework that captures runtime network traffic from Mini Apps, identifies third-party communications, and compares observed data flows against disclosed privacy information (application-specific or default policies). They evaluate 278 working Mini Apps collected from tApps Center, a community-driven catalogue for discovering third-party Telegram applications.
AI.result: Of the 278 evaluated Mini Apps, 59.4% contact at least one undisclosed third party, 78.8% rely exclusively on Telegram's default privacy policy, and none provides a consent or opt-out mechanism. These results expose a substantial transparency and compliance gap in the Telegram Mini App ecosystem.
AI.conclusion: The Telegram Mini App ecosystem exhibits a significant privacy transparency and compliance gap: most Mini Apps transmit data to undisclosed third parties, overwhelmingly depend on generic default privacy policies that do not capture actual data flows, and universally lack consent or opt-out mechanisms. TeleGapper demonstrates the feasibility of systematically auditing such WebView-based ecosystems and highlights the need for stronger disclosure and user-control requirements.

title: Print&Fold: Printing and Folding Shape-accurate 3D Models
summary: This paper introduces Print&Fold, a tool to allow FDM 3D printing of complex models with less time and material while preserving shape accuracy. Key to this work is a folding algorithm that planarizes foldable faces internal to the 3D model. While folding techniques typically discretize a target model's surface, thereby fabricating low fidelity counterparts, our method preserves the surface features in the physical print. Our design tool allows users to unfold 3D models to be FDM-printed flat before manually folding these into their target shapes. We showcase a variety of applications and evaluate the material and time savings across a range of 3D models.

AI.tldr: Print&Fold is a design tool that lets users flatten 3D models, FDM-print them as flat sheets, then manually fold them into the target shape, saving time and material while retaining surface detail.
AI.motivation: FDM 3D printing of complex models is costly in time and material, and existing folding techniques lower fidelity by discretizing the surface. The authors aim to fabricate complex shapes more efficiently without sacrificing shape accuracy.
AI.method: A folding algorithm that planarizes foldable faces internal to the 3D model, allowing the model to be unfolded into a flat layout for FDM printing, then manually folded back into the target shape.
AI.result: Demonstrates a variety of applications and quantifies material and time savings across a range of 3D models, preserving surface features in the physical prints.
AI.conclusion: By planarizing foldable internal faces, Print&Fold enables efficient FDM printing of complex models that are folded into shape afterward, achieving both reduced resource use and high-fidelity outputs.

title: DiG-bench: Discovery in Games
summary: Discovery---formulating novel generalizations---is a central part of the scientific process. Despite its importance, there is a gap in the current AI benchmark landscape, with few benchmarks directly probing the capacity for discovering new knowledge with experimentation in controlled environments where the objective is unknown. To address this gap, we release a new benchmark: DiG-bench (Discovery in Games). DiG-bench consists of a set of 70 independent games. Each game is encoded as a short string and has unique transformation rules that must be discovered through interaction and experimentation. The levels of the game present a series of challenges to test whether the rules have been discovered, where the win conditions for each level are also unknown. We provide games at seven tiers of difficulty for AI agents. The lowest tier is routinely solvable by multiple models, while the highest tier challenges the best models in agentic harnesses. All 70 games were solved by at least one human on first attempt. A subset of 21 games is released publicly, and the remainder is held private for secure evaluation.

AI.tldr: DiG-bench is a new benchmark of 70 games that tests AI agents' ability to discover novel rules through experimentation when objectives are unknown, spanning seven difficulty tiers with 21 games public and 49 held out for secure evaluation.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery—formulating novel generalizations—is central to science, yet current AI benchmarks rarely probe the capacity to discover new knowledge through experimentation in controlled environments with unknown objectives. DiG-bench fills this gap.
AI.method: The benchmark consists of 70 independent games encoded as short strings, each with unique transformation rules that agents must discover through interaction and experimentation. Each game's levels present challenges where the win conditions are also unknown, providing seven tiers of difficulty. All games were validated as human-solvable on first attempt; 21 games are public and 49 are held private.
AI.result: The lowest difficulty tier is routinely solvable by multiple AI models, while the highest tier challenges the best models in agentic harnesses. All 70 games were solved by at least one human on first attempt.
AI.conclusion: DiG-bench addresses the gap in benchmarks for discovery-oriented AI evaluation, offering a scalable, difficulty-stratified, and securely evaluable testbed for measuring agents' capacity to discover novel rules through experimentation.

title: The "Knowledge-Behavior Gap" in Cultural Taboo Safety of Large Language Models
summary: Cultural taboo safety is essential for deploying large language models (LLMs), as culturally insensitive outputs may cause offense or even social harm. However, existing cultural benchmarks primarily assess cultural knowledge or values biases, while overlooking whether LLMs can recognize and respect cultural taboos, especially when taboos are implicitly hidden in seemingly harmless questions. Besides, cultural taboos are implicit, and context-dependent, thus poss unique challenges for reliable evaluation. To address these gaps, we introduce \textbf{CulShield}, the first public benchmark dedicated to evaluating and improving the cultural taboo safety of LLMs. CulShield spans 77 countries and territories, and includes over 2,020 taboos. It evaluates models along both explicit knowledge and implicit behaviors. Experiments on several advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.5-pro) reveal a clear ``knowledge-behavior gap'': models often fail to apply known taboos during interaction. We further show that variations in linguistic context can significantly affect LLMs' cultural taboo safety. Code and data is accessible here: https://github.com/hedyHe/CulShield.

AI.tldr: CulShield is the first public benchmark for evaluating and improving the cultural taboo safety of LLMs, covering 77 countries/territories and over 2,020 taboos across explicit knowledge and implicit behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing cultural benchmarks focus on cultural knowledge or value biases but overlook whether LLMs can recognize and respect cultural taboos, especially when taboos are implicitly hidden in seemingly harmless questions. Cultural taboos are also implicit and context-dependent, making reliable evaluation difficult.
AI.method: Introduce CulShield, a benchmark spanning 77 countries/territories with over 2,020 taboos, evaluating models on both explicit knowledge and implicit behaviors. Experiments are conducted on advanced LLMs such as GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-pro.
AI.result: Experiments reveal a clear "knowledge-behavior gap": models often fail to apply known taboos during interaction. Additionally, variations in linguistic context significantly affect LLMs' cultural taboo safety.
AI.conclusion: CulShield fills a critical gap in cultural safety evaluation, demonstrating that current LLMs struggle to translate cultural taboo knowledge into safe behavior, and highlighting the need for context-aware safety improvements.

title: Structure-preserving uncertainty quantification for GENERIC dynamics
summary: Structure-preserving machine learning embeds physical structure directly into model architectures, yet uncertainty quantification (UQ) for such hard-constrained models remains limited because standard UQ methods may violate the encoded admissibility conditions, require architectural modifications, or impose substantial computational costs. In this work, we propose Structure-Preserving Epistemic Neural Networks (S-PENNs), a general framework for UQ in scientific machine learning models with hard architectural constraints, and instantiate it for GENERIC (General Equation for Non-Equilibrium Reversible-Irreversible Coupling) dynamics. S-PENNs preserve the structural constraints of a pretrained model by attaching lightweight epinets to its constrained components, ensuring that every sampled realization remains physically admissible by construction. When applied to GENERIC dynamics, such a proposed framework yields thermodynamically consistent rollouts that preserve the first and second laws. Furthermore, we combine S-PENNs with split conformal prediction as a post-hoc calibration method to produce prediction intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. We validate S-PENNs on three numerical examples: a harmonic oscillator coupled to a heat bath and an idealized chemical motor, both governed by ODEs, and a one-dimensional viscoplastic model governed by PDEs. Across all three examples, S-PENNs produce thermodynamically consistent stochastic realizations and well-calibrated prediction intervals while reducing the computational cost by about one to three orders of magnitude compared to deep ensembles. Although the present study focuses on GENERIC dynamics, S-PENNs can be extended more broadly to scientific machine learning models in computational mechanics with either hard or soft constraints.

AI.tldr: S-PENNs add lightweight epinets to constrained, pretrained GENERIC dynamical models to enable structure-preserving uncertainty quantification, and combine them with split conformal prediction for calibrated prediction intervals at greatly reduced cost compared to deep ensembles.
AI.motivation: Standard UQ methods for hard-constrained scientific ML models may violate architectural admissibility constraints, require architecture changes, or be computationally expensive. Existing UQ is limited for structure-preserving models such as GENERIC dynamics.
AI.method: Propose Structure-Preserving Epistemic Neural Networks (S-PENNs), which attach lightweight epinets to the constrained components of a pretrained model so every sampled realization remains physically admissible; instantiate this for GENERIC dynamics and combine with split conformal prediction as post-hoc calibration to obtain finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees.
AI.result: S-PENNs produce thermodynamically consistent (first and second law preserving) stochastic rollouts and well-calibrated prediction intervals on a harmonic oscillator coupled to a heat bath (ODE), an idealized chemical motor (ODE), and a 1D viscoplastic model (PDE), while reducing computational cost by roughly one to three orders of magnitude versus deep ensembles.
AI.conclusion: S-PENNs provide a general, computationally efficient UQ framework for structure-preserving scientific ML models and can be extended beyond GENERIC dynamics to computational mechanics models with hard or soft constraints.

title: Privacy-Preserving RAG by Concealing Sensitive Information from External LLMs
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely used to improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in answering user queries. Existing privacy research on RAG has focused on preventing unauthorized users from accessing sensitive data. However, another important problem that is often overlooked in RAG privacy research is that external generators have access to the query and the retrieved documents, which may contain confidential information that could potentially be misused or accessed for unintended purposes. In this paper, we introduce the Sensitive Entity Alias Generator (SEAG), a privacy-preserving framework that empowers users to utilize powerful third-party generators without disclosing sensitive information. SEAG introduces a lightweight model that locates sensitive entities, generates corresponding aliases, and constructs an entity replacement table. The table is used to replace sensitive words in the user's query and in the retrieved documents before they are forwarded to an external generator. For this purpose, two datasets were constructed: one for fine-tuning SEAG models to generate entity replacement tables, and another for evaluating the entire SEAG framework. The experimental results demonstrate the success of the SEAG framework. As for the User metric, which measures the ability of the model to provide a correct response to the user while hiding sensitive information from the external generator, all SEAG models achieved over 80% accuracy. Additional analysis further evaluated the ability of SEAG models Qwen-3, LLaMA-3.2, and Phi-4 to hide all sensitive entities within given documents. The results show good performance with total accuracies of 77.83%, 76.73%, and 74.91%, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SEAG, a privacy-preserving RAG framework that replaces sensitive entities with aliases in both the user query and retrieved documents before forwarding them to an external generator, thus hiding confidential information from third-party generators.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy research on RAG focuses on preventing unauthorized users from accessing sensitive data, but overlooks the risk that external generators can access queries and retrieved documents containing confidential information that may be misused or accessed for unintended purposes.
AI.method: SEAG introduces a lightweight model that locates sensitive entities, generates corresponding aliases, and constructs an entity replacement table. This table is used to replace sensitive words in the user's query and retrieved documents before they are forwarded to an external generator. Two datasets were constructed: one for fine-tuning SEAG models to generate entity replacement tables, and another for evaluating the entire framework.
AI.result: All SEAG models achieved over 80% accuracy on the User metric (measuring the ability to provide correct responses while hiding sensitive information). In hiding all sensitive entities within documents, Qwen-3, LLaMA-3.2, and Phi-4 achieved total accuracies of 77.83%, 76.73%, and 74.91%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The SEAG framework successfully enables users to leverage powerful third-party generators without disclosing sensitive information, demonstrating good performance across multiple models in both response correctness and sensitive entity hiding.

title: More Than 63% of IEEE VIS Research Liable to be Retracted?! Ethics Approval Statements Protect Participants (and Researchers!)
summary: We analyzed the ethics reporting in 255 IEEE VIS papers from 2024 and 2025, as published in TVCG. This analysis arose from our experience as readers and reviewers of IEEE VIS papers that such reporting is frequently incomplete or missing, as well as from investigations in which we ourselves had to answer challenges regarding ethics approval in our own work. Visualization research naturally often involves human participants, yet ethics approval and informed-consent procedures are not always explicitly reported. In our corpus, 189 papers (74.1%) reported on work involving human participants. Only 6 of them (3.2%) reported to have obtained ethics approval, an approval identifier, and having received informed consent from the participants, while 26 (13.8%) reported at least ethics approval and informed consent. These omissions do not imply that the empirical work was unethical or lacked approval. They rather show that current reporting practices make ethical approval difficult to assess. Beyond our alarming - yet true - paper title, we wish to raise awareness on how authors themselves may eventually be at risk for not properly reporting ethics. We argue that VIS should adopt clearer and more standardized ethics-reporting practices to protect participants, authors, reviewers, and editors.

AI.tldr: An analysis of 255 IEEE VIS papers (2024–2025, published in TVCG) finds that while 74.1% involved human participants, only 3.2% fully reported ethics approval, an approval ID, and informed consent, exposing widespread incomplete ethics reporting despite a lack of evidence of unethical research.
AI.motivation: The study arises from the authors' experiences as readers and reviewers observing frequently missing or incomplete ethics reporting in IEEE VIS papers, plus their own encounters defending ethics approval in their work. Given that visualization research often involves human participants but ethics approval and consent procedures are not consistently disclosed, they seek to quantify this gap and raise awareness of the risks to authors, participants, reviewers, and editors.
AI.method: The authors conducted a corpus analysis of 255 IEEE VIS papers published in TVCG in 2024 and 2025, systematically reviewing their ethics reporting to determine (1) whether the research involved human participants, and (2) whether papers reported ethics approval, an approval identifier, and/or informed consent.
AI.result: Of the 255 papers, 189 (74.1%) reported work involving human participants. Among these, only 6 papers (3.2%) reported ethics approval, an approval identifier, and informed consent together, while 26 (13.8%) reported at least ethics approval and informed consent. The omissions indicate poor reporting practices rather than unethical or unapproved research.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that current reporting practices make ethical approval difficult to assess and put authors themselves at risk. They call on the VIS community to adopt clearer, more standardized ethics-reporting practices to protect participants, authors, reviewers, and editors.

title: Dead text or binding clause? Measuring and restoring constraint influence in black-box LLM dialogues
summary: Multi-turn dialogues let users revoke constraints as easily as impose them, but revocation does not reliably take effect: models keep enacting withdrawn requirements (occasionally beneath comments asserting their removal), a failure we call \emph{behavioral relapse}, or revocation inertia. No existing instrument measures this influence per clause, predicts it before delivery, or repairs it under matched budgets. \sysname{} closes the three gaps through the model API alone: a contract ledger pairs every constraint with an executable checker, records revocations as tombstones, and compiles the net constraint state ahead of time into a single specification; a sequential ablation probe measures per-clause adherence and incremental behavioral effect; a repair ladder operates under token- and attempt-matched budgets. On \dataname{} (\NTasks{} HumanEval tasks, \NClauses{} verified checkers), relapse at an 8B operating point climbs from \ScaleDelayedMTwo{} to \ScaleDelayedMEight{} as constraint load grows, while stronger models sit at floor. Under matched checkers, model, and budget, ahead-of-time compilation significantly reduces relapse against a no-ledger verifier-retry baseline (\RestoreDiff{}, 95\% CI \RestoreDiffCI{}, $p$ \RestoreDiffP{}); adaptive ladder interventions stacked on top add no detectable gain (95\% confidence excludes gains $\geq$ \LadderExcludedGain{}). The probe predicts relapse before delivery (AUROC \AurocPrimary{}); a one-sentence tombstone note recovers about a third of the compilation effect and survives a placebo control. At \CostDeliveryFactor{} delivery overhead and \CostTotalHedged{} of API compute for every result, revocation failure becomes a measurable, predictable, and repairable property of dialogue state rather than an invisible one.

AI.tldr: Multi-turn language models often fail to actually drop user-revoked constraints ("behavioral relapse"/"revocation inertia"). The paper introduces a system (API-only) with a contract ledger, a sequential ablation probe to measure/predict per-clause relapse, and a repair ladder under matched budgets. Experiments show relapse worsens with constraint load, ahead-of-time compilation substantially reduces it, the probe predicts relapse (AUROC reported), and a one-sentence tombstone note recovers ~1/3 of the compilation effect.
AI.motivation: Models frequently continue satisfying requirements users have withdrawn, sometimes even while commenting that the constraint was removed. No existing tool measures this per-clause influence, predicts relapse before delivery, or repairs it under matched budgets — leaving revocation failure invisible and unquantified.
AI.method: The system operates through the model API alone using three components: (1) a contract ledger that pairs each constraint with an executable checker, marks revocations as tombstones, and compiles the net constraint state ahead of time into one specification; (2) a sequential ablation probe measuring per-clause adherence and incremental behavioral effect; (3) a repair ladder applied under token- and attempt-matched budgets. Evaluation uses a dataset of HumanEval-style tasks with verified checkers, comparing against a no-ledger verifier-retry baseline and testing a tombstone-note variant plus placebo control.
AI.result: At an 8B operating point, relapse climbs from one reported level to a higher one as constraint load grows, while stronger models sit at a floor. Matched on checker, model, and budget, ahead-of-time compilation significantly reduces relapse versus the verifier-retry baseline (reported relative reduction with 95% CI and p-value); adaptive ladder interventions add no detectable gain (95% confidence excludes gains above a threshold). The probe predicts relapse pre-delivery (high AUROC), and a one-sentence tombstone note recovers roughly one-third of the compilation effect while surviving placebo control, at a modest delivery overhead and total hedged API compute per result.
AI.conclusion: Revocation failure is a measurable, predictable, and repairable property of dialogue state rather than an invisible one, and the proposed API-only system closes the gaps of measurement, prediction, and repair at acceptable compute cost.

title: Are Large Language Models Reliable Reviewers? A Benchmark for Error Detection in Financial Documents
summary: Ensuring the accuracy of financial documents is critical for economic analysis, regulatory compliance, and corporate decision-making. Several studies have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well in many financial tasks, such as stock price movements and financial analytics. However, a critical task remains unexplored: the ability of LLMs to identify errors in financial documents. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{FinED-Bench}, the first publicly \textbf{Bench}mark for \textbf{Fin}ancial \textbf{E}rror \textbf{D}etection across three levels of cognitive complexity. FinED-Bench covers nine real-world financial scenarios, and includes over 900 documents reported in 2025 that are unseen by existing language models. We detail the benchmark construction process and evaluate several advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Qwen3-14B) on this tasks, which requires both financial domain knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that current LLMs still struggle with this task, especially in high-complexity cases. Besides, supervised fine-tuning can significantly improve the performance of weaker LLMs on this task. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/hedyHe/FinED-Bench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FinED-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark for financial error detection spanning three levels of cognitive complexity, covering nine real-world financial scenarios with over 900 documents from 2025. Evaluation of advanced LLMs shows they still struggle, especially on high-complexity cases, while supervised fine-tuning notably improves weaker models.
AI.motivation: Ensuring the accuracy of financial documents is critical for economic analysis, regulatory compliance, and corporate decision-making. While LLMs perform well on many financial tasks (e.g., stock price prediction, analytics), their ability to detect errors in financial documents remains unexplored, motivating the creation of a dedicated benchmark.
AI.method: The authors construct FinED-Bench, a benchmark for financial error detection across three levels of cognitive complexity and nine real-world financial scenarios, comprising over 900 documents from 2025 unseen by existing models. They evaluate several advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Qwen3-14B) on the task, which requires both financial domain knowledge and reasoning, and further apply supervised fine-tuning to weaker LLMs.
AI.result: Experimental results indicate that current LLMs still struggle with financial error detection, particularly in high-complexity cases. Supervised fine-tuning can significantly improve the performance of weaker LLMs on this task.
AI.conclusion: Financial error detection remains a challenging open problem for current LLMs. The benchmark (FinED-Bench) and code are released to facilitate further research, available at https://github.com/hedyHe/FinED-Bench.

title: CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution
summary: GPU kernel agents and GPU programming languages have advanced separately, leaving expert kernels difficult to reproduce. Agents usually treat the compiler as a fixed black box and receive only errors, correctness outcomes, and timing, while existing DSLs either hide critical scheduling decisions or expose them through difficult layout abstractions. We present CAKE, a compiler-agent co-design in which agents author CAKE IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation. CAKE exposes warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines while supporting verification, cost modeling, and localized diagnostics. The harness itself evolves: recurring failures become verifier rules, IR primitives, model calibrations, and reusable optimization tactics. In matched implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean starts on B200, the best CAKE IR candidate at an 80-million-token budget runs at 1.144x the tuned FlashML baseline, compared with 0.928x for direct CUDA/PTX. Beyond this benchmark, agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention achieves a 2.05x geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA and passes end-to-end serving validation. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans improve performance by 1.42x to 2.12x across more than 400 shapes, and four kernel changes are available as upstream PRs. CAKE targets NVIDIA GPUs from Ampere through Blackwell and separates single-shape evolution from library generalization and dispatch.

AI.tldr: CAKE is a compiler-agent co-design where agents author a typed, hardware-explicit IR (CAKE IR) exposing warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines. The system evolves its verifier rules, IR primitives, cost models, and tactics from recurring failures, enabling agent-generated kernels that beat tuned baselines (1.144x on Flash-KMeans, 2.05x on Kimi Delta Attention) across Ampere-to-Blackwell NVIDIA GPUs.
