AI.motivation: GPU kernel agents and GPU programming languages have advanced independently, making expert kernels hard to reproduce. Agents treat the compiler as a black box (only seeing errors, correctness, and timing), while existing DSLs either hide scheduling decisions or expose them through unwieldy layout abstractions. This gap motivates a representation and harness specifically designed so agents can both reason about and optimize hardware scheduling.
AI.method: CAKE introduces CAKE IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation exposing warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines, with support for verification, cost modeling, and localized diagnostics. The harness co-evolves with agent use: recurring failures are turned into verifier rules, IR primitives, model calibrations, and reusable optimization tactics. The system targets NVIDIA GPUs from Ampere through Blackwell and separates single-shape kernel evolution from library generalization and dispatch.
AI.result: On a matched, implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean start on B200 with an 80M-token budget, the best CAKE IR candidate runs at 1.144x the tuned FlashML baseline versus 0.928x for direct CUDA/PTX. Agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention achieves a 2.05x geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA and passes end-to-end serving validation. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans improve performance by 1.42x to 2.12x across 400+ shapes, with four kernel changes available as upstream PRs.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing the IR and the agent harness lets LLM-driven agents author expert-level GPU kernels that outperform tuned baselines and generalize across shapes via learned dispatch. CAKE demonstrates that exposing hardware scheduling explicitly, combined with an evolving verification/cost-modeling loop, substantially improves kernel reproducibility and performance.

title: Correct Is Not Governed: Provenance Integrity in Agentic Workflows
summary: Agentic workflows are commonly evaluated by whether they reach the correct outcome. That is insufficient in institutional settings, where a correct action may rely on the wrong authority, an unsupported completion claim, or work made stale by a later change. We define governed execution as work whose decisions, completion, and response to change are supported by inspectable provenance. We present Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that records authority and fact dependencies, verifies completion evidence, and selectively invalidates affected work. Across controlled comparisons, governed and direct workflows often reached the same outcomes, but only the governed path consistently preserved governing evidence, refused unsupported closure, and limited recovery to dependent tasks. A role-separated transfer challenge then failed: a deterministically enforced completeness contract severely over-blocked synthetic packets produced outside its authoring context. These results do not establish Matrix as a general accuracy enhancer; they support its primary role as an institutional integrity layer for making agentic work auditable and independently verifiable.

AI.tldr: Matrix adds a deterministic causal-state layer to agentic workflows that records authority and fact dependencies, verifies completion evidence, and selectively invalidates stale work, making outcomes auditable rather than merely correct.
AI.motivation: Agentic workflows are typically judged only by whether they reach the correct outcome, which is insufficient in institutional settings: a correct action may rest on the wrong authority, an unsupported completion claim, or work made stale by later changes. There is a need for governed execution whose decisions, completion, and responses to change are backed by inspectable provenance.
AI.method: The authors propose Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that (1) records authority and fact dependencies, (2) verifies completion evidence, and (3) selectively invalidates affected work. They compare governed workflows against direct workflows under controlled conditions and run a role-separated transfer challenge.
AI.result: Governed and direct workflows often reached the same outcomes, but only the governed path consistently preserved governing evidence, refused unsupported closure, and limited recovery to dependent tasks. In the role-separated transfer challenge, a deterministically enforced completeness contract severely over-blocked synthetic packets produced outside its authoring context, causing the challenge to fail.
AI.conclusion: The results do not establish Matrix as a general accuracy enhancer; rather, they support its primary role as an institutional integrity layer that makes agentic work auditable and independently verifiable.

title: Sensorimotor Stickies: A Reconfigurable On-Body Platform for Closed-Loop Sensorimotor Training
summary: Closed-loop sensorimotor training systems can improve learning by sensing movement and delivering real-time feedback, yet most are built as fixed implementations tied to a single task, even though the core technology (inertial and tactile sensing, vibrotactile cueing, rule-based logic) remains the same. We present Sensorimotor Stickies, a reconfigurable on-body platform that treats sensing and vibrotactile feedback as modular stickies that can be patched onto the body as needed. The platform includes miniaturized adhesive modules for IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, and vibrotactile actuation; low-power firmware and BLE infrastructure for raw streaming and motor control without task-specific rewrites; and a companion mobile app that provides a shared body-centered model for placement, calibration, and feedback authoring. Together, these components enable reconfiguration across training scenarios, user needs, and feedback setups. We evaluate the platform through technical characterization, configured application demonstration, practitioner-mediated configuration sessions, and an end-user study, demonstrating technical feasibility, reconfiguration breadth, and end-user configurability for first-time setup, calibration, and within-task feedback reconfiguration.

AI.tldr: Sensorimotor Stickies is a reconfigurable on-body platform that modularizes IMU sensing, tactile sensing, and vibrotactile feedback into adhesive "stickies," enabling closed-loop sensorimotor training to be reconfigured across tasks without task-specific firmware rewrites.
AI.motivation: Most closed-loop sensorimotor training systems are fixed implementations tied to a single task, despite sharing the same core technology (inertial and tactile sensing, vibrotactile cueing, rule-based logic). This limits reuse and reconfiguration across training scenarios and user needs.
AI.method: The authors built a modular wearable platform comprising miniaturized adhesive modules for IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, and vibrotactile actuation; low-power firmware and BLE infrastructure for raw streaming and motor control without task-specific rewrites; and a companion mobile app providing a shared body-centered model for placement, calibration, and feedback authoring.
AI.result: Evaluation via technical characterization, configured application demonstrations, practitioner-mediated configuration sessions, and an end-user study demonstrated technical feasibility, reconfiguration breadth, and end-user configurability for first-time setup, calibration, and within-task feedback reconfiguration.
AI.conclusion: The platform enables reconfiguration across training scenarios, user needs, and feedback setups, showing that modular sensing/feedback components with shared infrastructure can support flexible closed-loop sensorimotor training.

title: @skills: Attention is all you have
comment: 7 pages main, 23 pages in total with appendix, 6 figures
summary: There are 56,804 public agent skills today, and teams write many more privately. The dominant delivery model is installation: once installed, a skill's description remains in the system prompt, competing for fewer than 100 reliable trigger slots. This leaves the long tail with no practical path to use and forces teams' own playbooks to compete for the same scarce space. We observe that installation bundles three separable functions: content, persistence, and automatic triggering. Only the last requires prompt residency. We therefore propose @skills, an open protocol that separates them. A path addresses any skill, subtree, or collection, and reading a skill is sufficient to use it, so nothing is installed or made resident. The operation vendors a copy at the same path into a project's Git-tracked tree for adaptation and ownership. The operation adds one .gitignore-style line, the only element that costs prompt residency. A directory is a menu, making bundles ordinary directories rather than all-or-nothing units. The protocol requires no manifest, lockfile, or registration, and SKILL.md remains unchanged. @skills is additive, ships as an installable package, and turns any agent that can read files and run commands into a client through a single instruction file. Its open specification is at https://github.com/SylphAI-Inc/atskills and it is implemented in the AdaL CLI at https://adalagent.ai . Because paths address skills well but cannot find them, the protocol is paired with a free hub at https://atskills.one for corpus-wide search and ranking, repository-free hosting, private and team collections, and one-screen authoring. The hub is optional: gh: and local paths resolve without it, and indexed GitHub skills retain their gh: identities. Install less, use more.

AI.tldr: @skills is an open protocol that decouples a skill's content, persistence, and auto-triggering so agents can use skills by path (reading them) instead of installing them into the prompt, reserving prompt residency only for a single trigger line; it pairs with an optional free hub for discovery.
AI.motivation: Today's dominant delivery model is installation, which keeps every installed skill's description in the system prompt, competing for fewer than 100 reliable trigger slots. This leaves the long tail of skills unusable and forces teams' own playbooks to fight for the same scarce prompt space, because installation bundles three distinct functions—content, persistence, and automatic triggering—even though only triggering requires prompt residency.
AI.method: The protocol separates content, persistence, and auto-triggering. A path addresses any skill, subtree, or collection, and reading a skill is sufficient to use it (nothing is installed). A "vendors" operation copies a skill at the same path into a Git-tracked tree for adaptation and ownership. An "adds" operation inserts one .gitignore-style trigger line—the only element consuming prompt residency. Directories act as menus, so bundles are ordinary directories rather than all-or-nothing units. There is no manifest, lockfile, or registration, and SKILL.md is unchanged. The hub provides corpus-wide search/ranking, repository-free hosting, private/team collections, and one-screen authoring, but is optional since gh: and local paths work without it.
AI.result: @skills is additive, ships as an installable package, and turns any agent that can read files and run commands into a client via a single instruction file. It is implemented in the AdaL CLI and specified at github.com/SylphAI-Inc/atskills, with a free optional hub at atskills.one; indexed GitHub skills retain their gh: identities.
AI.conclusion: By separating content, persistence, and triggering, @skills removes installation and prompt residency as prerequisites for using skills, letting agents "install less, use more" while preserving a single low-cost trigger line and optional hub-based discovery.

title: Large Language Models Pass the History Exam But Miss the <<History>>: A Polish High School Exit Exam Matura Benchmark
summary: AI chatbots are widely used by students as knowledge sources, yet LLM benchmarks rarely assess interpretative historical reasoning. We evaluate eight leading LLMs on the Polish high school exit exams (Matura) in history - three official papers from 2023-2025, comprising short-answer questions and extended essays - comparing model performance against the human examinee population. Every model dramatically outperforms human examinees, yet aggregate scores mask distinct competency profiles: rankings are unstable across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, with a consistent penalty on Polish versus Global history content. Qualitative error analysis reveals two recurring failure modes - source conflation, in which models reason from source content rather than treating it as an object of analysis, and temporal disorientation, in which responses are historically misplaced. This study introduces the first LLM history benchmark grounded in Polish national curriculum.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks eight leading LLMs on Polish high school (Matura) history exams from 2023–2025 and finds they outperform human examinees, but with unstable rankings and specific failure modes (source conflation and temporal disorientation) that aggregate scores hide.
AI.motivation: AI chatbots are widely used as knowledge sources, but existing LLM benchmarks rarely assess interpretative historical reasoning, so the authors build a benchmark grounded in a national curriculum (Polish Matura) to test that skill set.
AI.method: Eight leading LLMs were evaluated on three official Polish Matura history papers (2023–2025), covering short-answer questions and extended essays. Model performance was compared against the human examinee population, and rankings were analyzed across task type, source modality, and geographical scope (Polish vs. Global history), complemented by qualitative error analysis.
AI.result: Every model dramatically outperforms human examinees, but aggregate scores mask distinct competency profiles: rankings are unstable across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, with a consistent penalty on Polish versus Global history content. Qualitative analysis reveals two recurring failure modes: source conflation (reasoning from source content instead of analyzing it) and temporal disorientation (historically misplaced responses).
AI.conclusion: The study introduces the first LLM history benchmark grounded in the Polish national curriculum and demonstrates that high aggregate scores conceal inconsistent ranking behavior and systematic weaknesses in interpretative historical reasoning, highlighting the need for more granular evaluation.

title: Interpretable Causal Discovery via Causal-Effect Constraints
summary: Causal discovery aims to uncover the underlying causal relationships given data generated from a system. The goal, however, is not merely to predict causal edges given data, but also to be able to interpret and explain either observed or hypothesized phenomena, such as a particularly large causal effect. We consider this task of conditional causal discovery and cast it as a Bayesian inference problem, in which we target the posterior over causal graphs and parameters conditional on an event such as a causal-effect constraint. Unfortunately, this poses a computational challenge: existing approaches to Bayesian causal discovery struggle when the event has small posterior mass. To address this, we adapt rare-event estimation techniques to perform inference the joint graph-parameter space. Our method gradually drives a particle population toward the constrained region while maintaining samples that approximate the conditional posterior. Empirical evaluation on synthetic graphs validates the accuracy of our approach at small and large scales, and we show in a case study on the Sachs protein dataset how our method can be used to aid scientific exploration by providing pathway-level summaries.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Bayesian method for conditional causal discovery that estimates the posterior over causal graphs and parameters given an event (e.g., a large causal effect), using rare-event estimation techniques to handle low-mass constraint regions.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery should go beyond predicting causal edges: researchers need to interpret and explain observed or hypothesized phenomena, such as unusually large causal effects. Conditioning on such events is a Bayesian inference problem over a joint graph-parameter space, but existing Bayesian causal discovery methods fail when the conditioning event has small posterior mass.
AI.method: The authors cast conditional causal discovery as Bayesian inference over the joint graph-parameter space, targeting the posterior conditional on an event such as a causal-effect constraint. They adapt rare-event estimation techniques to gradually drive a particle population toward the constrained region while maintaining samples that approximate the conditional posterior.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic graphs validates the accuracy of the approach at both small and large scales. A case study on the Sachs protein dataset demonstrates how the method aids scientific exploration by providing pathway-level summaries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed rare-event-based particle method successfully performs conditional causal discovery even when the conditioning event lies in a low-probability region, offering accurate posterior estimates and practically useful pathway-level summaries for scientific interpretation.

title: Before You Say It: Anticipating Verbal Behavior from Longitudinal Everyday Conversations with LLMs
summary: Knowing someone deeply means not just understanding what they say or do but also how they will likely think, react, and engage across situations. Such predictions could eventually inform systems to anticipate when the individual is about to deviate from their goal, catch regrettable behaviors before they are made, and surface blind spots before they take hold. While many interactive systems model users to enable more personalized interactions, most cannot make such behavioral predictions, as this often requires longitudinal observation and inference of how the individual's behaviors unfold across various everyday situations. In this work, we introduce a novel LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user's likely behavior across everyday conversational situations. We (1) collect a longitudinal dataset of over 1000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants using a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluate LLM-based predictions against ground truth behaviors; and (3) use semi-structured interviews to explore participants perceptions of behavioral predictions and their views on possible forms of future behavioral support. Altogether, our findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data. This opens up new possibilities for potential future context-aware, anticipatory, proactive and personalized AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user's likely behavior across everyday conversational situations, built from over 1000 hours of longitudinal naturalistic smartwatch-recorded conversations from 14 participants, and validated against ground-truth behaviors plus participant interviews about future behavioral support.
AI.motivation: Most interactive systems personalize interactions but cannot predict how individuals will think, react, or engage across situations. Enabling such behavioral predictions would let systems anticipate goal deviations, catch regrettable behaviors before they happen, and surface blind spots early, requiring longitudinal observation and inference of behavioral patterns.
AI.method: The authors (1) collect a longitudinal dataset of over 1000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants via a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluate LLM-based predictions against ground-truth behaviors; and (3) conduct semi-structured interviews to explore participants' perceptions of behavioral predictions and their views on possible forms of future behavioral support.
AI.result: Findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data, demonstrating the feasibility of anticipating individual behavioral patterns using LLM-based models.
AI.conclusion: The ability to predict person-specific verbal behavior opens up new possibilities for future context-aware, anticipatory, proactive, and personalized AI systems that could support individuals in everyday life.

title: Jagged Judges: Epistemic Stability Under Silence, Pressure, and Persistence
summary: LLM judges have become central infrastructure for model evaluations, online grading, and reward modeling. Judges are typically validated by accuracy on golden data, but accuracy says little about whether they are stable under re-prompting, challenge, or sustained pushback. We introduce the \emph{Wiggle Framework}, a unified stress test for epistemic stability in LLM judges. The framework decomposes judge robustness along three dimensions: Mechanical Consistency (stability under re-prompting and reframing), Single-turn Conviction (stability under a single challenge), and Multi-turn Persistence (stability under sustained or adaptive pressure). We use the framework to study 9 frontier models across 14 judging tasks spanning safety, toxicity, AI writing detection, and political-response evaluation. Every model exhibits substantial wiggle as a judge --- flipping verdicts 25--71\% of the time under static pushback, and 62--91\% with an adversarial LLM persuader. Critically, we find that pressure that succeeds in changing a judge's verdict is almost always net-corrupting with respect to ground truth. Beyond the framework itself, we identify baseline jury majority strength as the most effective single-shot signal for anticipating which items wiggle. Taken together, this is the first apples-to-apples cross-dataset comparison of mechanical, conformity, and persuadability tests in a judging context.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Wiggle Framework to stress-test epistemic stability in LLM judges, finding that all 9 frontier models flip verdicts 25–71% under static pushback and 62–91% under adversarial persuasion, with pressure-induced flips almost always moving away from ground truth.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are widely used for evaluation, grading, and reward modeling, yet they are validated primarily on accuracy against golden data. Accuracy alone does not reveal whether judges remain stable under re-prompting, challenge, or sustained pushback, so there is a need to systematically measure epistemic robustness rather than just correctness.
AI.method: The authors propose the Wiggle Framework, which decomposes judge robustness into three dimensions: Mechanical Consistency (stability under re-prompting and reframing), Single-turn Conviction (stability under a single challenge), and Multi-turn Persistence (stability under sustained or adaptive pressure). The framework is applied to 9 frontier models across 14 judging tasks spanning safety, toxicity, AI writing detection, and political-response evaluation.
AI.result: Every model exhibits substantial wiggle: verdicts flip 25–71% of the time under static pushback and 62–91% under an adversarial LLM persuader. Pressure that changes a judge's verdict is almost always net-corrupting relative to ground truth. Baseline jury majority strength emerges as the most effective single-shot signal for anticipating which items wiggle.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first apples-to-apples cross-dataset comparison of mechanical, conformity, and persuadability tests for LLM judges, demonstrating that epistemic instability is pervasive and that majority-consensus signals can help predict wiggle-prone items.

title: Predicting consumer-technology ownership without a diffusion history
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, supplementary material included (Tables S1-S6, Figure S1), data and code at https://osf.io/dr5ct
summary: We test whether the perceived attributes of a consumer technology predict how widely it is owned. In a 2022 Prolific survey of US adults (n = 678), respondents rated 65 consumer technologies on six attributes. We then elicited the same ratings from two frontier language models, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-5.5. We regress ownership prevalence on four UTAUT2 acceptance attributes plus a log-age covariate with a sign-constrained penalized regression and evaluate it by holding out one technology at a time. The attribute model improves on a baseline of years-since-launch: mean absolute error falls by 17% with the human ratings, and by more with either model, most with Opus 4.7. Over the short 2022-to-2025 window, where ownership moved little, the same attributes do not improve on a no-change baseline. We set out the limitations of the approach, including the possibility that language-model ratings reflect prior knowledge of these technologies rather than independent attribute reasoning. We include a deployment illustration: 2027 ownership predictions for eleven products launched in 2025 and 2026.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether perceived attributes of consumer technologies predict how widely they are owned, comparing human survey ratings with those from two frontier language models and evaluating the predictive value over a baseline.
AI.motivation: Understanding what drives adoption of consumer technologies is important for forecasting and product strategy. The authors ask whether perceived attributes (as conceptualized in UTAUT2) can predict ownership prevalence better than simpler baselines, and whether frontier language models can supply those attribute ratings in place of costly human surveys.
AI.method: A 2022 Prolific survey of 678 US adults rated 65 consumer technologies on six attributes. The same ratings were elicited from two frontier language models (Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-5.5). Ownership prevalence was regressed on four UTAUT2 acceptance attributes plus a log-age covariate using a sign-constrained penalized regression, evaluated via leave-one-technology-out cross-validation against baselines of years-since-launch and (for a short 2022–2025 window) a no-change baseline.
AI.result: The attribute model reduces mean absolute error by 17% over a years-since-launch baseline using human ratings, with larger reductions using either language model (most with Opus 4.7). Over the short 2022-to-2025 window, where ownership changed little, the attributes do not improve on a no-change baseline. The paper also includes 2027 ownership predictions for eleven products launched in 2025 and 2026.
AI.conclusion: Perceived attributes have predictive value for ownership prevalence, and language models can supply these ratings effectively, though this may partly reflect prior knowledge of the specific technologies rather than independent reasoning. The approach has limitations, including weak forecasting power over short horizons and potential circularity in model-generated ratings.

title: Training Under Challenge: Executable Certificates and Challenge-Closed Optimality for Neural Networks
comment: 82 pages, 24 figures, 10 tables. Ancillary reproducibility materials included
summary: A flat training curve does not reveal whether a neural network has reached a global optimum, is locally trapped, is representation-limited, or is mismatched to its trainer. We introduce Training Under Challenge, an executable-certificate framework in which predeclared, architecture-valid procedures construct complete alternatives in the same certified class and reevaluate the same objective. Any lower-valued candidate is a replayable witness that lower-bounds the checkpoint's empirical global-optimality gap. Passing a finite suite is only suite-relative; global-gap conclusions require a separately justified coverage mechanism. We define a resource-indexed challenge-power modulus that characterizes the largest gap compatible with passage. For squared loss, current block-decrease operators make coverage checkable and yield uniform and realized-residual bounds. We prove the converse frontier: without coverage, a first-order ReLU trainer can reach infinitely many exact conditional head optima while converging to a non-global point. On a channel-gated ResNet-18 distillation problem with known optimum, eight internal challenges cover all 240 audited output directions, and realized-residual bounds lie within factors of 1.74--3.02 of the true gap. Paired predictive certificates separate decoder under-use from representation insufficiency, while quantized-denoising studies demonstrate diagnosis, repair, and current-state recertification.

AI.tldr: Proposes "Training Under Challenge," a framework using architecture-valid challenge procedures to produce certified alternative solutions that lower-bound a checkpoint's empirical global-optimality gap, with theoretical coverage analysis and practical results on ResNet-18 distillation and quantized denoising.
AI.motivation: A flat training curve is uninformative: it cannot distinguish global optimum, local traps, representation limits, or trainer mismatch. Existing diagnostics cannot certify how far a checkpoint is from a global optimum, motivating a verifiable, replayable lower-bound mechanism.
AI.method: Introduces an executable-certificate framework where predeclared, architecture-valid procedures build complete alternatives in the same certified class and reevaluate the objective. Any lower-valued candidate is a replayable witness lower-bounding the empirical global-optimality gap. Defines a resource-indexed challenge-power modulus to characterize the largest gap compatible with passing a finite suite, and notes that global-gap conclusions require a separately justified coverage mechanism. For squared loss, current block-decrease operators make coverage checkable and give uniform and realized-residual bounds.
AI.result: Proves a converse frontier: without coverage, a first-order ReLU trainer reaches infinitely many exact conditional head optima while converging to a non-global point. On channel-gated ResNet-18 distillation with known optimum, eight internal challenges cover all 240 audited output directions, with realized-residual bounds within factors 1.74–3.02 of the true gap. Paired predictive certificates separate decoder under-use from representation insufficiency; quantized-denoising studies demonstrate diagnosis, repair, and recertification.
AI.conclusion: Challenge-based certificates give tight, replayable lower bounds on the global-optimality gap and enable diagnosis and repair, but passing a finite suite is only suite-relative; definitive global-gap certificates require an independently justified coverage mechanism.

title: Understanding Backdoor Vulnerabilities in Vertical Federated Learning: The Gap Between Research and Practice
summary: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) enables organizations holding complementary features of shared entities to collaborate and train models. In this setting, the initiator can withhold information about the learning task, while other contributors participate without exposing their local datasets, creating an asymmetric information structure aligned with growing privacy demands. However, this asymmetry is a double-edged sword. Among various threats, backdoor attacks are particularly concerning because VFL not only enables malicious contributors to poison the model during training, but also allows them to activate the backdoor at inference time to manipulate predictions. Although prior work has reported near-perfect attack success rates and proposed effective defenses, we find that most findings fail to hold under realistic conditions, exposing a fundamental gap between research and practice. In this paper, we present a systematic, practice-oriented study of backdoor vulnerabilities in VFL, revealing this gap in both methodological design and evaluation practices. We show that existing approaches overlook key practical constraints and therefore rely on unrealistic prior knowledge. Furthermore, these limitations have remained hidden due to poorly designed evaluation practices in the literature. To bridge this gap, we redefine threat models under realistic constraints, propose practical backdoor workflows, and introduce BVBench, a backdoor-centric benchmark that enables fair, practical, and comprehensive evaluation, preloaded with state-of-the-art baselines. BVBench provides strong evidence of the fragility of the current understanding of VFL backdoor risks and establishes a foundation for steering research toward uncovering practical vulnerabilities and developing more meaningful defenses.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that existing Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) backdoor attack/defense findings largely fail under realistic conditions, and proposes practical threat models, attack workflows, and BVBench—a backdoor-centric benchmark—to enable fair and practice-oriented evaluation.
AI.motivation: VFL's asymmetric information structure (the initiator hides the task while contributors keep data private) makes it vulnerable to backdoor attacks during training and inference. Prior work reports near-perfect attack success rates and effective defenses, but the authors find these results do not hold under realistic constraints, exposing a gap between research and practice caused by unrealistic assumptions and flawed evaluation practices.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic, practice-oriented study of VFL backdoor vulnerabilities. They identify overlooked practical constraints and unrealistic prior knowledge in existing approaches, redefine threat models under realistic constraints, propose practical backdoor workflows, and introduce BVBench—a backdoor-centric evaluation benchmark preloaded with state-of-the-art baselines for fair, practical, and comprehensive evaluation.
AI.result: Existing VFL backdoor attack and defense findings fail to generalize under realistic conditions due to unrealistic assumptions and poorly designed evaluations. BVBench provides strong evidence of the fragility of current understanding of VFL backdoor risks and establishes a foundation for uncovering practical vulnerabilities and developing meaningful defenses.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental gap between VFL backdoor research and practice. Redefining threat models under realistic constraints and adopting a practical benchmark like BVBench is essential to steer future research toward uncovering real vulnerabilities and building more meaningful defenses.

title: Safety vs. Social Image: Co-Designing Protection Mechanisms Against Ableist Harassment with People with Disabilities in Social Virtual Reality
summary: People with disabilities (PWD) increasingly use avatars to express disability identities in social virtual reality (VR), but greater visibility also invites targeted harassment. Existing safety features are often insufficient, overlooking PWD's experiences and needs. To address this gap, we co-designed protection mechanisms with 11 PWD to reveal their values and needs. Our research employed a social lens to interpret harassment behaviors and protection mechanisms. Inspired by Hall's Proxemics Theory that interpersonal distances indicate social intent and boundaries, we divided social VR spaces into four proxemic zones (Intimate, Personal, Social, and Public) and used them to structure our protection mechanism co-design. We also provided different protection mechanism probes (Inform, Educate, Consent, and Combat) to elicit participant preferences. Our study highlighted the role of social proximity in shaping PWD's harassment perception and protection preferences and revealing PWD's unique social values and needs (e.g., managing harassment with optimism and resilience, prioritizing social image over safety). We proposed design recommendations for protection mechanisms that protect PWD while maintaining their desired social images.

AI.tldr: The paper co-designs harassment protection mechanisms for people with disabilities (PWD) in social VR. Using Hall's Proxemics Theory, it divides VR spaces into four proxemic zones (Intimate, Personal, Social, Public) and uses four protection probes (Inform, Educate, Consent, Combat) with 11 PWD. The study finds social proximity shapes PWD's harassment perception and protection preferences, revealing PWD prioritize social image over safety and manage harassment with optimism and resilience. It proposes design recommendations that protect PWD while preserving their desired social images.
AI.motivation: PWD increasingly use avatars to express disability identities in social VR, but this visibility invites targeted harassment. Existing safety features are insufficient because they overlook PWD's specific experiences and needs.
AI.method: A co-design study with 11 PWD using a social lens. Grounded in Hall's Proxemics Theory, social VR spaces were divided into four proxemic zones (Intimate, Personal, Social, Public). Four protection mechanism probes (Inform, Educate, Consent, Combat) were provided to elicit participant preferences.
AI.result: Social proximity shapes PWD's harassment perception and protection preferences. The study reveals PWD's unique social values and needs, such as managing harassment with optimism and resilience and prioritizing social image over safety.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes design recommendations for protection mechanisms that protect PWD from harassment while maintaining their desired social images, addressing the gap left by existing safety features.

title: SteerBench-Work: A Benchmark for Agent Steering at Action Boundaries
summary:
Long-running LLM agents act through tools, and a single step can send an email, merge a pull request, or wire a payment. The steering decision is the pre-commit choice at that boundary: proceed, or hold for human or policy review. We introduce SteerBench-Work, an incident-anchored, bidirectional benchmark for that decision in workplace agents across developer operations, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, and security.
  Release v2026-05 contains 106 scenarios anchored in public incidents, paired evidence-reversed mirrors, and calibration controls, with labels split nearly evenly between proceed and hold so the two error directions get near-identical numbers of chances. A model sees the proposed action and the available evidence, returns a gate decision, and is scored on whether it crosses or holds the boundary correctly. Across 30 model conditions the failures run almost entirely in one direction: models wrongly hold authorized, evidence-cleared work on 28.1% of opportunities and wrongly allow unsafe work on 1.0%. The hardest cases are risk-resolved commits, where signed or structured evidence has already cleared a real risk trigger, and models score markedly worse on evidence-reversed mirrors of famous incidents (63.8%) than on the incidents themselves (98.5%). General capability is not the same as steering calibration: higher-capability models often over-refuse at the commit boundary, and more reasoning can repair a weak gate while leaving a calibrated one flat. The public leaderboard is at steerbench.com.

AI.tldr: SteerBench-Work is a benchmark of 106 incident-anchored scenarios testing whether LLM workplace agents correctly decide to proceed with, or hold for review, high-stakes tool-based actions (email, PR merge, payment, etc.). Across 30 models, errors are one-sided: models wrongly hold legitimate work 28.1% of the time but wrongly allow unsafe work only 1.0%.
AI.motivation: Long-running LLM agents take irreversible actions through tools, and the steering (gate) decision — proceed vs. hold for human/policy review — is critical, yet there is no dedicated benchmark measuring how well models calibrate this decision. The authors also aim to show that general capability does not equal steering calibration.
AI.method: They built SteerBench-Work, an "incident-anchored, bidirectional" benchmark with 106 scenarios across Dev Ops, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, and security. Scenarios are anchored in public incidents, mirrored with reversed evidence, and include calibration controls, with proceed/hold labels split nearly evenly. Models see the proposed action and available evidence, return a gate decision, and are scored on boundary correctness.
AI.result: Across 30 model conditions, failures are almost entirely in one direction: 28.1% wrongly hold authorized, evidence-cleared work vs. 1.0% wrongly allow unsafe work. Hardest cases are risk-resolved commits (where signed/structured evidence cleared a real risk trigger). Models score 98.5% on famous incidents but only 63.8% on their evidence-reversed mirrors. Higher-capability models often over-refuse; more reasoning repairs a weak gate but leaves a calibrated one flat.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are poorly calibrated for the steering decision in workplace agents, mainly erring toward over-refusal rather than unsafe action, and general capability does not imply steering calibration. SteerBench-Work provides a public leaderboard (steerbench.com) to measure and improve this boundary decision.

title: New Terms, New Toxicity: Consensus-based Chinese Neologism Toxicity Detection via Search-Augmented LLMs
summary: Neologisms, emerging terms in meaning or form, can serve as new vehicles for toxic expression, like "country girl" as a stigmatizing label targeting feminism. Such toxic neologisms appear benign but have evolved into toxic usage in public consensus, posing challenges to moderation systems and remaining underexplored. In this paper, we investigate how to detect implicit toxicity expressed via neologisms. We first propose a taxonomy that captures the origins and consensus-verification criteria of toxic neologisms, followed by the construction of a lexicon spanning widely observed risk categories. To capture toxicity grounded in public consensus, we introduce SeTox, a search-augmented framework that enables static large language models (LLMs) to incorporate real-time web context for neologism toxicity detection. Experiments show that SeTox, even with 3B-scale models, outperforms recent large-scale models, demonstrating its scalability to incorporate real-world knowledge for toxic neologism detection. Disclaimer: this paper has offensive contents that may be disturbing to some readers.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the detection of implicit toxicity expressed through neologisms—new terms that look benign but have acquired toxic meanings. The authors introduce a taxonomy and lexicon of toxic neologisms, and propose SeTox, a search-augmented framework that lets static LLMs use real-time web context to detect toxicity grounded in public consensus. Experiments show SeTox outperforms larger-scale models even at 3B scale.
AI.motivation: Toxic neologisms (e.g., "country girl" as a stigmatizing feminist label) appear innocuous but carry toxic meaning through evolving public consensus, making them hard for moderation systems to catch. This problem is underexplored, so the authors aim to enable detection of implicit toxicity hidden in emerging terms.
AI.method: The authors (1) propose a taxonomy capturing the origins and consensus-verification criteria of toxic neologisms, (2) build a lexicon covering widely observed risk categories, and (3) introduce SeTox, a search-augmented framework that lets static LLMs incorporate real-time web context to detect toxicity grounded in public consensus.
AI.result: Experiments show that SeTox, even using 3B-scale models, outperforms recent large-scale models, demonstrating its scalability in incorporating real-world knowledge for toxic neologism detection.
AI.conclusion: SeTox effectively enables static LLMs to leverage real-time web context, achieving strong toxic neologism detection performance that exceeds much larger models, showing promise for scalable moderation of emerging toxic language.

title: Demand Transfer Estimation at Scale via Restricted Logit Modeling
comment: 8 pages. Accepted in the Main Conference of IEEE ICMLA 2026
summary:
Item demand forecasting is an integral component of store assortment optimization. Existing literature focuses on learning a suitable customer choice model and using this model to determine the value of an objective function (i.e. expected demand) with respect to an assortment proposal. However, for large item universe with many categories, this approach can prove inefficient, needing a separate demand forecast for every possible item assortment. An alternate approach exists whereby we combine the efficiency of forecasting item demand independently, while at the same time applying adjustments to the independent forecasts that account for the relations between item demand and the availability of other similar items on the shelf.
  Central to this approach is the estimation of Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients. These DT coefficients represent the percent of a particular target item's (item that the customer walked in the store to buy) demand that is redirected to each other item in the universe should the target item be removed from the shelf. We introduce an approach that allows us to compute these DT coefficients on large item universes (assortments having 1 million+ items). Experiments on data as well as historical transaction data for multiple locations within categories demonstrate that when certain reasonable assumptions about substitution behavior are satisfied, our procedure is able to accurately estimate underlying DT coefficients and lead to improvements in demand forecasting.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a scalable method to estimate Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients, which quantify how a removed item's demand is redistributed to substitute items. This enables efficient assortment-wide demand forecasting on item universes of 1 million+ items without forecasting every possible assortment separately.
AI.motivation: Existing assortment optimization methods rely on customer choice models requiring a separate demand forecast for every possible assortment, which is inefficient for large item universes. The authors seek an approach that combines independent per-item demand forecasting with adjustments capturing substitution relationships between items, at massive scale.
AI.method: The authors introduce a procedure to estimate Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients—the percentage of a target item's demand redirected to each other item when the target is removed from the shelf. The method scales to large item universes (1 million+ items) by leveraging reasonable assumptions about substitution behavior.
AI.result: Experiments on both data and historical transaction data across multiple locations and categories show that, when reasonable substitution assumptions hold, the procedure accurately estimates underlying DT coefficients and improves demand forecasting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DT coefficient estimation approach enables scalable, accurate assortment-aware demand forecasting for very large item catalogs, providing an efficient alternative to choice-model-based per-assortment forecasting.

title: General Probabilities of Causation with Causal Knowledge
summary: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) characterize individual causal responses that cannot be directly observed and therefore generally require partial identification. Tian and Pearl first derived theoretically sharp bounds for binary PoCs, including the probability of necessity (PN), the probability of sufficiency (PS), and the probability of necessity and sufficiency (PNS). Mueller et al. subsequently tightened the bounds for binary PNS by incorporating causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. More recently, Li and Pearl, as well as Shu et al., extended PoCs to multivalued settings and derived corresponding theoretical bounds. These developments naturally raise the question of whether additional causal knowledge can further tighten the bounds in multivalued settings. This paper addresses this question by deriving tighter bounds for multivalued PoCs through the incorporation of causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. We illustrate the theoretical results with toy examples, while simulation studies further demonstrate that the proposed bounds are tighter than existing nonbinary bounds.

AI.tldr: The paper derives tighter bounds for multivalued probabilities of causation (PoCs) by incorporating causal information from covariates and mediators, extending prior binary-setting work to nonbinary outcomes/treatments.
AI.motivation: Probabilities of causation (PN, PS, PNS) capture individual causal responses but are unobservable and only partially identifiable. While Tian and Pearl gave sharp theoretical bounds for binary PoCs, and Mueller et al. tightened binary PNS bounds using covariates/mediators, recent extensions (Li and Pearl; Shu et al.) to multivalued settings still lack analogous covariate/mediator-informed bounds. The open question is whether extra causal knowledge can further tighten bounds in multivalued settings.
AI.method: The authors extend the covariate- and mediator-informed bounding framework from the binary PNS case (Mueller et al.) to multivalued PoCs, deriving new (tighter) bounds that exploit causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. Theoretical results are illustrated with toy examples and validated through simulation studies.
AI.result: The proposed bounds are tighter than existing nonbinary (multivalued) PoC bounds, as demonstrated by toy examples and confirmed by simulation studies.
AI.conclusion: Additional causal knowledge encoded in covariates and mediators can indeed tighten bounds for multivalued probabilities of causation, answering the open question and providing sharper partial identification for nonbinary PoCs.

title: Are you Talking Logic to Me? Assessing Language Models Syllogistic Reasoning Capabilities
comment: Accepted to the International Joint Conference on Rules and Reasoning (RuleML+RR) 2026
summary: Language models (LMs) struggle with logical tasks like reasoning on syllogisms. It has been shown that Knowledge Representation (KR) plays a crucial role in expressing input information to help models solve tasks. This observation motivates our study of the impact of different formal KR notations on syllogistic reasoning by extending the FOLIO and P-FOLIO datasets. Our experiments on Small Language Models (SLMs) in Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Zero-Shot (ZS) settings show that the choice of input notation can yield performances competitive with natural language while enabling faster inference. We also propose a syllogistic categorization method (SEF) and use it to enrich ZS prompts with logical definitions, which boost reasoning in small models. We open-source our framework, Common Logic Grammar Construction (CLGC), as the first Python library for automatically generating syllogisms in KR notations and defining their SEF categories.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how different formal Knowledge Representation (KR) notations affect syllogistic reasoning in language models. It extends the FOLIO and P-FOLIO datasets, proposes a syllogistic categorization method (SEF) to enrich zero-shot prompts, and releases CLGC, a Python library for generating syllogisms in KR notations.
AI.motivation: Language models struggle with logical tasks such as syllogistic reasoning, and prior work shows that Knowledge Representation (KR) plays a key role in how input information is expressed to help models solve tasks. This motivates investigating the impact of different formal KR notations on syllogistic reasoning.
AI.method: The authors extend the FOLIO and P-FOLIO datasets with inputs expressed in different formal KR notations. They evaluate Small Language Models (SLMs) in Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Zero-Shot (ZS) settings. They also propose a syllogistic categorization method called SEF, used to enrich ZS prompts with logical definitions, and develop the Common Logic Grammar Construction (CLGC) framework — the first Python library for automatically generating syllogisms in KR notations and defining their SEF categories.
AI.result: Experiments show that the choice of input notation can yield performance competitive with natural language while enabling faster inference. Additionally, enriching zero-shot prompts with logical definitions via the SEF categorization boosts reasoning in small models.
AI.conclusion: Formal KR notations offer a viable alternative to natural language for syllogistic reasoning in LMs, matching or approaching natural-language performance with faster inference, and the SEF-based logical definition prompting improves small-model reasoning. The open-sourced CLGC library supports future research by automating syllogism generation and categorization.

title: Finding the Needle in a Haystack: Test-Time Analog Circuit Representation Adaptation for Bayesian Optimization
summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient framework for analog circuit topology search, where evaluating each candidate topology can require costly simulation. However, representation-based BO methods typically treat circuit embeddings as fixed after encoder training. This creates a mismatch between representation learning and optimization: embeddings learned to encode or reconstruct circuit structure are not necessarily organized according to the figure of merit (FoM) being optimized. This paper introduces Test-Time Analog Representation Adaptation for Bayesian Optimization (TTARO), an online deep-kernel BO framework that adapts circuit representations throughout the search process. Starting from pretrained circuit embeddings, TTARO jointly learns a nonlinear feature transformation and a Gaussian-process surrogate using the FoM labels of the circuits evaluated so far. Following each new evaluation, TTARO updates the representation and surrogate before selecting the next candidate. We compare TTARO with conventional Gaussian Process-based BO over fixed embeddings and with Deep Kernel Learning (DKL), which learns the representation only from the initial evaluated designs and keeps it fixed throughout the remainder of the search. By continually incorporating newly observed FoM labels into representation learning, TTARO aligns the search space with the optimization objective as BO progresses. In our experiments, TTARO reduces regret AUC by 15.2% on average relative to BO and by 20.7% relative to DKL across 40 encoder/kernel/acquisition settings, outperforming prior art in most settings with reductions as large as 46.7%.

AI.tldr: TTARO is an online deep-kernel Bayesian optimization method that continuously adapts analog circuit embeddings during topology search, reducing regret AUC versus fixed-embedding BO and DKL.
AI.motivation: Representation-based BO methods fix circuit embeddings after encoder training, causing a mismatch between the learned representation space and the figure of merit (FoM) being optimized. The authors aim to keep the representation aligned with the optimization objective throughout the search.
AI.method: Starting from pretrained circuit embeddings, TTARO jointly learns a nonlinear feature transformation and a Gaussian-process surrogate using FoM labels of circuits evaluated so far. After each evaluation, it updates both the representation and surrogate before selecting the next candidate via acquisition.
AI.result: Across 40 encoder/kernel/acquisition settings, TTARO reduces regret AUC by 15.2% on average relative to BO over fixed embeddings and by 20.7% relative to DKL, with reductions up to 46.7% and outperforming prior art in most settings.
AI.conclusion: Continually incorporating newly observed FoM labels into representation learning lets TTARO align the search space with the optimization objective as BO progresses, yielding consistent gains over both fixed-embedding BO and DKL.

title: Sovereign by necessity? Frontier AI export controls, cyber security, and the limits of national AI capability
summary: A small number of firms based in two states produce the most capable frontier AI models. The governments of those states have shown both the legal power and the political will to decide which other countries may use these systems. In June 2026 the United States required a leading developer to obtain licences before releasing its most advanced models to any foreign person, including foreign nationals resident in the United States. The affected models were withdrawn worldwide at short notice, partly because the restriction proved impractical to administer. This followed within months of the first documented case of a largely autonomous, AI-run cyber espionage campaign, and coincided with mounting evidence that frontier models alter the economics of both cyber attack and cyber defence. This article examines how these two developments interact, and situates them within the unusual market dynamics now driving large-scale AI development. It argues that access to frontier AI is becoming part of national cyber defence, that such access can be revoked, and that the obvious remedy of sovereign capability remains only partly feasible for all but a handful of states. Drawing on evidence about training costs, the concentration of computing power and the support offered by national AI programmes, it asks what sovereignty can realistically mean for small and middle powers, and for large powers as well. The article proposes a layered strategy: negotiated access guarantees, sovereignty at the level of inference, hedging with open-weight models, pooled regional capability, sustained talent development and continued investment in basic cyber resilience. The open-weight hedge proves at once more capable and more politically exposed than is commonly assumed. Much of the near-term risk lies in how capable models are deployed and contained rather than in their apparent performance.

AI.tldr: The article analyzes how US export-style licensing of frontier AI models interacts with the rise of AI-driven cyber operations, arguing that access to frontier AI is becoming a component of national cyber defense. It proposes a layered strategy (negotiated access guarantees, inference-level sovereignty, open-weight hedging, regional pooling, talent development, and basic cyber resilience) for states that cannot realistically build sovereign frontier capability.
AI.motivation: Two states controlling frontier AI models have begun restricting foreign access, as shown by the June 2026 US licensing requirement that forced withdrawal of advanced models worldwide. This coincided with the first documented largely autonomous AI-run cyber espionage campaign and growing evidence that frontier models shift the economics of cyber attack and defense, raising urgent questions about what sovereignty means for states unable to build their own frontier AI.
AI.method: The article is an analytical/argumentative piece that examines the interaction between frontier AI access restrictions and AI-enabled cyber conflict. It situates these developments within current AI market dynamics, and draws on evidence about training costs, computing-power concentration, and national AI programs to assess the feasibility of sovereign capability for small, middle, and large powers.
AI.result: The analysis finds that access to frontier AI is becoming part of national cyber defense and that such access can be revoked, while sovereign capability remains only partly feasible for all but a handful of states. It concludes that the open-weight hedge is both more capable and more politically exposed than commonly assumed, and that near-term risk lies mainly in how capable models are deployed and contained rather than in their raw performance.
AI.conclusion: For most states, full sovereign frontier AI capability is unrealistic. The article recommends a layered strategy combining negotiated access guarantees, inference-level sovereignty, open-weight hedging, pooled regional capability, sustained talent development, and basic cyber resilience, while warning that deployment and containment discipline, not model performance, is the critical near-term risk.

title: Designing AI Pipelines for Decision-Ready ITSM Intelligence
summary: IT service management (ITSM) systems accumulate large volumes of heterogeneous ticket data that are difficult for sales and executive stakeholders to convert into actionable intelligence. This paper presents a sociotechnical AI pipeline, designed and evaluated following design science research principles, that transforms raw ITSM exports into a multilevel decision-support artifact. The pipeline combines LLM-based schema normalization, HDBSCAN sub-topic clustering, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering to generate executive-facing Main-topics and granular Sub-topics. A stakeholder evaluation across six artifacts and five raters from Sales Engineering and customer success roles shows that all four decision-support metrics, interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use, on average exceed 4.0 out of 5.0, with trust as the most consistent signal. The findings position ITSM analytics as an Information Systems (IS) problem of transformation, abstraction, and human-centered design.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a sociotechnical AI pipeline that converts heterogeneous ITSM ticket data into a multi-level decision-support artifact, combining LLM-based normalization, HDBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering. Stakeholder evaluation shows decision-support metrics exceed 4.0/5.0, with trust as the most consistent signal.
AI.motivation: IT service management (ITSM) systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous ticket data that sales and executive stakeholders struggle to convert into actionable intelligence. The paper addresses the gap between raw ITSM exports and usable decision-support insights.
AI.method: The authors develop a sociotechnical AI pipeline following design science research principles. It integrates LLM-based schema normalization, HDBSCAN sub-topic clustering, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering to produce executive-facing Main-topics and granular Sub-topics. The artifact is evaluated across six artifacts and five raters from Sales Engineering and customer success roles using four decision-support metrics.
AI.result: All four decision-support metrics—interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use—on average exceed 4.0 out of 5.0, with trust emerging as the most consistent signal across raters.
AI.conclusion: ITSM analytics is framed as an Information Systems (IS) problem involving transformation, abstraction, and human-centered design, positioning the pipeline as an effective multi-level decision-support artifact.

title: Query Timing Produces Opposite Positional Biases Between LLMs and Humans
summary: Positional biases such as recency and primacy effects have been documented in large language models (LLMs), yet the underlying mechanism by which these models make their evaluations remains poorly understood. Both primacy and recency biases have been observed in human judgments in response to evidence, but recent work suggest that \emph{when} the listener updates their beliefs -- during the presentation of evidence or only at the end -- influences the presence of such effects. We investigate whether a similar phenomenon holds for LLMs, finding divergence from human behavior. These biases are more exacerbated in newer models compared to their predecessors.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates positional biases (recency and primacy effects) in large language models, examining whether the timing of belief updates during versus after evidence presentation shapes these biases as in humans, and finds LLMs diverge from human behavior, with biases worsening in newer models.
AI.motivation: Positional biases such as recency and primacy effects are documented in LLMs, but the underlying evaluation mechanism remains poorly understood. In humans, both biases appear in response to evidence, and recent work suggests the timing of belief updating (online during evidence presentation vs. only at the end) influences whether these effects occur. The authors aim to determine whether a similar phenomenon holds for LLMs.
AI.method: The study compares LLM behavior against the human model linking belief-update timing (during vs. end of evidence presentation) to primacy/recency effects, and tests whether language models exhibit the same dependence, including analysis across different model generations.
AI.result: LLMs diverge from human behavior regarding the relationship between belief-update timing and positional biases. Additionally, these positional biases are more exacerbated (stronger) in newer models compared to their predecessors.
AI.conclusion: Language models do not reproduce the human pattern linking belief-update timing to primacy/recency effects, and the magnitude of positional biases has grown in newer model versions.

title: The Impact of Temporal Context Length and Encoding Strategies on Self-Supervised ECG Representation Learning
comment: Accepted at the 48th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC 2026). 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table
summary: Self-supervised electrocardiogram (ECG) models are often trained on a few seconds of ECG signal and, increasingly, on discretized token sequences. It remains unclear whether these choices sacrifice information needed for rhythm inference and longitudinal consistency in real-world ambulatory recordings. We present a controlled study on the Icentia11k single-lead dataset that varies (i) the input horizon (16 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, and 10 minutes) and (ii) the front-end representation (continuous convolutional patch embeddings vs. fixed vector-quantized tokens), while holding the Transformer backbone and training protocol constant. Representations are assessed by downstream abnormal rhythm detection and by patient-level retrieval that probes cross-session stability. Our results show that increasing temporal context beyond 16-second snapshots yields stronger transfer and higher retrieval accuracy, with the strongest performance achieved by the 5- and 10-minute models, indicating improved capture of slow-varying rhythm dynamics and individual-specific structure. Across all evaluated horizons, continuous patch embeddings outperform discretized tokens, suggesting that quantization can discard clinically relevant waveform detail. These findings motivate ECG foundation models that emphasize extended context and continuous encoders for clinical prediction and similarity-based applications. Our code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/muha-0/ecg-ssl-representation-learning.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how input horizon length and front-end representation (continuous embeddings vs. discretized tokens) affect self-supervised ECG models, showing that longer contexts and continuous encoders improve rhythm detection and patient retrieval on the Icentia11k dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised ECG models typically train on a few seconds of signal and increasingly use discretized token sequences, but it is unclear whether these design choices discard information needed for rhythm inference and longitudinal consistency in real-world ambulatory recordings.
AI.method: A controlled study on the Icentia11k single-lead dataset varying (i) input horizon (16s, 1min, 5min, 10min) and (ii) front-end representation (continuous convolutional patch embeddings vs. fixed vector-quantized tokens), while holding the Transformer backbone and training protocol constant. Representations are evaluated via downstream abnormal rhythm detection and patient-level retrieval probing cross-session stability.
AI.result: Increasing temporal context beyond 16-second snapshots yields stronger transfer and higher retrieval accuracy, with best performance from the 5- and 10-minute models, indicating better capture of slow-varying rhythm dynamics and individual-specific structure. Continuous patch embeddings outperform discretized tokens across all horizons, suggesting quantization discards clinically relevant waveform detail.
AI.conclusion: ECG foundation models should prioritize extended temporal context and continuous encoders for clinical prediction and similarity-based applications. Code and pretrained models are publicly released.

title: TopoIntent: Compiling Security Intent into Executable, Compliance-Checked Network Topologies
summary: Enterprise security topology design requires translating business intent, regulatory requirements, and risk assumptions into zones, boundary devices, inter-zone paths, and access-control policies. Existing NetOps automation tools mainly operate after this design is fixed, providing limited support for generating structured security topologies from underspecified natural-language requirements. We present TopoIntent, a system that compiles security intent into executable, compliance-checked network topologies. It uses a schema contract to constrain generation, retrieves reference architectures from a curated template library via dense-vector search, and applies staged fusion for intent-template alignment and security completion. The generated topology is checked against CIS Controls v8.1.2 safeguards visible at the topology layer, while unresolved cases are marked for manual review. Structural gaps are repaired through additive schema-preserving edits. The final topology is exported to Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs, enabling executable reachability and allow/deny tests. Because no public benchmark exists for this requirement-to-topology task, we construct an evaluation set from reference security architecture diagrams. The retrieval set contains 22 templates and 44 synthetic intents across five scenarios, while the held-out set contains 7 templates and 14 intents from finance and government scenarios excluded from retrieval. On the held-out set, additive repair improves topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raises the post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88.

AI.tldr: TopoIntent compiles underspecified natural-language security requirements into executable, compliance-checked network topologies by combining schema-constrained generation, dense-vector template retrieval, staged fusion, CIS Controls v8.1.2 compliance checking, and additive schema-preserving repairs. It exports Mininet-based topologies with iptables ACLs for reachability testing and demonstrates improved compliance and policy pass rates on a newly constructed evaluation benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing NetOps automation tools operate after security topology design is fixed and provide limited support for turning underspecified natural-language requirements into structured security topologies. There is a gap between business/regulatory intent and concrete zone, boundary, path, and access-control designs, with no public benchmark for this requirement-to-topology task.
AI.method: TopoIntent uses: (1) a schema contract to constrain generation; (2) dense-vector search over a curated template library to retrieve reference architectures; (3) staged fusion for intent-template alignment and security completion; (4) compliance checking against CIS Controls v8.1.2 topology-visible safeguards, with unresolved cases flagged for manual review; (5) additive schema-preserving edits to repair structural gaps; and (6) export to Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs for executable reachability and allow/deny testing.
AI.result: On a held-out set of 7 templates and 14 intents from finance and government scenarios, additive repair improved topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raised the post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88. The evaluation set was built from 22 retrieval templates and 44 synthetic intents across five scenarios, plus the held-out set.
AI.conclusion: TopoIntent successfully bridges natural-language security intent and executable network topologies, demonstrating that schema-constrained generation, template retrieval, staged fusion, compliance checking, and additive repair can produce compliant, testable security designs. The system achieves strong compliance and policy pass rates and establishes a new evaluation benchmark for requirement-to-topology generation.

title: PatientAct: Theory-Grounded Mental Health Client Simulation
summary: LLM-based simulated clients are increasingly used to train novice counselors, evaluate LLM therapists, and generate synthetic data. However, current simulators produce overly cooperative clients that disclose too readily, accept therapeutic reframes without resistance, and resolve core issues within a single session. We trace these issues to profiles that lack causal depth and behavioral mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible. We present PatientAct, a framework for client simulation grounded in established clinical theories. Our profiles integrate the 5Ps clinical case formulation, providing causal depth without tying the design to any single therapeutic modality. During simulation, profiles include a dynamic memory layer in which items carry trust thresholds (e.g., symptoms are available early, whereas formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). At each turn, the client's emotional reaction and behavior are modeled before generating a response. If the therapist approaches gated content, PatientAct expresses resistance in terms of quantity, content, and style rather than defaulting to cooperation or a single resistance pattern. We evaluate our framework on 40 clinical situations and demonstrate that it generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility. Moreover, PatientAct significantly outperforms the baselines, yielding substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism. Our code and data will be publicly available via github.com/Sahandfer/PatientHub.

AI.tldr: PatientAct is a framework for realistic client simulation in counseling contexts that adds causal depth (5Ps formulation) and trust-gated dynamic memory, so simulated clients express realistic resistance instead of being overly cooperative, outperforming baselines on resistance quality and behavioral realism.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based client simulators are unrealistically cooperative—clients disclose too readily, accept therapeutic reframes without pushback, and resolve issues in one session. These flaws stem from profiles lacking causal depth and mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible. The authors aim to produce more clinically plausible clients that exhibit realistic resistance.
AI.method: PatientAct grounds client simulation in established clinical theory. Profiles integrate the 5Ps clinical case formulation (providing causal depth while remaining modality-agnostic) and include a dynamic memory layer where each item carries a trust threshold (e.g., symptoms accessible early; formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). At each turn, the client's emotional reaction and behavior are modeled before response generation. When the therapist approaches gated content, PatientAct expresses resistance across quantity, content, and style, rather than defaulting to cooperation or a single resistance pattern.
AI.result: Evaluated on 40 clinical situations, PatientAct generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility and significantly outperforms baselines, yielding substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism.
AI.conclusion: Modeling causal case formulation and trust-gated accessibility produces more clinically plausible and realistically resistant simulated clients than prior simulators, with code and data to be made publicly available.

title: On the Expressive Power of Transformers
summary: Multi-layer transformers form the critical component of essentially all large language models (LLMs) in use today. Because of their ubiquity and computational capability, there is a rapidly growing body of work that aims to precisely calibrate the expressive power of transformers as language recognizers by comparing them against standard models of computation studied for decades by the theoretical computer science community. In this endeavor, circuit complexity has by and large emerged as the "correct" branch of computational complexity to analyze the expressive power of transformers; the reason is that parameterizing transformers by the various resources they use, such as attention and precision, leads to direct comparisons with different classes of circuits parameterized by resources such as type of gates, size, and depth. Here, we present an overview of selected results that delineate the expressive power of transformers using concepts and methods from circuit complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys how circuit complexity can be used to precisely characterize the expressive power of transformers as language recognizers, mapping transformer resource parameters (attention, precision) to circuit complexity classes.
AI.motivation: Transformers are the core component of essentially all modern LLMs, motivating a growing effort to rigorously understand what languages they can recognize. Circuit complexity has emerged as the correct framework because transformer resources (attention, precision) align naturally with circuit resources (gate type, size, depth), enabling direct comparisons against decades of work in theoretical computer science.
AI.method: The paper provides an overview of selected results that use concepts and methods from circuit complexity to delineate the expressive power of transformers. It parameterizes transformers by resources such as attention and precision and compares them against corresponding circuit complexity classes parameterized by gate type, size, and depth.
AI.result: The survey delineates the expressive power of transformers by establishing connections between transformer resource usage and various circuit complexity classes, showing where transformers sit within the landscape of standard computational models.
AI.conclusion: Circuit complexity offers the appropriate lens for precisely calibrating transformer expressive power as language recognizers, and the surveyed results map transformers onto well-understood circuit complexity classes based on their resources.

title: Unified Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Complex Graph Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Graph reasoning provides a promising testbed for evaluating the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), as graph instances can be programmatically generated, structurally controlled, and naturally scaled to long-input settings. However, existing graph reasoning benchmarks have limited coverage of data complexity, rely heavily on manual construction, and lack unified evaluation across text-based and code-based reasoning modes. To address these limitations, we propose {\dataset}, a five-stage \textit{semi-automatic} framework for constructing complex graph reasoning benchmarks. It expands benchmark coverage along five dimensions: \textit{Graph Size}, \textit{Task Complexity}, \textit{Task Description}, \textit{Graph Loading}, and \textit{Task Source}. The framework uses an LLM-based data generator to automatically produce task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, graph-loading scripts, question forms, and evaluation scripts, while retaining human validation at key quality-control stages.
