Based on it, we construct a benchmark with $202$ tasks and evaluate LLMs under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings. Experiments show that the complexity dimensions reveal model limitations that are less visible in existing benchmarks; existing fine-tuned models struggle to generalize to GraphGym, whereas retrieval-augmented methods show scenario-dependent adaptability, improving textual reasoning but not consistently improving coding reasoning. These findings suggest that ours serves as a challenging and diagnostic benchmark for graph reasoning and provides empirical guidance for future enhancement methods. Code and dataset will be published soon.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a semi-automatic benchmark framework for complex graph reasoning in LLMs, covering five complexity dimensions, and evaluates models under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings. Results reveal model limitations not visible in existing benchmarks, poor cross-benchmark generalization of fine-tuned models, and scenario-dependent benefits of retrieval augmentation.
AI.motivation: Existing graph reasoning benchmarks have limited coverage of data complexity, rely heavily on manual construction, and lack unified evaluation across text-based and code-based reasoning modes. The authors aim to fill these gaps with a scalable, semi-automatic benchmark that probes model limitations more thoroughly.
AI.method: The authors propose a five-stage semi-automatic framework that expands benchmark coverage along five dimensions: Graph Size, Task Complexity, Task Description, Graph Loading, and Task Source. An LLM-based data generator automatically produces task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, graph-loading scripts, question forms, and evaluation scripts, while human validation is retained at key quality-control stages. Using this framework, they construct a benchmark of 202 tasks and evaluate LLMs under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings.
AI.result: Experiments show the complexity dimensions expose model limitations less visible in existing benchmarks. Existing fine-tuned models struggle to generalize to the new benchmark (GraphGym), and retrieval-augmented methods show scenario-dependent adaptability, improving textual reasoning but not consistently improving coding reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark serves as a challenging and diagnostic tool for graph reasoning and offers empirical guidance for future enhancement methods. Code and dataset will be released.

title: A Contract-Grade Verifier for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels, and a Native Blackwell Backward for the Gated-Linear-Recurrence Family
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures. Also archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21563213
summary: Systems that generate GPU kernels with language models report high correctness rates. Those rates come from a single loose test: run the kernel on a few random inputs at one fixed shape and accept it if the output is close to a reference. A kernel can pass that test and still be silently wrong. It can return an ordinary number where the true answer is a NaN or an infinity, differ from run to run, break when the shape changes, or accumulate in fp16 where the reference keeps an fp32 total. We build the instrument that checks correctness properly: a contract-grade verifier of twelve adversarial gates, each a property a correct kernel must satisfy, several of them tolerance-free, so no choice of threshold can explain a failure away. Aimed outward, the verifier audits 2,638 machine-generated kernels that a public system's own harness had already accepted as correct. It finds 39.5% broken beyond any tolerance argument and 62.1% carrying at least one violation. The field's standard test accepts 1,487 kernels the verifier rejects, against only 14 the other way. We defend the finding four independent ways: a 7/7 positive control, a threshold-calibration sweep, 98.5% agreement with the reference benchmark's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. Aimed inward, the verifier judges a kernel of our own: the first native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward for the gated-linear-recurrence (GDN) family, including the reverse-state stage the field still runs on a fallback. We establish its correctness independently, against a double-precision oracle, and train five family members through it. The correctness signal behind reported progress in kernel generation is far weaker than the numbers suggest, and a set of tolerance-free contracts would close most of the gap.

AI.tldr: The paper exposes that high reported correctness rates for LLM-generated GPU kernels rest on a weak test (few random inputs at one fixed shape), building a contract-grade verifier with 12 adversarial, several tolerance-free gates that finds 39.5% of previously "accepted" kernels broken and 62.1% with at least one violation.
AI.motivation: Existing correctness evaluation for machine-generated GPU kernels uses a loose, single-shape, few-random-inputs test with tolerance-based comparison, which lets silently wrong kernels pass (NaN/inf mishandling, non-determinism, shape sensitivity, fp16 accumulation drift). The field's reported correctness rates therefore overstate real reliability.
AI.method: The authors construct a contract-grade verifier composed of twelve adversarial gates, each a property a correct kernel must satisfy, with several gates being tolerance-free so no threshold choice can mask failures. They apply it outward to audit 2,638 machine-generated kernels that a public system's harness had already accepted, and inward to verify their own native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward kernel for the gated-linear-recurrence (GDN) family, validated against a double-precision oracle.
AI.result: The verifier finds 39.5% of accepted kernels broken beyond any tolerance argument and 62.1% carrying at least one violation. The standard test accepts 1,487 kernels the verifier rejects while the verifier accepts only 14 the standard test does not. Findings are defended by a 7/7 positive control, a threshold-calibration sweep, 98.5% agreement with the reference benchmark's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. The authors' own GDN backward kernel passes verification and trains five family members.
AI.conclusion: The correctness signal behind reported kernel-generation progress is much weaker than the headline numbers suggest, and a set of tolerance-free contracts would close most of the evaluation gap.

title: Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging: A Semantic Superposition and Contextual Lamination Framework for Malpractice-Resilient Online Assessment
summary: Contemporary online assessment systems rely primarily on browser lockdown, webcam monitoring, and behavioural analytics, yet remain vulnerable to attacks that extract the assessment content itself through screenshots, screen sharing, optical character recognition, and automated scraping. This paper extends the Multi-dimensional Spatio-Temporal Context Camouflaging Model (MSCCM) within the MARS (Multi-modal Assessment Resilience Suite) by introducing the Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging Theory (MCCT), a mathematical framework that protects rendered assessment content through semantic superposition. Authentic assessment content and synthetically generated camouflage are represented as a unified rendering while remaining recoverable only by legitimate candidates. The framework models the adversarial extraction process through an explicit extraction-channel operator and develops six coupled constructs: the Context Inversion Operator, Contextual Lamination Operator, Separation Channel, Human Readability Functional, Computational Ambiguity Functional, and Context Camouflage Tensor. Computational ambiguity is formulated using conditional entropy, yielding a closed-form expression that quantifies uncertainty during unauthorized extraction, while legitimate recovery is guaranteed through an exact filtering identity. We further establish theoretical properties governing ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, and temporal multiplexing, and present a rendering algorithm with computational complexity and a pre-registered evaluation protocol. MCCT provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for behaviorally adaptive, accessibility-aware, and computationally resilient digital assessment by securing rendered assessment content while preserving readability for legitimate users.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging Theory (MCCT), a mathematical framework that protects online assessment content by superimposing synthetic camouflage onto authentic content in a single rendering, recoverable only by legitimate candidates while remaining ambiguous to extractors.
AI.motivation: Existing online assessment security (browser lockdown, webcam monitoring, behavioral analytics) cannot prevent attacks that directly extract assessment content via screenshots, screen sharing, OCR, or automated scraping. There is a need for a principled, mathematically rigorous defense that secures the rendered content itself while keeping it readable for legitimate users.
AI.method: Extends the Multi-dimensional Spatio-Temporal Context Camouflaging Model (MSCCM) within MARS by developing six coupled constructs: Context Inversion Operator, Contextual Lamination Operator, Separation Channel, Human Readability Functional, Computational Ambiguity Functional, and Context Camouflage Tensor. It models adversarial extraction via an explicit extraction-channel operator, formulates computational ambiguity using conditional entropy with a closed-form uncertainty expression, guarantees legitimate recovery through an exact filtering identity, establishes theoretical properties (ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, temporal multiplexing), and provides a rendering algorithm with complexity analysis and a pre-registered evaluation protocol.
AI.result: The framework yields a closed-form expression for computational ambiguity during unauthorized extraction, an exact filtering identity ensuring legitimate recovery, and formal theorems governing ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, and temporal multiplexing, together with a rendering algorithm and evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: MCCT provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for behaviorally adaptive, accessibility-aware, and computationally resilient digital assessment by securing rendered content while preserving readability for legitimate users.

title: Lines and Ladders: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Large-Scale Retail Price Taxonomy
comment: 8 pages. Accepted in the Main Conference of IEEE ICMLA 2026
summary: Maintaining price consistency and executing an Every Day Low Price strategy is critical for global retailers. However, with catalogs spanning millions of active items, manual governance of price relationships is infeasible. Inconsistent pricing across item variants distorts customer value perception and cannibalizes sales. To address this, we present a scalable, context-aware Multi-Agent Framework designed to automate the construction of "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomies. Our framework employs specialized LLM agents to construct these coherent pricing structures by identifying key attributes, extracting multi-modal values, and applying hierarchical grouping logic. Evaluated on real-world enterprise data and deployed in production, our 3-Agent system achieves an F1-score of 0.83 for Lines, outperforming single-agent baselines by mitigating cognitive overload. The system achieves >90% precision and >75% recall in Food & Consumables, and 80.2% assignment accuracy in the unstructured General Merchandise catalog.

AI.tldr: A production-deployed 3-Agent LLM framework automates "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomy construction, achieving F1 0.83 for Lines and high precision/recall across catalog domains.
AI.motivation: Global retailers need to maintain Every Day Low Price consistency across catalogs with millions of items, making manual governance of price relationships infeasible. Inconsistent pricing across item variants distorts customer value perception and cannibalizes sales.
AI.method: A scalable, context-aware Multi-Agent Framework using specialized LLM agents that construct "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomies by identifying key attributes, extracting multi-modal values, and applying hierarchical grouping logic. Evaluated with a 3-Agent system against single-agent baselines on real-world enterprise data.
AI.result: The 3-Agent system achieves an F1-score of 0.83 for Lines, outperforming single-agent baselines by mitigating cognitive overload. It reaches >90% precision and >75% recall in Food & Consumables, and 80.2% assignment accuracy in the unstructured General Merchandise catalog.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent LLM framework is viable for production-scale pricing taxonomy automation, delivering coherent Lines and Ladders structures with strong precision and recall across structured and unstructured catalogs.

title: DIVE: Unlocking Self-Improvement in Frozen Language Models Through Diversity-Driven Skill Evolution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) cannot retain post-deployment experience without parameter updates. We introduce DIVE, a diversity-driven framework that enables frozen LLMs to improve by evolving persistent natural-language skills from task experience and verifier feedback. These skills encode reusable reasoning procedures, verification strategies, common failure modes, and output constraints and are both executed and revised by the same underlying model without access to a teacher model. Since natural-language skill evolution is a stochastic, non-convex search process, optimizing a single skill trajectory can overfit to sampled experience or converge to a suboptimal solution. DIVE mitigates this optimization variance by independently evolving multiple skill populations from bootstrapped experience, adaptively refining them through diverse transformations, and jointly selecting a complementary set of skills. Across six mathematical and logical reasoning tasks and multiple model families, DIVE consistently outperforms existing reasoning methods, prompt-optimization approaches, skill-development frameworks, and memory-based baselines. It achieves rapid self-improvement from accumulated experience, obtaining substantially larger performance gains with fewer rollouts than parameter-based methods such as SFT and GRPO, and prompt optimization with GEPA. Further, the resulting skills transfer across model scales and families, enabling smaller models such as GPT-5-nano to match or outperform larger counterparts, i.e., GPT-5, under conventional prompting. These results establish diversity-driven skill evolution as an effective, interpretable, and parameter-free approach to LLM self-improvement.

AI.tldr: DIVE is a diversity-driven, parameter-free framework that lets frozen LLMs self-improve by evolving persistent natural-language skills from task experience and verifier feedback, avoiding optimization variance through multiple independently evolved skill populations.
AI.motivation: LLMs cannot retain post-deployment experience without parameter updates, so weights-based fine-tuning is costly and incompatible with frozen/deployed models. The authors propose parameter-free self-improvement via natural-language skills. Because skill evolution is a stochastic, non-convex search, optimizing a single skill trajectory risks overfitting to sampled experience or converging to suboptimal solutions; this motivates diversity-driven evolution of multiple populations.
AI.method: DIVE evolves persistent natural-language skills that encode reusable reasoning procedures, verification strategies, common failure modes, and output constraints, executed and revised by the same frozen model without a teacher. It mitigates optimization variance by (1) independently evolving multiple skill populations from bootstrapped experience, (2) adaptively refining them via diverse transformations, and (3) jointly selecting a complementary skill set.
AI.result: Across six mathematical and logical reasoning tasks and multiple model families, DIVE consistently outperforms existing reasoning methods, prompt-optimization methods (GEPA), skill-development frameworks, and memory-based baselines. It achieves rapid self-improvement with fewer rollouts and larger gains than parameter-based methods (SFT, GRPO). Evolved skills transfer across model scales and families, letting smaller models (e.g., GPT-5-nano) match or outperform larger ones (GPT-5) under conventional prompting.
AI.conclusion: Diversity-driven skill evolution is an effective, interpretable, and parameter-free approach to LLM self-improvement, enabling frozen models to accumulate reusable skills that transfer across scales and families.

title: Federated Compositional Muon Optimizer for Matrix-Wise Models
summary: Muon, a more recently developed optimizer, is useful for matrix-wise models in AI areas. Although many works have studied Muon and its variants, these methods are still not particularly well-suited for hierarchical structured problems. To fill this gap, we propose an effective federated compositional Muon (FedCoMuon) optimizer to solve distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization problems. Specifically, our FedCoMuon optimizer builds on compositional gradient tracking and orthogonalized momentum. Moreover, we propose a variance reduced variant of FedCoMuon (FedCoMuon-VR) based on a momentum-based variance reduced technique. In theory, we analyze the convergence properties of our algorithms under the non-i.i.d. and non-convex settings. In particular, we prove that our FedCoMuon-VR obtains a lower sample complexity of $O(ε^{-3})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary solution than the existing FedMuon algorithms. Extensive numerical experiments on robust federated learning and task-distributed risk-sensitive meta learning show that our proposed methods are competitive with existing compositional baselines and achieve the best reported accuracy in several settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FedCoMuon, a federated compositional variant of the Muon optimizer for distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization, along with a variance-reduced version FedCoMuon-VR, and proves improved sample complexity O(ε^{-3}) for finding ε-stationary solutions.
AI.motivation: Muon and its variants are useful for matrix-wise models in AI, but existing methods are not well-suited for hierarchical structured problems. Therefore, there is a need for an effective optimizer that handles distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization problems.
AI.method: The authors propose FedCoMuon, which combines compositional gradient tracking with orthogonalized momentum. They further develop FedCoMuon-VR using a momentum-based variance reduced technique to improve convergence.
AI.result: Under non-i.i.d. and non-convex settings, FedCoMuon-VR achieves a lower sample complexity of O(ε^{-3}) for finding an ε-stationary solution than existing FedMuon algorithms. Extensive experiments on robust federated learning and task-distributed risk-sensitive meta learning show competitive performance with existing compositional baselines and the best reported accuracy in several settings.
AI.conclusion: FedCoMuon and FedCoMuon-VR effectively address distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization, with the variance-reduced variant offering improved sample complexity and superior empirical accuracy across tested federated learning and meta learning tasks.

title: EEG Decoding Using CNN and LSTM Network
summary: Motor imagery (MI) brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a promising approach for establishing flexible communication pathways between the human brain and external devices , particularly for individuals affected by stroke or neurodegenerative disorders. Reliable decoding of motor-imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) remains challenging because EEG recordings contain substantial noise and exhibit complex, weakly informative relationships with the underlying brain activity. Although deep learning provides an effective means of learning representations directly from EEG signals, its application to MI-EEG feature learning remains comparatively limited. This study introduces a hybrid deep-learning architecture that integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a bidirectional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) network. The CNN is used to learn high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG recordings, whereas the bi-LSTM models temporal dependencies and relationships among the extracted features. The proposed approach is evaluated using both a publicly available dataset and a privately acquired dataset obtained with an EEG acquisition system. The experimental results indicate that the CNN\&bi-LSTM architecture provides robust performance for both two- and three-class motor-imagery classification and demonstrates promising subject-independent decoding capability across the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: A hybrid CNN + bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) architecture is proposed for motor-imagery EEG classification, achieving robust performance on both public and private datasets for two- and three-class tasks and showing promising subject-independent decoding.
AI.motivation: Motor imagery BCIs enable flexible brain–device communication, especially for stroke and neurodegenerative disorder patients. However, reliable MI-EEG decoding is difficult because EEG signals are noisy and weakly informative, and deep-learning-based feature learning for MI-EEG remains comparatively limited.
AI.method: The study proposes a hybrid deep-learning model combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a bidirectional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) network. The CNN learns high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG, while the bi-LSTM models temporal dependencies among the extracted features. Evaluation uses a public dataset and a privately acquired dataset collected with an EEG acquisition system.
AI.result: The CNN+bi-LSTM architecture achieves robust performance for both two-class and three-class motor-imagery classification and demonstrates promising subject-independent decoding capability across the evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid CNN+bi-LSTM approach is an effective solution for MI-EEG decoding, delivering robust classification and promising cross-subject generalization, which supports its potential for practical BCI applications.

title: Intensional Anaphora
comment: 49 pages. Published in Semantics and Pragmatics
summary: Intensional operators are often treated as quantifiers over possible worlds, parallel to the treatment of determiners as quantifiers over individuals. Yet individuals introduced in intensional contexts cannot serve as antecedents to later pronouns as easily as those introduced in merely quantificational contexts. For instance, "Everyone is eating a cheeseburger" may be followed by "They are large", where "they" refers to the cheeseburgers being eaten. However, as Stone (1999) points out, the similar "Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger" does not support later anaphoric references such as "It is large" or "They are large". Stone (1999), Stone and Hardt (1999), and Brasoveanu (2010) address this by requiring a pronoun's value (its referents) to exist in the world of evaluation, ruling out anaphora from non-veridical intensional contexts. We show, however, both cases where such anaphora is disallowed even when the pronoun's referents clearly exist and cases where it is allowed even though they might not exist. We argue that intensional anaphora is best captured using a description-based rather than value-based account. A pronoun presupposes that its corresponding antecedent description is instantiated in each world of the context set. Thus, there must be a cheeseburger being eaten by Andrea in every candidate world for "It is large" to be felicitous after "Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger". We implement our proposal via a new logic, building on Keshet (2018) and Abney and Keshet (2022), called Plural Intensional Presuppositional predicate calculus (PIP). Each PIP formula translates directly into standard first-order predicate calculus with set abstraction, providing a classical foundation for this work.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that anaphora out of intensional (modal) contexts is governed by a description-based presupposition rather than by the existence of referents in the evaluation world, and formalizes this via a new logic (PIP) translatable into classical first-order logic.
AI.motivation: Existing accounts (Stone 1999, Stone & Hardt 1999, Brasoveanu 2010) explain intensional anaphora by requiring a pronoun's referents to exist in the world of evaluation, which wrongly predicts both undergeneration (ruling out felicitous anaphora where referents might not exist) and overgeneration (allowing anaphora even when it is infelicitous despite existing referents).
AI.method: The authors propose a description-based (rather than value-based) account: a pronoun presupposes that its antecedent description is instantiated in every world of the context set. They implement this in a new logic, Plural Intensional Presuppositional predicate calculus (PIP), building on Keshet (2018) and Abney and Keshet (2022); each PIP formula translates directly into standard first-order predicate calculus with set abstraction, giving a classical foundation.
AI.result: The authors show cases where intensional anaphora is disallowed even when the pronoun's referents clearly exist, and cases where it is allowed even though the referents might not exist, demonstrating that value-based existence accounts are both too restrictive and too permissive. Their description-based presupposition correctly captures these patterns, illustrated by the contrast between "Everyone is eating a cheeseburger" (supports "They are large") and "Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger" (does not support "It is large").
AI.conclusion: Intensional anaphora is best captured description-based: a pronoun presupposes its antecedent description is instantiated in each world of the context set. The PIP logic provides a classical, compositional foundation for this presuppositional account.

title: Perturbation-based Regional Interpretability through Subtraction Mapping (PRISM): naming-error dissociations in language models and post-stroke aphasia
comment: 49 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Supplementary methods, 6 tables and 5 figures included
summary: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models lacks spatially resolved, falsifiable tools for testing whether internal components are specialized for distinct cognitive operations. We adapt subtraction analysis, the standard framework of human neuroimaging, from biological brains to perturbed transformers, and apply the same logic to both substrates in parallel. Building on the Brain-LLM Unified Model (BLUM), which showed that layer-perturbed LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-13B error profiles match the lesion patterns of aphasic patients, we develop PRISM (Perturbation-based Regional Interpretability through Subtraction Mapping). PRISM maps the seven clinical Philadelphia Naming Test categories, subtracts error classes pairwise, and treats each perturbation seed as a subject in a group analysis with threshold-free cluster enhancement along the layer axis. We run a structurally matched analysis on 213 chronic post-stroke aphasia patients using correlation-difference lesion-symptom mapping, and replicate both sides on held-out splits. The designs match in subject dimension (seeds, patients), spatial dimension (layers, atlas-parcellated cortex) and thresholding, but the contrast operator differs: a within-subject error-proportion difference for the LLM, a between-subject correlation difference for the cortex. Both substrates recover a robust phonemic-favoring dissociation, a deep layer cluster and a frontal-perisylvian cortical cluster, both replicating; the semantic-favoring direction is a consistently signed but non-significant trend on both. PRISM thus gives a falsifiable, spatially resolved test of functional-specialization claims in transformer language models. A confirmatory ROI-level intervention (PRISM Stage 3) licensing the strongest causal-mechanism claim is left to subsequent work.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts subtraction analysis from human neuroimaging to transformers, introducing PRISM to test whether LLM layers are specialized for distinct cognitive operations by matching methodology to lesion-symptom mapping in aphasia patients. Both substrates show a replicable phonemic-favoring dissociation (deep layer / frontal-perisylvian cortex), while semantic-favoring effects remain non-significant trends, providing a falsifiable, spatially resolved test of functional specialization in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models lacks spatially resolved, falsifiable tools for testing whether internal components (e.g., layers) are specialized for distinct cognitive operations. Existing work (BLUM) showed error-profile matches between layer-perturbed LLaVA and aphasic patients but did not provide a formal, spatially explicit subtraction framework with matched statistics across substrates.
AI.method: PRISM (Perturbation-based Regional Interpretability through Subtraction Mapping) maps seven clinical Philadelphia Naming Test categories, subtracts error classes pairwise, and treats each perturbation seed as a subject in a group analysis with threshold-free cluster enhancement along the layer axis. In parallel, a structurally matched analysis is run on 213 chronic post-stroke aphasia patients using correlation-difference lesion-symptom mapping (atlas-parcellated cortex). Both are replicated on held-out splits. The designs match in subject dimension (seeds/patients), spatial dimension (layers/cortex), and thresholding; the contrast operator differs (within-subject error-proportion difference for the LLM vs. between-subject correlation difference for cortex).
AI.result: Both substrates recover a robust phonemic-favoring dissociation—a deep layer cluster in the LLM and a frontal-perisylvian cortical cluster in patients—both of which replicate on held-out splits. The semantic-favoring direction is a consistently signed but non-significant trend in both substrates.
AI.conclusion: PRISM provides a falsifiable, spatially resolved test of functional-specialization claims in transformer language models, with cross-substrate validation against human lesion data. A confirmatory ROI-level causal intervention (PRISM Stage 3) to license the strongest causal-mechanism claim is left to subsequent work.

title: Concept Drift Detection and Adaptive Retraining of Malware Classification Models
comment: To appear as a chapter in the book "Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Defense in Emerging Threats", to be published by Springer by early 2027
summary: Concept drift refers to changes over time in the statistical properties of data, as compared to the data that was used to train a learning model. Machine learning models for malware detection or classification are particularly susceptible to performance degradation caused by concept drift, as attackers constantly modify existing malware. In this chapter, we analyze two machine learning-based approaches to automated concept drift detection-a novel approach based on One-Class Support Vector Machines (OCSVM) and a previously-studied technique based on Minibatch K-Means (MK-Means). For comparison we also consider Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), a statistical technique for detecting changes in multidimensional data. We conduct an extensive series of experiments comparing the effectiveness of four learning models, namely, Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting. For each of these models, we consider three distinct scenarios: A static scenario where no model retraining occurs, a periodic scenario where models are constantly retrained irrespective of concept drift, and a drift-aware scenario where models are only retrained when concept drift is detected. Under the drift-aware scenario, we analyze the tradeoff between accuracy and training efficiency using Pareto Front analysis. We find that all three concept drift detection techniques achieve classification accuracy comparable to periodic retraining, while offering substantially greater efficiency in terms of the number of models that must be retrained. In addition, drift-aware retraining based on our OCSVM technique generally outperforms the MK-Means and MMD approaches. Overall, these results provide strong evidence that we can accurately detect concept drift in malware classification models.

AI.tldr: The paper compares three concept drift detection methods (a new OCSVM approach, Minibatch K-Means, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy) across four malware classification models, showing that drift-aware retraining matches periodic retraining's accuracy while being far more efficient, with OCSVM generally performing best.
AI.motivation: Malware classification models suffer performance degradation from concept drift because attackers constantly modify malware, altering data statistical properties relative to training data. The authors seek efficient, automated ways to detect this drift so models can be retrained selectively rather than constantly.
AI.method: The authors analyze two machine learning-based concept drift detection approaches: a novel One-Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM) technique and a previously-studied Minibatch K-Means (MK-Means) technique, plus the statistical Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) method. They test four learning models (Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting) under three scenarios: static (no retraining), periodic (always retraining), and drift-aware (retrain only when drift is detected). They use Pareto Front analysis to evaluate the accuracy-vs-training-efficiency tradeoff in the drift-aware scenario.
AI.result: All three concept drift detection techniques achieve classification accuracy comparable to periodic retraining while substantially reducing the number of models that must be retrained. The drift-aware retraining based on the OCSVM technique generally outperforms the MK-Means and MMD approaches.
AI.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence that concept drift in malware classification models can be accurately and efficiently detected, with the OCSVM-based method being the most effective among those tested.

title: The Role of Natural Language Understanding in Multimodal Video-Based Dengue Diagnosis
summary: Detecting infection-related behavioral changes in mosquitoes from video data is challenging because mosquitoes are small, move rapidly and irregularly, and are affected by environmental factors such as background, lighting, and shadows, which can make reliable feature extraction difficult. In this study, a YOLO- and Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based vision-language framework is proposed to classify mosquito flight frames of uninfected and Dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV2)-infected mosquitoes. First, YOLO is used to isolate mosquito regions from the background. Then, visual features extracted from video frames are aligned with biologically meaningful textual prompts in a shared embedding space. The multimodal model was fine-tuned using supervised bidirectional contrastive learning and evaluated through frame-level image-text similarity-based classification. The results show that the proposed method achieved 98.54% accuracy and 99.91% sensitivity at the frame level. After temporal aggregation of frame-level information, the model achieved complete video-level performance. The ablation results showed that fine-tuning and CLIP-based representations were essential for this domain, while the textual branch provided semantic image-text alignment rather than an accuracy advantage over the vision-only model. These findings suggest that vision-language models can provide a useful framework for analyzing infection-related biological behaviors from video data.

AI.tldr: A YOLO + CLIP vision-language framework classifies flight video frames of uninfected vs. DENV2-infected mosquitoes, achieving 98.54% frame-level accuracy and near-perfect video-level performance after temporal aggregation.
AI.motivation: Detecting infection-related behavioral changes in mosquitoes from video is difficult due to their small size, rapid and irregular movement, and sensitivity to environmental factors (background, lighting, shadows), which hinder reliable feature extraction. This motivates a vision-language approach that can leverage semantic alignment to analyze subtle biological behaviors.
AI.method: First, YOLO isolates mosquito regions from the background. Visual features extracted from video frames are then aligned with biologically meaningful textual prompts in a shared embedding space. The multimodal model is fine-tuned using supervised bidirectional contrastive learning and evaluated via frame-level image-text similarity-based classification. Frame-level predictions are temporally aggregated for video-level decisions.
AI.result: The method achieved 98.54% accuracy and 99.91% sensitivity at the frame level, and complete (100%) video-level performance after temporal aggregation. Ablations showed fine-tuning and CLIP-based representations were essential for this domain, while the textual branch contributed semantic image-text alignment but no accuracy advantage over the vision-only model.
AI.conclusion: Vision-language models provide a useful framework for analyzing infection-related biological behaviors from video data, despite the textual branch mainly enabling semantic alignment rather than boosting accuracy.

title: When Explanations Betray Backdoors: Black-Box Auditing for Language Model Classifiers
summary: Language model classifiers with explanations are used for moderation, routing, topic triage, and low-resource annotation. We study black-box auditing when the defender has only clean calibration data without trigger information but can ask the classifier for a label plus a short rationale or quoted evidence. We introduce Groundedness Drift, a lightweight score measuring whether the answer summary remains grounded in the input. Across two 7B backbones, five datasets, and four common non-adaptive OpenBackdoor-style attack families, Groundedness Drift achieves higher AUROC and lower residual target ASR than every compared detector in all cases at a nominal 5\% clean-FPR budget. We then evaluate Unsupported Groundedness, a multi-probe escalation for explanation-camouflage stress cases. Unsupported Groundedness improves signals but does not close the adaptive gap.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Groundedness Drift, a lightweight black-box audit score that detects backdoor/poisoning attacks on LLM classifiers by measuring whether the model's explanation (answer summary) stays grounded in the input. It outperforms all compared detectors across datasets and attack families at a fixed clean false-positive budget, and a follow-up multi-probe method (Unsupported Groundedness) improves signals for camouflage cases but still leaves an adaptive gap.
AI.motivation: LLM classifiers with explanations are widely deployed for moderation, routing, topic triage, and low-resource annotation, making them attractive targets for backdoor attacks. Existing auditing often assumes access to trigger information, which is unrealistic. The authors aim to enable black-box auditing using only clean calibration data (no trigger information) by exploiting the rationales/evidence the classifier produces, and to test whether explanation-based signals can detect even explanation-camouflaged attacks.
AI.method: The paper proposes Groundedness Drift, a lightweight score that measures whether an answer summary remains grounded in the input, computed from the classifier's label plus its short rationale or quoted evidence. It is evaluated across two 7B backbones, five datasets, and four common non-adaptive OpenBackdoor-style attack families, compared against existing detectors at a nominal 5% clean false-positive rate. A second method, Unsupported Groundedness, is a multi-probe escalation designed for explanation-camouflage stress cases, which probes the model multiple times to improve detection signals.
AI.result: Groundedness Drift achieves higher AUROC and lower residual target attack success rate (ASR) than every compared detector in all cases at a nominal 5% clean-FPR budget. Unsupported Groundedness improves detection signals on explanation-camouflage stress cases but does not close the adaptive gap (an adaptive attacker can still evade).
AI.conclusion: Explanation-groundedness auditing via Groundedness Drift is a practical, trigger-free black-box defense that outperforms prior detectors, though adaptive attacks that explicitly camouflage explanations remain a challenge that the multi-probe Unsupported Groundedness mitigates but does not fully solve.

title: MAG: MAnifold Guided Semi-Supervised Multi-modal In-Context Learning
summary: Few-shot in-context learning (ICL) with multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) enables task adaptation without parameter updates, but its performance is highly sensitive to the quality and coverage of the selected demonstrations. While unlabeled multi-modal data is abundant, it remains elusive how to exploit them for ICL. We propose MAG (MAnifold-Guided semi-supervised in-context demonstra- tion selection), an efficient framework that leverages unlabeled data to improve multi-modal ICL. MAG formulates demonstration selection as a semi-supervised propagation problem on a multi-modal graph and adopts a two-stage strategy: (i) relevance score propagation identifies a compact set of high-impact unlabeled samples for pseudo-labeling, reducing MLLM inference cost; (ii) multi-modal relevance is used to select the final demonstrations. We show that textual represen- tations are more effective for relevance propagation, while both visual and textual modalities are crucial for high-quality demonstration selection. Experiments on eight multi-modal benchmarks demonstrate that MAG consistently outperforms strong baselines in label-scarce regimes, achieving significant gains with a limited pseudo-labeling budget.

AI.tldr: MAG is a framework for semi-supervised in-context demonstration selection in multimodal LLMs that treats selection as graph-based relevance propagation over unlabeled data, using text-only propagation to cheaply pseudo-label a compact set and then combined visual+text cues to pick the final demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Few-shot in-context learning with multimodal LLMs is highly sensitive to the quality and coverage of chosen demonstrations. Unlabeled multimodal data is abundant but underutilized, so the paper seeks an efficient way to exploit it to improve ICL without parameter updates.
AI.method: MAG formulates demonstration selection as semi-supervised propagation on a multimodal graph with a two-stage approach: (1) relevance score propagation identifies a compact, high-impact subset of unlabeled samples for pseudo-labeling to cut MLLM inference cost, and (2) multimodal relevance is used to select final demonstrations. Textual representations are used for propagation, while both visual and textual modalities inform final selection.
AI.result: Text representations are more effective for relevance propagation, whereas both visual and textual modalities are crucial for high-quality demonstration selection. Across eight multimodal benchmarks, MAG consistently beats strong baselines in label-scarce settings, yielding significant gains even with a limited pseudo-labeling budget.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MAG framework efficiently leverages unlabeled multimodal data to boost few-shot in-context learning, reducing inference cost via targeted pseudo-labeling and improving demonstration quality by combining visual and textual relevance, with robust gains demonstrated across diverse benchmarks.

title: Beyond the Best Guess: Improving LLM Solution Coverage with Evolution Strategies
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in discovery domains such as math and science. The usual approach is to present the problem to the model and use its answer as the proposed solution. However, beyond this best guess, discovery can be enhanced by increasing test-time compute. In a process called pass@k, the model is allowed to explore the solution space and generate diverse candidate solutions. Unfortunately, the standard approach to post-training LLMs through Reinforcement Learning (RL) may limit pass@k: the model's output distribution narrows around high-reward outputs, causing the solution coverage to collapse. The alternative is to use Evolution Strategies (ES), a population-based, gradient-free post-training method that optimizes directly in weight space through random perturbations. As this paper shows, ES achieves consistently higher pass@k than RL and produces a broader output distribution with greater solution coverage. This coverage in turn makes it possible to achieve better results in e.g. standard math benchmarks. Thus, ES provides a better foundation for post-training in discovery problems and other domains where diverse solution coverage is critical.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Evolution Strategies (ES) outperform Reinforcement Learning (RL) for post-training LLMs in discovery domains, because RL narrows the output distribution and collapses solution coverage, while ES yields higher pass@k and broader solution diversity.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in discovery domains (math, science) where exploring diverse candidate solutions is valuable, but standard RL post-training collapses the model's output distribution around high-reward outputs, limiting pass@k performance and solution coverage.
AI.method: The authors post-train LLMs using Evolution Strategies (ES), a population-based, gradient-free method that optimizes directly in weight space via random perturbations, and compare it against standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training.
AI.result: ES consistently achieves higher pass@k than RL and produces a broader output distribution with greater solution coverage, which leads to better results on standard math benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ES provides a better foundation for post-training in discovery problems and other domains where diverse solution coverage is critical, since it preserves distributional diversity that RL tends to collapse.

title: A Cloud-Edge System for Multimodal Clinical Screening in Resource-Constrained Rural Settings
comment: 31 pages, 3 figures. In Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Volume 340, 2026 (Machine Learning for Healthcare Conference)
summary: Medical AI has demonstrated specialist-level diagnostic accuracy, yet these capabilities remain largely inaccessible in resource-constrained rural settings where bandwidth is scarce, compute is limited, and clinical decision-making requires integrating heterogeneous modalities. We introduce a cloud--edge collaborative architecture that addresses these constraints: lightweight, domain-specific models on the edge transform raw medical data into compact structured outputs, while a cloud LLM synthesizes these outputs into clinical summaries. An LLM-based orchestrator dynamically selects diagnostic tools based on patient context, promoting comprehensive modality coverage without processing irrelevant inputs. We evaluate on 20 multimodal clinical cases spanning cardiac, obstetric, trauma, and screening scenarios under three simulated network profiles (500,kbps--5,Mbps). The hybrid system achieves 98--99% diagnostic tool recall with 92--96% precision, matches or exceeds cloud-only baselines on clinical accuracy, and maintains bandwidth-invariant latency (25--35,s) at 4--15x lower token cost. These results highlight the role of architectural design in enabling efficient multimodal integration and improving factual grounding compared to cloud-only approaches under deployment constraints.

AI.tldr: A cloud–edge collaborative architecture lets edge devices run lightweight domain models to compress raw medical data into compact structured outputs, while a cloud LLM synthesizes clinical summaries and an LLM-based orchestrator selects only relevant diagnostic tools. Tested on 20 multimodal cases under constrained networks, it achieves high tool recall/precision, matches cloud-only accuracy, and keeps latency bandwidth-invariant at much lower token cost.
AI.motivation: Specialist-level medical AI remains inaccessible in resource-constrained rural settings due to scarce bandwidth, limited compute, and the need to integrate heterogeneous modalities during clinical decision-making. The paper seeks to make multimodal medical AI deployable under these constraints without sacrificing accuracy or factual grounding.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-tier architecture: (1) lightweight, domain-specific edge models transform raw medical data (e.g., imaging, signals) into compact structured outputs; (2) a cloud LLM synthesizes these outputs into clinical summaries; and (3) an LLM-based orchestrator dynamically selects diagnostic tools based on patient context to ensure comprehensive modality coverage while avoiding irrelevant inputs. The system is evaluated on 20 multimodal clinical cases across cardiac, obstetric, trauma, and screening scenarios under three simulated network profiles (500 kbps–5 Mbps).
AI.result: The hybrid system achieves 98–99% diagnostic tool recall with 92–96% precision, matches or exceeds cloud-only baselines on clinical accuracy, maintains bandwidth-invariant latency of 25–35 seconds, and reduces token cost by 4–15x compared to cloud-only approaches.
AI.conclusion: Architectural design (edge compression plus cloud orchestration/summarization) enables efficient multimodal integration and improves factual grounding relative to cloud-only systems under real deployment constraints, making specialist-grade medical AI viable in resource-limited environments.

title: Spatial Memory Agent: Experience-Grounded Procedure Memory for Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial intelligence is becoming a foundation for embodied agents, robotic planning, and multimodal assistants. To improve the spatial reasoning ability of VLM agents, existing work has mainly followed two lines. One line uses post-training methods, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Another line adopts an agentic paradigm in which the model calls external spatial tools, such as depth estimation and 3D reconstruction tools, to gather intermediate spatial evidence. We study a complementary and underexplored route: Can a frozen VLM agent improve its spatial reasoning through \textbf{parameter-update-free self-evolution}, without depending on external expert spatial tools at inference time? We present \textbf{Spatial Memory Agent (SMA)}, an \textbf{experience-grounded runtime framework} that converts verified spatial experience into reusable transferable lessons. In a verifiable spatial environment, SMA queries the frozen VLM, obtains a predicted answer and reward, and uses \textbf{verifier-guided reflection} to distill compact transferable lessons from spatial experience. SMA further assigns each lesson a \textbf{Transfer Reliability Score (TRS)}, which is initialized uniformly and calibrated from later retrieval outcomes as visit evidence of future transfer reliability. During \textbf{read-only deployment}, SMA retrieves lessons by semantic filter and similarity-TRS combined ranking, allowing the retrieved memory to guide frozen model inference. Across five representative spatial benchmarks and four base VLMs, SMA achieves the highest macro average in every base-model block and the best accuracy among the evaluated methods in most of the 20 evaluations, establishing a practical parameter-update-free path for spatial self-evolution across the evaluated frozen model scales and environments.

AI.tldr: SMA enables a frozen VLM to improve spatial reasoning without parameter updates or external spatial tools, by converting verified spatial experiences into reusable, transferable lessons with reliability scoring, and retrieves them at inference time to guide the model.
AI.motivation: Improving spatial reasoning in VLM agents has relied on post-training (SFT/RL) or agentic use of external spatial tools. The authors explore a complementary, underexplored route: whether a frozen VLM can self-evolve its spatial reasoning in a parameter-update-free manner, avoiding costly training and dependence on external expert spatial tools at inference time.
AI.method: SMA is an experience-grounded runtime framework operating in a verifiable spatial environment. It queries the frozen VLM for an answer and reward, then applies verifier-guided reflection to distill compact, transferable lessons from spatial experience. Each lesson is assigned a Transfer Reliability Score (TRS), initialized uniformly and calibrated from subsequent retrieval outcomes as evidence of future transfer reliability. During read-only deployment, SMA retrieves lessons via a semantic filter combined with similarity-TRS ranking, and the retrieved memory guides frozen model inference—all with no parameter updates.
AI.result: Across five representative spatial benchmarks and four base VLMs, SMA achieves the highest macro average in every base-model block and the best accuracy among evaluated methods in most of the 20 evaluations, validating its effectiveness across frozen model scales and environments.
AI.conclusion: SMA establishes a practical, parameter-update-free path for spatial self-evolution of frozen VLMs, demonstrating that verified experience can be distilled into transferable, reliability-scored lessons that effectively guide inference without external spatial tools or fine-tuning.

title: Novels generated by language models show compressed formal variation
summary: While large language models can generate entire novels, there is little information about the level of formal variation in their output over many generations. Rather than asking whether individual passages can be identified as AI-generated, this study asks whether repeated AI generation can produce the same range of diversity which is found across human corpora. This paper contrasts six corpora based on generation source and target style: twenty novels generated using GPT-5.5 Thinking in a nineteenth-century British realist style, twenty novels generated using Qwen3-14B in a nineteenth-century British realist style, twenty novels generated using each of these models in a contemporary zero style, 205 nineteenth-century human-written British novels, and sixty-five contemporary human-written Zero-Style novels. At the document level, the research includes MATTR-500, Shannon entropy, average sentence length, readability, and punctuation rate measurements. The most robust and reliable result is compression of sentence structure. Repeated generations produce novels that vary far less from one another in sentence structure than human novels do. Compression is also present in the measures of readability, punctuation, and sentence length variability within novels. Lexical measures tend to be similarly compressed, with the exception of Qwen Zero-Style MATTR. Despite having distinct mean stylistic profiles, GPT and Qwen lack a stable pattern of cross-measure correlation. This article therefore distinguishes between variance overclosure, which represents a limited formal range between novels, and a more specific phenomenon of correlational overclosure. This means that an individual AI-generated novel may resemble human fiction stylistically, while a collection of AI-generated novels occupies a much narrower formal range.

AI.tldr: Repeated AI novel generation produces far less formal variation than is found across human-written novels, a phenomenon the paper terms "variance overclosure," with a distinct subtype of "correlational overclosure."
AI.motivation: Existing research on AI-generated text focuses on detecting individual AI passages, but little is known about whether repeated large-scale generation can reproduce the formal diversity found across human corpora.
AI.method: The study contrasts six corpora by generation source and target style: 20 novels generated with GPT-5.5 Thinking and 20 with Qwen3-14B in a nineteenth-century British realist style; 20 novels from each model in a contemporary "zero" style; 205 nineteenth-century human-written British novels; and 65 contemporary human-written Zero-Style novels. It measures MATTR-500, Shannon entropy, average sentence length, readability, punctuation rate, and analyzes cross-measure correlations and within-novel variability.
AI.result: The most robust finding is compression of sentence structure: AI-generated novels vary far less from one another than human novels do. Compression also appears in readability, punctuation, and sentence-length variability within novels, and in most lexical measures (except Qwen Zero-Style MATTR). Despite distinct mean stylistic profiles, GPT and Qwen show no stable cross-measure correlation patterns.
AI.conclusion: The paper distinguishes variance overclosure (limited formal range between novels) from correlational overclosure (lack of stable cross-measure relationships). An individual AI-generated novel may resemble human fiction stylistically, yet a collection of AI novels occupies a much narrower formal range.

title: Decentralized Multi-Player Q-Learning in Episodic Markov Decision Processes with Information Asymmetry
summary: We study decentralized multi-player reinforcement learning in episodic tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) under three forms of information asymmetry: (A) unobserved actions with common rewards, (B) observed actions with independent rewards, and (C) unobserved actions with independent rewards. Players cannot communicate during learning but may agree on a protocol a priori. For Problems A and B we propose \texttt{mQ-learning} and \texttt{mQ-learning-intervals}, achieving $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^4 S A_{\text{joint}}\, T})$ regret, where $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the state count, $T = KH$ the total steps, and $A_{\text{joint}} = \prod_{i=1}^M |\mathcal{A}_i|$ the joint action space across $M$ players. For Problem C we give \texttt{mEXC} and \texttt{mEXC-Bellman}, two-phase explore-then-commit algorithms with regret $\tilde{O}(H (S A_{\text{joint}})^{1/3} T^{2/3})$. Against the centralized joint-action benchmark, decentralized learning under information asymmetry matches the single-agent Q-learning rate of \cite{jin2018q} up to logarithmic factors. Because $A_{\text{joint}}$ grows exponentially in $M$, the bounds are most meaningful for small $M$ or small per-player action sets.

AI.tldr: The paper studies decentralized multi-player reinforcement learning in episodic tabular MDPs under three information asymmetry settings (unobserved actions/common rewards, observed actions/independent rewards, unobserved actions/independent rewards). It proposes mQ-learning and mQ-learning-intervals for Problems A and B achieving ~O(√(H⁴ S A_joint T)) regret, and mEXC/mEXC-Bellman for Problem C with ~O(H (S A_joint)^(1/3) T^(2/3)) regret, matching centralized single-agent Q-learning rates up to log factors.
AI.motivation: Players cannot communicate during learning but can agree on a protocol beforehand. The goal is to achieve near-optimal regret in decentralized multi-player RL under different forms of information asymmetry, matching the centralized joint-action benchmark without communication.
AI.method: The paper proposes model-free algorithms: mQ-learning and mQ-learning-intervals for Problems A (unobserved actions, common rewards) and B (observed actions, independent rewards); and mEXC and mEXC-Bellman, two-phase explore-then-commit algorithms, for Problem C (unobserved actions, independent rewards). Regret is analyzed against the centralized joint-action benchmark.
AI.result: For Problems A and B, regret is ~O(√(H⁴ S A_joint T)); for Problem C, regret is ~O(H (S A_joint)^(1/3) T^(2/3)). Both match the single-agent Q-learning rate of Jin et al. (2018) up to logarithmic factors. Here H is horizon, S state count, T = KH total steps, and A_joint = Π|A_i| the product action space.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized learning under information asymmetry attains the centralized joint-action benchmark. Because A_joint grows exponentially in the number of players M, the bounds are most meaningful for small M or small per-player action sets.

title: Excess Separability: Nuisance-Controlled Residual-Stream Probing for Benchmark Contamination Detection
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, 7 tables. Code and artefacts: https://github.com/mabushi-lab/residual-stream-contamination-probing
summary:
Benchmark contamination is diagnosed today with n-gram overlap, with likelihood-based membership inference, or with canary strings, and each needs something usually unavailable: the training corpus, a well-chosen test statistic, or foresight at dataset release. A recent alternative reads contamination off a linear probe on internal activations. We show that the natural way to do this does not work, and specify one that survives measurement.
  The protocol reports a zero-sum contrast on the depth profile of probe accuracy, recentred on a level-matched placebo baseline, tested against a label-permutation null, with the reference set twice the size of the suspect set. Each choice replaces a simpler alternative we measured and rejected. Reporting the level of excess separability rather than its shape makes the false positive rate track the size of the analyst's own control set, from 0.03 to 0.99 under a true null. Contrasting against a flat depth profile fails in both directions, rejecting a true null 0.72 of the time when surface decodability rises with depth and losing all power when it falls. An item bootstrap holds the fitted probe fixed and rejects up to 0.09 of the time where a permutation null that refits it holds 0.02. A half-size baseline triples the error rate.
  On real transformers, baseline depth profiles are measurably not flat, spanning up to 29.1 accuracy points on a temporal split, and their non-flatness tracks the surface difference between the item sets (correlation 0.87 over 6 audits), so the correction is largest exactly where it is needed. All 4 well-matched Pile arms return null, and the protocol refuses a verdict on the temporal split rather than reporting one. What this does not establish is whether transformers carry a familiarity direction at all: the only positive sits on the split where exchangeability fails. Implementation, tests and audits are released.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a probe-based method for detecting benchmark contamination in language models. It finds that the natural (naive) linear-probe approach fails, and develops a corrected protocol—centered zero-sum depth-profile contrast against a matched placebo baseline with a label-permutation null—then validates its false-positive behavior and audits real transformers.
AI.motivation: Existing contamination diagnostics (n-gram overlap, likelihood-based membership inference, canary strings) each require something usually unavailable: the training corpus, a well-chosen test statistic, or foresight at dataset release. A recent alternative reads contamination from a linear probe on internal activations, but its natural implementation does not actually work. The authors aim to establish which probe-based protocol can survive measurement and report trustworthy false-positive rates.
AI.method: The protocol computes a zero-sum contrast on the depth profile of probe accuracy, recentered on a level-matched placebo baseline, and tests it against a label-permutation null, with the reference set twice the size of the suspect set. Each design choice replaces a simpler alternative that the authors measured and rejected (e.g., shape-based reporting, flat-depth contrast, item bootstrap, half-size baseline). They validate false-positive rates under a true null and audit real transformers on matched Pile arms and a temporal split, measuring baseline non-flatness and its correlation with surface differences between item sets.
AI.result: The natural probe approach fails. In the corrected protocol, reporting excess separability level (not shape) makes the false-positive rate track the analyst's control-set size (0.03 to 0.99 under a true null). Contrasting against a flat depth profile fails both directions: it rejects a true null 0.72 of the time when surface decodability rises with depth and loses all power when it falls. An item bootstrap rejects up to 0.09 where the refitting permutation null holds 0.02. A half-size baseline triples the error rate. On real transformers, baseline depth profiles are measurably non-flat (up to 29.1 accuracy points on a temporal split), and this non-flatness tracks surface differences between item sets (correlation 0.87 over 6 audits). All 4 well-matched Pile arms return null, and the protocol refuses a verdict on the temporal split. The only positive occurs where exchangeability fails, so whether transformers carry a familiarity direction remains unestablished.
AI.conclusion: A probe-based contamination detector can be made valid by centering on a matched placebo baseline, using a zero-sum depth-profile contrast, and testing with a label-permutation null; each simpler alternative fails measurably. However, the protocol cannot establish that transformers encode a familiarity direction, since the sole positive sits on a split where exchangeability fails, and it correctly refuses a verdict on the temporal split.

title: Beyond Outcome Rewards: Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization for Deep Search Agents
summary: Deep search agents operate over trajectories spanning dozens of steps, yet standard reinforcement learning provides only a single outcome reward per trajectory, which is far too sparse for effective credit assignment. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) addresses this by using the model's own logits as dense token-level teachers, but extending it to search agents introduces a fundamental tension: the teacher, having access to privileged information such as the correct answer, produces a distribution that differs systematically from the student's exploration-based reasoning, and naive distillation causes the student to inherit this information asymmetry rather than learn better search strategies. We resolve this tension through two contributions. First, we construct Evidence Anchors, which are concise, step-level evidence snippets extracted from the web, as privileged information that captures key reasoning steps without revealing the entire answer path. Second, we propose Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO), which converts teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights within GRPO, applied exclusively to incorrect trajectories. This design decouples what to update from how much to update: the outcome reward determines the direction of policy change, while the teacher modulates its magnitude at each step. Correct trajectories are left untouched, preserving their diversity. On Qwen3-8B, SSPO consistently outperforms GRPO across BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES, surpassing or matching GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps while adding only about 5 percent overhead per step from a single additional forward pass.

AI.tldr: SSPO improves credit assignment for deep search agents by distilling privileged "evidence anchors" into step-level advantage weights inside GRPO, applied only to incorrect trajectories, outperforming GRPO on BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES at roughly 5% overhead.
AI.motivation: Deep search agents span many steps but receive only one sparse outcome reward, making credit assignment hard. Existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is unsuitable because the teacher has privileged information (e.g., the correct answer), causing its distribution to diverge from the student's exploration-based reasoning, so naive distillation makes the student inherit information asymmetry instead of learning better search.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) Evidence Anchors—concise, step-level evidence snippets extracted from the web—serve as privileged information capturing key reasoning steps without revealing the full answer path. (2) Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO) converts teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights within GRPO, applied only to incorrect trajectories. The outcome reward sets the direction of policy change (what to update) while the teacher modulates magnitude per step (how much to update); correct trajectories are left untouched to preserve diversity.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B, SSPO consistently outperforms GRPO on BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES, surpassing or matching GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps while adding only about 5% overhead per step from a single additional forward pass.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling update direction (outcome reward) from update magnitude (teacher-modulated step weights) and restricting distillation to incorrect trajectories, SSPO resolves the teacher-student information asymmetry and yields efficient, stronger search-agent training.

title: PROVE-RT: Generating Mechanized Theorem Prover Scripts for Real-Time Systems using LLMs
summary:
Schedulability analysis is essential for certifying real-time systems, but existing tests are often developed through pen-and-paper proofs that are difficult to scale, validate, and maintain. Mechanized verification in PROSA/ROCQ offers a rigorous alternative, yet manually constructing such proofs requires substantial domain expertise and proof-engineering effort. Recent successes of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks make them promising candidates for generating PROSA/ROCQ scripts for mechanized theorem provers. However, state-of-the-art LLMs often lack the PROSA-specific knowledge required to correctly use its modeling abstractions and proof patterns.
  This paper introduces PROVE-RT, an LLM-assisted framework for generating PROSA/ROCQ scripts to mechanize schedulability analyses in real-time systems literature. PROVE-RT guides generation through dependency-aware informal sketches, retrieval from processed PROSA documentation, staged skeleton generation, and proof completion. We construct a mechanization-oriented corpus from 1, 191 real-time systems papers, containing 13, 134 informal sketches with dependency information. On a curated evaluation set, direct prompting of state-of-the-art LLMs fails to reliably generate valid PROSA mechanizations, whereas PROVE-RT achieves a success rate of 44.7%. These results show that retrieval-guided and staged LLM assistance can improve automated mechanization of schedulability analysis in PROSA/ROCQ.

AI.tldr: PROVE-RT is an LLM-assisted framework that generates PROSA/ROCQ mechanized proofs for real-time schedulability analysis, using dependency-aware sketches, retrieval, staged skeleton generation, and proof completion to achieve a 44.7% success rate where direct LLM prompting fails.
AI.motivation: Existing schedulability analysis tests rely on pen-and-paper proofs that are hard to scale, validate, and maintain. Mechanized verification in PROSA/ROCQ is rigorous but manually constructing proofs demands heavy domain expertise and proof-engineering effort. LLMs are promising for proof generation but lack the PROSA-specific knowledge needed to correctly use its abstractions and proof patterns.
AI.method: PROVE-RT combines four components: (1) dependency-aware informal sketches to guide generation, (2) retrieval from a processed PROSA documentation corpus, (3) staged skeleton generation, and (4) proof completion. The authors built a mechanization-oriented corpus from 1,191 real-time systems papers containing 13,134 informal sketches with dependency information, and evaluated on a curated test set against direct prompting of state-of-the-art LLMs.
AI.result: Direct prompting of state-of-the-art LLMs fails to reliably generate valid PROSA mechanizations, while PROVE-RT achieves a 44.7% success rate on the curated evaluation set, demonstrating that retrieval-guided and staged LLM assistance improves automated mechanization.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-guided and staged LLM assistance can meaningfully improve automated mechanization of schedulability analysis in PROSA/ROCQ. PROVE-RT shows that combining domain-specific retrieval, dependency-aware sketches, and staged generation enables LLMs to produce valid proofs where direct prompting fails, advancing automated certification of real-time systems.

title: ERSkill: Evolving for Skill-Guided Adaptive Memory Retrieval
summary: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on long-term memory for persistent interactions, the retrieval mechanisms governing this memory are rarely treated as evolvable components. This static approach limits performance on heterogeneous memory queries, which often demand diverse evidence construction strategies. To address this, we introduce \textbf{ERSkill}, a retrieval-centric framework for self-evolving, skill-guided memory access. ERSkill compiles interaction histories into a structured memory store and represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills composed of fundamental primitives. At inference time, a trained router dynamically matches each query to the optimal skill to construct tailored evidence for answer generation. To enable continuous improvement, ERSkill co-evolves the skill set and the router during training. It employs an experience trie to efficiently record explored retrieval paths, alongside a double-frontier mechanism that safely decouples the expansion of new skill capabilities from stable, router-facing deployment. Experiments across multiple agent memory benchmarks demonstrate that ERSkill substantially outperforms strong non-evolving and self-evolving baselines. Notably, it improves the overall average across F1, BLEU-1, and LLM-judge scores by 31.3\% with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and by 28.1\% with GPT-5.4-nano.

AI.tldr: ERSkill is a self-evolving, retrieval-centric framework for LLM agent memory that treats retrieval mechanisms as evolvable skills. It matches queries to optimal skills via a trained router, and co-evolves both skills and router during training using an experience trie and a double-frontier mechanism, significantly outperforming baselines across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly depend on long-term memory, but retrieval mechanisms are typically static and not treated as evolvable components. This limits performance on heterogeneous memory queries that require diverse evidence construction strategies, motivating a framework where retrieval behavior can continuously improve.
AI.method: ERSkill compiles interaction histories into a structured memory store and represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills built from fundamental primitives. At inference, a trained router dynamically maps each query to the optimal skill to construct tailored evidence. During training, an experience trie efficiently records explored retrieval paths, and a double-frontier mechanism safely decouples the expansion of new skill capabilities from stable router-facing deployment, enabling co-evolution of the skill set and router.
AI.result: Across multiple agent memory benchmarks, ERSkill substantially outperforms strong non-evolving and self-evolving baselines, improving the overall average of F1, BLEU-1, and LLM-judge scores by 31.3% with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and by 28.1% with GPT-5.4-nano.
AI.conclusion: Treating memory retrieval as a self-evolving, skill-guided process substantially improves LLM agent memory performance, validating the ERSkill framework for continuous, safe improvement of retrieval mechanisms.

title: CoMedBench: A Multi-Source Benchmark of Synthetic Medical Data Fidelity and Downstream Utility
summary: Access to clinical data is essential for developing reliable healthcare machine learning systems, but direct use of electronic health records is constrained by privacy regulation, institutional review, data-use agreements, and the risk of re-identification. Synthetic data promises a practical alternative: it can preserve useful statistical and clinical structure while reducing exposure of sensitive patient records. Prior studies often evaluate a single generator, one dataset, or a narrow downstream task, making it difficult to know when synthetic data can support model development and when it fails to preserve task-critical signal. We introduce CoMedBench, a reproducible benchmark that evaluates a family of generators under a common clinical-validity framework and one shared training and evaluation engine, spanning static tabular and temporal downstream tasks on established critical-care datasets. In total the benchmark spans 37 dataset-task pairs across two modalities consists of 20 static tabular and 17 temporal ICU time-series-drawn from seven public data sources: three intensive-care databases (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU) together with the UCI Machine Learning Repository, the CDC BRFSS diabetes cohort (2015), NHANES (1999-2014), and the pycox survival datasets (GBSG and METABRIC). The benchmark evaluates both statistical fidelity and task utility by comparing models trained and tested across real and synthetic data. In these settings, synthetic training data preserves most of the downstream signal: on tabular tasks the reference generator CoMed-CTGAN retains a mean AUROC utility (the synthetic-to-real performance ratio) of 90.6%, rising to 97.3% for the strongest generator, CoMed-TVAE. Temporal ICU tasks are harder and more generator-sensitive: CoMed-CTGAN retains 81.6% (AUROC) and only 64.0% under the imbalance-sensitive AUPRC, whereas CoMed-TVAE still retains ~95% (AUROC).

AI.tldr: CoMedBench is a reproducible benchmark for evaluating synthetic health data generators across 37 dataset-task pairs (20 tabular, 17 temporal ICU time-series) from seven public sources, measuring both statistical fidelity and downstream task utility.
AI.motivation: Real clinical data is limited by privacy regulation, IRB review, and re-identification risk, motivating synthetic data as an alternative. However, prior studies evaluate only a single generator, one dataset, or a narrow task, making it unclear when synthetic data preserves task-critical signal.
AI.method: The authors introduce CoMedBench, a common clinical-validity framework with a shared training/evaluation engine covering static tabular and temporal tasks. It spans 37 dataset-task pairs (20 static tabular, 17 temporal ICU time-series) from seven sources: MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, eICU, UCI ML Repository, CDC BRFSS diabetes (2015), NHANES (1999-2014), and pycox survival datasets (GBSG, METABRIC). It evaluates statistical fidelity and task utility by comparing models trained and tested across real and synthetic data.
AI.result: Synthetic training data retains most downstream signal. On tabular tasks, CoMed-CTGAN retains mean AUROC utility of 90.6%, rising to 97.3% for CoMed-TVAE. Temporal ICU tasks are harder and more generator-sensitive: CoMed-CTGAN retains 81.6% AUROC and only 64.0% AUPRC, while CoMed-TVAE still retains ~95% AUROC.
