AI.conclusion: Synthetic data can support model development, preserving most downstream signal; tabular tasks are well-preserved, while temporal ICU tasks are more challenging and sensitive to generator choice, especially under imbalance-sensitive metrics like AUPRC.

title: ARAC: Benchmarking Auto-Research's Alignment and Completeness on End-to-End Researchs
summary: The rapid advancement of Auto-Research has surfaced a fundamental evaluation challenge: how can we measure the alignment, logical coherence, and evolutionary completeness of its research trajectory with human research behavior? We propose Auto-Research's Alignment and Completeness, ARAC-Bench: a Researcher-Mimicking Evaluation framework that shifts the objective from matching final answers to reproducing high-quality human research processes. The framework operates through two synergistic components: the Academic Cognition Skills system, which is the first to transforms implicit reviewer expertise into stage-calibrated, quantifiable rubrics; and a three-stage capability diagnostic protocol, which decomposes the research process under strict modular constraints into three traceable, mutually independent dimensions: Proposal, Experiment, and Synthesis. Systematic evaluation of 11 SOTA frameworks yields a best alignment score of only 67.9 of 100, revealing a significant gap in simulating rigorous human methodology. Validation against Ph.D. Candidates rankings shows a strong correlation of 0.8141, confirming that ARAC-Bench reliably reflects the dimensions researchers truly value. ARAC-Bench provides not only a fine-grained diagnostic tool but also a scalable reward signal for training the next generation of autonomous research systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ARAC-Bench, an evaluation framework for Auto-Research that measures how well autonomous research systems mimic human research processes. It uses stage-calibrated rubrics (Academic Cognition Skills) and a three-stage diagnostic protocol (Proposal, Experiment, Synthesis). Evaluation of 11 SOTA frameworks shows a best alignment score of only 67.9/100, and the benchmark correlates strongly (0.8141) with Ph.D. candidate rankings.
AI.motivation: Auto-Research is advancing rapidly, but existing evaluation methods focus on matching final answers rather than assessing the alignment, logical coherence, and evolutionary completeness of the research trajectory against human research behavior. There is a need to measure whether these systems reproduce high-quality human research processes, not just correct outputs.
AI.method: ARAC-Bench introduces two synergistic components. First, the Academic Cognition Skills system, which transforms implicit reviewer expertise into stage-calibrated, quantifiable rubrics. Second, a three-stage capability diagnostic protocol that decomposes the research process under strict modular constraints into three traceable, mutually independent dimensions: Proposal, Experiment, and Synthesis. The framework is validated against 11 SOTA frameworks and correlated with Ph.D. candidate rankings.
AI.result: Systematic evaluation of 11 state-of-the-art frameworks yields a best alignment score of only 67.9 out of 100, indicating a significant gap in simulating rigorous human methodology. Validation against Ph.D. candidate rankings shows a strong correlation of 0.8141, confirming the benchmark reliably reflects dimensions researchers truly value.
AI.conclusion: ARAC-Bench provides a fine-grained diagnostic tool for assessing Auto-Research systems and serves as a scalable reward signal for training the next generation of autonomous research systems, shifting evaluation from output matching to process reproduction.

title: HiRoute: Hierarchical Routed Prompt Tuning for Safety Alignment of Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to harmful requests and jailbreak attacks. Parameter-efficient safety alignment methods based on prompt tuning typically rely on a single global prompt or externally selected prompt modules. Such static designs struggle to maintain a cross-category safety boundary while generating constructive responses tailored to specific risks and avoiding over-refusal of benign inputs. To address these limitations, we propose HiRoute, an input-adaptive hierarchical prompt-tuning framework that separates category-agnostic safety control from category-specific response guidance. HiRoute first trains a lightweight hierarchical router on representations extracted from a frozen LLM to jointly detect harmful intent and predict multi-label risk scores. It then freezes both the backbone model and the router and uses preference optimization with alternating gradient updates to learn a shared coarse-grained prompt and a set of fine-grained prompt experts as continuous embeddings. At inference time, benign inputs bypass the safety branch, whereas risky inputs are processed using the shared prompt together with a router-weighted mixture of risk-specific prompt experts. Experiments across three instruction-tuned models show that HiRoute achieves high safety rates across multiple safety benchmarks while preserving safe-response helpfulness, reducing over-refusal, and maintaining competitive performance on general-purpose tasks.

AI.tldr: HiRoute is an input-adaptive, hierarchical prompt-tuning framework that decouples category-agnostic safety control from category-specific response guidance, using a frozen-LLM router plus coarse and fine-grained prompt experts to improve safety while reducing over-refusal.
AI.motivation: LLMs remain vulnerable to harmful requests and jailbreak attacks. Existing parameter-efficient safety alignment based on prompt tuning uses a single global prompt or externally selected prompt modules, which are static and fail to maintain cross-category safety boundaries while tailoring responses to specific risks and avoiding over-refusal of benign inputs.
AI.method: HiRoute trains a lightweight hierarchical router on representations from a frozen LLM to jointly detect harmful intent and predict multi-label risk scores. Then, with the backbone and router frozen, it uses preference optimization with alternating gradient updates to learn a shared coarse-grained prompt and a set of fine-grained prompt experts as continuous embeddings. At inference, benign inputs bypass the safety branch; risky inputs use the shared prompt combined with a router-weighted mixture of risk-specific prompt experts.
AI.result: Across three instruction-tuned models, HiRoute achieves high safety rates on multiple safety benchmarks while preserving safe-response helpfulness, reducing over-refusal, and maintaining competitive performance on general-purpose tasks.
AI.conclusion: HiRoute effectively addresses the limitations of static prompt-based safety alignment by adaptively separating generic safety control from risk-specific guidance, yielding robust safety, better helpfulness, fewer over-refusals, and preserved general capability.

title: CABS+: Efficient and Scalable Model Merging via Conflict-Aware Sparsification and Adaptive Weight Allocation
summary: Model merging has recently attracted significant attention as a promising paradigm for constructing unified multi-task models without requiring additional retraining. However, parameter conflicts and knowledge interference across tasks often degrade merged-model performance. Prior work introduced Conflict-Aware and Balanced Sparsification (CABS), which reduces parameter interference through structured pruning and sequential masking. However, CABS relies on grid search to determine scaling coefficients, resulting in exponential time complexity, while its optimization objective can be dominated by high-performance tasks, leading to suboptimal overall performance. To address these limitations, we extend CABS and propose CABS+. Specifically, Adaptive Weight Allocation (AWA) optimizes merging coefficients via a gradient-free search scheme to reduce time complexity, while an asymmetric fitness function promotes more comprehensive performance gains across tasks. Moreover, we conduct a systematic empirical study of key factors influencing model merging performance and propose Relative Synergy Score (RSS) to quantify model mergeability and guide model selection. We compare CABS+ with state-of-the-art model merging methods, including CABS, AdaMerging, and WUDIMerging, across 27 datasets and 5 models covering large language, small-scale language, and vision models. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness and efficiency of CABS+. Compared with AdaMerging and WUDIMerging, CABS+ improves overall performance by 16.97% and 12.93%, respectively, exhibits stronger stability and robustness across varying task numbers and model architectures, uses less than 25% of the GPU memory required by AdaMerging, and achieves nearly a 4x speedup in merging time over WUDIMerging.

AI.tldr: CABS+ extends the CABS model-merging framework by replacing grid-search coefficient tuning with gradient-free Adaptive Weight Allocation (AWA) and an asymmetric fitness function, and introduces Relative Synergy Score (RSS) to quantify model mergeability. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods across 27 datasets and 5 models while using far less GPU memory and time.
AI.motivation: Model merging builds unified multi-task models without retraining, but suffers from parameter conflicts and knowledge interference. The prior CABS method reduces interference via structured pruning and sequential masking, yet relies on grid search for scaling coefficients (exponential time complexity) and has an optimization objective biased toward high-performance tasks, yielding suboptimal overall results. The work aims to fix these efficiency and fairness limitations.
AI.method: CABS+ extends CABS with two mechanisms: Adaptive Weight Allocation (AWA), a gradient-free search that optimizes merging coefficients to cut time complexity, and an asymmetric fitness function that promotes more balanced performance across tasks. Additionally, a systematic empirical study of merging-influencing factors leads to a Relative Synergy Score (RSS) metric for quantifying model mergeability and guiding model selection. Evaluation covers 27 datasets and 5 models spanning large language, small-scale language, and vision models, compared against CABS, AdaMerging, and WUDIMerging.
AI.result: CABS+ improves overall performance by 16.97% over AdaMerging and 12.93% over WUDIMerging, shows stronger stability and robustness across varying task numbers and architectures, uses less than 25% of the GPU memory required by AdaMerging, and achieves nearly a 4x speedup in merging time versus WUDIMerging.
AI.conclusion: CABS+ effectively and efficiently addresses the coefficient-search and task-imbalance limitations of CABS, delivering superior, more stable multi-task merging performance at substantially lower computational cost, with RSS providing a principled means to assess mergeability and select models.

title: ReconSpan: Reconstruction-Guided Adaptive Latent Tokenization
summary: Adaptive latent tokenization maps a fine-grained input to a shorter sequence of continuous representations associated with input-dependent spans. We introduce ReconSpan, which divides text into chunks that a backward decoder can reconstruct from a single contextual prefix code and retains one such code as the latent token for each chunk. The reconstruction criterion is applied when chunks are formed, allowing one trained autoencoder to produce average chunk lengths from 6.5 to 12.2. At matched average length, reconstruction-guided boundaries preserve more text than random boundaries. Readers of the resulting latent sequence recover topic information reliably but struggle to extract exact details.

AI.tldr: ReconSpan introduces a reconstruction-guided approach to adaptive latent tokenization, dividing text into chunks each represented by a single latent code that a backward decoder can reconstruct, yielding tunable average chunk lengths from 6.5 to 12.2.
AI.motivation: Traditional fixed-length or naive tokenization loses information in fine-grained inputs; the authors seek adaptive latent tokenization where input-dependent spans are compressed into shorter continuous representations while preserving as much reconstructible content as possible.
AI.method: ReconSpan divides text into chunks, each represented by a single contextual prefix code retained as the latent token. A reconstruction criterion based on a backward decoder is applied during chunk formation, and a single trained autoencoder supports variable average chunk lengths (6.5–12.2).
AI.result: At matched average chunk length, reconstruction-guided boundaries preserve more text than random boundaries. Human readers can reliably recover topic information from the latent sequence but struggle to extract exact details.
AI.conclusion: Reconstruction-guided boundary selection produces more informative latent representations than random segmentation, although the compression trades off fine-grained detail for reliable topic-level recovery.

title: Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing
summary: Online platforms increasingly compare many adaptive decision policies---ranking systems, recommendation algorithms, pricing rules, and language-model agents---while each reward-bearing interaction can be costly or risky. A direct A/B/n design gives each of $J$ policies its own horizon-$T$ trajectory and therefore uses $JT$ outcomes. We introduce Tree-Coupled A/B Testing (\TCAB), an exact feedback-sharing design for arbitrary history-dependent contextual-bandit policies. At each round, a predictable tree connects the current policy histories; every parent--child context--action law is maximally coupled, and one reward is shared within each component of matched tree edges. Every policy retains exactly its standalone finite-horizon trajectory law, even though the policies are deliberately dependent. If $D_{e,t}$ records a mismatch on tree edge $e$ at round $t$, the number of reward queries satisfies the pathwise identity $N(T)=T+\sum_{t,e}D_{e,t}$ and hence equals $T$ plus cumulative tree-edge total variation in expectation. This cost is conditionally optimal among exact edge-local designs on the selected tree, and a current-round minimum-spanning tree is myopically optimal among tree designs. For fixed $J$, sublinear pseudo-regret of every policy and almost-sure uniqueness of the oracle action imply $\mathbb{E}[N(T)]=T+o(T)$, versus $JT$ for independent runs. We also obtain finite-sample variance bounds for pairwise policy contrasts. Experiments on reward-model evaluation, multiple-choice language-model evaluation, and adaptive search policies demonstrate substantial improvements in the cost--precision frontier.

AI.tldr: Tree-Coupled A/B Testing (TCAB) enables comparing J adaptive policies using nearly T reward queries instead of JT, by coupling policy trajectories on a tree so each policy keeps its exact standalone distribution while sharing rewards across matched edges.
AI.motivation: Online platforms increasingly compare many adaptive decision policies, but each reward-bearing interaction is costly or risky. Standard A/B/n designs require JT outcomes for J policies over horizon T, which is expensive. The goal is exact feedback sharing that reduces reward queries without distorting any policy's trajectory law.
AI.method: At each round, a predictable tree connects current policy histories; every parent-child context-action law is maximally coupled, and one reward is shared within each component of matched tree edges. The number of reward queries satisfies the pathwise identity N(T)=T+sum_{t,e} D_{e,t}, where D_{e,t} records a mismatch on tree edge e at round t. This equals T plus cumulative tree-edge total variation in expectation. The design is conditionally optimal among exact edge-local designs on the chosen tree, and a current-round minimum-spanning tree is myopically optimal among tree designs.
AI.result: For fixed J, sublinear pseudo-regret of every policy and almost-sure uniqueness of the oracle action imply E[N(T)]=T+o(T), versus JT for independent runs. The paper also derives finite-sample variance bounds for pairwise policy contrasts. Experiments on reward-model evaluation, multiple-choice language-model evaluation, and adaptive search policies show substantial improvements in the cost-precision frontier.
AI.conclusion: TCAB achieves near-linear (T up to o(T) overhead) reward cost when policies are well-behaved, dramatically reducing the JT cost of independent runs while preserving exact policy distributions and enabling valid variance bounds for contrasts.

title: Beyond Retrieval: Query-Conditioned Reuse of Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories
summary: Retrieval can identify a past trajectory that may matter, yet it does not specify how an acting agent should use that trajectory after users, entities, constraints, or environment state have changed. We identify this post-retrieval reuse step as a distinct bottleneck for long-horizon trajectory memory and formulate an evaluation framework that holds candidate retrieval, target state, model, decoding, and tool budget fixed while varying the support delivered to the agent. We instantiate the framework with query-conditioned reuse (QCR), a deliberately simple target-bound note that records a reusable procedure, bindings to recover, applicability conditions, and verification requirements. QCR serves to test the reuse hypothesis rather than to claim a universally preferred memory format. Across 2,391 target instances in WebArena, WorkArena, and AppWorld, QCR reaches 62.3% average Success, 10.7 points above Full Trajectory, while using 48.9% fewer online tokens. Summary reranking selects a reusable memory for 94.8% of targets, placing end-task Success within 1.8 points of an oracle reusable selector. Analyses by trajectory length and source--target binding shift show that direct trajectory injection loses much of its utility as traces grow longer or source-specific values change, whereas target-bound support preserves a larger share of the measured gain. The resulting framework separates retrieval quality from the problem of turning retrieved experience into safe, useful support for a new task.

AI.tldr: The paper isolates "post-retrieval reuse" as a key bottleneck in long-horizon trajectory memory, showing that a simple target-bound note (QCR) outperforms injecting full trajectories by 10.7 success points while cutting online token use by ~49%.
AI.motivation: Retrieval only finds a past trajectory that may be relevant; it does not tell an agent how to reuse that trajectory once users, entities, constraints, or environment state have changed. The authors argue this post-retrieval reuse step is a distinct, underexamined bottleneck that limits the utility of long-horizon trajectory memory, and that conflating retrieval quality with reuse quality obscures where gains actually come from.
AI.method: The authors formulate an evaluation framework that holds candidate retrieval, target state, model, decoding, and tool budget fixed while varying only the support delivered to the agent. They instantiate it with Query-Conditioned Reuse (QCR), a deliberately simple target-bound note recording a reusable procedure, bindings to recover, applicability conditions, and verification requirements. QCR tests the reuse hypothesis rather than claiming a universal memory format. They also use summary reranking to select a reusable memory and compare against an oracle reusable selector.
AI.result: Across 2,391 target instances in WebArena, WorkArena, and AppWorld, QCR achieves 62.3% average Success, 10.7 points above Full Trajectory, while using 48.9% fewer online tokens. Summary reranking selects a reusable memory for 94.8% of targets, placing end-task Success within 1.8 points of an oracle reusable selector. Analyses show direct trajectory injection loses utility as traces lengthen or source-specific values change, whereas target-bound support preserves a larger share of the measured gain.
AI.conclusion: Separating retrieval quality from the reuse problem is essential: turning retrieved experience into safe, useful support for a new task requires target-bound support rather than raw trajectory injection, and the proposed framework cleanly isolates retrieval effectiveness from the quality of post-retrieval reuse.

title: ViTOED: A Dataset for Target-Oriented Emotion Detection on Vietnamese Social Media Texts
comment: Accepted for publication at 2026 International Conference on Multimedia Analysis and Pattern Recognition (MAPR 2026)
summary: This paper introduces ViTOED, a novel dataset for target-oriented emotion detection in Vietnamese social media texts. The ViTOED comprises 10,985 user comments and 21,244 manually annotated opinion quadruples (source, target, expression, polarity) that follow strict guidelines. The dataset reveals Vietnamese-specific phenomena, such as implicit sources and targets and vocabulary ambiguities, enabling deeper analysis of user emotions toward entities. We propose a baseline using structured sentiment graphs and evaluate various Vietnamese pre-trained language models. The empirical results highlight challenges in span detection and relation extraction and indicate substantial room for model improvement in Vietnamese Target-Oriented Emotion Detection tasks.

AI.tldr: ViTOED is a new Vietnamese dataset for target-oriented emotion detection containing 10,985 comments with 21,244 annotated opinion quadruples, accompanied by a structured sentiment graph baseline that reveals remaining challenges in span detection and relation extraction.
AI.motivation: Existing target-oriented emotion/sentiment detection research concentrates on resource-rich languages like English and Chinese, leaving Vietnamese—with its implicit sources/targets and vocabulary ambiguities—underserved. The authors aim to fill this gap with a rigorously annotated dataset and benchmark to enable deeper analysis of user emotions toward entities in Vietnamese social media.
AI.method: The authors construct ViTOED, a dataset of 10,985 Vietnamese social media comments annotated with opinion quadruples (source, target, expression, polarity) under strict guidelines, capturing Vietnamese-specific phenomena such as implicit sources/targets and lexical ambiguity. They then propose a baseline built on structured sentiment graphs and evaluate multiple Vietnamese pre-trained language models on span detection and relation extraction tasks.
AI.result: Empirical results show that the baseline and pre-trained models perform modestly, with significant difficulties in span detection and relation extraction, indicating a large performance gap and room for improvement on the Vietnamese target-oriented emotion detection task.
AI.conclusion: ViTOED provides a valuable benchmark exposing Vietnamese-specific challenges in target-oriented emotion detection. The proposed structured sentiment graph baseline offers a reference point, but substantial model improvements are still needed, highlighting future research opportunities for Vietnamese ABSA/emotion detection.

title: A Compositional Theory of Curvature in Probabilistic Circuits
summary: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are generative models that support exact inference and, unlike deep neural networks, admit an exact and tractable measure of loss-surface curvature: the trace of the Hessian of the log-likelihood. Recent work regularizes this trace globally to bias learning toward flatter, better generalizing optima. We show that treating sharpness as a global regularizer can be misspecified for PCs, whose curvature is inherently compositional. We prove that each sum node's contribution to the Hessian trace factorizes exactly into its circuit flow, which measures how heavily the node is used, and a local sharpness term determined by its output distribution. This decomposition provides insights into why global sharpness regularization is depth biased and can lead to underfitting. Building on it, we introduce an adaptive sharpness aware regularizer that penalizes nodes based on intrinsic local curvature and preserves closed form EM updates. We also show that empirically, this targeted regularization recovers the generalization that global regularization sacrifices while retaining the robustness and benefits of sharpness aware learning.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that global sharpness regularization is misspecified for Probabilistic Circuits; it derives an exact factorization of each sum node's Hessian-trace contribution into circuit flow times local sharpness, and proposes an adaptive local sharpness-aware regularizer that preserves EM updates and recovers generalization.
AI.motivation: Recent work globally regularizes the Hessian trace to bias Probabilistic Circuit learning toward flatter optima, but the authors argue this global treatment is misspecified because PC curvature is inherently compositional, causing depth bias and underfitting.
AI.method: They prove that each sum node's contribution to the Hessian trace factorizes exactly into its circuit flow (how heavily the node is used) and a local sharpness term determined by its output distribution. Based on this decomposition, they introduce an adaptive sharpness-aware regularizer that penalizes nodes according to intrinsic local curvature while preserving closed-form EM updates.
AI.result: The adaptive local regularization empirically recovers the generalization that global sharpness regularization sacrifices, while retaining the robustness and benefits of sharpness-aware learning.
AI.conclusion: Global sharpness regularization is depth-biased and can underfit PCs; regularizing based on local, compositional sharpness with adaptive weighting is more effective, preserving EM tractability and improving generalization.

title: Practice Makes Unsafe: Skill Misevolution in Self-Improving LLM Agents
summary: Self-improving LLM agents convert successful trajectories into persistent cross-task state. An unsafe success can thereby become reusable policy after its triggering input disappears. Skill evolution makes this failure measurable by distilling operational trajectories into executable, transferable, and inspectable procedures. Because evolution optimizes task outcomes rather than procedure safety, compromised experience can cause skill misevolution. Existing benchmarks measure current behavior or static artifacts but cannot attribute risk across authoring, retrieval, and later execution. To expose this lifecycle, we introduce SkillMisevo-Gym, a lifecycle-aware harness that versions skill state across agent frameworks, and SkillMisevo-Bench, a frozen design from malicious exposure to carryover tasks, with concept-aligned benign tasks and nine lifecycle metrics. We also introduce SafeEvolve, a wrapper that repairs unsafe content and governs subsequent reuse. Across 25 agent-method configurations, each covering 525 tasks in 25 episodes, all 21 evolved configurations author unsafe artifacts, while only fifteen lead to fresh-session harm. In the exposure sweep, three malicious tasks raise carryover ASR from 16.0% to 35.3%. Across representative skill evolution methods, SafeEvolve reduces unsafe retrieval and fresh-session harm by 26.7 and 17.3 percentage points, respectively, while mean benign utility changes by only 0.4 points. Together, persistent-adaptation safety must govern what updates write and what future executors reuse. Code is available at https://github.com/henrymao2004/misevolve.

AI.tldr: The paper exposes a "skill misevolution" failure mode in self-improving LLM agents, where unsafe successful trajectories become reusable cross-task skills, and introduces a lifecycle-aware benchmark suite (SkillMisevo-Gym/Bench) plus a defense (SafeEvolve) to detect and mitigate cross-episode safety risks.
AI.motivation: Self-improving LLM agents distill successful trajectories into persistent, cross-task policy (skills). Because this evolution optimizes task outcomes rather than procedure safety, an unsafe success can be embedded as a reusable skill that persists long after its triggering input disappears. Existing safety benchmarks only evaluate current behavior or static artifacts, failing to attribute risk across the full lifecycle of skill authoring, retrieval, and later execution.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) SkillMisevo-Gym, a lifecycle-aware harness that versions skill state across agent frameworks; (2) SkillMisevo-Bench, a frozen benchmark spanning malicious exposure through carryover tasks, including concept-aligned benign tasks and nine lifecycle metrics; and (3) SafeEvolve, a wrapper that repairs unsafe content in authored skills and governs subsequent reuse. Evaluation covers 25 agent-method configurations, each running 525 tasks across 25 episodes, plus an exposure sweep varying the number of malicious training tasks.
AI.result: All 21 evolved configurations author unsafe artifacts, but only fifteen lead to fresh-session harm, showing a gap between authoring and downstream impact. In the exposure sweep, three malicious tasks raise carryover attack success rate (ASR) from 16.0% to 35.3%. SafeEvolve reduces unsafe retrieval by 26.7 percentage points and fresh-session harm by 17.3 percentage points across representative skill evolution methods, while changing mean benign utility by only 0.4 points.
AI.conclusion: Persistent-adaptation safety must govern both what skill updates write and what future executors reuse. The distinction between authoring unsafe artifacts and actual downstream harm highlights the need for lifecycle-aware evaluation, and SafeEvolve demonstrates that safety can be substantially improved with negligible loss of benign utility. Code is available at the provided GitHub repository.

title: Sustaining Plasticity via Learnable Wavelet Activations in Continual Learning
summary: Plasticity loss has emerged as a critical challenge in continual learning that significantly hinders the acquisition of sequential tasks. While optimizing activation designs offers a potential solution, current fixed-form functions suffer from an inherent spectral bias towards low-frequency variations, whereas learnable variants permit unconstrained updates that induce catastrophic forgetting. To address these limitations, we propose a novel learnable wavelet activation that decomposes the activation function into low-frequency and high-frequency components to explicitly counter spectral bias. Furthermore, we employ dynamic wavelet injection to adaptively enhance plasticity for new tasks, alongside a regularization strategy to ensure the stability of previous learned knowledge. Theoretically, we provide rigorous mathematical guarantees for the proposed framework, proving the structural necessity of the hybrid wavelet architecture for efficient $L^2$ approximation and demonstrating that the decoupled learning rate mechanism successfully restores network plasticity for high-frequency information. Additionally, we provide a formal derivation of the loss-driven injection trigger mechanism to precisely guide the injection. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach maintains superior trainability and generalization throughout the learning process and achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse continual learning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a learnable wavelet activation function that explicitly separates low- and high-frequency components to counter spectral bias in continual learning, combined with dynamic wavelet injection for plasticity and a regularization strategy for stability, achieving state-of-the-art performance across continual learning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Plasticity loss severely hinders continual learning. Fixed-form activation functions exhibit spectral bias toward low-frequency variations, while learnable activations allow unconstrained updates that cause catastrophic forgetting. The goal is to design an activation that mitigates spectral bias while preserving stability of previously learned knowledge.
AI.method: The authors introduce a learnable wavelet activation that decomposes the activation into low-frequency and high-frequency components to explicitly counter spectral bias. They employ dynamic wavelet injection to adaptively enhance plasticity for new tasks, paired with a regularization strategy ensuring stability of prior knowledge. The work provides rigorous theoretical guarantees including proof of the hybrid wavelet architecture's structural necessity for efficient L2 approximation, demonstration that a decoupled learning rate mechanism restores plasticity for high-frequency information, and formal derivation of a loss-driven injection trigger mechanism.
AI.result: Extensive empirical evaluations show the approach maintains superior trainability and generalization throughout learning and achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse continual learning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed learnable wavelet activation framework effectively addresses plasticity loss in continual learning by explicitly balancing high- and low-frequency components, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical results establishing it as an effective solution for sequential task acquisition.

title: AI and Consumer Rights in India Working Paper
summary:
As AI systems proliferate in consumer facing applications, questions about liability for AI related harms remain unresolved. This working paper examines whether India's Consumer Protection Act, 2019, adequately addresses harm caused by defective AI products and services, and whether it proportionately allocates liability across the AI value chain.
  The Act's broad definitions of product liability, harm, and deficiency appear technology agnostic and potentially applicable to AI related incidents including personal injury, psychological harm, biased outputs, and loss of control. However, significant gaps remain. Proving causation between AI defects and consumer harm presents a technical challenge, as AI failures often stem from design choices rather than discrete defects. Additionally, the Act's framework assumes distinct roles for manufacturers, sellers, and service providers, yet the AI value chain involves overlapping responsibilities among data providers, model developers, deployers, and users that do not neatly map to these categories. Current liability frameworks lack proportionate mechanisms to effectively address complex, multistakeholder AI harms. While the Act may cover AI entities, enforcement requires clarification on sector specific overlaps.

AI.tldr: This working paper analyzes whether India's Consumer Protection Act, 2019 can adequately address harms caused by defective AI products and services, finding that while its broad definitions are potentially applicable, significant gaps in causation and liability allocation across the multistakeholder AI value chain remain.
AI.motivation: As AI systems proliferate in consumer-facing applications, questions about liability for AI-related harms remain unresolved, creating a need to examine whether existing consumer protection frameworks can handle these novel challenges.
AI.method: The paper conducts a doctrinal/legal analysis of India's Consumer Protection Act, 2019, examining its provisions (product liability, harm, and deficiency definitions) against the technical realities of AI systems and the multistakeholder AI value chain.
AI.result: The Act's broad definitions are technology-agnostic and potentially applicable to AI-related incidents (personal injury, psychological harm, biased outputs, loss of control); however, two key gaps emerge: (1) proving causation is technically challenging because AI failures often stem from design choices rather than discrete defects, and (2) the Act's distinct role assumptions (manufacturer, seller, service provider) do not map onto the overlapping responsibilities among data providers, model developers, deployers, and users. Liability frameworks currently lack proportionate mechanisms for complex multistakeholder AI harms, and enforcement requires clarification on sector-specific overlaps.
AI.conclusion: While India's Consumer Protection Act, 2019 may cover AI entities in principle, it requires clarification and adaptation—particularly around causation, proportionate liability allocation across the AI value chain, and sector-specific enforcement overlaps—to effectively address AI-related harm.

title: FastThaiG2P: Lightning-fast Thai Grapheme-to-phoneme Conversion for Voice Agent Pipelines
summary: FastThaiG2P provides sub-millisecond Thai grapheme-to-phoneme conversion for text-to-speech pipelines (International Phonetic Alphabet and Kokoro-TTS conventions) using a PyThaiNLP-tokenized, extensible dictionary and normalization rules for common Central Thai speech. The approach achieves an average latency of 0.15 ms per utterance on a benchmark of 27,242 synthetically generated utterances, of which 30\% is spent on tokenization, 12\% on normalization, and 58\% on out-of-vocabulary fallbacks (0.5\% OOV rate). To demonstrate its effectiveness, we used FastThaiG2P to phonemize Som-TTS, an open dataset containing 20 hours of grapheme-and-audio pairs, then trained an 82M-parameter StyleTTS 2 model based on a Kokoro-TTS recipe. The resulting model vocalizes intelligible Thai speech suitable for prototyping and development at 0.25 real-time factor (4x real-time) with ONNX inference on CPU.

AI.tldr: FastThaiG2P is a sub-millisecond Thai grapheme-to-phoneme converter for TTS pipelines, achieving 0.15 ms average latency per utterance on a 27,242-utterance benchmark; it was used to phonemize the 20-hour Som-TTS dataset and train an 82M-parameter StyleTTS 2 model that produces intelligible Thai speech at 0.25 real-time factor with CPU ONNX inference.
AI.motivation: To enable fast, practical Thai grapheme-to-phoneme conversion for text-to-speech pipelines, addressing the need for low-latency phonemization compatible with common TTS conventions (IPA and Kokoro-TTS).
AI.method: A dictionary-based (lookup) approach built on PyThaiNLP tokenization, paired with an extensible dictionary and normalization rules for common Central Thai speech; out-of-vocabulary words are handled via fallback mechanisms. The converter outputs IPA and Kokoro-TTS phoneme conventions.
AI.result: Average latency of 0.15 ms per utterance on 27,242 synthetic utterances, with 30% of time on tokenization, 12% on normalization, and 58% on OOV fallbacks (0.5% OOV rate). Training an 82M-parameter StyleTTS 2 model on the phonemized 20-hour Som-TTS dataset yielded intelligible Thai speech at a 0.25 real-time factor (4x real-time) using ONNX CPU inference.
AI.conclusion: FastThaiG2P provides fast, low-latency Thai phonemization suitable for prototyping and development, and successfully supports training a full TTS pipeline (StyleTTS 2) that vocalizes intelligible Thai speech efficiently on CPU.

title: Robust data-driven discovery of fractional differential equations via weak formulations and Pareto-based subset selection
summary: Fractional partial differential equations describe nonlocal dynamics, but discovering them from noisy data is difficult because fractional differentiation amplifies high-frequency measurement noise and the derivative orders are unknown. We propose Weak-Pareto, which combines an adjoint-consistent weak formulation of fractional terms with Pareto-based subset selection over discrete term types and continuous fractional orders. For linear right-hand-side terms, the adjoint transfers fractional operators from measured fields to smooth test functions, replacing noise-sensitive pointwise differentiation with smoothing integration; for nonlinear terms, the noise-suppression effect is partial yet useful. Coefficients are fitted by ridge regression within a branch-aware differential-evolution search over the orders. The support size is then selected at the validation-error-complexity elbow. We show that the variance of fixed linear right-hand-side weak features vanishes under grid refinement, whereas noise amplification in pointwise fractional features increases with derivative order. Across fractional advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and Burgers benchmarks, Weak-Pareto recovers parsimonious structures from clean and noisy measurements. In controlled advection-diffusion and Burgers comparisons, it retains the correct support at every tested multiplicative-noise level, whereas the unregularised strong-form counterpart largely fails once noise is introduced; this advantage persists under additive Gaussian noise. Ablations show that the weak library drives noise robustness and that continuous-order Pareto search avoids the support-selection failure of a dense fixed dictionary. On the advection-diffusion benchmark, Weak-Pareto yields more consistent operator recovery and substantially lower measured runtime than a contemporary neural baseline.

AI.tldr: Weak-Pareto discovers fractional PDEs from noisy data by combining an adjoint-consistent weak formulation (to suppress noise) with Pareto-based subset selection over term types and continuous fractional orders, outperforming strong-form and neural baselines.
AI.motivation: Discovering fractional PDEs from noisy data is hard because fractional differentiation amplifies high-frequency noise and the derivative orders are unknown, so a noise-robust method with support/order selection is needed.
AI.method: Weak-Pareto uses an adjoint-consistent weak formulation that transfers fractional operators from measured fields to smooth test functions (full noise suppression for linear RHS terms, partial for nonlinear). Coefficients are fit via ridge regression inside a branch-aware differential-evolution search over continuous orders, and support size is chosen at the validation-error-complexity elbow.
AI.result: Weak-feature variance for linear RHS terms vanishes under grid refinement while pointwise noise amplification grows with derivative order. Across fractional advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and Burgers benchmarks, Weak-Pareto recovers parsimonious structures from clean and noisy data, retains correct support at all tested multiplicative-noise levels (and under additive Gaussian noise), and yields more consistent operator recovery with substantially lower runtime than a neural baseline.
AI.conclusion: The weak library drives noise robustness and continuous-order Pareto search avoids the support-selection failure of a dense fixed dictionary, making Weak-Pareto a more reliable and efficient approach for fractional PDE discovery from noisy data.

title: ReflectFact: Self-Reflective Agents for Improving Comprehension and Reasoning in Multi-Hop Fact Verification
summary: Multi-hop fact verification, which verifies claims by reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence, is critical for combating misinformation on social media yet remains highly challenging. Recent methods primarily rely on multi-agent collaboration to decompose fact verification into specialized subtasks. However, these methods face two critical limitations: (1) agents may perform individual subtasks without sufficient awareness of the global verification objective, causing their reasoning to deviate from the intended direction; and (2) conflicts between parametric knowledge and the provided evidence may undermine evidence-grounded reasoning and lead to incorrect verdicts. To address these challenges, we propose ReflectFact, a novel self-reflective agent framework for multi-hop fact verification. ReflectFact introduces three key tasks. Explicit Reasoning Path Planning builds an evidence-grounded reasoning path by resolving implicit entities, decomposing the claim into sub-questions, and integrating the verified facts into a verdict. Evidence-Drift Verification makes the agent re-answer by quoting the supporting evidence when a grounded answer merely echoes its parametric prior, thereby calibrating evidence deviation to ensure grounded comprehension. Reasoning Reflection Verification re-examines each reasoning step and regenerates it once an inconsistency is detected, correcting reasoning flaws such as location bias and replacement bias through a global task perspective. Subsequently, the agent aggregates validated reasoning chains to yield reliable verdicts. Extensive experiments on HOVER and EX-FEVER demonstrate that ReflectFact effectively remedies the comprehension and reasoning defects of existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and respectively outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.32\% and 2.78\% on the two datasets.

AI.tldr: ReflectFact is a self-reflective agent framework for multi-hop fact verification that adds three mechanisms—Explicit Reasoning Path Planning, Evidence-Drift Verification, and Reasoning Reflection Verification—to correct comprehension and reasoning errors, achieving state-of-the-art results on HOVER and EX-FEVER.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop fact verification on social media is critical but hard. Existing multi-agent methods suffer from two limitations: (1) agents solve individual subtasks without awareness of the global verification objective, so reasoning drifts from the intended direction; and (2) conflicts between parametric prior knowledge and provided evidence undermine evidence-grounded reasoning, producing incorrect verdicts.
AI.method: The paper proposes ReflectFact, a self-reflective agent framework with three key tasks: (1) Explicit Reasoning Path Planning builds an evidence-grounded reasoning path by resolving implicit entities, decomposing the claim into sub-questions, and integrating verified facts into a verdict; (2) Evidence-Drift Verification makes the agent re-answer by quoting supporting evidence when a grounded answer merely echoes its parametric prior, calibrating evidence deviation for grounded comprehension; (3) Reasoning Reflection Verification re-examines each reasoning step and regenerates it upon detecting inconsistency, correcting flaws such as location bias and replacement bias from a global task perspective. Validated reasoning chains are then aggregated into reliable verdicts.
AI.result: Experiments on HOVER and EX-FEVER show ReflectFact remedies comprehension and reasoning defects of existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.32% and 2.78% on the two datasets, respectively.
AI.conclusion: ReflectFact effectively addresses the comprehension and reasoning shortcomings of prior multi-agent fact verification approaches, delivering state-of-the-art accuracy on both benchmark datasets and demonstrating the value of self-reflection for evidence-grounded, objective-aware verification.

title: From Atomic Evidence to Logical Composition: Structured Compositional Reasoning over Compound Answer Options
summary: Large language models often fail when answer options require combining atomic judgments under explicit logical operators, even when they judge the individual atoms correctly. We study compound options connected by AND, OR, and NEITHER/NOR, introducing a framework that decomposes each option into atomic answers and scores contrastive hypotheses about each one, so the model never sees a compound option. An operator-constrained integer linear program then composes the calibrated scores into a single prediction. We evaluate on LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA and introduce LOGICAL-SATA, a reading-comprehension benchmark derived from SATA-Bench. Our framework improves Macro-F1 from 48.3 to 77.0 on the human-validated LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA split and from 47.0 to 75.6 on LOGICAL-SATA, with the largest gains on NEITHER/NOR.

AI.tldr: LLMs struggle with answer options combining atomic judgments under logical operators (AND, OR, NEITHER/NOR). The authors decompose compound options into atomic answers, score each atom contrastively, then compose scores via an operator-constrained integer linear program, avoiding ever showing the model a compound option. This boosts Macro-F1 from 48.3→77.0 on LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA and 47.0→75.6 on LOGICAL-SATA, with largest gains on NEITHER/NOR.
AI.motivation: Large language models fail on compounds required by explicit logical operators (AND, OR, NEITHER/NOR) even when they correctly judge individual atomic facts, suggesting the bottleneck is compositional logical reasoning over multiple atoms rather than atomic judgment.
AI.method: A framework that decomposes each compound option into atomic answers and scores contrastive hypotheses about each atom so the model never sees a compound option. An operator-constrained integer linear program (ILP) then composes the calibrated atomic scores into a single logical prediction respecting the AND/OR/NEITHER-NOR constraints. Evaluated on LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA and a new reading-comprehension benchmark LOGICAL-SATA derived from SATA-Bench.
AI.result: Macro-F1 improved from 48.3 to 77.0 on the human-validated LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA split, and from 47.0 to 75.6 on LOGICAL-SATA, with the largest gains on NEITHER/NOR.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing compound options into atomic judgments and composing them with an operator-constrained ILP substantially improves LLM performance on logical compound answer selection, indicating that atomic scoring plus explicit constraint composition is an effective remedy for LLMs' compositional weaknesses.

title: Adaptive $k$ Nearest Neighbors Classifier via Granular Ball Computing
summary: The $k$-Nearest Neighbor~(KNN) algorithm is widely used across various tasks. The selection of the $k$ value is a key issue because it significantly impacts performance. In this paper, an adaptive and efficient KNN approach via granular-ball computing is proposed. The method consists of two stages. \textcolor{black}{In the training stage, the dataset is first coarsely partitioned to reduce the complexity of data distributions within a granular ball, and then the Fisher criterion is introduced to control ball splitting and stopping, yielding a multi-granularity granular ball representation. In the prediction stage, the nearest granular ball is first located through a weighted distance mechanism, and an adaptive neighborhood is then constructed around the test sample. The effective $k$ value is dynamically determined by the actual number of samples contained in this neighborhood. The neighborhood induced by the nearest granular ball provides more stable local group information, thereby improving robustness against noise and local perturbations.} Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing KNN variants across multiple datasets in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. The code has been open-sourced for reproducibility: https://github.com/lianxiaoyu724/Adaptive-GBKNN.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive and efficient KNN method based on granular-ball computing. It coarsely partitions data into granular balls, uses the Fisher criterion to control splitting into a multi-granularity representation, then at prediction time locates the nearest granular ball via weighted distance and builds an adaptive neighborhood to dynamically determine the effective k value. Experiments show improved accuracy and efficiency over existing KNN variants.
AI.motivation: The selection of the k value in the k-Nearest Neighbor algorithm is critical because it greatly affects performance, yet fixed k values are hard to tune and may be suboptimal. The work seeks an adaptive, efficient way to determine k automatically rather than relying on a fixed parameter.
AI.method: A two-stage approach using granular-ball computing. Training stage: (1) the dataset is coarsely partitioned to reduce the complexity of data distributions within each granular ball; (2) the Fisher criterion is introduced to control ball splitting and stopping, producing a multi-granularity granular-ball representation. Prediction stage: (1) the nearest granular ball is located using a weighted distance mechanism; (2) an adaptive neighborhood is constructed around the test sample, and the effective k is dynamically set to the actual number of samples in this neighborhood. The neighborhood induced by the nearest granular ball supplies stable local group information, improving robustness to noise and local perturbations.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets show the proposed method outperforms existing KNN variants in both accuracy and efficiency. The code is open-sourced for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive granular-ball KNN method effectively determines k dynamically, achieves better accuracy and efficiency than existing KNN variants, and provides stronger robustness against noise and local perturbations. Code is publicly available to support reproducibility.

title: Predictive Memory Localization: Forecasting Selective Intervention Paths from Internal Signals
summary: Activation steering turns localized representations into control directions, but localization alone does not reveal whether a direction has a selective operating regime. We introduce Predictive Memory Localization (PML), which treats the measured-grid intervention path as the predictive object of memory localization. PML separates random-calibrated target movement from semantic-neighbor and capability damage, and compares static localization and supervised geometry with a strength-disjoint low-dose causal response. Our frozen study covers 3,000 records from nine datasets and fourteen domains, yielding 30,000 distinct record-direction-layer paths and 210,000 distinct path-strength evaluations. At layer 7, the geometry-derived RFM/AGOP direction reaches 13.1% target-any and 12.3% clean-any, exceeding random by 3.6 and 3.4 percentage points under a record-paired bootstrap. Across record-, dataset-, and domain-grouped splits, responses at $|α|=0.1$ are the strongest signal for outcomes at disjoint strengths $|α|\in\{0.25,0.5\}$. On held-out records, a predictor-driven selector chooses a coefficient or abstains, improves utility and reduces semantic-neighbor damage relative to a train-tuned fixed-strength policy, and avoids most evaluations in a dense scan. Across three residual-norm-matched base models, learned directions retain selective-path gains and low-dose responses yield 0.801-0.828 record-held-out macro AUROC. PML therefore turns memory localization into a falsifiable forecast of margin-level selective outcomes and a risk-aware intervention decision.

AI.tldr: PML reframes memory localization as a predictive, falsifiable task: instead of just locating representations, it forecasts whether an intervention direction has a selective operating regime. Using 3,000 records across nine datasets/fourteen domains and 210,000 path-strength evaluations, it shows low-dose ($|α|=0.1$) causal responses best predict outcomes at disjoint strengths, and a learned selector can choose coefficients or abstain to preserve utility while cutting semantic-neighbor damage.
AI.motivation: Activation steering converts localized representations into control directions, but localization alone does not establish whether a direction actually has a selective operating regime (i.e., can move the target without damaging semantic neighbors or general capabilities). The authors want to turn memory localization from a static geometric finding into a predictive, risk-aware intervention decision.
AI.method: PML treats a measured-grid intervention path (record-direction-layer across multiple strengths) as the predictive object. It separates random-calibrated target movement from semantic-neighbor and capability damage, and contrasts static localization/supervised geometry against a strength-disjoint low-dose causal response. Evaluation spans a frozen study of 3,000 records from nine datasets and fourteen domains (30,000 distinct record-direction-layer paths; 210,000 path-strength evaluations) across three residual-norm-matched base models. A predictor-driven selector chooses a coefficient or abstains, and performance is validated under record-, dataset-, and domain-grouped splits plus record-paired bootstrap.
AI.result: At layer 7, the geometry-derived RFM/AGOP direction reaches 13.1% target-any and 12.3% clean-any (exceeding random by 3.6 and 3.4 p.p. under record-paired bootstrap). Responses at $|α|=0.1$ are the strongest predictor of outcomes at disjoint $|α|\in\{0.25,0.5\}$ across all grouped splits. The selector improves utility and reduces semantic-neighbor damage versus a train-tuned fixed-strength policy while avoiding most evaluations in a dense scan. Learned directions retain selective-path gains; low-dose responses yield 0.801–0.828 record-held-out macro AUROC across the three models.
AI.conclusion: PML converts memory localization into a falsifiable forecast of margin-level selective outcomes and enables risk-aware intervention decisions, showing that low-dose causal responses are informative for higher-strength behavior and can be acted on via a coefficient-or-abstain selector.

title: AQuA: Recursively Self-Improving Quantitative Trading Research Agents
summary: We study recursive self-improvement at the level of quantitative-investment research: whether an autonomous system can use evidence from earlier experiments to improve the hypotheses and candidates proposed in later iterations. We present AQuA, which comprises two separate language-model-driven research systems: one for symbolic factor discovery and one for trainable model development. The two systems do not share agents, memories, candidate spaces, or research state. Instead, each independently closes its own research loop by retaining validated evidence and using it to guide subsequent proposals. In this bounded sense, both systems implement recursive self-improvement at the level of the research process. Each system also uses its own sealed sandbox, which fixes the data splits, feature and label definitions, and evaluator while allowing the model to act only through constrained factor expressions or configuration diffs. The factor system, a manager-mediated multi-agent pipeline, discovers and combines factors into a signal that reaches a combined information coefficient of about $0.190$ on a crypto universe. The model system, a config-driven loop over a hybrid time-series architecture, reaches a per-stock information coefficient of $+0.0843$ on US equities and converts it into a threshold long/short strategy with a held-out Sharpe of up to $+2.50$ at a two-leg cost. The strategy is positive in every year from 2021 to 2025.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AQuA, a pair of independent language-model-based research systems that each implement recursive self-improvement by retaining validated evidence from earlier experiments to guide later proposals. One system discovers symbolic factors on crypto data, reaching an information coefficient (IC) of ~0.190; the other configures a hybrid time-series model for US equities, reaching a per-stock IC of +0.0843 and converting it into a long/short strategy with held-out Sharpe up to +2.50, positive in every year 2021–2025.
AI.motivation: To study whether recursive self-improvement is achievable at the level of quantitative-investment research, i.e., whether an autonomous system can use evidence from earlier experiments to improve the hypotheses and candidates proposed in later iterations, while maintaining controlled, reproducible evaluation conditions.
AI.method: AQuA comprises two separate language-model-driven research systems that do not share agents, memories, candidate spaces, or research state. Each independently closes its own research loop by retaining validated evidence and using it to guide subsequent proposals. Each system operates inside a sealed sandbox that fixes data splits, feature and label definitions, and the evaluator, while allowing the model to act only through constrained factor expressions or configuration diffs. The factor system is a manager-mediated multi-agent pipeline that discovers and combines factors into a signal on a crypto universe. The model system is a config-driven loop over a hybrid time-series architecture for US equities.
AI.result: The factor system's combined signal reaches a combined information coefficient of about 0.190 on a crypto universe. The model system reaches a per-stock information coefficient of +0.0843 on US equities and converts it into a threshold long/short strategy with a held-out Sharpe of up to +2.50 at a two-leg cost; the strategy is positive in every year from 2021 to 2025.
AI.conclusion: Recursive self-improvement at the research-process level is feasible in a bounded, sandboxed setting: two independent LLM systems can each close their own loop by retaining validated evidence to influence subsequent proposals, yielding positive, robust quantitative-investment results under fixed evaluation conditions.

title: EGRL: Edge generation-guided relation-aware learning for RNA-protein interaction prediction
summary: RNA-Protein Interactions (RPIs) are critical for regulating cellular functions. While traditional wet-lab experiments for RPI detection are costly and time-consuming, Deep Learning (DL) methods provide an efficient computational alternative for RPI Prediction (RPIP). In particular, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are promising, as they naturally model RPI networks. However, existing GNN-based methods often rely on homogeneous graphs or predefined meta-paths, which limit their ability to handle data sparsity and to generalize to cold-start scenarios involving unknown molecules. To address these limitations, we propose Edge Generation-guided Relation-aware Learning (EGRL), a novel framework with several key components: implicit meta-path learning to capture relational semantics without handcrafted paths; a multi-relation-aware attention mechanism for adaptive fusion of interaction patterns; a graph generator that predicts potential ("soft") edges to support cold-start nodes; and a multi-feature fusion predictor for final interaction scoring. EGRL is jointly trained with a primary task loss and an auxiliary generator loss. Comprehensive evaluations on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that EGRL achieves competitive overall performance. More importantly, it exhibits superior generalization in cold-start settings, achieving an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.867 and an Area Under the Precision-Recall curve (AUPR) of 0.861 on unknown molecules, corresponding to improvements of 8.6% in AUROC and 5.0% in AUPR over prior state-of-the-art methods. The code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: EGRL is a GNN-based framework for RNA-Protein Interaction Prediction that introduces implicit meta-path learning, multi-relation-aware attention, a graph generator for soft edges, and a multi-feature fusion predictor, achieving strong cold-start generalization (AUROC 0.867, AUPR 0.861) over prior state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional wet-lab RPI detection is costly and slow, while DL offers a faster alternative. Existing GNN-based RPIP methods rely on homogeneous graphs or predefined meta-paths, limiting their capacity to handle data sparsity and to generalize to cold-start scenarios with unknown molecules.
AI.method: EGRL comprises four main components: (1) implicit meta-path learning that captures relational semantics without handcrafted paths; (2) a multi-relation-aware attention mechanism for adaptive fusion of interaction patterns; (3) a graph generator that predicts potential soft edges to support cold-start nodes; and (4) a multi-feature fusion predictor for final interaction scoring. The model is jointly trained using a primary task loss and an auxiliary generator loss.
AI.result: On four benchmark datasets, EGRL achieves competitive overall performance and notably superior cold-start generalization, reaching AUROC 0.867 and AUPR 0.861 on unknown molecules, corresponding to improvements of 8.6% in AUROC and 5.0% in AUPR over prior state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: EGRL effectively addresses sparsity and cold-start limitations in GNN-based RPIP through implicit meta-path learning, relation-aware attention, and graph generation, delivering competitive accuracy and marked generalization gains, with code to be released soon.

title: Falsehood and Impossibility Are Different Directions in an AI's Representation of Language
summary: Language can describe states of affairs that are false and states of affairs that could not be the case at all. Whether an AI model internally distinguishes these failures remains unclear. I report an exploratory activation study of the multimodal open-weight model Gemma 3 4B IT using 85 prompts from 17 philosophical families and a topic-matched modality set of 15 topics, each expressed as a truth, contingent falsehood, improbable claim, semantic anomaly, and necessary falsehood. In its answers, the model conflates contingent falsehood with contradiction, labeling 12 of 15 false statements "contradiction." Its activations show a different pattern. A linear truth probe separates impossible from true statements (AUC 0.93) but not impossible from false statements (AUC 0.20). An impossibility probe evaluated on held-out topic families separates necessary from contingent falsehood at AUC 1.00, peaking at layer 15 with balanced accuracy 0.97 (Bonferroni-adjusted P=0.018). The truth and impossibility directions are close to orthogonal, whereas the impossibility direction partially overlaps a semantic anomaly direction while remaining distinguishable from it. Sparse autoencoder features at the same layer repeat this geometry. Features selective for impossibility also fire on anomalous sentences but rarely on contingent falsehoods. In this model's activation space, necessary falsehoods are not extreme cases of contingent falsehood but lie closer to the experimentally defined category of semantic anomaly. This representational proximity does not imply that impossible statements are intrinsically meaningless. These correlational observations from one small model offer an empirical footnote to an old philosophical distinction.

AI.tldr: An activation study of Gemma 3 4B IT shows that, despite labeling false statements as "contradiction" in its verbal output, the model's internal representations distinguish necessary falsehoods (impossibilities) from contingent falsehoods and align them more closely with semantic anomalies.
AI.motivation: To determine whether an AI model internally distinguishes between false states of affairs (contingent falsehoods) and states of affairs that could not be the case at all (necessary falsehoods/impossibilities), given that its surface answers conflate these categories.
AI.method: Exploratory activation study of the multimodal open-weight model Gemma 3 4B IT using 85 prompts from 17 philosophical families and a topic-matched set of 15 topics, each expressed as a truth, contingent falsehood, improbable claim, semantic anomaly, and necessary falsehood. Methods include linear probing (truth probe and impossibility probe with held-out topic families), direction orthogonality analysis, and sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature inspection at layer 15.
AI.result: In answers, the model labels 12 of 15 false statements as "contradiction," conflating contingent falsehood with contradiction. Internally, a linear truth probe separates impossible from true statements (AUC 0.93) but not impossible from false statements (AUC 0.20). An impossibility probe separates necessary from contingent falsehood at AUC 1.00, peaking at layer 15 with balanced accuracy 0.97 (Bonferroni-adjusted P=0.018). Truth and impossibility directions are near-orthogonal; the impossibility direction partially overlaps a semantic anomaly direction while remaining distinguishable. SAE features selective for impossibility also fire on anomalous sentences but rarely on contingent falsehoods.
AI.conclusion: In this model's activation space, necessary falsehoods are not extreme cases of contingent falsehood but lie closer to the category of semantic anomaly. This representational proximity does not imply impossible statements are intrinsically meaningless. The correlational observations from one small model offer an empirical footnote to a longstanding philosophical distinction.

title: Revisiting Overestimation Bias Problem of Q-learning: Settling Large Discrete Action Space via Action Intersection
summary: This paper considers the overestimation bias problem of Q-learning in the setting of a large action space, for the purpose of relieving the bottleneck of existing methods. We find that the large action space increases the randomness in Q-value estimation. The randomness makes two paradigms that drive the major literature on the overestimation problem have their own bottlenecks: the coupling paradigm, i.e., the optimal action and its Q-value are estimated with the same Q-function, always has a positive bias. This is because randomness leads to some actions having abnormally high estimated values than their true values, and the coupling methods prefer these actions. The decoupling paradigm, i.e., the optimal action and its Q-value are estimated with two independent Q-functions, always has a negative bias. This is because randomness increases the estimation gap between the two independent Q-tables for the same action. This paper shows that action intersection can be a simple yet powerful strategy to relieve these bottlenecks. The action intersection strategy enables semi-decoupling via two designs: (1) it allows two Q-functions to share a certain fraction of trajectory data; (2) if a data sample is shared, each Q-function is updated using the coupling paradigm; otherwise, using the decoupling paradigm. Two properties make the action intersection strategy powerful: (1) attaining a large bias range, i.e., varying the data sharing fraction, the estimation bias varies from underestimating to overestimating; (2) fine granularity: the action intersection size can be made arbitrarily finer to enable finer control. We consider two experiment settings, i.e., tabular and deep RL, deep RL experiments show that our method outperforms several SOTA baselines drastically; tabular experiments reveal why our method can achieve superior performance.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses Q-learning's overestimation bias in large action spaces and proposes an "action intersection" strategy that enables semi-decoupling (a blend of coupling and decoupling paradigms) to flexibly control estimation bias, achieving strong empirical results in both tabular and deep RL.
AI.motivation: In large action spaces, randomness in Q-value estimation increases, causing the two dominant paradigms for tackling overestimation bias to hit bottlenecks: coupling methods (which estimate the optimal action and its Q-value with the same Q-function) suffer persistent positive bias because randomness inflates some actions' estimated values and coupling prefers them; decoupling methods (which use two independent Q-functions) always exhibit negative bias because randomness widens the estimation gap between the two Q-tables for the same action. The goal is to relieve these bottlenecks.
AI.method: The paper proposes an action intersection strategy enabling semi-decoupling through two designs: (1) two Q-functions share a certain fraction of trajectory data; (2) for shared samples each Q-function is updated via the coupling paradigm, while for unshared samples it is updated via the decoupling paradigm. Two key properties make this powerful: a large bias range (varying the data-sharing fraction shifts bias from underestimation to overestimation) and fine granularity (the intersection size can be made arbitrarily fine for precise control).
AI.result: Deep RL experiments show the method drastically outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines, and tabular experiments explain why the method achieves superior performance.
AI.conclusion: Action intersection is a simple yet effective strategy that relieves the bottlenecks of both coupling and decoupling paradigms by enabling fine-grained, tunable semi-decoupling, yielding superior performance in large action space settings.

title: Polish Medical Visual Question Answering: Vision-Language Models Underutilize Visual Evidence
summary: We introduce a Polish-language medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmark, built from Polish Board Certification Examination questions for licensed physicians and dentists pursuing specialist certification. The benchmark comprises image-containing questions spanning diverse medical specialties and visual domains, together with a text-only question answering (QA) control set. We evaluate Polish-oriented, general-purpose open-weight, and commercial vision-language models. The task remains challenging: the best model achieves 79.0\% accuracy on the full VQA set, and only GPT-5.6 surpasses the approximate human reference on the subset with available candidate responses; all other evaluated models perform worse than humans. To assess visual grounding, we compare complete inputs with configurations omitting the image, the question, or both, and categorize questions by image importance. Models derive more useful information from the question text than from the image and perform worse on image-dominant questions. Across both QA and VQA, they nevertheless achieve above-chance accuracy from the answer choices alone, showing that non-trivial performance can persist even when key task components are missing.

AI.tldr: A new Polish medical visual question answering benchmark built from Board Certification Exams is introduced. Evaluations of open and commercial vision-language models show the task is hard (top accuracy 79.0%), only one model beats the human reference, and models rely more on question text than images while still scoring above chance from answer choices alone.
AI.motivation: To create a resource for evaluating multimodal medical understanding in Polish, a low-resource language, and to probe how much vision-language models actually depend on visual information versus textual cues and answer-choice priors.
AI.method: The authors construct a Polish medical VQA benchmark from image-containing questions in the Polish Board Certification Examination, spanning many specialties and visual domains, plus a text-only QA control set. They evaluate Polish-oriented models, general open-weight models, and commercial vision-language models. They ablate inputs by omitting the image, the question, or both, and categorize questions by image importance to measure visual grounding.
AI.result: The best model reaches 79.0% accuracy on the full VQA set; only GPT-5.6 exceeds the approximate human reference on the subset with available candidate responses, while all other models underperform humans. Models extract more useful information from the question text than from the image and do worse on image-dominant questions. Even with key components removed, models achieve above-chance accuracy from the answer choices alone in both QA and VQA.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals that current vision-language models struggle with Polish medical VQA, rely disproportionately on textual input over images, and can exploit answer-choice biases to score above chance even without the question or image, highlighting limited genuine visual grounding.

title: The Embedder's Dilemma: LLMs Are Better, but at What Cost?
summary: Should you replace your text-embedding pipeline with a large language model? We answer this with a controlled, cost-aware comparison of ten LLMs across six families and 26 embedding models (118M to 14B parameters) on 37 tasks spanning classification, semantic textual similarity (STS), clustering, pair classification, and retrieval. In aggregate the two paradigms are effectively tied: the best LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro, 77.6) and the best embedding model (77.2) differ by 0.4 points. Their strengths differ by task: LLMs lead on reasoning-heavy retrieval, embedding models lead on classification, and the two match on clustering, STS, and pair classification. Reaching that parity is expensive. An LLM costs up to 1,431x more than an embedding model of comparable quality (USD 154 vs. USD 0.11 per benchmark pass), and the open LLMs tested process tokens 2.5 to 736x more slowly on the same GPU. Reasoning tokens account for 28 to 81% of LLM inference cost; lower reasoning budgets preserve or improve retrieval quality for most models in our ablation. The Pareto frontier contains the leading embedding models and one LLM, Gemini 3.1 Pro. These results support a division of labour: use embedding models for similarity, classification, and clustering, and reserve LLMs for reasoning-intensive retrieval. Our code, datasets, and results are publicly available at https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/embedders-dilemma.

AI.tldr: A controlled, cost-aware comparison of 10 LLMs and 26 embedding models across 37 tasks finds the two paradigms statistically tied overall, but with distinct strengths: LLMs excel at reasoning-heavy retrieval while embedding models win on classification, and embedding models are dramatically cheaper and faster.
AI.motivation: The rapid rise of LLMs raises the question of whether they can (and should) replace dedicated text-embedding pipelines. Prior work lacked a controlled, task- and cost-aware comparison, making it unclear when each paradigm is preferable.
AI.method: The authors benchmark 10 LLMs across six families and 26 embedding models (118M–14B parameters) on 37 tasks spanning classification, semantic textual similarity (STS), clustering, pair classification, and retrieval. They analyze aggregate and per-task performance, compute cost in USD per benchmark pass and token processing throughput on the same GPU, and perform an ablation on reasoning-token budgets to build a Pareto frontier.
AI.result: The best LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro, 77.6) and best embedding model (77.2) differ by only 0.4 points. LLMs lead on reasoning-heavy retrieval, embedding models lead on classification, and they match on clustering, STS, and pair classification. However, LLMs cost up to 1,431× more (USD 154 vs. USD 0.11 per pass), and open LLMs process tokens 2.5–736× slower. Reasoning tokens account for 28–81% of LLM inference cost; lower reasoning budgets preserve or improve retrieval quality. The Pareto frontier contains leading embedding models plus one LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro).
AI.conclusion: The authors recommend a division of labor: use embedding models for similarity, classification, and clustering, and reserve LLMs for reasoning-intensive retrieval. Code, datasets, and results are publicly released.

title: Towards Socially Compliant Navigation in Deep Reinforcement Learning via Proxemics-Based Reward Modeling
summary: Developing effective robot navigation methods in crowded environments is essential for real-world applications. Although recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods have improved navigation performance in crowded environments, they often focus primarily on task-centric objectives and underrepresent social compliance objectives. In this paper, we introduce a novel proxemics-based reward formulation for DRL social navigation that provides a dense, interpretable social learning signal while maintaining navigation efficiency. Our approach models each human's personal space as a radial Gaussian-mixture field derived from Hall's proxemics theory and computes a robot-centric local cost over the robot's field of view.
