We integrate the proposed reward into established DRL navigation methods and evaluate it in simulation across multiple crowd scenarios, reward baselines, and crowd densities using both navigation metrics and social metrics. Results show that the proposed reward consistently improves social metrics in simulation while maintaining competitive navigation performance relative to the compared reward models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a proxemics-based reward function for deep reinforcement learning social navigation, modeling human personal space as radial Gaussian-mixture fields to provide a dense social learning signal, and shows it improves social metrics without hurting navigation performance in simulation.
AI.motivation: Existing deep reinforcement learning methods for robot navigation in crowds focus primarily on task-centric objectives (reaching the goal efficiently) and underrepresent social compliance objectives, limiting socially acceptable behavior around humans.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel reward formulation grounded in Hall's proxemics theory. Each human's personal space is modeled as a radial Gaussian-mixture field, and a robot-centric local cost is computed over the robot's field of view. This dense, interpretable social reward is integrated into established DRL navigation methods and evaluated in simulation across multiple crowd scenarios, reward baselines, and crowd densities using both navigation and social metrics.
AI.result: The proposed reward consistently improves social metrics in simulation while maintaining competitive navigation performance relative to the compared reward models.
AI.conclusion: Modeling personal space via proxemics-based Gaussian-mixture fields yields a dense, interpretable reward that better balances social compliance with navigation efficiency in DRL-based crowd navigation, suggesting it is a promising approach for socially aware robot navigation.

title: FlashDrive: Flash Vision-Language-Action Inference for Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise to bring end-to-end reasoning to autonomous driving, but their computational cost remains far too high for real-time control. The core challenge is structural: VLA inference is not a single bottleneck but a cascade of four. Visual encoding wastes compute on overlapping video frames; language-model prefill recomputes context that could be carried over from the previous timestep; reasoning tokens are generated serially despite low entropy; and flow-matching denoising applies uniform compute to a non-uniform velocity field. Addressing any one stage in isolation leaves the others untouched. We propose FlashDrive, an algorithm-system co-design framework that targets all four stages simultaneously. Our key insight is that each bottleneck admits a distinct, lightweight algorithmic shortcut: temporal overlap enables streaming KV-cache reuse across frames; the low per-token entropy and strong intra-block correlations of driving-domain reasoning make a non-autoregressive diffusion drafter highly effective for speculative decoding; and the velocity field's structure---sharp at the endpoints, flat in the middle---permits adaptive step caching that concentrates compute where it matters. Layered on system-level CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion, these techniques compound. Applied to Alpamayo 1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization, FlashDrive reduces end-to-end latency from 717ms to 151ms (4.7x) while leaving accuracy essentially unchanged: minADE6@6.4s shifts by only 0.08m, minADE1 improves, and closed-loop collision and off-road rates improve in simulation. By raising a 10B-parameter reasoning VLA from 1.4~Hz to 6.6~Hz on a single GPU, FlashDrive moves end-to-end autonomous driving substantially closer to real-time deployment.

AI.tldr: FlashDrive is an algorithm-system co-design framework that accelerates Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving by attacking all four inference bottlenecks (visual encoding, language prefill, autoregressive reasoning, and flow-matching denoising) simultaneously, achieving a 4.7× latency reduction with essentially unchanged accuracy.
AI.motivation: VLA models promise end-to-end reasoning for autonomous driving, but their computational cost is too high for real-time control. The bottleneck is structural: it is a cascade of four stages—visual encoding wastes compute on overlapping video frames, language-model prefill recomputes carry-over context, reasoning tokens are generated serially despite low entropy, and flow-matching denoising applies uniform compute to a non-uniform velocity field. Solving any single stage leaves the others untouched.
AI.method: FlashDrive targets all four stages with distinct lightweight algorithmic shortcuts: (1) temporal overlap enables streaming KV-cache reuse across frames in visual encoding; (2) low per-token entropy and strong intra-block correlations of driving-domain reasoning are exploited via a non-autoregressive diffusion drafter for speculative decoding; (3) the velocity field's structure (sharp at endpoints, flat in the middle) enables adaptive step caching in flow-matching denoising to concentrate compute where it matters; (4) CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion layer on system-level optimizations. Evaluated on Alpamayo 1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization.
AI.result: FlashDrive reduces end-to-end latency from 717ms to 151ms (4.7×), raising throughput from 1.4 Hz to 6.6 Hz on a single GPU. Accuracy is essentially unchanged: minADE6@6.4s shifts by only 0.08m, minADE1 improves, and closed-loop collision and off-road rates improve in simulation.
AI.conclusion: By co-designing lightweight algorithmic shortcuts with system-level optimizations across all four inference stages, FlashDrive brings a 10B-parameter reasoning VLA substantially closer to real-time deployment, achieving 4.7× lower latency without meaningful accuracy loss and improving closed-loop driving safety metrics.

title: When Your Agent Opens the Chat App: Agent-Controlled Search over Raw Chat Logs Rivals Structured Memory
summary: Agent-memory systems increasingly buy retrieval quality with structure, transforming raw conversation histories into summaries, embeddings, trees, or knowledge graphs before any question is asked. We ask how much of that benefit comes from the structure itself, rather than from competent retrieval over the raw history. We present ReFind, an agent-controlled search interface that builds no semantic structure at all: it leaves the conversation archive unmodified, indexes it lexically at turn granularity, and combines a generic iterative keyword-search loop with four chat-native controls grounded in empirical refinding work: session-aware rank fusion, local context expansion, temporal narrowing, and skipping already-inspected sessions. A separate reasoning stage answers from the collected evidence. Across a broad suite of conversational-memory tasks (single- and multi-hop QA, event ordering, and fact consolidation), roughly 2,800 questions on precise-retrieval and fact-tracking capabilities evaluated under the incremental multi-turn setting of MemoryAgentBench, ReFind attains the highest mean accuracy (58.2) of any system compared, above the strongest graph- and tree-based memory systems (HippoRAG 2, 53.2), all under a GPT-4o-mini backbone matched to every reused baseline. Controlled comparisons to single-shot BM25, a matched generic-agentic BM25 control, component removals, and agentic dense/hybrid variants separately support the roles of agent control, chat-native controls, and lexical retrieval. On LongMemEval-S/M, the same interface reaches 93.2 +/- 3.3 and 89.3 +/- 6.0 with GPT-5-mini. The results indicate that for precise, evidence-grounded questions over chat archives, much of the benefit credited to elaborate memory structures is recoverable by giving an agent controllable search over the unmodified record, with no LLM-based index construction at all.

AI.tldr: ReFind shows that an agent-controlled lexical search interface over unmodified chat archives, with no semantic structure or LLM-built index, matches or beats structured graph/tree memory systems on conversational-memory tasks.
AI.motivation: Agent-memory systems increasingly invest in elaborate semantic structure (summaries, embeddings, trees, knowledge graphs) built before queries; the paper questions how much of the retrieval benefit actually comes from the structure versus from competent retrieval over the raw conversation history.
AI.method: ReFind leaves the conversation archive unmodified, indexes it lexically at turn granularity, and combines a generic iterative keyword-search loop with four chat-native controls grounded in empirical refinding work: session-aware rank fusion, local context expansion, temporal narrowing, and skipping already-inspected sessions. A separate reasoning stage answers from the collected evidence. Evaluated on ~2,800 questions (single/multi-hop QA, event ordering, fact consolidation) under MemoryAgentBench's incremental multi-turn setting, with GPT-4o-mini matched across all baselines; also tested on LongMemEval-S/M with GPT-5-mini.
AI.result: ReFind achieves the highest mean accuracy (58.2), above HippoRAG 2 (53.2) and other graph/tree systems. Controlled comparisons to single-shot BM25, a matched generic-agentic BM25 control, component ablations, and agentic dense/hybrid variants support the roles of agent control, chat-native controls, and lexical retrieval. On LongMemEval-S/M it reaches 93.2 +/- 3.3 and 89.3 +/- 6.0.
AI.conclusion: For precise, evidence-grounded questions over chat archives, much of the benefit attributed to elaborate memory structures is recoverable by giving an agent controllable search over the unmodified record, with no LLM-based index construction at all.

title: Momentum as Residual-Driven Multiplier Correction for Deep Learning Optimization
summary: Momentum-based optimizers are widely used in modern deep learning, yet the relations among momentum recursion, update geometry, and acceleration remain only partially understood. We develop an $\textbf{A}$DMM-$\textbf{I}$nspired $\textbf{M}$omentum (AIM) framework based on residual-penalty variable splitting, which interprets momentum as a multiplier-like correction driven by the splitting residual. AIM recovers the exponential moving average of gradients from an ADMM-style multiplier update and separates two mechanisms that are usually intertwined in practical optimizers: the residual penalty determines the update geometry, whereas the approximation of the objective-related subproblem determines the acceleration form. Building on AIM, we propose $\textbf{R}$elativistic $\textbf{A}$daptive gradient $\textbf{D}$escent with $\textbf{A}$ccelerated $\textbf{R}$esidual (RADAR), which combines relativistic adaptive geometry, decoupled residual correction, and second-order momentum filtering to improve the update direction and momentum estimation. We establish stochastic convergence through a variance-perturbed Lyapunov drift analysis. Experiments on supervised vision learning, language modeling, and reinforcement learning show that RADAR achieves consistent improvements over strong adaptive optimizer baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the ADMM-Inspired Momentum (AIM) framework, which reinterprets momentum as a multiplier-like correction from an ADMM variable-splitting view, and uses it to build RADAR, a new optimizer that outperforms strong adaptive baselines across vision, language, and RL tasks.
AI.motivation: Momentum-based optimizers dominate modern deep learning, yet the relationships among momentum recursion, update geometry, and acceleration are only partially understood. The authors aim to disentangle mechanisms usually intertwined in practical optimizers to clarify how geometry and acceleration arise and to design better optimizers.
AI.method: The authors develop the AIM framework based on residual-penalty variable splitting, interpreting momentum as a multiplier-like correction driven by the splitting residual. AIM recovers the exponential moving average of gradients from an ADMM-style multiplier update and separates two mechanisms: the residual penalty (which determines update geometry) and the approximation of the objective-related subproblem (which determines the acceleration form). Based on AIM, they propose RADAR (Relativistic Adaptive gradient Descent with Accelerated Residual), combining relativistic adaptive geometry, decoupled residual correction, and second-order momentum filtering. Convergence is shown via a variance-perturbed Lyapunov drift analysis.
AI.result: RADAR achieves consistent improvements over strong adaptive optimizer baselines in supervised vision learning, language modeling, and reinforcement learning experiments.
AI.conclusion: The AIM framework clarifies the separation between update geometry and acceleration form in momentum optimizers, and the resulting RADAR optimizer demonstrates practical gains across diverse learning settings, supporting the value of the ADMM-inspired perspective.

title: Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, and Fragility in Perturbation Responses
summary: Perturbation methods explain model decisions by measuring prediction changes under altered inputs, but response magnitude tells us only how much a model reacts, not what that reaction means. The same magnitude can support the final factual-counterfactual difference, oppose it, or arise strongly along the perturbation path yet vanish at the endpoint. We therefore track how the contrast develops as paired inputs are progressively revealed, using the final contrast to interpret the trajectory. We introduce DECAF (Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, And Fragility), which routes aligned, opposed, and endpoint-null responses into evidence E, contradiction C, and fragility F. The decomposition preserves ordinary magnitude exactly, Abs = E + C + F, and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms. Across controlled vision and tabular settings, the three components track independently measured behavior. In a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit, we compare cases with nearly identical response magnitude but different independently measured behaviors. The largest DECAF component agrees with an observed behavior in 96.4% of cases, compared with 35.0% for magnitude alone. Changing only the reveal path increases total response by nearly 80%, yet evidence barely changes while fragility grows by more than 4x. On FunnyBirds and ImageNet-1k, short forward-only DECAF trajectories outperform the tested general-purpose attribution baselines. On a 1B-scale DINOv2 model, a short trajectory matches a strong gradient-based baseline with 4.75x lower wall time and 2.36x lower peak memory.

AI.tldr: DECAF decomposes a model's total response magnitude into three interpretable components—Evidence (E), Contradiction (C), and Fragility (F)—by tracking how the contrast between paired inputs develops along a progressive reveal path. The decomposition is exact (Abs = E + C + F), unique under endpoint-relative axioms, and outperforms magnitude alone at predicting a model's actual behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing perturbation-based explanation methods measure only how much a model reacts (response magnitude), not what that reaction means. The same magnitude can align with the final factual-counterfactual difference, oppose it, or be large along the perturbation path yet vanish at the endpoint—so magnitude alone is ambiguous and misleading for interpreting model decisions.
AI.method: The authors introduce DECAF, which progressively reveals paired inputs and uses the final contrast as an endpoint to interpret the trajectory. Responses are routed into three components: evidence E (aligned responses), contradiction C (opposed responses), and fragility F (responses that arise strongly along the path but vanish at the endpoint). The decomposition satisfies Abs = E + C + F and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms. Attribution is obtained from short forward-only DECAF trajectories.
AI.result: In controlled vision and tabular settings, E, C, and F track independently measured behavior. In a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit of cases with nearly identical response magnitude but different measured behaviors, the largest DECAF component agrees with observed behavior in 96.4% of cases versus 35.0% for magnitude alone. Changing only the reveal path increases total response by ~80% while evidence barely changes and fragility grows >4x. On FunnyBirds and ImageNet-1k, short DECAF trajectories outperform tested general-purpose attribution baselines. On a 1B-scale DINOv2 model, a short trajectory matches a strong gradient-based baseline with 4.75x lower wall time and 2.36x lower peak memory.
AI.conclusion: Magnitude alone is insufficient to interpret model decisions; the trajectory of how contrast develops under progressive input reveal carries the semantic meaning of a perturbation response. DECAF's endpoint-relative decomposition of magnitude into evidence, contradiction, and fragility provides an exact, unique, and behaviorally faithful interpretation, and yields efficient, competitive attribution at scale.

title: BavGround: A Benchmark for Regional Cultural Grounding and Dialect Competence in Bavarian
summary: Cultural evaluation of large language models (LLMs) often focuses on high-resource standard languages, leaving regional culture and dialect communities underrepresented. We introduce BavGround, a benchmark for evaluating Bavarian regional cultural grounding and dialect competence across English, German and Bavarian. BavGround contains 206 multiple-choice source questions across eight cultural domains per language, yielding 618 multi-parallel instances, with items covering both broadly accessible cultural knowledge and source-grounded regional knowledge from journalism, historical sources, and specialist literature. We evaluate fifteen 7B-10B open-weight instruction-tuned models and one closed-model reference. Strong multilingual models perform best overall, but performance drops on Bavarian items and source-grounded questions, indicating persistent difficulty with dialectal and localized cultural knowledge. We further show that conclusions depend strongly on evaluation protocol: raw answer-letter scoring, shuffled-letter scoring, option-text likelihood, generated-answer parsing, and semantic matching can produce different absolute scores and rankings, especially for regionally adapted models. Finally, an exploratory analysis of GENBA-10B checkpoints suggests that continued pretraining improves answer-content likelihood unevenly across domains, while dialect competence remains comparatively weak. BavGround supports localized, protocol-aware evaluation of cultural representation in LLMs.

AI.tldr: BavGround is a multi-parallel benchmark (206 questions × 3 languages, 8 cultural domains) for evaluating Bavarian regional cultural grounding and dialect competence in LLMs. Evaluation of 15 open-weight 7B–10B models plus one closed reference shows strong multilingual models lead overall but degrade on Bavarian and source-grounded items, and reveals that score rankings are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol choices.
AI.motivation: Existing cultural evaluations of LLMs concentrate on high-resource standard languages, underrepresenting regional cultures and dialect communities such as Bavarian. There is a need for benchmarks that capture localized cultural knowledge and dialectal competence across multiple languages.
AI.method: The authors build BavGround, a benchmark of 206 multiple-choice source questions across eight cultural domains, translated into English, German, and Bavarian (618 multi-parallel instances), mixing broadly accessible knowledge with source-grounded regional content drawn from journalism, historical sources, and specialist literature. They evaluate fifteen 7B–10B open-weight instruction-tuned models and one closed model using five scoring protocols: raw answer-letter scoring, shuffled-letter scoring, option-text likelihood, generated-answer parsing, and semantic matching. They also run an exploratory analysis of GENBA-10B checkpoints to assess the effect of continued pretraining.
AI.result: Strong multilingual models perform best overall, but accuracy drops on Bavarian-language items and source-grounded questions, signaling persistent difficulty with dialectal and localized cultural knowledge. Different evaluation protocols produce different absolute scores and rankings, particularly for regionally adapted models. Continued pretraining improves answer-content likelihood unevenly across domains while dialect competence remains comparatively weak.
AI.conclusion: BavGround provides a localized, protocol-aware framework for assessing cultural representation in LLMs, demonstrating that both regional dialect knowledge and evaluation-protocol choices materially affect measured model performance and rankings.

title: H-VAEP and H-xT: Valuing Offensive On-the-Ball Actions in Handball by Estimating Probabilities
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 13th Workshop on Machine Learning and Data Mining for Sports Analytics (MLSA 2026), co-located with ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Traditional player evaluation in professional handball relies on basic box-score metrics or heuristic indices, which fail to credit the multi-player build-up chain. While football (soccer) analytics has adopted Expected Threat (xT) and Valuing Actions by Estimating Probabilities (VAEP), these event-based action valuation frameworks have not yet been adapted to handball. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive adaptation and evaluation of xT and VAEP for handball, utilizing five seasons of tracking-derived event data from the Handball Bundesliga. We develop Handball-xT (H-xT) using a handball-native court zoning layout, demonstrating via simulations that it is systematically more robust than standard rectangular grids. We optimize Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP) by tailoring its feature space and selecting the context length to limit team-identity leakage. Our evaluation shows that H-VAEP yields exceptionally stable, discriminative, and intuitive player ratings that highlight build-up play. Finally, we release our complete code repository to help professional clubs deploy these models.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts two soccer action-valuation frameworks—Expected Threat (xT) and VAEP—into handball, producing H-xT and H-VAEP, and validates them on five seasons of Handball Bundesliga event data, showing stable ratings that better credit build-up play.
AI.motivation: Traditional handball player evaluation relies on basic box-score metrics or heuristic indices that fail to credit the multi-player build-up chain. Soccer analytics has solved comparable problems with event-based action valuation (xT and VAEP), but these frameworks had not been adapted to handball.
AI.method: The authors adapt xT and VAEP to handball using tracking-derived event data from five Handball Bundesliga seasons. They design Handball-xT (H-xT) with a handball-native court zoning layout, verifying via simulation that it is more robust than standard rectangular grids. They optimize Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP) by tailoring the feature space and choosing a context length that limits team-identity leakage.
AI.result: H-VAEP produces exceptionally stable, discriminative, and intuitive player ratings that effectively highlight build-up play. Simulations confirm the handball-native zoning layout makes H-xT systematically more robust than standard rectangular grids.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first comprehensive adaptation of xT and VAEP to handball, delivering practical, deployable player-evaluation tools. The authors release their complete code repository to help professional clubs adopt the models.

title: Moose: Latent concept learning with reasoning-shortcut awareness in $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$
summary: The OWL 2 EL profile is used in some of the largest production ontologies, including the Gene Ontology and SNOMED CT. Existing neuro-symbolic (NeSy) learning methods accept propositional theories or Datalog, and reasoning-shortcut (RS) awareness has not been investigated in ontology settings. We present Moose, a method that compiles an $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ TBox and finite ABox to a Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD). The SDD acts as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer, and we add closure clauses outside the $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ profile on declared exhaustive families to overcome the limited expressivity of $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ under partial supervision. We show termination, soundness, completeness, and polynomial intermediate sizes, and validate the proofs in Lean. We then define the first formal partial-supervision latent-concept-learning task over an OWL EL ontology, i.e., learning per-individual classifiers for latent concepts from observed ABox literals, and evaluate Moose on MNIST-with-ontology and Pizzaïolo. Moose improves over propositional-NeSy, fuzzy-logic, and ontology embedding baselines, and presents the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in an OWL EL setting.

AI.tldr: Moose is a neuro-symbolic method that compiles an EL++ TBox and ABox into a Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD) used as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer, enabling reasoning-shortcut-aware latent-concept learning over OWL 2 EL ontologies.
AI.motivation: OWL 2 EL is widely used in large production ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, SNOMED CT), but existing neuro-symbolic (NeSy) learning methods only handle propositional theories or Datalog, and reasoning-shortcut (RS) awareness has not been studied in ontology settings. There is also a need to overcome EL++'s limited expressivity under partial supervision.
AI.method: Moose compiles an EL++ TBox and finite ABox to an SDD, which acts as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer. It adds closure clauses outside the EL++ profile on declared exhaustive families to increase expressivity. The authors prove termination, soundness, completeness, and polynomial intermediate sizes, with proofs validated in Lean. They define the first formal partial-supervision latent-concept-learning task over an OWL EL ontology (learning per-individual classifiers for latent concepts from observed ABox literals) and evaluate on MNIST-with-ontology and Pizzaïolo.
AI.result: Moose outperforms propositional-NeSy, fuzzy-logic, and ontology-embedding baselines, and provides the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in an OWL EL setting.
AI.conclusion: Moose enables sound, complete, and scalable neuro-symbolic learning over OWL 2 EL ontologies with reasoning-shortcut awareness, addressing a gap in prior NeSy methods and demonstrating improved performance over existing baselines.

title: Prompts in the Wild: A Large Analyzed Collection of Transactional Prompts in Code
summary: The behavior of contemporary generative Large Language Models (LLMs) is directly shaped by prompts, unstructured texts that describe the desired output and model behavior. In this paper we argue that prompts are linguistic objects that merit investigation in their own right. To this end, we collect 57.5K unique samples of prompts from GitHub. Specifically, we focus on transactional prompts: reproducible natural language instructions that are integrated into software. To enable the empirical, quantitative study of prompts, we introduce a structured ontology, capturing the properties of prompts as well as their formal and semantic components. Based on this ontology, we transform prompts from unstructured raw texts into richly structured linguistic objects. Analysis of these structured data reveals significant diversity of usage patterns across languages, domains, tasks, and modalities, in a typical Zipf-like distribution where some clearly prevail and others, more diverse, appear in the long tail. To validate the reliability of the ontology-based annotation of the prompts, we perform a comprehensive error analysis across all fields, providing a detailed assessment of annotation quality. We release the dataset together with a browsing and exploration interface (https://github.com/OnlpLab/transactionalPromptsCollection ).

AI.tldr: The paper treats prompts as linguistic objects, builds a 57.5K-sample dataset of transactional prompts from GitHub, introduces an ontology for their structured annotation, analyzes usage diversity, evaluates annotation quality, and releases the dataset with a browsing interface.
AI.motivation: Prompts directly shape modern LLM behavior yet are understudied as linguistic objects in their own right. The authors argue for systematic, empirical study of prompts and aim to provide a structured dataset and ontology to enable quantitative analysis.
AI.method: Collect 57.5K unique transactional prompt samples from GitHub; define a structured ontology capturing prompt properties plus formal and semantic components; transform raw prompts into richly structured linguistic objects; perform Zipf-like distribution analysis and a comprehensive error analysis across all annotation fields to assess quality.
AI.result: Analysis reveals significant diversity in usage patterns across languages, domains, tasks, and modalities, following a typical Zipf-like distribution where a few categories prevail and many diverse cases lie in the long tail. Annotation quality is validated via error analysis, and the dataset plus a browsing/exploration interface are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: Prompts are linguistic objects deserving dedicated study; the released ontology, structured dataset, and interface enable reproducible empirical research on transactional prompts.

title: Multi-perspective Imbalance-Conscious 6G Beamforming Optimization and Performance
summary: The study presents a systematic machine learning (ML) study of 6G-IoT beamforming optimization (6GBO) using supervised and unsupervised approaches. We compared the predictive power of network, environmental, device, and vision feature groups for 6GBO. Additionally, it addressed other unsupervised perspectives that can enhance 6GBO, including clustering network scenarios using methods such as K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering. Several imbalance-aware experiments revealed that network features possess better prediction power than device, environmental, and vision feature groups, as evidenced by their recall, F1-score and ROC-AUC values. For unsupervised ML exploration (assessed using Elbow, Silhouette score, and Davies-Bouldin Index methods), the results indicate that the deployment environment and type of device primarily influence clustering, rather than mobility-based attributes. Furthermore, the explainability analysis showed that bandwidth, IoT sensors, and mobility possess higher global feature importance across the feature groups. In the future, we would apply deep and reinforcement learning techniques to predict throughput/latency or to optimize rewards determined by performance indicators like SNR enhancement

AI.tldr: A systematic ML study of 6G-IoT beamforming optimization (6GBO) comparing supervised and unsupervised approaches, finding that network features best predict 6GBO performance, while clustering is driven by deployment environment and device type rather than mobility.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate and improve 6G-IoT beamforming optimization (6GBO) by identifying which feature groups (network, environmental, device, vision) have the strongest predictive power, and to explore unsupervised methods for analyzing network scenarios.
AI.method: Supervised and unsupervised machine learning approaches were applied. Supervised imbalance-aware experiments compared the predictive power of network, environmental, device, and vision feature groups using recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. Unsupervised clustering used K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering, evaluated with the Elbow method, Silhouette score, and Davies-Bouldin Index. Explainability analysis assessed global feature importance.
AI.result: Network features showed the best prediction power over device, environmental, and vision groups. Clustering was primarily influenced by deployment environment and device type rather than mobility-based attributes. Explainability analysis revealed that bandwidth, IoT sensors, and mobility have higher global feature importance across groups.
AI.conclusion: Network features are most informative for 6GBO prediction, and environment/device type dominate clustering. Future work will apply deep learning and reinforcement learning to predict throughput/latency or optimize rewards based on performance indicators such as SNR enhancement.

title: Decoupled Contrastive Decoding via Expert-Aligned Drafting
summary: Contrastive Decoding (CD) improves generation quality, but its amateur-model pass makes decoding expensive. Accelerating CD with speculative decoding raises a proposal-alignment question: should the contrastive signal shape the drafter, or should it remain only in verification? We study this question in the lightweight feature-level drafter regime. Two controlled diagnostics, matched Cross-alpha training and an Approximate Dual-Drafter decomposition, give the same diagnosis: contrastive-aware drafting does not consistently improve over expert-aligned drafting because the contrastive correction is usually weaker than drafter error, and reconstruction can amplify that error. We introduce Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which drafts with an expert-aligned lightweight proposer and applies the amateur only in unchanged CD verification. Standard speculative verification preserves the vanilla-CD output distribution. Across the main 8B settings, EAGLE3-based DCD achieves average greedy speedups of 1.65 to 1.95x over vanilla CD and reduces MMLU proposal-path latency by about 5 to 12x relative to amateur-coupled proposal paths.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to make speculative decoding work efficiently with Contrastive Decoding (CD). It finds that making the drafter contrastive-aware does not reliably help, and proposes Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which drafts with an expert-aligned proposer and applies the amateur only during CD verification, achieving 1.65–1.95x speedups over vanilla CD.
AI.motivation: Contrastive Decoding improves generation quality but its amateur-model pass makes decoding expensive. Accelerating it with speculative decoding raises a key design question: should the contrastive signal shape the drafter, or should it be applied only in verification? The paper aims to answer this for lightweight feature-level drafters.
AI.method: Two controlled diagnostics are used: matched Cross-alpha training and an Approximate Dual-Drafter decomposition. These isolate the effect of contrastive-aware drafting. The authors then propose Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which uses an expert-aligned lightweight proposer for drafting and applies the amateur model only in the (unchanged) CD verification stage, relying on standard speculative verification to preserve the vanilla-CD output distribution.
AI.result: Both diagnostics give the same diagnosis: contrastive-aware drafting does not consistently beat expert-aligned drafting, because the contrastive correction is usually weaker than drafter error, and reconstruction can amplify that error. Across main 8B settings, EAGLE3-based DCD achieves average greedy speedups of 1.65–1.95x over vanilla CD and reduces MMLU proposal-path latency by roughly 5–12x compared to amateur-coupled proposal paths.
AI.conclusion: The contrastive signal is better kept in verification rather than in the drafter. DCD decouples drafting (expert-aligned) from the amateur correction (verification-only), preserving the vanilla-CD output distribution while significantly accelerating contrastive decoding.

title: Diagnosing JEPA World Models with Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models that predict in a compact latent space rather than in pixels, reducing the pressure to model nuisance appearance. Yet this provides no guarantee against visual perturbations: they can still alter the encoded representation and affect subsequent action-conditioned predictions. Bisimulation captures this requirement precisely: two observations should be treated as the same state only when their action-conditioned consequences agree. Guided by this criterion, we introduce Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC), a diagnostic that measures how far a clean history and a visually perturbed view of it diverge after being rolled forward under the same action sequence. We prove that this divergence bounds the perturbation-induced change in multi-step prediction error and planner cost. Building on pairwise ACPC, we define two complementary measures: the Invariance Radius (IR) summarizes clean-perturbed rollout spread, while the Separation Rate (SR) checks whether different states remain distinguishable after rollout. Experiments on four visual control tasks show that pairwise ACPC predicts perturbation-induced prediction and cost changes. On LeWM, the IR-SR screen transfers across tasks, and the joint diagnostic remains informative under blur and resize. PLDM exhibits similar diagnostic trends under a different architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC), a diagnostic measuring how much a clean observation and its visually perturbed version diverge after rolling forward under the same action sequence, proving this divergence bounds changes in multi-step prediction error and planner cost. It also defines two complementary measures—Invariance Radius (IR) and Separation Rate (SR)—and validates them on four visual control tasks.
AI.motivation: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) reduce pressure to model nuisance appearance by predicting in latent space, but they do not guarantee robustness to visual perturbations, which can still alter encoded representations and downstream action-conditioned predictions. Bisimulation formalizes the required property: two observations should be treated as the same state only when their action-conditioned consequences agree. The paper aims to provide a diagnostic grounded in this criterion to quantify perturbation-induced degradation.
AI.method: The authors define Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC), which measures the divergence between a clean history and a visually perturbed view of it after rolling both forward under the same action sequence. They prove this divergence bounds the perturbation-induced change in multi-step prediction error and planner cost. Extending pairwise ACPC, they introduce two complementary measures: the Invariance Radius (IR) summarizing clean-perturbed rollout spread, and the Separation Rate (SR) checking whether different states remain distinguishable after rollout.
AI.result: On four visual control tasks, pairwise ACPC predicts perturbation-induced prediction and cost changes. On LeWM, the IR-SR screen transfers across tasks, and the joint diagnostic remains informative under blur and resize perturbations. PLDM exhibits similar diagnostic trends under a different architecture.
AI.conclusion: ACPC, along with its IR and SR extensions, provides an effective, bisimulation-grounded diagnostic for measuring visual-perturbation robustness in joint-embedding world models, with the joint IR-SR measure transferring across tasks and remaining informative under varied perturbations and architectures.

title: Foundations of MT-PDCL: Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic
summary: Standard probabilistic logic programming frameworks typically rely on grounding logic programs into discrete propositional representations. This operational requirement restricts exact inference to finite domains and discrete probability distributions. In this paper, we introduce Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic (MT-PDCL), a generalized foundational framework that eliminates this finite-domain restriction. By explicitly defining stochastic variables over bounded index domains and equipping the interpretation space with standard Borel $σ$-algebras, MT-PDCL allows logical variables to operate natively over continuous measurable spaces. Building on Continuous Distribution Semantics, MT-PDCL models probabilistic rules as mutually independent causal events. However, rather than aggregating these derivations via finite boolean circuits, declarative entailment is formally defined through exact Lebesgue integration over the continuous measure space. We introduce a continuous immediate consequence operator that unifies the integration of continuous prior distributions with the evaluation of exact continuous observations. We demonstrate that this approach replaces the combinatorial bottleneck of discrete grounding with exact, algebraic, and structurally differentiable inference. While this transition trades discrete combinatorics for the geometric curse of dimensionality, it achieves the expressive power of continuous probabilistic models while preserving the pure declarative syntax of definite clause logic.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MT-PDCL, a measure-theoretic probabilistic logic programming framework that removes the finite/discrete grounding restriction by integrating over continuous Borel measure spaces via exact Lebesgue integration, while preserving definite clause syntax.
AI.motivation: Standard probabilistic logic programming (PLP) relies on grounding into discrete propositional representations, which restricts exact inference to finite domains and discrete distributions. The authors aim to lift this operational limitation so logical variables can operate natively over continuous measurable spaces.
AI.method: MT-PDCL defines stochastic variables over bounded index domains and equips the interpretation space with standard Borel σ-algebras. Built on Continuous Distribution Semantics, it models probabilistic rules as mutually independent causal events, but defines declarative entailment through exact Lebesgue integration over the continuous measure space instead of finite boolean circuits. A continuous immediate consequence operator unifies integration of continuous priors with evaluation of exact continuous observations.
AI.result: The approach replaces the combinatorial bottleneck of discrete grounding with exact, algebraic, and structurally differentiable inference. It trades discrete combinatorics for the geometric curse of dimensionality while achieving the expressive power of continuous probabilistic models and preserving pure declarative definite clause syntax.
AI.conclusion: MT-PDCL generalizes probabilistic logic programming to continuous measurable domains, enabling exact continuous inference at the cost of geometric dimensionality, thereby expanding the expressive power of the framework while keeping its declarative syntax intact.

title: Unifying Depth and Width Pruning for LLMs via Binary Knapsack Optimization
summary: Structured pruning is a promising approach for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet existing methods rely heavily on greedy heuristics that produce myopic decisions, and often fail to precisely meet target compression budgets. We present SNIPER, a two-stage structured pruning framework that solves a knapsack optimization over coarse-granularity components to yield conditionally optimal parameter allocations with respect to fixed importance estimates, followed by a fine-grained pruning stage to meet strict budget constraints. We introduce the Compression Ratio Adherence Factor (CRAFT) to quantify budget fidelity, showing that while existing pruners deviate from target compression ratios by up to 33%, SNIPER achieves near-exact adherence with a CRAFT score of 0.98. Evaluations across four diverse architectures over a set of 18 tasks spanning five domains demonstrate SNIPER's consistent improvements in average performance retention and task-level stability over six state-of-the-art pruners. Across all pruning configurations, SNIPER achieves an excellent mean rank of 1.25, indicating its robust cross-architectural generalizability and excellent reliability.

AI.tldr: SNIPER is a two-stage structured pruning framework for LLMs that replaces greedy heuristics with knapsack-based optimal allocation, followed by fine-grained pruning to meet strict budgets, achieving near-exact compression ratio adherence (CRAFT 0.98) and top performance across diverse architectures and tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing structured pruning methods rely on greedy heuristics that lead to myopic decisions and frequently fail to precisely meet target compression budgets, motivating the need for an optimization-driven approach with verifiable budget fidelity.
AI.method: SNIPER is a two-stage framework. Stage one solves a knapsack optimization over coarse-granularity components to produce conditionally optimal parameter allocations given fixed importance estimates. Stage two performs fine-grained pruning to satisfy strict budget constraints. The authors also introduce CRAFT (Compression Ratio Adherence Factor) to quantify budget fidelity.
AI.result: While existing pruners deviate from target compression ratios by up to 33%, SNIPER achieves near-exact adherence with a CRAFT score of 0.98. Across four architectures and 18 tasks spanning five domains, SNIPER shows consistent improvements in average performance retention and task-level stability over six state-of-the-art pruners, attaining a mean rank of 1.25 across all pruning configurations.
AI.conclusion: SNIPER demonstrates robust cross-architectural generalizability and excellent reliability, substantially improving both compression-ratio adherence and performance retention over existing structured pruning methods.

title: CardioState-JEPA: Delay-Aware Cross-Modal Learning of a Shared Cardiac Representation
summary: Electrocardiography (ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and phonocardiography (PCG) provide complementary views of the same cardiac cycle, yet existing cardiac foundation models are trained for a single sensing modality, leaving the shared physiology across sensors unexploited. We introduce CardioState-JEPA, a cardiac foundation model to learn a single shared representation jointly across ECG, PPG, and PCG, built on a physiology-aware joint-embedding predictive architecture. The model maps heterogeneous waveforms into a common token space, processes them with a single shared Transformer encoder, and learns by predicting masked latent cardiac states, placing the pretraining target on shared physiology rather than sensor-specific waveform appearance. To handle the temporal offsets between electrical, mechanical, and hemodynamic events, cross-modal prediction uses a learned delay aligner that matches signals at the corresponding cardiac time. Because synchronized multi-sensor recordings are scarce, CardioState-JEPA first learns within-modality structure from abundant unimodal data and then uses paired data to align modalities in latent cardiac time. Evaluated as a frozen encoder across 25 downstream tasks spanning ECG, PPG, and PCG, our encoder improves average PPG classification by 8.2 AUROC points, PCG murmur detection by 18.8 AUROC points, and ECG classification by 15.5 AUROC points over the best self-supervised signal baseline and matches or exceeds cardiac models trained with privileged clinical text or supervised labels on several ECG benchmarks. These results establish that heterogeneous cardiac signals can mutually supervise a single foundation model of cardiac physiology.

AI.tldr: CardioState-JEPA is a multi-modal cardiac foundation model that learns a shared latent representation across ECG, PPG, and PCG using a physiology-aware joint-embedding predictive architecture, achieving large gains on 25 downstream tasks over single-signal baselines.
AI.motivation: ECG, PPG, and PCG capture complementary views of the same cardiac cycle, but existing cardiac foundation models are trained on a single modality, wasting shared physiology. The authors aim to jointly learn from all three signals, despite the scarcity of synchronized multi-sensor recordings and inherent temporal offsets between electrical, mechanical, and hemodynamic events.
AI.method: CardioState-JEPA maps heterogeneous waveforms (ECG/PPG/PCG) into a common token space and processes them with a single shared Transformer encoder. Pretraining targets masked latent cardiac state prediction (JEPA) to focus on shared physiology rather than waveform reconstruction. A learned delay aligner handles cross-modal temporal offsets by matching signals in "latent cardiac time." Training is staged: first learn within-modality structure from abundant unimodal data, then align modalities using paired data.
AI.result: As a frozen encoder across 25 downstream tasks, CardioState-JEPA improves average PPG classification by 8.2 AUROC points, PCG murmur detection by 18.8 AUROC points, and ECG classification by 15.5 AUROC points over the best self-supervised signal baseline. It also matches or exceeds cardiac models trained with privileged clinical text or supervised labels on several ECG benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous cardiac signals can mutually supervise a single foundation model of cardiac physiology, demonstrating that multi-modal pretraining leverages shared physiology to substantially improve downstream performance across all three modalities.

title: From Local Mismatch to Global Impact: Optimizing Cache Reuse Policy for Efficient Diffusion
summary: Diffusion models have achieved dominant performance in visual generation but suffer from substantial inference overhead. While cache-based acceleration has emerged as a promising solution, existing policies rely on local similarity heuristics, which we identify as being significantly misaligned with final generation quality. This discrepancy stems from the non-uniform propagation and accumulation of errors along the denoising trajectory. To address this, we propose Global-Impact Cache (GCache). We first establish a rigorous theoretical characterization of the error propagation upper bound. Recognizing that this bound can be overly conservative for complex, highly non-convex diffusion models, we further reparameterize the propagation exponent with a Bernstein form and reformulate cache policy search as a bilevel optimization problem. In detail, GCache identifies an optimal reuse policy in the inner objective while aligning the error-weighting function with generation quality loss in the outer objective. This framework effectively reconciles theoretical rigor with empirical performance, learning to prioritize computation where it most impacts visual fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GCache consistently outperforms prior caching strategies on both video and image generation. Notably, on the state-of-the-art Wan2.1 video diffusion model, GCache maintains a 2.17x speedup while significantly enhancing generation quality, reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.

AI.tldr: GCache proposes a globally-aware caching policy for diffusion models that corrects the misalignment between local similarity heuristics and final generation quality, achieving 2.17x speedup on Wan2.1 while reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models are computationally expensive at inference. Existing cache-based acceleration relies on local similarity heuristics, which the authors find to be misaligned with final generation quality because errors propagate and accumulate non-uniformly along the denoising trajectory. This motivates a globally-aware caching policy that prioritizes computation where it most affects visual fidelity.
AI.method: GCache first derives a rigorous upper bound on error propagation along the denoising trajectory. Since this bound is overly conservative for highly non-convex diffusion models, it reparameterizes the propagation exponent using a Bernstein form and reformulates cache policy search as a bilevel optimization problem. The inner objective identifies an optimal reuse policy, while the outer objective aligns the error-weighting function with generation quality loss.
AI.result: GCache consistently outperforms prior caching strategies on both video and image generation. On the state-of-the-art Wan2.1 video diffusion model, it achieves a 2.17x speedup while significantly improving generation quality, reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.
AI.conclusion: By reconciling theoretical rigor with empirical performance, GCache learns to allocate computation where it most impacts visual fidelity, offering an effective cache-based acceleration framework that improves both speed and quality of diffusion model inference.

title: LycheeMemory V2: Efficient Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents via Semantic Segment-Level Consolidation
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents must preserve information from past interactions to support future tasks. Existing memory systems typically rely on eager consolidation, invoking LLMs after each interaction to extract, summarize, or update memories. This design makes memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization can reduce construction cost but risks discarding fine-grained contextual evidence, whereas larger retrieval contexts or multi-hop LLM reasoning shift the overhead to query time. We present LycheeMemory V2, an efficient long-term memory framework that replaces turn-level consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation. Instead of consolidating every interaction, LycheeMemory batches multiple exchanges into segments and encodes each finalized segment into context-independent typed memory records. Segment-level batching lowers LLM encoding frequency, while semantic boundary detection helps preserve coherent event-level and temporal evidence compared with fixed-window batching. The resulting records are organized with lightweight structured indexes for query-planned evidence retrieval. Experiments using GPT-4.1-Mini show that LycheeMemory achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S without increasing query-time token usage. More broadly, our results suggest that the accuracy--cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on what information is retained, but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated.

AI.tldr: LycheeMemory V2 is an efficient long-term memory framework for LLM agents that replaces turn-level eager memory consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation, reducing construction cost while preserving retrieval quality and achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing long-horizon LLM agent memory systems rely on eager consolidation, invoking the LLM after every interaction to extract/summarize/update memories, which makes memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization cuts cost but risks losing fine-grained contextual evidence, while enlarging retrieval contexts or multi-hop LLM reasoning merely moves overhead to query time. The paper seeks a better accuracy--cost trade-off by changing the granularity of consolidation.
AI.method: LycheeMemory V2 batches multiple exchanges into semantic segments and consolidates each finalized segment once into context-independent typed memory records, instead of consolidating every turn. Segment-level batching lowers LLM encoding frequency, while semantic boundary detection preserves coherent event-level and temporal evidence better than fixed-window batching. Lightweight structured indexes organize the resulting records to enable query-planned evidence retrieval.
AI.result: Using GPT-4.1-Mini, LycheeMemory V2 attains state-of-the-art performance of 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S without increasing query-time token usage.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy--cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on which information is retained but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated; segment-level consolidation offers a more efficient balance than turn-level consolidation.

title: I-SDPO: Instance-Level Adaptive Self-Distillation Policy Optimization
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) learns from reward differences within a rollout group, but receives no useful relative signal when every sampled response is incorrect. Privileged self-distillation can fill this gap with dense token supervision, yet applying it throughout training creates a different failure mode: the teacher is a biased, low-variance surrogate for the reward objective, so persistent imitation can oppose reward-improving updates after the policy becomes capable of producing successful trajectories. We introduce I-SDPO (Instance-Level Adaptive Self-Distillation Policy Optimization), which treats teacher reliance as capability-dependent. I-SDPO makes one routing decision per input instance and shares it across that instance's rollout group: all-incorrect groups use a privileged self-distillation objective, whereas any-success groups remain intact for GRPO. This design uses imitation only where group-relative rewards are uninformative. A local analysis characterizes when teacher and reward directions align and shows that a non-vanishing biased distillation weight induces an optimization bias floor. The routing rule automatically reduces the expected distillation rate as success probability rises, withdrawing teacher influence without a hand-designed schedule. On SciKnowEval, I-SDPO obtains the best result in all four scientific domains and improves average mean@16 accuracy from 56.67% with GRPO to 70.31%, with a maximum domain gain of 18.24 points.

AI.tldr: I-SDPO adaptively routes between privileged self-distillation and GRPO per instance: it uses teacher imitation only when a rollout group has no correct answer (where reward differences are uninformative), and switches back to pure GRPO once any success appears, removing the biased-distillation failure mode of persistent imitation.
AI.motivation: GRPO learns only from reward differences within a rollout group, so it gets no useful relative signal when every sampled response is incorrect. Privileged self-distillation provides dense token supervision to fill this gap, but applying it throughout all of training makes the teacher a biased, low-variance surrogate that can oppose reward-improving updates once the policy itself can produce successful trajectories.
AI.method: I-SDPO makes teacher reliance capability-dependent via one routing decision per input instance, shared across that instance's rollout group. All-incorrect groups use a privileged self-distillation objective; any-success groups stay intact for GRPO. A local analysis characterizes when teacher and reward directions align and shows that a non-vanishing biased distillation weight induces an optimization bias floor. The routing rule automatically reduces the expected distillation rate as success probability rises, withdrawing teacher influence without any hand-designed schedule.
AI.result: On SciKnowEval, I-SDPO achieves the best result in all four scientific domains and raises average mean@16 accuracy from 56.67% (GRPO) to 70.31%, with a maximum single-domain gain of 18.24 points.
AI.conclusion: Treating teacher reliance as capability-dependent lets I-SDPO use imitation only where group-relative rewards are uninformative, avoiding the optimization bias floor of persistent distillation and outperforming GRPO substantially on scientific knowledge evaluation.

title: BoardroomAI: Dependency-Aware Human-Steerable Multi-Agent Deliberation through Evolving Decision Graphs
summary: Organizational decisions are co-created while evidence, constraints, and human priorities continue to evolve. In conventional transcript-based multi-agent systems, humans typically provide an initial problem, agents deliberate internally, and the system returns a final response. BoardroomAI instead treats the human as a persistent participant who can intervene by challenging assumptions, modifying constraints, changing priorities, introducing evidence, or redirecting the decision process. We operationalize this human--agent coexistence through four components: (i) a typed decision graph representing evidence, assumptions, constraints, claims, objections, alternatives, risks, decisions, semantic dependencies, and specialist responsibility; (ii) an intervention compiler that converts confirmed human actions into explicit graph updates; (iii) dependency-aware propagation that identifies affected subgraphs, preserves unaffected artifacts, and selectively reactivates relevant specialists; and (iv) an evaluation framework measuring intervention impact, repair coverage, preservation, recomputation, and decision validity. Across 600 generated decision-DAG interventions, propagation matched exhaustive impact computation while inspecting only 14.59% of nodes. In a 12-case exploratory pilot, selective repair recomputed 62.11% of canonical nodes, preserved all gold-unaffected nodes, and produced valid updated decisions in six cases while abstaining in the remaining six. These abstentions show that correct intervention routing may still provide insufficient context for synthesis, motivating a \emph{decision-sufficient context closure} for human-steered multi-agent deliberation. All results are synthetic and prototype-level.

AI.tldr: BoardroomAI reimagines multi-agent deliberation as an ongoing human-in-the-loop process where users can intervene in decisions via typed graph updates, dependency-aware propagation, and selective specialist reactivation, rather than a one-shot transcript-based pipeline.
AI.motivation: Conventional transcript-based multi-agent systems treat humans as providing only an initial problem and receiving a final answer, ignoring that organizational decisions evolve as evidence, constraints, and priorities shift. The paper seeks to enable persistent human participation that can challenge assumptions, modify constraints, change priorities, add evidence, or redirect decision processes, and to route these interventions correctly without discarding unaffected work.
AI.method: The authors introduce four components: (1) a typed decision graph encoding evidence, assumptions, constraints, claims, objections, alternatives, risks, decisions, semantic dependencies, and specialist responsibility; (2) an intervention compiler that turns confirmed human actions into explicit graph updates; (3) dependency-aware propagation that finds affected subgraphs, preserves unaffected artifacts, and selectively reactivates relevant specialists; and (4) an evaluation framework measuring intervention impact, repair coverage, preservation, recomputation, and decision validity. They test on 600 generated decision-DAG interventions and a 12-case exploratory pilot.
AI.result: Dependency-aware propagation matched exhaustive impact computation while inspecting only 14.59% of nodes on 600 generated decision-DAG interventions. In a 12-case pilot, selective repair recomputed 62.11% of canonical nodes, preserved all gold-unaffected nodes, and yielded valid updated decisions in six cases while abstaining in the remaining six. Abstentions indicate that correct intervention routing can still provide insufficient context for synthesis, motivating a decision-sufficient context closure. All results are synthetic and prototype-level.
AI.conclusion: Human-steered multi-agent deliberation is feasible via graph-based intervention routing, but correct routing alone is insufficient for decision synthesis when context is lacking. This motivates a decision-sufficient context closure to ensure agents have enough context to produce valid updated decisions.

title: The Objective Is the Bottleneck: Latent World Models Encode What Their Planners Cannot Use
comment: Follow-up to arXiv:2608.10145. All experiments run on a laptop CPU; no model was trained or fine-tuned. Code, checkpoints and every measurement: github.com/joyjeet-singh/tinylab
summary:
Latent world models are judged by how well they predict, so when planning fails at long horizons the natural reading is that the predictor degrades. On a reproduction of LeWorldModel on TwoRoom we show the binding constraint is the planner's objective instead.
  The predictor is not the limit: its imagined state seventy-five environment steps ahead is still only 0.189 as wrong as assuming the world froze, while the planner never imagines beyond twenty-five. The objective is. Cross-entropy-method planning minimises squared latent distance, which tracks true distance at r = 0.426, saturates by about eighty arena units and decreases beyond a hundred and twenty, so moving away from the goal can lower the cost. The information is present throughout: a ridge probe recovers position from the frozen embedding at R^2 0.9922.
  The pathology is the method's, not one reimplementation's. It is present in the authors' released weights, and across four checkpoints long-horizon success rank-orders exactly with metric quality and inversely with prediction accuracy.
  Replacing only the objective, with nothing retrained and no GPU, lifts goals reached at offset 100 from 26.0% to 98.0%, equals the 98.0% at offset 25, and reaches 92.0% under a third of the budget: planning stops depending on the horizon. The best cost is not the most accurate. A head learned from frame separation alone predicts spatial distance worse than a position probe (r = 0.819 against 0.9897) yet plans better, charging 24% more to cross the environment's dividing wall where squared latent distance charges 4% less. It has learned reachability, not proximity.

AI.tldr: A reproduction of the LeWorldModel on the TwoRoom task shows that long-horizon planning failures are caused by the planner's objective (squared latent distance in cross-entropy-method planning), not by degraded world-model prediction. Replacing only the cost function dramatically improves goal-reaching while removing dependence on planning horizon.
AI.motivation: Latent world models are typically judged by prediction accuracy, so long-horizon planning failures are usually attributed to predictor degradation. The authors challenge this assumption by investigating whether the planner's objective, rather than the predictor, is the limiting factor in long-horizon planning.
AI.method: The authors reproduce LeWorldModel on two connected rooms (TwoRoom). They measure whether the imagined state 75 steps ahead degrades versus a "frozen world" baseline, analyze squared latent distance as the planning cost (its correlation with true distance, saturation, and non-monotonic behavior beyond ~120 arena units), probe the frozen embedding with ridge regression to check if position is recoverable, test across four checkpoints and the authors' released weights, then replace only the planning objective. A successor head learned purely from frame separation predicts spatial distance worse than a position probe (r=0.819 vs 0.9897) yet plans better, indicating it has learned reachability rather than proximity.
AI.result: The imagined state 75 steps ahead is only 0.189 as wrong as freezing the world, while the planner never imagines beyond 25 steps. Squared latent distance tracks true distance at r=0.426, saturates around 80 arena units, and decreases beyond 120 units. A ridge probe recovers position at R²=0.9922. Long-horizon success across four checkpoints rank-orders with metric quality and inversely with prediction accuracy. Replacing only the objective lifts goals reached at offset 100 from 26.0% to 98.0% (equal to the 98.0% at offset 25) and reaches 92.0% under a third of the budget, with no retraining and no GPU. The learned reachability head charges 24% more to cross a dividing wall where squared latent distance charges 4% less.
AI.conclusion: The pathology is inherent to the method, not to a single reimplementation: prediction accuracy is not the bottleneck, and the standard squared latent distance objective saturates and becomes non-monotonic at long horizons. Replacing the objective with reachability-based costs removes horizon dependence in planning and dramatically improves long-horizon performance, suggesting world-model evaluation and planner design should focus on the objective rather than solely on prediction accuracy.

title: DMDIntel: Interpreting Large Language Models via Dynamic Mode Decomposition
summary: In this work, we introduce DMDIntel which uses dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to make the predictions made by LLMs in a classification task interpretable. It develops an input attribution pipeline, that first decomposes the hidden states of an LLM into prominent patterns, also known as modes, and then associates ranks to the input tokens based on the projection values on those modes. Rigorous experiments across three datasets and three model families consistently show that the ranked attribution of input tokens obtained using DMDIntel by far outperforms state-of-the-art techniques such as principal component analysis, integrated gradients and SHAP.

AI.tldr: DMDIntel uses dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to make LLM classification predictions interpretable by decomposing hidden states into modes and ranking input tokens by their projection values, outperforming PCA, integrated gradients, and SHAP.
AI.motivation: LLM predictions are opaque, and existing interpretability methods (PCA, integrated gradients, SHAP) provide suboptimal token-level attributions. The authors aim to develop a more faithful input-attribution method grounded in the dynamics of hidden states.
AI.method: DMDIntel builds an input attribution pipeline: it applies dynamic mode decomposition to the hidden states of an LLM to extract prominent dynamic patterns (modes), then ranks input tokens according to their projection values onto these modes to obtain token-level attributions.
AI.result: Experiments across three datasets and three model families consistently show that DMDIntel's ranked token attributions significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods including principal component analysis, integrated gradients, and SHAP.
AI.conclusion: DMDIntel demonstrates that dynamic mode decomposition of hidden states yields a more effective and interpretable token attribution technique for LLM classification tasks than existing state-of-the-art approaches.

title: VALG: An Agentic System for ML Theory Research
summary:
Machine learning theory studies learning procedures through mathematical setups in which the data model, training protocol, oracle access, loss, metric, and randomness define the phenomenon that a theorem is meant to explain. Solving an open problem therefore requires the problem formulation, theorem target, and proof mechanism to be developed in concert. Researchers formulate hypotheses, test them through preliminary theoretical or empirical analysis, and refine both assumptions and proofs. We investigate whether this process can be organized as an autonomous agentic workflow for ML theory research.
  We develop VALG, an agentic system that combines multi-level Verification, Adaptive formulation of Learning-theory problems, and Graph-structured proof development. Within each source-relative theorem branch, VALG maintains a fixed mathematical specification, checks the theorem-level composition of a typed proof-dependency graph, and constructs and reviews local proofs in dependency order. When a proof attempt fails, VALG identifies whether the obstruction lies in a derivation, the proof structure, or the theorem formulation and routes the next attempt accordingly. Formulation-level obstructions initiate an explicitly related variant or relaxation, preserving the mathematical relation between the resulting theorem and the source problem.
  We evaluate VALG on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems. Two runs produce internally finalized theorem candidates that match the scope of their source briefs; the remaining seven yield restricted-method results, special cases, or conditional theorems. These case studies show how VALG keeps source-scope matches, relaxations, conditional results, and blocked attempts mathematically distinct. VALG is open source at https://github.com/DechenZhang/VALG-ML-Theory-Agent.

AI.tldr: VALG is an agentic system that automates ML theory research by combining verification, adaptive problem formulation, and graph-structured proof development, and it is evaluated on nine subproblems from COLT 2026 open problems, producing two full theorem candidates and seven restricted/conditional results.
AI.motivation: Solving open problems in machine learning theory requires jointly developing the problem formulation, theorem target, and proof mechanism. The authors investigate whether this iterative process—hypothesizing, testing, and refining assumptions and proofs—can be organized as an autonomous agentic workflow for ML theory research.
AI.method: VALG combines multi-level Verification, Adaptive formulation of Learning-theory problems, and Graph-structured proof development. Within each source-relative theorem branch, it maintains a fixed mathematical specification, checks theorem-level composition of a typed proof-dependency graph, and constructs and reviews local proofs in dependency order. When a proof attempt fails, it classifies the obstruction as either a derivation issue, a proof-structure issue, or a theorem-formulation issue and routes the next attempt accordingly; formulation-level obstructions lead to an explicitly related variant or relaxation that preserves the mathematical relation to the source problem.
AI.result: Evaluated on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems, VALG produced internally finalized theorem candidates matching their source briefs in two runs, while the remaining seven yielded restricted-method results, special cases, or conditional theorems. The case studies demonstrate that VALG keeps source-scope matches, relaxations, conditional results, and blocked attempts mathematically distinct.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that an autonomous agentic workflow can organize ML theory research by coordinating verification, adaptive formulation, and graph-structured proof development, producing distinct and clearly classified outcomes (full matches, relaxations, conditional results, or blocked attempts) and is released open source.

title: Comment on "Modeling rapid language learning by distilling Bayesian priors into artificial neural networks"
summary: McCoy & Griffiths (2025, henceforth M&G) suggest that a Bayesian prior can be distilled into Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) through Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML, Finn et al., 2017). They support this empirically by showing that meta-trained networks demonstrate formal language learning abilities comparable to Yang & Piantadosi (2023)'s Bayesian learner, significantly outperforming standard ANNs. We point out that under the standard interpretation of a prior, M&G's procedure does not actually instill one; it merely initializes network weights favorably, leaving the objective function unchanged. We then consider a more permissive interpretation, where the system as a whole can be seen as implementing a Bayesian learner even without an explicit prior in the objective. We show that this interpretation faces nontrivial challenges. Finally, we assess how well MAML approximates the empirical results of Bayesian learning, showing that unlike genuine Bayesian learners, M&G's model overfits and generalizes poorly to unseen data.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques McCoy & Griffiths (2025)'s claim that MAML instills a Bayesian prior in ANNs, arguing that MAML only improves weight initialization without altering the objective function, that the broader "system-as-Bayesian" interpretation is problematic, and that MAML models overfit and generalize worse than genuine Bayesian learners.
AI.motivation: To challenge the claim that meta-learning (MAML) can distill a Bayesian prior into neural networks, and to clarify what it actually takes for a model to be a genuine Bayesian learner.
AI.method: The authors provide a conceptual critique of M&G's setup under two interpretations (standard and permissive), and conduct an empirical comparison showing that MAML-trained networks overfit and generalize poorly to unseen data relative to true Bayesian learners.
AI.result: Under the standard interpretation, MAML only initializes weights favorably and leaves the objective unchanged, so no prior is instilled. The permissive system-level interpretation faces nontrivial challenges. Empirically, MAML models overfit and generalize poorly to unseen data, unlike genuine Bayesian learners.
AI.conclusion: McCoy & Griffiths' MAML procedure does not actually implement a Bayesian prior; it merely produces a favorable initialization, and its empirical behavior (overfitting, poor generalization) diverges from genuine Bayesian learning.

title: Uniform Herding: Exemplar Replay with Representation Refresh
summary: As the feature representation changes, replay must preserve the earlier classes. However, only a bounded active exemplar set can be replayed. We propose Uniform Herding, which allocates the current active set across observed classes and uses a bounded candidate pool to refresh their chosen exemplars in the current representation. On CIFAR-100 with ten class-incremental tasks, a ResNet-18 backbone, active budget $M=2{,}000$, retrieval budget $b=64$, and three seeds, Uniform Herding obtains $44.00\pm0.51\%$ final average accuracy and $17.22\pm0.43\%$ forgetting, compared with $42.33\pm1.20\%$ and $24.87\pm1.11\%$ for iCaRL. Within the Uniform Herding protocol, final accuracy decreased when NME or herding was replaced with the tested alternatives, while forgetting increased when distillation was removed. Changing the retrieval budget has a smaller effect across the tested range than changing the active budget. The comparison with iCaRL is end-to-end. It does not isolate the effect of refresh from the other protocol differences. These results are limited to the tested protocol.

AI.tldr: Uniform Herding is a class-incremental learning replay method that evenly allocates a bounded active exemplar set across observed classes and periodically refreshes exemplars from a bounded candidate pool in the current feature representation. On CIFAR-100 it achieves 44.00% final average accuracy and 17.22% forgetting, outperforming iCaRL (42.33% accuracy, 24.87% forgetting) end-to-end.
AI.motivation: In class-incremental learning, replay must preserve earlier classes even as the feature representation changes, but only a bounded active exemplar set can be stored. This creates a tension between allocating the limited budget across a growing number of classes and keeping exemplars representative of the current feature space, motivating a method that both allocates and refreshes exemplars efficiently.
AI.method: Uniform Herding allocates the current active budget uniformly across all observed classes, then uses a bounded candidate pool (retrieval budget b=64) to refresh the chosen exemplars within the current feature representation via herding. The approach is evaluated on CIFAR-100 with ten class-incremental tasks, a ResNet-18 backbone, an active budget M=2,000, and three seeds, compared against iCaRL.
