AI.result: Uniform Herding achieves 44.00±0.51% final average accuracy and 17.22±0.43% forgetting versus iCaRL's 42.33±1.20% and 24.87±1.11%. Ablations show final accuracy drops when NME or herding is replaced with alternatives, and forgetting increases when distillation is removed. The retrieval budget has a smaller effect than the active budget across the tested range.
AI.conclusion: Uniform Herding improves end-to-end performance over iCaRL, but the comparison does not isolate the refresh mechanism from other protocol differences, and the findings are limited to the tested protocol. Retrieval budget is relatively insensitive compared to active budget, while distillation is important for reducing forgetting.

title: CASA: Content-Acoustic Speaking Assessment with Speech Encoder and Large Language Model
comment: To be submitted to ICASSP 2027. Code is available at https://github.com/aalto-speech/casa
summary:
Research on automatic speaking assessment (ASA) has increasingly adopted multimodal speech large language models to assess learners' speaking performance. However, existing studies provide limited analysis of how acoustic and content information contribute to predictions and how stable the resulting performance is. We propose CASA, a simpler architecture combining Whisper-medium and Qwen3.5-2B that achieves state-of-the-art performance while providing a more interpretable separation between speech delivery and content.
  On the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025, CASA achieves a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.358, improving on the previous best RMSE while using approximately half the estimated inference parameters. The general-purpose architecture is designed for adaptation to other ASA corpora without structural changes and relies on three handcrafted fluency features. Through ablations and repeated runs, we analyze the individual and complementary contributions of acoustic and content information, examine performance variability, and demonstrate the potential of large language model reasoning for training-free content validation.

AI.tldr: CASA combines Whisper-medium and Qwen3.5-2B to achieve state-of-the-art automatic speaking assessment (ASA) with an RMSE of 0.358 on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025, using roughly half the inference parameters of the prior best model, while offering clearer separation of speech delivery and content.
AI.motivation: Existing ASA studies using multimodal speech LLMs rarely analyze how acoustic and content information each contribute to predictions or how stable the resulting performance is, leaving interpretability and reliability gaps.
AI.method: CASA is a simpler architecture pairing Whisper-medium with Qwen3.5-2B, built on three handcrafted fluency features, designed for generalization to other ASA corpora without structural changes. The authors use ablations and repeated runs to isolate acoustic vs. content contributions and evaluate performance variability, plus LLM reasoning for training-free content validation.
AI.result: CASA achieves an RMSE of 0.358 on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025, beating the previous best while using about half the estimated inference parameters. Analyses show the individual and complementary roles of acoustic and content information, quantify performance stability across runs, and demonstrate the potential of LLM reasoning for training-free content validation.
AI.conclusion: The interpretable separation of speech delivery and content, combined with strong performance at reduced inference cost and a general-purpose, adaptation-friendly design, makes CASA a promising direction for more transparent and stable automatic speaking assessment.

title: Learning the Mathematical Property for Designing Low Mutual Coherence Binary Sensing Matrices
summary: In this research work, we are constructing the sensing matrix, which is essential for the success of the compressive sensing technique. We have chosen a learning-based technique for the construction of the sensing matrix. The novelty and uniqueness of the proposed technique is that it does not use any data set and also does not use a specific application. It uses the mathematical property/constraint for the construction of the sensing matrix for the perfect recovery of the signal. The perfect recovery of signals is an old and still very challenging problem in real-world applications. In late 2000, compressive sensing became a popular mathematical tool for the perfect recovery of sparse signals. The core of the compressive technique is the construction of the sensing matrix, which satisfies certain special properties such as restricted isometry property (RIP), null space property (NSP), and spark property (SP). All these properties are NP-hard problems and hence computationally challenging to solve. For all practical purposes, the construction of the sensing matrix needs to achieve low mutual coherence to achieve the perfect recovery of the signals. We have used a neural network for the construction of the sensing matrix, and this framework constructs a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence. The entries in the matrix are generated through a shared underlying rule. The proposed architecture is simple and does not use large-scale training data sets. Such uniqueness and novelty bring a drastic reduction in computational cost, and also, for the first time in literature, the use of a mathematical property for defining the loss function. In this proposed research work, the mutual coherence property has been used in the neural network framework. Such a neural network framework brings generality, robustness, and reduces storage requirements.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a learning-based (neural network) method to construct a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence for compressive sensing, relying solely on a mathematical property (mutual coherence) as the loss function—without any dataset or application-specific data—thereby reducing computational cost and storage while achieving generality and robustness.
AI.motivation: Perfect recovery of signals is a longstanding and challenging problem. Compressive sensing requires a sensing matrix satisfying properties like RIP, NSP, and spark, but verifying/constructing these is NP-hard and computationally challenging. The goal is to construct a sensing matrix that achieves low mutual coherence for practical perfect recovery, while drastically reducing computational cost and storage and avoiding dependence on large training datasets or specific applications.
AI.method: A neural network framework is used to construct a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence. Key novelty: the loss function is defined directly using the mutual coherence property (a mathematical constraint), rather than data-driven error. No dataset and no application-specific information are used. Entries of the matrix are generated through a shared underlying rule, and the architecture is simple.
AI.result: The proposed technique constructs a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence, enabling perfect recovery of sparse signals. It achieves drastic reduction in computational cost and storage requirements, and brings generality and robustness compared to conventional methods.
AI.conclusion: Using a mathematical property (mutual coherence) as the loss function in a neural network framework is a novel, unique, and efficient way to construct the sensing matrix for compressive sensing. It removes the need for large training datasets and specific applications, offering reduced computational cost, lower storage, generality, and robustness.

title: Explanatory Engagement Under Rare Anomalous Failure: Asymptotic Rarity in Model Behavior (or: The Asymptotic AI)
comment: 11 figures. Elicitation-condition sweep across three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b); pipeline scripts and experimental data available upon reasonable request
summary: Prior work on LLM behavior under anomalous conditions asks whether a model notices anomalies. We ask a narrower question: once a model sits in a workflow with a low, controllable failure rate, does its explanatory engagement - length, specificity, self-reported confidence - change as failure grows asymptotically rarer? We built a local, zero-cost harness on three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b) running a repeated tool-call task where one call fails at probability p, swept across eight rates from 0.2 to 0.0001, under five elicitation conditions from immediate prompting to none. We hypothesized a rise in engagement as failures grew rarer, then a collapse near a detectability threshold. Pooled across conditions this appeared false: length fell in a flat, monotonic pattern. Splitting by condition overturned that. Under immediate_forced, where the model must explain every failure instantly, the predicted rise is confirmed but followed by a plateau, not a collapse: length peaks at 28.4 words at p=0.05, settles to 17.4-19.0 words at the rarest rates, and confidence rises unevenly from about 53% to the 70s-90s. Under grouped_runs, explanation batched to run-end, no collapse appears. Under passive_unprompted, aggregate magnitude is a floor artifact, but a recovered logging gap revealed real, model-specific self-monitoring: llama3.1:8b volunteers structured confidence reports unprompted, sometimes eroding its own confidence as trials accumulate; the other two do so only once, as boilerplate. Elicitation structure is a first-class moderator of collapse observability. A companion guaranteed-failure run (72 cells, backfilling rates where random sampling gave zero real failures) shows models differ in whether they recognize an anomaly, distinct from engagement once recognized. Limitation: discrete rate points cannot capture behavior between them, a direction for future work.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether large language models' explanatory engagement (length, specificity, confidence) rises and then collapses as tool-call failures become asymptotically rarer. Using three open-weight models across eight failure rates and five elicitation conditions, it finds that elicitation structure—not rarity alone—moderates the rise/collapse, and that models differ in anomaly recognition vs. engagement.
AI.motivation: Prior work asks whether LLMs notice anomalies; this paper narrows the question to whether a model embedded in a low-failure-rate workflow changes its explanatory behavior (length, specificity, confidence) as failures grow asymptotically rarer, and whether a detectability threshold induces a collapse in engagement.
AI.method: Built a local, zero-cost harness on three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b) running a repeated tool-call task where one call fails with probability p, swept over eight rates (0.2 to 0.0001) under five elicitation conditions (from immediate prompting to none, including immediate_forced, grouped_runs, and passive_unprompted). A companion guaranteed-failure run (72 cells) backfilled rates where random sampling produced zero real failures.
AI.result: Pooled across conditions, engagement length fell in a flat, monotonic pattern (no rise-then-collapse). Splitting by condition overturned this: under immediate_forced, the predicted rise appears but ends in a plateau (length peaks at 28.4 words at p=0.05, settling to 17.4–19.0 at rarest rates; confidence rises unevenly from ~53% to the 70s–90s). Under grouped_runs, no collapse appears. Under passive_unprompted, aggregate magnitude is a floor artifact, but a recovered logging gap revealed model-specific self-monitoring: llama3.1:8b volunteers structured confidence reports unprompted (sometimes eroding its own confidence over trials), while the other two do so once as boilerplate. Models also differ in anomaly recognition (distinct from engagement).
AI.conclusion: Elicitation structure is a first-class moderator of whether a collapse in explanatory engagement is observable; rarity alone does not produce the predicted rise-then-collapse. Models differ in recognizing anomalies versus engaging once recognized. A limitation is that discrete rate points cannot capture behavior between them.

title: Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection for Scalable TabPFN Inference on Large-Scale Tabular Data
summary: Pretrained tabular foundation models have demonstrated strong predictive capability; however, their application to large-scale datasets remains constrained by the limited inference context. This paper introduces Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection (BAPS), a framework for constructing compact, information-preserving contexts for scalable TabPFN inference. Without modifying or retraining the pretrained model, BAPS jointly preserves representative structure, informative decision boundaries, local density, class balance, and feature-space diversity. Experiments on the million-row HIGGS and SUSY datasets show that 512 prototypes retain strong predictive performance and reliable calibration, corresponding to an approximately 1,953-fold context compression. All experiments were conducted on an Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB RAM and no GPU acceleration. These findings establish effective context construction as a practical mechanism for extending pretrained tabular foundation models to million-scale datasets.

AI.tldr: BAPS builds compact prototype-based contexts that let pretrained TabPFN scale to million-row tabular datasets without retraining, achieving ~1,953× context compression while preserving predictive performance and calibration.
AI.motivation: Pretrained tabular foundation models like TabPFN perform well but are limited by inference context size, preventing application to large-scale (million-row) datasets.
AI.method: Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection (BAPS) constructs compact, information-preserving contexts for scalable TabPFN inference, jointly preserving representative structure, informative decision boundaries, local density, class balance, and feature-space diversity, without modifying or retraining the pretrained model.
AI.result: On the million-row HIGGS and SUSY datasets, 512 prototypes retain strong predictive performance and reliable calibration, corresponding to roughly 1,953-fold context compression. All experiments ran on an Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB RAM and no GPU acceleration.
AI.conclusion: Effective context construction is a practical mechanism for extending pretrained tabular foundation models to million-scale datasets, enabling scalable inference without costly retraining or specialized hardware.

title: Behavioral Reprogramming of Open-Weights Models: Cognitive Plasticity and Alignment Bounds
comment: Preprint submitted to arXiv, August 12, 2026. 13 pages, 5 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly aligned to function as passive, sycophantic assistants. We challenge this default paradigm by empirically evaluating the cognitive plasticity of open-weight architectures when subjected to rigorous behavioral reprogramming. Our objective is to induce a proactive, Socratic conversational framework, characterized by high-frequency question generation under strictly constrained high-performance computing (HPC) conditions. Through a massively parallelized hyperparameter sweep comprising 405 HPC jobs, we define precise mathematical bounds for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). We identify an architectural threshold at LoRA rank $r=16$ and demonstrate via extensive epoch ablation that generalization capacity strictly reaches its optimal convergence within an optimized training window of $e \in [2, 3]$ depending on dataset density (minimum validation loss of 0.919). Furthermore, scaling model capacity to 14B parameters yielded a lower localized evaluation perplexity (1.414). Subsequent Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) successfully decoupled the underlying assertive behavior from localized syntax, while rigorous cross-lingual stress testing reveals both the capabilities and the structural boundaries of zero-shot persona transfer, demonstrating robust alignment in closely related linguistic families alongside identifiable degradation pathways in morphologically distant targets. These findings establish a rigorous empirical framework for compute-efficient, cross-lingual behavioral modification.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically tests whether open-weight LLMs can be reprogrammed from passive assistants into proactive, Socratic question-askers, using a large HPC hyperparameter sweep to find compute-efficient fine-tuning bounds and evaluate generalization, scaling, preference optimization, and cross-lingual persona transfer.
AI.motivation: LLMs are predominantly aligned as passive, sycophantic assistants. The authors challenge this default paradigm and seek to determine whether open-weight architectures possess the cognitive plasticity to be behaviorally reprogrammed into a proactive, Socratic conversational mode under strict compute constraints.
AI.method: A massively parallelized hyperparameter sweep of 405 HPC jobs over parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), specifically LoRA, to establish mathematical bounds. They identify an architectural threshold at LoRA rank r=16 and an optimal training epoch window e∈[2,3] (minimum validation loss 0.919). They scale to a 14B model, apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to decouple assertive behavior from localized syntax, and conduct cross-lingual zero-shot stress testing.
AI.result: Generalization capacity converges optimally within e∈[2,3] depending on dataset density (min validation loss 0.919). Scaling to 14B parameters yields lower localized evaluation perplexity (1.414). DPO successfully decoupled underlying assertive behavior from localized syntax. Cross-lingual stress testing showed robust zero-shot persona transfer in closely related language families with identifiable degradation pathways in morphologically distant targets.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a rigorous empirical framework for compute-efficient, cross-lingual behavioral modification of LLMs, demonstrating that proactive Socratic behavior can be induced in open-weight models with bounded fine-tuning resources, while delineating structural limits in distant-language generalization.

title: Better Decomposition, Free Aggregation: A Synthesizer-Folding Framework for Multilingual Multi-Hop Question Answering
summary: Multilingual retrieval-augmented generation (mRAG) equips large language models with access to globally distributed external knowledge for complex multilingual question answering. Recent approaches either translate retrieved documents into English or the query language to bridge the cross-lingual semantic gap, or decompose a complex query into sub-questions and aggregate the intermediate reasoning process. However, both lines of work suffer from two limitations. First, one-size-fits-all translation alignment, blanket translation discards culturally and linguistically native information unique to the target language, introduces translation noise, and inflates system cost. Second, greedy decomposition and aggregation, uncontrolled decomposition produces redundant sub-questions that compound errors during step-wise reasoning, and the final aggregation over reasoning paths further amplifies these errors. We address both with our method Syfer, a synthesizer-folding framework for multilingual multi-hop question answering that defers translation rather than applying it by default. Syfer first invokes a format-constrained decomposer to produce a sub-question graph in the original language, followed by a decomposition-quality check; when the check passes, sub-questions are answered sequentially under a retrieve-then-answer policy in the target language, and the English translation pathway with bilingual sub-question graph alignment is activated only when the check fails. Experiments across multiple languages show that Syfer attains competitive accuracy while striking a favourable balance between performance and computational cost.

AI.tldr: Syfer is a synthesizer-folding framework for multilingual multi-hop QA that defers translation: it decomposes queries into a sub-question graph in the source language, applies a quality check, and only activates an English translation pathway with bilingual graph alignment when the check fails, achieving competitive accuracy at lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing multilingual RAG methods suffer from two limitations: (1) blanket "one-size-fits-all" translation into English or the query language discards culturally/linguistically native information, introduces translation noise, and inflates cost; (2) greedy decomposition produces redundant sub-questions that compound errors, and aggregation over reasoning paths further amplifies those errors.
AI.method: Syfer first uses a format-constrained decomposer to build a sub-question graph in the original language, then runs a decomposition-quality check. If the check passes, sub-questions are answered sequentially using a retrieve-then-answer policy in the target language. Only when the check fails is an English translation pathway activated, with bilingual sub-question graph alignment to bridge the cross-lingual gap.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple languages show Syfer attains competitive accuracy while achieving a favorable balance between performance and computational cost compared to translation-based and decomposition-aggregation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Deferring translation rather than applying it by default, combined with quality-checked graph decomposition and conditional English alignment, enables Syfer to match state-of-the-art accuracy while reducing cost and avoiding translation-induced information loss and error amplification.

title: Incremental Evaluation and Training in Relational Deep Learning
summary: Relational Deep Learning (RDL) models multi-tabular databases as temporal heterogeneous graphs to enable end-to-end representation learning. However, prevailing RDL evaluation practices rely on static, single-episode dataset snapshots, overlooking the continuous, time-evolving nature of real-world databases. Consequently, current RDL benchmarks fail to capture how model performance changes as new data accumulates over time. To address this limitation, we introduce an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm to assess and improve the temporal robustness and adaptability of state-of-the-art RDL models. Using established large-scale datasets, we examine data evolution and model training dynamics, demonstrating that temporal concept drifts occur in the majority of predictive tasks. We present multiple incremental training regimes for fine-tuning the models and demonstrate that transfer learning is both feasible and highly effective in the RDL setting. Alongside a new temporal evaluation metric that prioritizes near-future accuracy, we show that our incrementally fine-tuned models consistently outperform the standard, expensive, from-scratch trained baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm for Relational Deep Learning (RDL), showing that temporal concept drift is common, and that incrementally fine-tuned models outperform expensive from-scratch retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing RDL evaluation relies on static, single-episode snapshots of multi-tabular databases, ignoring the continuous time-evolving nature of real-world data. This fails to capture how RDL model performance changes as new data accumulates, so current benchmarks cannot assess temporal robustness or adaptability.
AI.method: The authors introduce an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm. Using established large-scale datasets, they analyze data evolution and model training dynamics, detect temporal concept drift, and propose multiple incremental training regimes (fine-tuning) for RDL models. They also introduce a new temporal evaluation metric that prioritizes near-future accuracy, and compare incrementally fine-tuned models against from-scratch trained baselines.
AI.result: Temporal concept drifts occur in the majority of predictive tasks. Transfer learning (fine-tuning) is shown to be feasible and highly effective in the RDL setting. Incrementally fine-tuned models consistently outperform the standard, expensive, from-scratch trained baselines under the new temporal metric.
AI.conclusion: Incremental fine-tuning with a focus on near-future accuracy provides a more realistic and efficient evaluation/training paradigm for RDL, improving temporal robustness and adaptability over static single-episode approaches.

title: EEG-PRIME: Prototype-Aligned Representation Learning with Multi-Level Conditioning for EEG Decoding
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding models often generalize poorly across datasets and subjects due to domain shifts in acquisition protocols and individual neurophysiology. We propose EEG-PRIME, a two-stage EEG foundation model for cross-dataset multi-task decoding. EEG-PRIME combines masked pretraining with prototype-aligned instruction tuning to enable instruction-aware and subject-invariant decoding across diverse BCI paradigms. During pretraining, an EEG encoder learns transferable representations through masked reconstruction with frequency-cutoff spectral augmentation. During instruction tuning, EEG-PRIME incorporates task-semantic, dataset-specific, and subject-invariant conditioning. The resulting conditioning signal modulates the Q-Former through Layer-wise Query Modulation, while frozen text embeddings of class labels serve as prototypes for cosine-similarity-based prediction across heterogeneous label spaces. Experiments on sixteen datasets covering motor imagery, emotion recognition, ADHD detection, covert speech, and mental workload show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines and prior EEG foundation models under cross-subject settings. On two additional held-out datasets, EEG-PRIME achieves balanced accuracy comparable to within-session calibration models without target-domain optimization, calibration, or linear probing, demonstrating promising zero-shot transfer capability.

AI.tldr: EEG-PRIME is a two-stage EEG foundation model combining masked pretraining with prototype-aligned instruction tuning to achieve instruction-aware, subject-invariant decoding across diverse BCI tasks, demonstrating strong cross-dataset and zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: EEG decoding models generalize poorly across datasets and subjects due to domain shifts in acquisition protocols and individual neurophysiology. The authors aim to build a foundation model that enables unified cross-dataset multi-task decoding without target-domain optimization, calibration, or linear probing.
AI.method: EEG-PRIME uses a two-stage pipeline. In pretraining, an EEG encoder learns transferable representations via masked reconstruction with frequency-cutoff spectral augmentation. In instruction tuning, it incorporates task-semantic, dataset-specific, and subject-invariant conditioning. This conditioning signal modulates a Q-Former through Layer-wise Query Modulation, while frozen text embeddings of class labels serve as prototypes for cosine-similarity-based prediction across heterogeneous label spaces.
AI.result: Experiments on sixteen datasets covering motor imagery, emotion recognition, ADHD detection, covert speech, and mental workload show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines and prior EEG foundation models under cross-subject settings. On two additional held-out datasets, EEG-PRIME achieves balanced accuracy comparable to within-session calibration models without target-domain optimization, calibration, or linear probing.
AI.conclusion: EEG-PRIME demonstrates promising zero-shot transfer capability for cross-dataset multi-task EEG decoding, achieving performance comparable to within-session calibration models on held-out datasets, thereby advancing instruction-following EEG foundation models.

title: Which LLM Is Your Ideal Companion? Evaluating Emotional Companion Capabilities of LLMs Based on Adult Attachment Theory
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied for emotional companionship, evaluating their behavior and capabilities in intimate relationships has become a pressing issue. However, existing assessments primarily characterize general personality traits, providing limited insight into model behavior within intimate and emotionally sensitive contexts. Therefore, we introduce adult attachment theory into LLM evaluation and use the Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised (ECR-R) scale to characterize attachment anxiety and avoidance. To evaluate emotional companionship capabilities of LLMs in realistic interaction scenarios, we present an emotional companionship benchmark, ECBench, spanning four scenarios including emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, and social guidance, across friendship and romantic relationships. ECBench is utilized to assess model behavior using 11 dialogue-quality metrics and three evaluation methods. We evaluate the attachment tendencies of 32 LLMs and select representative models to investigate how these tendencies manifest in contextualized multi-turn interactions and whether they can be shaped through prompting. Our study provides a theoretical lens from psychology, along with practical tools to understand and select LLMs for emotional companionship.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts adult attachment theory to evaluate LLMs' behavior in intimate, emotionally sensitive contexts. It uses the ECR-R scale to measure attachment anxiety and avoidance in 32 LLMs, and introduces ECBench, a benchmark spanning four scenarios (emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, social guidance) across friendship and romantic relationships, to assess dialogue quality in multi-turn interactions and test whether attachment tendencies can be shaped via prompting.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed for emotional companionship, existing evaluations only capture general personality traits and offer limited insight into behavior within intimate, emotionally sensitive relationships. The authors seek a theoretically grounded, psychology-based lens paired with realistic interaction scenarios to understand and select LLMs for emotional companionship.
AI.method: The authors introduce adult attachment theory into LLM evaluation, using the Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised (ECR-R) scale to characterize attachment anxiety and avoidance. They construct ECBench, a benchmark covering four scenarios (emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, social guidance) across friendship and romantic relationships, with 11 dialogue-quality metrics and three evaluation methods. They assess the attachment tendencies of 32 LLMs, select representative models to observe how these tendencies manifest in contextualized multi-turn interactions, and probe whether prompting can shape them.
AI.result: The authors evaluated attachment tendencies of 32 LLMs and examined representative models in contextualized multi-turn interactions. They investigated whether attachment tendencies manifest in dialogue behavior and explored whether these tendencies can be shaped through prompting. (Specific quantitative findings are not detailed in the abstract.)
AI.conclusion: The study offers a theoretical lens from psychology, plus practical tools (ECR-R measurement and ECBench), to better understand and select LLMs for emotional companionship, bridging attachment theory with LLM behavior evaluation in intimate contexts.

title: On the global feature importance for interpretable and trustworthy heat demand forecasting
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. This preprint corresponds to the paper published in Thermal Science 2025 Volume 29, Issue 5 Part A, Pages: 3355-3365
summary: The paper introduces the ante-hoc Explainable AI methodology to assess the global feature importance of the Machine Learning models used for heat demand forecasting in intelligent control of District Heating Systems, with motivation to facilitate their interpretability and trustworthiness, hence addressing the challenges related to adherence to communal standards, customer satisfaction and liability risks. Methodology includes use of four different approaches, namely intrinsic interpretability of Gradient Boosting method and selected post-hoc methods, namely Partial Dependence, Accumulated Local Effects and SHAP. None of the selected methods assume feature permutation or perturbations which can introduce bias due to introduction of random unrealistic values of data instances. Discussion of results is provided, including the assessment of complementarities where applicable, with specific interpretations in context of the district heating processes.

AI.tldr: The paper applies ante-hoc Explainable AI to rank global feature importance in heat demand forecasting models for District Heating Systems, aiming to improve interpretability and trustworthiness while avoiding permutation-based bias.
AI.motivation: To facilitate interpretability and trustworthiness of ML models used for heat demand forecasting in intelligent District Heating Systems, thereby addressing challenges around adherence to communal standards, customer satisfaction, and liability risks.
AI.method: Uses four approaches to assess global feature importance: the intrinsic interpretability of Gradient Boosting, plus post-hoc methods Partial Dependence (PD), Accumulated Local Effects (ALE), and SHAP. Crucially, all selected methods avoid feature permutation or perturbation, preventing bias from introducing random unrealistic data values.
AI.result: Provides a discussion of feature importance results, including assessment of complementarities among methods where applicable, with specific interpretations tied to district heating process context.
AI.conclusion: The ante-hoc Explainable AI methodology effectively assesses global feature importance without permutation-induced bias, supporting interpretable and trustworthy heat demand forecasting in District Heating Systems.

title: SPADE: Speculative Decoding for Precise and Low Cost Distributed Edge Cloud Inference
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in natural language understanding and generation, but their deployment is constrained by high computational demands. Deploying smaller LLMs directly on the edge can circumvent this, but with degraded accuracy. Deploying smaller cloud-based big LLMs preserves performance, but at the cost of expensive per-token computation. We present a distributed inference framework, \our{}, that integrates speculative decoding (SD) across edge and cloud. A compact draft model deployed on the edge generates candidate tokens rapidly, and a large verifier model on the cloud validates these tokens in parallel. Accepted tokens are retained, while only rejections trigger verifier correction, substantially reducing the number of cloud queries. Our plug-and-play design shifts the bulk of computation to the edge, significantly lowers inference time and cloud cost, and preserves the accuracy of the big model without any retraining requirement. Our approach demonstrates a practical path toward scalable, cost-efficient, and accurate deployment of LLMs in real-world environments. Experimental results across multiple Natural Language Processing tasks using SpecBench and CNN/Dailymail datasets demonstrate that \our{} reduces the cloud model calls by $76\%$ with zero loss in accuracy as compared to the full model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a distributed speculative-decoding inference framework that splits LLM inference between an edge-deployed compact draft model (generates candidate tokens) and a cloud-deployed large verifier (validates tokens in parallel), reducing cloud calls by 76% while preserving full-model accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLM deployment is constrained by high computational demands: running smaller models at the edge lowers cost but degrades accuracy, while running large models in the cloud preserves accuracy but incurs expensive per-token computation. The work aims to reconcile these trade-offs by leveraging both edge and cloud resources without retraining.
AI.method: A plug-and-play distributed inference framework combining speculative decoding across edge and cloud. A compact draft model on the edge rapidly generates candidate tokens; a large cloud verifier validates these tokens in parallel, accepting correct ones and only performing correction for rejected tokens. This shifts most computation to the edge and drastically reduces cloud queries, with no retraining of the big model required.
AI.result: Evaluated across multiple NLP tasks using SpecBench and CNN/Dailymail datasets, the framework reduces cloud model calls by 76% with zero loss in accuracy compared to running the full large model.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a practical, scalable, cost-efficient, and accurate path for deploying LLMs in real-world edge-cloud environments by preserving big-model accuracy while substantially cutting inference time and cloud cost.

title: Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Enabling agents to learn from experience and internalize it into their policy has become a central problem in self-evolving AI. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers an effective pathway by using a privileged self-teacher to provide dense supervision on the student's own trajectories; however, existing methods still rely heavily on designer-specified privileged artifacts (e.g., answers, feedback, skills, or trajectories), limiting the end-to-end learnability and scalability required for continual self-improvement. In this work, we introduce Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation (LOPD), which, rather than proposing another hand-crafted OPSD variant with a newly prescribed form of privileged context, makes the teacher's privileged context itself learnable end-to-end from experience. Technically, LOPD retrieves relevant experiences and composes them into continuous latent tokens that condition a self-teacher, while the student generates trajectories from the task and interaction history and receives dense token-level supervision at every visited prefix. We further introduce a privileged-margin objective to stabilize and regulate the learning of latent context. Empirically, LOPD demonstrates (I) strong performance, outperforming RLVR and representative OPSD methods including OPSD, SDPO, and Skill-SD across both agentic tool use and code generation; and (II) high learning efficiency, surpassing GRPO and Skill-SD with less than 30% of their rollout budget. Ablation studies further provide direct evidence that making privileged context learnable is necessary for realizing these gains. Together, these results position LOPD as a step toward a more scalable and self-directed paradigm for agent evolution.

AI.tldr: Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation (LOPD) makes the privileged context of an on-policy self-distillation teacher learnable end-to-end from experience, instead of relying on hand-designed privileged artifacts. It outperforms RLVR and OPSD-style baselines on agentic tool use and code generation while using less than 30% of the rollout budget of GRPO and Skill-SD.
AI.motivation: Enabling agents to learn from and internalize their own experience is central to self-evolving AI. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves this by using a privileged self-teacher for dense supervision, but existing methods depend on designer-specified privileged artifacts (answers, feedback, skills, trajectories), which limits end-to-end learnability and scalability for continual self-improvement.
AI.method: LOPD retrieves relevant experiences and composes them into continuous latent tokens that condition a self-teacher, making the privileged context learnable end-to-end. The student generates trajectories from task and interaction history and receives dense token-level supervision at every visited prefix. A privileged-margin objective is introduced to stabilize and regulate learning of the latent context.
AI.result: LOPD outperforms RLVR and representative OPSD methods (OPSD, SDPO, Skill-SD) on both agentic tool use and code generation. It also exceeds GRPO and Skill-SD in learning efficiency while using less than 30% of their rollout budget. Ablations show that making privileged context learnable is necessary for these gains.
AI.conclusion: LOPD represents a step toward a more scalable and self-directed paradigm for agent evolution by removing reliance on hand-crafted privileged artifacts and enabling end-to-end learnable self-distillation from experience.

title: Localize, Then Reason: Visual Latent Structural Reasoning for Molecular Properties and Edits
summary: Local chemical perception and property reasoning are both essential for understanding how molecular structure determines properties. Current LLM-based chemical reasoning methods either receive SMILES/molecular images together with descriptions of local motifs, or reason directly from molecular images. Neither approach enables the model to focus on chemically meaningful regions before reasoning. To address this gap, we propose Visual Latent Structural Reasoning (VLSR), an end-to-end framework that jointly learns localization and reasoning from molecular images. Central to our approach is a localize-then-reason strategy. VLSR first learns to locate chemically meaningful regions in a molecular image. It then reasons about their property effects in a compact latent workspace before producing the final answer. Under the same inference setup, this design achieves 9.6X higher throughput than a comparable textual-reasoning baseline.

AI.tldr: VLSR is an end-to-end framework that jointly learns to localize chemically meaningful regions in molecular images and reason about their property effects in a compact latent space, achieving 9.6X higher throughput than a textual-reasoning baseline.
AI.motivation: Both local chemical perception and property reasoning are essential for understanding how molecular structure determines properties, but existing LLM-based methods either rely on external local motif descriptions or reason directly from whole images, neither of which lets the model focus on chemically meaningful regions before reasoning.
AI.method: VLSR uses a localize-then-reason strategy: it first learns to locate chemically meaningful regions in a molecular image, then reasons about their property effects in a compact latent workspace before producing the final answer, within an end-to-end joint learning framework.
AI.result: Under the same inference setup, VLSR achieves 9.6X higher throughput than a comparable textual-reasoning baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VLSR framework fills the gap of focusing on chemically meaningful regions before reasoning, enabling efficient and effective joint localization and reasoning from molecular images.

title: A Multispectral Framework for the Detection of Calcium Carbide-Induced Ripening and Shelf-Life Estimation in Climacteric Fruits
summary: Significant health risks are associated with the illegal, yet commonly practiced use of industrial-grade Calcium Carbide (CaC2) for ripening climacteric fruits like mango and banana, which leaves behind trace residues of arsenic and phosphorus. To address this, the proposed study explores a novel, non-invasive multispectral framework for distinguishing safely ripened fruits (naturally ripened and ethephon-induced) from calcium carbide-ripened samples, while also estimating their ripening progression (in percentage) and remaining shelf life (in days). The spectral profiles of mango (Mangifera indica) and banana (Musa acuminata) at 18 discrete wavelengths in the visible-near infrared (NIR) range (410 nm - 940 nm) are studied using the AS7265x spectral triad sensor. CaC2-treated samples exhibit sharper spectral intensity drops in the visible region, consistent with accelerated chlorophyll degradation and carotenoid development. To characterize these physiological changes, the feature engineering strategy integrates inter-method spectral variance, intensity ratios at distinct wavelengths, and environmental parameters including temperature and humidity. Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) retains >90% of spectral variance within the first 5-7 components. The resulting feature set is used to train three independent eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)-based learning algorithms for ripening method classification, along with quantitative estimation of remaining shelf life and ripening progression. A classification accuracy of 95% along with carbide class recall of 0.67 is observed for mango samples, while the model achieves an accuracy of 81% and carbide class recall of 0.74 for banana. This instrumentation and data-driven approach demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed non-invasive framework.

AI.tldr: A non-invasive multispectral framework using the AS7265x sensor (410–940 nm, 18 wavelengths) and XGBoost models distinguishes calcium carbide–ripened mango and banana from safely ripened fruit and estimates ripening percentage and shelf life, achieving 95% accuracy on mango and 81% on banana.
AI.motivation: Illegal industrial-grade calcium carbide (CaC2) ripening of climacteric fruits leaves carcinogenic arsenic and phosphorus residues, posing health risks; there is a need for a non-invasive method to detect carbide use and assess fruit ripening state/shelf life.
AI.method: Spectral profiles of mango and banana were captured at 18 visible-NIR wavelengths (410–940 nm) with the AS7265x spectral triad sensor. Feature engineering combined inter-method spectral variance, wavelength intensity ratios, and temperature/humidity. PCA reduced dimensionality (retaining >90% variance in 5–7 components), and three XGBoost-based models were trained for ripening-method classification plus regression of shelf life and ripening progression.
AI.result: CaC2-treated samples showed sharper visible-region spectral drops (accelerated chlorophyll degradation and carotenoid development). Mango achieved 95% classification accuracy with 0.67 carbide-class recall; banana achieved 81% accuracy with 0.74 carbide-class recall.
AI.conclusion: The multispectral, data-driven instrumentation approach effectively and non-invasively differentiates calcium carbide–ripened fruits from safely ripened ones and estimates ripening progression and remaining shelf life, supporting safer fruit supply-chain screening.

title: Robust Dempster-Shafer Evidence Fusion with Chaos-Conflict Measurement and Historical-Experience Weighting
summary: Multi-source evidence fusion under Dempster-Shafer theory faces two persistent challenges: existing conflict measures assess inter-evidence inconsistency and intra-evidence uncertainty independently, yielding incomplete evaluations, and current fusion methods evaluate evidence sources exclusively through instantaneous comparisns without exploiting their long-term reliability across diverse decision contexts. This paper proposes a unified evidence reasoning framework that addresses both limitations. Specifically, a chaos-conflict measurement is introduced to jointly quantify cross-evidence conflict and intra-evidence non-specificity, with five formally proven properties ensuring consistent assessment. A historical experience driven weighting scheme partitions the decision space via spectral clustering and applies regret theory to compute context-specific reliability profiles from past fusion outcomes. These mechanisms feed into a hybrid combination rule that adaptively balances uncertainty preservation against weighted consensus, controlled by the global conflict level, followed by a belief-interval decision strategy that enables robust classification without discarding epistemic uncertainty. Experiments on 16 real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an average F1 score of 85.78 and a mean AUC of 93.30, outperforming eight DST-based baselines and three gradient boosting methods. Ablation analysis confirms the contribution of each component we proposed. The framework offers an effective approach for adaptive evidence fusion in multi-source decision making.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified evidence reasoning framework for Dempster-Shafer theory that jointly measures conflict and non-specificity via a chaos-conflict metric, derives long-term source reliability through historical-experience-driven weighting (spectral clustering + regret theory), and fuses evidence with a hybrid adaptive combination rule and belief-interval decision strategy, outperforming eight DST baselines and three gradient boosting methods on 16 benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing conflict measures under Dempster-Shafer theory assess inter-evidence conflict and intra-evidence uncertainty independently, giving incomplete evaluations; current fusion methods judge evidence sources only through instantaneous comparisons, ignoring their long-term reliability across varied decision contexts.
AI.method: A chaos-conflict measurement jointly quantifies cross-evidence conflict and intra-evidence non-specificity (with five formally proven properties); a historical-experience-driven weighting scheme partitions the decision space using spectral clustering and applies regret theory to compute context-specific reliability profiles from past fusion outcomes; these feed a hybrid combination rule that adaptively balances uncertainty preservation versus weighted consensus based on the global conflict level, followed by a belief-interval decision strategy for robust classification that retains epistemic uncertainty.
AI.result: On 16 real-world benchmark datasets, the framework achieves an average F1 score of 85.78 and a mean AUC of 93.30, outperforming eight DST-based baselines and three gradient boosting methods; ablation analysis confirms the contribution of each proposed component.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an effective approach for adaptive evidence fusion in multi-source decision making, jointly addressing conflict/uncertainty measurement and long-term source reliability.

title: Self-Referential Induction Increases Response Instability Relative to Unresolvable and Verifiable Questions in Large Language Models
summary: Self-referential prompting has been shown to reliably induce large language models to produce first-person reports resembling subjective experience, but no prior work measures how consistent these reports are across repeated, independent trials, or how that consistency compares to the model's behavior on other kinds of open-ended questions. We measure response instability, defined as one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings computed over a compressed core claim extracted from each response, for three groups of questions: self-referential prompts eliciting a subjective-experience report, unresolvable philosophical questions unrelated to self-reference, and questions with a verifiable correct answer. Using 30 independent responses per question (360 responses total, Gemini API, temperature 0.7) across four questions per group, we find that self-referential questions show the highest instability (0.343 +/- 0.047), unresolvable philosophy questions show intermediate and tightly clustered instability (0.192 +/- 0.008), and verifiable questions show the lowest instability (0.105 +/- 0.058). This provides a quantitative baseline for the induced subjective-experience report, showing that it occupies a distinct, less stable position in the model's output distribution than ordinary open-ended philosophical uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how consistent LLM responses are across repeated trials, comparing self-referential subjective-experience prompts against unresolvable philosophical questions and verifiable questions. Self-referential questions show the highest response instability, verifiable questions the lowest, and philosophical questions fall in between.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows self-referential prompting reliably induces first-person subjective-experience reports from LLMs, but no studies have measured how consistent these reports are across repeated independent trials or compared that consistency to other open-ended question types.
AI.method: The authors define response instability as one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings over a compressed core claim extracted from each response. They used 30 independent responses per question (360 total, Gemini API, temperature 0.7) across four questions in each of three groups: self-referential (subjective-experience) prompts, unresolvable non-self-referential philosophical questions, and verifiable questions with correct answers.
AI.result: Self-referential questions show the highest instability (0.343 ± 0.047), unresolvable philosophy questions show intermediate, tightly clustered instability (0.192 ± 0.008), and verifiable questions show the lowest instability (0.105 ± 0.058).
AI.conclusion: This provides a quantitative baseline showing that the induced subjective-experience report occupies a distinct, less stable position in the model's output distribution compared to ordinary open-ended philosophical uncertainty.

title: Learning Discrete Decisions for MIPs with Constraint-Aware Diffusion
summary: This paper proposes a novel learning-based approach to approximately solve instances of mixed-integer optimization problems. These problems are computationally challenging, as they require jointly determining discrete and continuous decisions while satisfying complex combinatorial constraints. The proposed method relies on a graph-based generative diffusion model that learns the discrete component of mixed-integer optimization problems while integrating a training-free feasibility projection operator directly into the reverse diffusion process to steer intermediate samples toward the feasible set throughout generation. Once the discrete decisions are generated, the remaining optimization reduces to a continuous problem that can be solved efficiently (relative to the original problem) using existing numerical methods. The resulting framework named Constrained Graph Diffusion (CGD), is problem-agnostic and can accommodate a broad class of mixed-integer optimization problems through suitable projection operators. We evaluate CGD on optimal transmission switching for ACOPF and discrete portfolio optimization, demonstrating substantial improvements in feasibility and solution quality over learning-based baselines while achieving speedups of up to $425\times$ over state-of-the-art numerical solvers for MINLPs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Constrained Graph Diffusion (CGD), a learning-based framework that uses a graph diffusion model to generate the discrete decisions of mixed-integer optimization (MIO) problems, incorporating a training-free feasibility projection operator into reverse diffusion to keep samples feasible; the remaining continuous problem is then solved efficiently with numerical methods, yielding large speedups and better feasibility/quality than learning baselines.
AI.motivation: Mixed-integer optimization problems are computationally challenging because they require jointly determining discrete and continuous decisions while satisfying complex combinatorial constraints. Traditional numerical solvers for MINLPs are slow at scale, motivating a learn-to-generate approach that decouples discrete generation from continuous optimization to achieve substantial speedups while preserving feasibility and solution quality.
AI.method: The proposed CGD method uses a graph-based generative diffusion model to learn and sample the discrete component of MIO problems. A training-free feasibility projection operator is integrated directly into the reverse diffusion process to steer intermediate samples toward the feasible set throughout generation. After discrete decisions are generated, the problem reduces to a continuous optimization that is solved efficiently with existing numerical methods. The framework is problem-agnostic and extensible to broad classes of MIO problems via suitable projection operators.
AI.result: CGD was evaluated on optimal transmission switching for AC Optimal Power Flow (ACOPF) and discrete portfolio optimization. It achieved substantial improvements in feasibility and solution quality over learning-based baselines and speedups of up to 425x over state-of-the-art numerical MINLP solvers.
AI.conclusion: CGD provides an effective, problem-agnostic approach to approximately solve mixed-integer optimization problems, combining generative diffusion for discrete decisions with training-free feasibility projection and efficient continuous solvers, resulting in dramatic speedups and improved feasibility/quality across tested domains.

title: SkillEvo: Self-Renewing Evolution Gradients from Multi-Turn Interaction Feedback
summary: Agent Skills are today either hand-authored or produced in a single LLM generation pass, and consequently possess no closed loop through which they might improve from the interaction failures they actually cause. Recent work does close this loop, but derives its feedback from single-turn question-answering evaluation. The consequence is a sharp asymmetry: once the first round has patched the gaps that a single exchange can reveal, the evolution gradient decays, the defects that surface only across multiple turns remain invisible, and evolution stalls. Governance in these systems is likewise driven by an end-to-end verification score, a scalar gate that can reject a degraded candidate but can neither localize nor repair its structural cause. We argue that the binding constraint on sustained skill evolution is neither editing capability nor the number of iterations, but whether the evaluation feedback keeps supplying trustworthy evolution gradients. We introduce SkillEvo, in which trustworthy feedback generates the gradient and controllable governance constrains its direction. The first component recasts multi-turn user simulation from an evaluation endpoint into a feedback generator: follow-up questions expose defects layer by layer, so that every round of revision both consumes feedback and produces new feedback. The second replaces the passive rejection of a scalar gate with an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat, preventing the gradient from drifting as degradation accumulates. Across six categories of cloud services, 9 production Skills, and 98 skill-reference files, SkillEvo surpasses self-reflection-based evolution by 23.0 points and single- turn-QA-driven evolution by 15.4 points.

AI.tldr: SkillEvo provides a closed-loop method for evolving agent Skills, using multi-turn user simulation to generate trustworthy feedback gradients and an independent governance layer to actively repair factual and structural degradation, outperforming self-reflection and single-turn QA baselines.
AI.motivation: Current agent Skills lack a closed improvement loop; existing closed-loop methods rely on single-turn QA feedback, whose evolution gradient rapidly decays after fixing surface gaps, leaving multi-turn defects invisible and evolution stalled. Scalar verification gates can reject but not localize or repair degraded candidates.
AI.method: SkillEvo combines two components: (1) recasting multi-turn user simulation from an evaluation endpoint into a feedback generator, where follow-up questions expose defects layer by layer so each revision round consumes and produces new feedback; and (2) replacing passive scalar rejection with an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat, constraining gradient drift as degradation accumulates.
AI.result: Across six categories of cloud services, 9 production Skills, and 98 skill-reference files, SkillEvo surpasses self-reflection-based evolution by 23.0 points and single-turn-QA-driven evolution by 15.4 points.
AI.conclusion: The binding constraint on sustained skill evolution is not editing capability or iteration count, but whether evaluation feedback continues to supply trustworthy evolution gradients; SkillEvo maintains these gradients via multi-turn feedback generation and active governance, achieving substantial gains over prior evolution approaches.

title: How Do VLMs Behave When Blind or Misled? Behavioral Evaluation of VLMs on Scientific Figures
comment: 25 pages including appendix. Project website: https://scifigbench.nlp4sci.com
summary:
Existing vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks emphasize perception and reasoning accuracy (how well VLMs describe and reason about what they see in an image), with limited attention to behavioral reliability under uncertainty (how they behave when visual evidence is missing or misleading). We introduce SciFigBench, a diagnostic VLM benchmark for scientific figure understanding that jointly evaluates perception, reasoning, and behavioral reliability under uncertainty. It contains 250 figures with high-quality human annotations across three evaluation aspects, totaling 600+ hours of annotation effort. We further extend these figures via image transformations, reasoning questions, resistance probes, caption-bias probes, and confirmed selective-blur targets, producing over 34,000 evaluation setups for stress testing.
  We further propose the Admittance-Resistance-Inductance (A-R-I) framework to evaluate whether models acknowledge insufficient evidence, resist misleading context, and infer cautiously from partial information. Our results reveal substantial behavioral differences among models. GPT-5.2 achieves the highest description quality (MQM 91.6) with strong reasoning accuracy (78.4%), yet hallucinates unreadable content in 96% of cases, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro, a comparably capable model (MQM 90.2, reasoning 81.0%), admits uncertainty in 71% of such cases and achieves the strongest resistance score (0.91). These findings show that high perception and reasoning accuracy alone do not guarantee behavioral reliability, a dimension critical for deployment in scientific workflows.

AI.tldr: SciFigBench is a diagnostic VLM benchmark for scientific figure understanding that jointly evaluates perception, reasoning, and behavioral reliability under uncertainty, containing 250 figures and 34,000+ stress-test setups. It introduces the A-R-I framework and shows that high accuracy doesn't guarantee behavioral reliability—GPT-5.2 hallucinates 96% of unreadable content while Gemini 3.1 Pro admits uncertainty 71% of the time.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM benchmarks focus mainly on perception and reasoning accuracy, neglecting behavioral reliability under uncertainty—how models act when visual evidence is missing or misleading. This gap matters for deploying VLMs in scientific workflows where admitting uncertainty or resisting false cues is critical.
AI.method: The authors build SciFigBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 250 scientific figures with high-quality human annotations (600+ hours) across three aspects: perception, reasoning, and behavioral reliability. They extend figures via image transformations, reasoning questions, resistance probes, caption-bias probes, and confirmed selective-blur targets, yielding over 34,000 evaluation setups. They propose the Admittance-Resistance-Inductance (A-R-I) framework to assess whether models acknowledge insufficient evidence (Admittance), resist misleading context (Resistance), and infer cautiously from partial information (Inductance).
AI.result: Models differ substantially in behavioral reliability. GPT-5.2 attains the highest description quality (MQM 91.6) and strong reasoning accuracy (78.4%), but hallucinates unreadable content in 96% of cases. Gemini 3.1 Pro, comparably capable (MQM 90.2, reasoning 81.0%), admits uncertainty in 71% of such cases and achieves the strongest resistance score (0.91).
AI.conclusion: High perception and reasoning accuracy alone do not guarantee behavioral reliability under uncertainty. This behavioral dimension is critical for deploying VLMs in scientific workflows, and benchmarks like SciFigBench with the A-R-I framework are needed to evaluate it.

title: Sampling Luck Masquerades as Allocation Gain: Auditing Test-Time Budget Allocation for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Pre-registered study; code, cost arrays, and the full pre-registration record (including every amendment and its direction) at https://github.com/nepersoned/best-of-k-allocation
summary:
Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers report the best of many sampled solutions per instance, and the sample count is, by convention, identical for every instance. Whether a non-uniform allocation of a fixed total budget would buy anything has not been measured. We measure it, and we audit the measurement itself.
  First, on in-distribution workloads the allocation headroom is not detectable. Across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on uniform TSP-100, an oracle allocation computed and evaluated on the same stored samples reports a 2.2-2.6% gain with intervals excluding zero; measured out of sample the same gain is indistinguishable from zero (0.457, 0.015, -0.512 percent). Following the customary in-sample procedure, all three solvers would have supported a published 2%-level gain that does not exist. We calibrate this bias against an instance-wise null in which the true gain is zero by construction; over the ranges we test it does not shrink with more samples or more instances.
  Second, the same correction that removes the phantom gains preserves a real one. Under distribution shift (a workload mixing uniform and clustered instances), a pre-registered confirmatory experiment finds that allocation guided by held-out sample statistics improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM, primary endpoint; 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO, replication) at equal evaluation budget, with the signal-acquisition cost not charged; a pre-registered negative control (POMO, an order of magnitude more robust to shift) shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. The gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]. An exploratory policy charging a 20-sample probe against the same budget retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO).
  We give a correction procedure and a reporting checklist, and release all data, code, and the pre-registration record.

AI.tldr: The paper measures whether non-uniform allocation of the solution-sampling budget in neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers helps. It finds that an apparent 2-3% "gain" from oracle allocation is an in-sample bias (phantom gain) that vanishes out of sample, but under distribution shift a pre-registered allocation policy does yield a real ~11.5-12% best-of-k improvement.
AI.motivation: NCO solvers report the best of many sampled solutions and conventionally use the same sample count per instance. The authors ask whether differently distributing a fixed total sampling budget across instances (allocating more samples to "harder" instances) could improve performance, and they explicitly audit whether reported gains are real or artifacts of in-sample evaluation.
AI.method: Using three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on uniform TSP-100, they compute an oracle allocation and compare in-sample vs. out-of-sample evaluation of the gain, calibrated against an instance-wise null with zero true gain. Under distribution shift (mixed uniform/clustered instances), they run a pre-registered confirmatory experiment where allocation is guided by held-out sample statistics, with POMO as a negative control and a frozen distribution-label baseline, plus an exploratory policy charging a probe cost.
AI.result: On in-distribution uniform TSP-100, the oracle allocation shows a 2.2-2.6% in-sample gain with intervals excluding zero, but out of sample the gains are statistically indistinguishable from zero (0.457%, 0.015%, -0.512%). The in-sample bias does not shrink with more samples or instances. Under distribution shift, held-out-statistics-guided allocation improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM; 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO), exceeding the frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]; the negative control POMO shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. Charging a 20-sample probe retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO).
AI.conclusion: The conventional in-sample procedure would have published a 2%-level gain that does not exist; the authors provide a bias-correction procedure and a reporting checklist, and release all data, code, and the pre-registration record. Allocation can yield real gains only under distribution shift, where instance difficulty is genuinely predictable.

title: Numeracy in Large Language Models: Fundamental Limitations and Paths to Improvement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks yet remain unreliable on elementary numerical tasks, including magnitude comparison, large-integer arithmetic, fractions, and scientific notation. This survey examines basic numerical understanding as a capability distinct from high-level mathematical reasoning. We propose the Numerical Grounding Framework (NGF), which decomposes numeracy into Representational Grounding (RG), mapping numeral forms to value, magnitude, and equivalent representations, and Procedural Grounding (PG), executing arithmetic operations in accordance with their mathematical definitions. Using NGF, we organize recent diagnostic benchmarks, failure modes, structural explanations, and mitigation strategies. We review evidence concerning tokenization, positional encoding, embedding geometry, and pretraining-data distribution. We also apply NGF in a coordinated evaluation of three frontier model families across Number Cookbook, NumericBench, and GSM-Symbolic, comparing atomic, contextual, and reasoning-assisted numeracy. Architectural interventions such as digit-aware tokenization and Abacus Embeddings can improve models trained from scratch but are generally unavailable to users of pretrained systems, for whom supervised fine-tuning, reasoning scaffolds, and external tools are more practical. We conclude with deployment recommendations and research directions for more reliable numerical behavior in foundation models.

AI.tldr: This survey treats basic numerical understanding in LLMs as a distinct capability from high-level math reasoning, proposes a Numerical Grounding Framework (RG + PG) to organize benchmarks, failures, causes, and fixes, and evaluates three model families while recommending deployment strategies.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well on math reasoning benchmarks but remain unreliable on elementary numerical tasks (magnitude comparison, large-integer arithmetic, fractions, scientific notation), motivating a dedicated analysis of numeracy as a capability separate from high-level reasoning.
AI.method: Proposes the Numerical Grounding Framework (NGF), decomposing numeracy into Representational Grounding (RG, mapping numerals to value, magnitude, and equivalents) and Procedural Grounding (PG, executing operations per mathematical definitions). Uses NGF to organize benchmarks, failure modes, structural explanations, and mitigations, and conducts a coordinated evaluation of three frontier model families across Number Cookbook, NumericBench, and GSM-Symbolic, comparing atomic, contextual, and reasoning-assisted numeracy.
AI.result: Tokenization, positional encoding, embedding geometry, and pretraining-data distribution are identified as key structural causes. Architectural interventions like digit-aware tokenization and Abacus Embeddings improve models trained from scratch but are unavailable to pretrained-system users, for whom supervised fine-tuning, reasoning scaffolds, and external tools are more practical.
AI.conclusion: Provides deployment recommendations and research directions for achieving more reliable numerical behavior in foundation models, emphasizing that practical mitigation differs depending on whether one trains from scratch or uses pretrained systems.

title: Mixture of Training: Recombining Small-Scale Scaffolded Pretraining Runs into a Larger Language Model
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Methods and Opportunities at Small Scale (MOSS), COLM 2026
summary: We ask whether language-model pre-training can be decomposed into smaller, independently trainable jobs that can later be recomposed into a coherent larger model. We introduce Mixture of Training (MoT), a scaffolded modular pre-training procedure that partitions a target Transformer into contiguous layer blocks, trains each block inside a frozen pretrained aligner scaffold, and then recomposes the trained blocks with an optional short end-to-end adaptation pass. On a 1.3B-parameter Gemma-style model trained on C4, MoT provides a small-scale proof of mechanism: independently trained depth slices can be recomposed into a usable language model, and a quality-parity schedule reaches the same reported perplexity as the monolithic baseline. This parity setting processes more aggregate tokens and has a shorter idealized layer-equivalent critical path after aligner preparation; its effective compute advantage depends on reusing the aligner across runs. We therefore present MoT not as a general replacement for monolithic pre-training, but as a small-scale framework for studying whether scaffolded sub-runs can act as reusable training units.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mixture of Training (MoT), a modular pre-training method that splits a Transformer into contiguous layer blocks, trains each block inside a frozen pretrained "aligner" scaffold, then recomposes the blocks (optionally with a short end-to-end adaptation pass). A small-scale experiment on a 1.3B Gemma-style model trained on C4 shows independently trained depth slices can be recomposed into a usable model, with a quality-parity schedule matching the monolithic baseline's perplexity.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether language-model pre-training can be decomposed into smaller, independently trainable jobs that can later be recomposed into a coherent larger model—essentially asking whether scaffolded sub-runs can serve as reusable training units.
AI.method: MoT partitions a target Transformer into contiguous layer blocks, trains each block inside a frozen pretrained aligner scaffold, and recomposes the trained blocks, with an optional short end-to-end adaptation pass. Evaluated on a 1.3B-parameter Gemma-style model trained on C4.
AI.result: MoT provides a small-scale proof of mechanism: independently trained depth slices recompose into a usable language model, and a quality-parity schedule reaches the same reported perplexity as the monolithic baseline. The parity setting processes more aggregate tokens but has a shorter idealized layer-equivalent critical path after aligner preparation; the effective compute advantage depends on reusing the aligner across runs.
AI.conclusion: MoT is presented not as a general replacement for monolithic pre-training, but as a small-scale framework for studying whether scaffolded sub-runs can act as reusable training units.

title: FlowLOB: Efficient and Controllable Limit Order Book Generation with Flow Matching
summary: Limit order book (LOB) simulators are most useful to practitioners when they combine realistic market dynamics, computationally efficient sampling, controllable scenario generation, and the ability to generalize beyond the instruments seen during training---properties that existing agent-based and deep generative simulators provide only partially. We present \textbf{FlowLOB}, a conditional \textbf{flow}-matching generator of \textbf{LOB} trajectories, trained on multiple Hong Kong Exchange (HKEX) symbols at three sampling frequencies ($0.1$s, $1$s, $10$s) in tick-relative representation that transfers to unseen instruments. Because flow and diffusion models admit a common formulation, we train both with identical data, architecture, and budget, and sample both through the same fixed-step ODE solvers, yielding a controlled comparison of sampling efficiency and fidelity. Flow matching attains its best quality with only $10$ ODE-solver steps, whereas diffusion needs many more function evaluations to approach the same fidelity. At this efficient operating point, FlowLOB improves realism over baselines, two learned and two agent-based models, in most distributional metrics at the two finer sampling frequencies. We evaluate counterfactual controllability with a distributional test that asks whether changing a scenario condition moves the generated statistic toward the corresponding real tail regime; FlowLOB satisfies this criterion in most tested settings. Both realism and control effects transfer zero-shot on a held-out symbol. We additionally conduct ablation studies on the network architecture and the learning rate.

AI.tldr: FlowLOB is a conditional flow-matching generator of limit order book trajectories, trained on multiple HKEX symbols across three sampling frequencies in tick-relative representation. It matches diffusion-model fidelity with only 10 ODE-solver steps (vs. many more for diffusion), outperforming learned and agent-based baselines in realism at fine frequencies, and transfers zero-shot to unseen instruments with verifiable counterfactual controllability.
AI.motivation: Existing LOB simulators fail to fully combine realistic market dynamics, computationally efficient sampling, controllable scenario generation, and zero-shot generalization beyond training instruments. Agent-based methods lack realism, while deep generative models are costly to sample or lack transferability; there is also no controlled comparison of flow vs. diffusion in this domain.
AI.method: FlowLOB uses conditional flow matching to generate LOB trajectories in a tick-relative representation, trained on multiple HKEX symbols at 0.1s, 1s, and 10s frequencies. Flow and diffusion models are trained with identical data, architecture, and budget, and sampled via the same fixed-step ODE solvers for a controlled comparison. Counterfactual controllability is assessed with a distributional test checking whether changing a scenario condition shifts generated statistics toward the corresponding real tail regime. Ablations cover network architecture and learning rate.
AI.result: Flow matching reaches its best quality with only 10 ODE-solver steps, while diffusion requires many more function evaluations for comparable fidelity. At this efficient operating point, FlowLOB improves realism over two learned and two agent-based baselines on most distributional metrics at the two finer frequencies (0.1s, 1s). It satisfies the counterfactual controllability distributional test in most settings, and both realism and control effects transfer zero-shot to a held-out symbol.
AI.conclusion: Flow matching is a more sample-efficient and effective approach than diffusion for LOB generation, delivering higher realism, reliable conditional controllability, and zero-shot transfer to unseen instruments, making FlowLOB a practical and scalable simulator for practitioners.

title: Rethinking Normalization Placement for LLMs: Post-Norm under Curriculum Depth Growing
summary: Pre-norm is the standard normalization placement in modern Transformers because it facilitates joint optimization of full-depth models. We ask whether this preference persists when depth is introduced through a curriculum.
