In curriculum depth growth, each appended block receives the boundary representation produced by a trained prefix, making normalization placement relevant to forward conditioning. We therefore test whether placement and training curriculum interact. In a controlled distillation study with a Qwen3-8B teacher and a nine-layer student, pre-norm and post-norm are indistinguishable under joint training, differing by $0.0004$ validation CE, while post-norm improves over pre-norm by $0.0328$ under curriculum growth, an order of magnitude larger. A post-joint control matched by student active-layer tokens remains worse than post-grow, which rules out compute as the sole explanation. The ranking crosses over during the curriculum: post-norm takes the lead once blocks are appended. Single-block and freeze controls localize the ranking change to block appending rather than shallow-block quality or retraining. Boundary diagnostics associate post-norm with stable residual scales and pre-norm with structural-token scale drift; on a fixed batch, the final pre-grow block is also nearly identity-mapped. Together with the phase-wise crossover, these observations are consistent with boundary-scale conditioning after new blocks are appended. The results motivate treating normalization placement and training curriculum as coupled design choices in this distillation setting.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how normalization placement (pre-norm vs. post-norm) interacts with training curriculum in Transformers, showing that while the two are indistinguishable under joint training, post-norm substantially outperforms pre-norm when depth is introduced gradually via curriculum growth.
AI.motivation: Pre-norm is the standard in modern Transformers because it enables joint optimization of deep models, but this preference may not hold when depth is introduced through a curriculum. Under curriculum depth growth, each newly appended block receives the boundary representation from a trained prefix, making normalization placement relevant to forward conditioning. The authors ask whether normalization placement and training curriculum interact.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled distillation study using a Qwen3-8B teacher and a nine-layer student. They compare pre-norm and post-norm under two regimes: joint training (all layers trained together) and curriculum growth (blocks appended progressively). Controls include a post-joint setup matched by student active-layer tokens, single-block and freeze controls to isolate effects, and boundary diagnostics measuring residual scales, structural-token scale drift, and identity-mapping behavior of the final pre-grow block.
AI.result: Under joint training, pre-norm and post-norm differ by only 0.0004 validation CE (indistinguishable). Under curriculum growth, post-norm improves over pre-norm by 0.0328, an order of magnitude larger. A compute-matched post-joint control remains worse than post-grow, ruling out compute alone. The ranking crosses over during the curriculum: post-norm takes the lead once blocks are appended. Controls localize this change to block appending rather than shallow-block quality or retraining. Boundary diagnostics show post-norm is associated with stable residual scales, while pre-norm shows structural-token scale drift, and the final pre-grow block is nearly identity-mapped.
AI.conclusion: Normalization placement and training curriculum are coupled design choices in the distillation setting; post-norm is preferable when growing depth via curriculum, contrary to the standard pre-norm preference under joint training. The authors recommend treating the two factors jointly rather than independently when designing models.

title: Refusing Intent, Not Form: Wrapper-Based Intent-Group Supervision for LLM Safety
summary: Safety tuning can improve harmful refusal, but models may learn surface-form shortcuts: wrapped harmful prompts bypass safety, while similarly wrapped benign prompts are over-refused. We propose Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation (WIFA), an automatic intent-group augmentation method that pairs wrapped harmful examples with structurally matched wrapped benign counterexamples, requiring no external teacher or manual per-wrapper intent labels. We use WIFA as a common data layer for two complementary fine-tuning routes: WIFA-Boost, a two-stage high-safety recipe, and Anchored Group-Consistent Refusal Training (A-GCRT), which regularizes refusal/compliance decision scores across same-intent wrappers and anchors harmful and benign groups on opposite sides of a margin. In the Qwen setting, WIFA-Boost reaches the strongest transformed-harmful refusal, while A-GCRT reduces OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7\% for the base model to 17.4\%; reproduced baselines do not match these operating points. Llama results and ablations over data structure, two-stage order, and A-GCRT components support this intent-group interpretation without claiming universal below-base over-refusal.

AI.tldr: To stop models from relying on surface-form shortcuts (bypassing harmful wrapped prompts while over-refusing benign wrapped ones), the authors introduce WIFA, an automatic intent-group data augmentation that pairs wrapped harmful examples with wrapped benign counterexamples. WIFA feeds two fine-tuning routes: WIFA-Boost (two-stage, high-safety) and A-GCRT (margin-based, group-consistent refusal regularization). Results show strongest transformed-harmful refusal (WIFA-Boost) and large over-refusal reduction (A-GCRT, 25.7%→17.4% on OR-Bench) in Qwen, with Llama results and ablations supporting the intent-group interpretation.
AI.motivation: Safety tuning improves harmful refusal, but models acquire shallow surface-form shortcuts: harmful intent hidden behind wrappers evades refusal, while benign prompts wrapped the same way are wrongly refused. The goal is a method that captures underlying intent rather than surface wrapper patterns, without external teachers or manual wrapper-based labels.
AI.method: WIFA (Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation) automatically builds intent groups by pairing wrapped harmful examples with structurally matched wrapped benign counterexamples. It serves as a shared data layer for two fine-tuning approaches: (1) WIFA-Boost, a two-stage high-safety recipe; (2) Anchored Group-Consistent Refusal Training (A-GCRT), which regularizes refusal/compliance decision scores across same-intent wrappers and uses a margin to anchor harmful and benign groups on opposite sides.
AI.result: In the Qwen setting, WIFA-Boost attains the strongest refusal of transformed harmful prompts, while A-GCRT cuts OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7% (base) to 17.4%. Reproduced baselines cannot reach these operating points. Llama results and ablations over data structure, two-stage order, and A-GCRT components support the intent-group interpretation, without claiming universally below-base over-refusal.
AI.conclusion: Grouping examples by intent (via WIFA) and training with either the two-stage WIFA-Boost or the margin-anchored A-GCRT reliably improves harmful refusal and reduces over-refusal more effectively than baselines. The work supports an intent-group interpretation of safety failures while carefully avoiding claims of universal below-base over-refusal.

title: Branch and Bound for Relational Verification of Neural Networks
comment: The full version of the paper accepted by EMSOFT 2026
summary:
Verification of neural networks against relational specifications, such as global robustness, is crucial for safety-critical applications of cyber-physical systems (CPS), given their increasing adoption of AI components. Compared to simple trace properties (e.g., local robustness), verifying relational specifications requires reasoning about the relationship between multiple network inferences, which brings significant technical challenges. Existing research has explored abstraction techniques based on sound and convex over-approximation of neural network outputs; however, since these approaches are inherently incomplete and may raise false alarms, they further underscore the need of effective abstraction refinement.
  In this paper, we propose a branch-and-bound (BaB) framework to mitigate the issue, which iteratively splits the problem until all sub-problems are verified. Specifically, our BaB framework features splitting of relational neurons rather than individual neurons as prior works do, and as the core of our technique, we devise a relational neuron selection strategy based on the dual formulation of the verification problem, which allows us to efficiently select the (most likely) optimal relational neuron that maximizes the refinement brought by problem splitting. We evaluate SaBRe on 817 verification problems across ACAS Xu, MNIST-F, MNIST-C, CIFAR and GTSRB. The results show that SaBRe outperforms different baseline approaches, in terms of the number of solved instances and verification efficiency, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed techniques.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SaBRe, a branch-and-bound (BaB) verification framework for neural networks against relational specifications (e.g., global robustness). Unlike prior works that split individual neurons, SaBRe splits relational neurons and uses a dual-formulation-based selection strategy to choose the most effective relational neuron for refinement, thereby mitigating incompleteness and false alarms in abstraction-based verification.
AI.motivation: Verifying neural networks against relational specifications (such as global robustness) is essential for safety-critical cyber-physical systems increasingly using AI. Relational specifications require reasoning about relations between multiple network inferences, unlike simple trace properties like local robustness. Existing abstraction methods rely on sound but convex over-approximations of network outputs and are inherently incomplete, often producing false alarms, which motivates the need for effective abstraction refinement.
AI.method: The authors propose a branch-and-bound (BaB) framework that iteratively splits the verification problem until all sub-problems are verified. The key novelty is splitting relational neurons instead of individual neurons, and a relational neuron selection strategy based on the dual formulation of the verification problem that efficiently selects the (most likely) optimal relational neuron maximizing the refinement from problem splitting.
AI.result: SaBRe was evaluated on 817 verification problems across ACAS Xu, MNIST-F, MNIST-C, CIFAR, and GTSRB. It outperforms various baseline approaches in terms of the number of solved instances and verification efficiency, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SaBRe framework effectively addresses the incompleteness of abstraction-based relational verification via relational neuron splitting guided by dual-formulation selection, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks and validating its practical benefit for safety-critical neural network verification.

title: SkillShapley: Boundary-Adaptive Shapley Valuation for Skill Step Attribution in LLM Agents
summary: Agent skills are crucial external instructions that enable language agents to execute long procedural tasks such as coding or document processing. Existing agent skills are primarily created through human manual crafting or agent execution traces, with limited understanding of how each step contributes to overall skill performance on specific tasks; i.e., there remains an open problem in quantifying the contribution of individual steps within an agent skill. To address this issue, we first model skill-step attribution as a Shapley value-based contribution estimation problem, and then propose SkillShapley, a step-level attribution framework for agent skills. Notably, SkillShapley operates in two phases, motivated by key empirical insights, i.e., discretized benchmark rewards that create sharp performance cliffs, and step interactions that are largely additive rather than synergistic. Specifically, it first identifies informative coalitional regions, and then adaptively samples new coalitions that can yield reusable marginal evidence. Experiments on skills from the widely adopted SkillsBench demonstrate that our SkillShapley can effectively and efficiently identify high- or low-value skill steps, providing several key takeaways for agent skill creation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SkillShapley, a Shapley value-based framework that attributes the contribution of individual steps within agent skills, enabling effective and efficient identification of high- or low-value steps to inform skill creation.
AI.motivation: Agent skills (external instructions for long procedural tasks) are currently built via manual crafting or execution traces, with no principled way to quantify how each individual step contributes to overall skill performance on specific tasks—a gap that motivates step-level contribution attribution.
AI.method: SkillShapley models skill-step attribution as a Shapley value-based contribution estimation problem. It operates in two phases driven by empirical insights: (1) discretized benchmark rewards create sharp performance cliffs, so it first identifies informative coalitional regions; (2) step interactions are largely additive rather than synergistic, so it adaptively samples new coalitions that yield reusable marginal evidence for efficient Shapley estimation.
AI.result: Experiments on skills from the widely used SkillsBench benchmark show SkillShapley effectively and efficiently identifies high- or low-value skill steps, yielding several key takeaways for agent skill creation.
AI.conclusion: SkillShapley provides a principled, efficient step-level attribution method for agent skills, bridging the gap between coarse skill construction and fine-grained step understanding, with practical implications for improving skill creation.

title: Beyond Local Accuracy: A Protocol-Level Identifiability Audit for Controlled LLM Reasoning Evaluation
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Ning Huang, Ziqi Sha, and Wenxuan Tang contributed equally as second authors. Wei Deng is the corresponding author
summary: LLM benchmark scores can be precise even when the observation protocol does not identify the behavioral property they are intended to measure. In a controlled, solver-grounded setting, we formalize a protocol-level identifiability audit over a finite behavioral policy class: given policies H, observation support O, and estimand $τ$, we test whether O separates every pair with different $τ$. The audit requires zero model calls and resolves our diagnostic case: base-only observation collapses seven frozen deterministic policies into one equivalence class; full support yields seven classes and no cross-estimand collisions; every leave-one-out support retains a constructive collision witness. Empirically, both constrained-generation variants have pair-validity 1.0, yet base accuracy and selective-response fidelity diverge - 0.620 versus 0.324 across six balanced oracle-transition directions (cluster-bootstrap 95% CI [0.600, 0.642] vs. [0.304, 0.345]) - and the gap recurs on a second deterministic source (0.646 vs. 0.331). The audit also synthesizes a minimum identifying support $O^*$ for the frozen policy class: two cells instead of the full 36-cell tensor. This case shows how evaluation-design validity can be checked structurally before model inference and why base correctness does not determine intervention-response fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a model-free "identifiability audit" that checks whether an observation protocol (support) can statistically separate policies with different behavioral estimates, and applies it to show that high base benchmark accuracy does not imply correct intervention-response fidelity.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores can be numerically precise yet fail to measure the behavioral property they claim to. The authors want a structural, pre-inference way to verify validity of an evaluation design, specifically to diagnose why base correctness does not determine selective-response fidelity.
AI.method: In a controlled, solver-grounded setting, they formalize a protocol-level identifiability audit over a finite policy class H with observation support O and estimand τ. The audit tests whether O separates every pair of policies with different τ, requiring zero model calls. They apply it to a frozen set of seven deterministic policies, including leave-one-out support variants, and empirically compare two constrained-generation variants on pair-validity, base accuracy, and selective-response fidelity using balanced oracle-transition directions with cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Base-only observation collapses seven frozen deterministic policies into one equivalence class; full support yields seven classes with no cross-estimand collisions; every leave-one-out support retains a constructive collision witness. Both constrained-generation variants achieve pair-validity 1.0, yet base accuracy and selective-response fidelity diverge (0.620 vs 0.324; CI [0.600, 0.642] vs [0.304, 0.345]), recurring on a second deterministic source (0.646 vs 0.331). The audit synthesizes a minimum identifying support O* of just two cells instead of the full 36-cell tensor.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation-design validity can be checked structurally before model inference, and base correctness does not determine intervention-response fidelity. The audit offers a zero-call diagnostic for whether an observation protocol can identify the intended behavioral estimand.

title: ProME: Prototype-Margin Environments with Repair-Aware Selection for Group-Robust Learning
summary: Group-robust learning is crucial for maintaining accuracy on rare subpopulations when training-group labels are unavailable. However, existing methods often infer environments from a separate reference model and select representations before fitting the classifier used at deployment, leaving both decisions misaligned with the deployed predictor. In this work, we formulate group robustness without training-group labels as the endogenous environments with repair-aware selection (ERAS) problem, and propose ProME (Prototype-Margin Environments) to align both decisions with the deployed predictor. ProME splits prototype margins at their median to construct approximately balanced environments along the training trajectory, and fits a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data to rank the resulting predictors by validation worst-group accuracy. We theoretically bound the worst risk across the inferred environments for a fixed predictor and partition, showing that this bound transfers to the oracle groups under an explicit alignment condition. Extensive experiments show that prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples, classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation, and ProME achieves the highest average worst-group accuracy among the compared methods with the same group-label access.

AI.tldr: ProME tackles group robustness without training-group labels by jointly aligning environment inference and classifier selection with the deployed predictor; it uses median-split prototype margins to build balanced environments and a group-balanced linear head to rank candidates by validation worst-group accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art average worst-group accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing group-robust methods infer environments with a separate reference model and select representations before fitting the deployed classifier, so both environment inference and selection are misaligned with the final predictor. The paper aims to align environment construction and candidate selection directly with the deployed classifier to improve worst-group accuracy without training-group labels.
AI.method: ProME formulates the task as the endogenous environments with repair-aware selection (ERAS) problem. It splits prototype margins at their median to create approximately balanced environments along the training trajectory, then fits a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data to rank candidate predictors by validation worst-group accuracy. The paper also provides a theoretical bound on worst risk across inferred environments for a fixed predictor and partition, which transfers to oracle groups under an explicit alignment condition.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples and classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation. ProME attains the highest average worst-group accuracy among compared methods with the same group-label access.
AI.conclusion: By aligning environment inference and selection with the deployed predictor, ProME effectively improves worst-group accuracy under limited group-label access, demonstrating that repair-aware, predictor-aligned environment construction is key to group-robust learning.

title: Teach the Magnitude, Not the Direction: Verifier-Bounded Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn Multi-step LLM Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers a verifier-bounded performance ceiling for training multi-turn tool-use agents, yet its trajectory-level credit assignment conflates heterogeneous per-turn outcomes into a single reward signal. On-policy distillation provides dense per-token supervision but is either teacher-bounded or prone to gradient concentration collapse. We introduce $\textbf{CrEST}$, a hierarchical credit assignment framework that retains RL's verifier-bounded ceiling while incorporating dense token-level signals from a privileged self-teacher. $\textbf{CrEST}$ resolves credit at two levels: turn-segmented verified advantages address inter-turn dilution, while entropy-gated self-teacher modulation refines intra-turn token contributions. Experiments on BFCL V3 and WildToolBench show that $\textbf{CrEST}$ consistently outperforms both RL and distillation baselines across two model scales, with the largest gains on long-trajectory and strict session-level metrics. Our work demonstrates that the teacher's role in policy optimization can be reduced from determining update directions to modulating update magnitudes, unlocking dense credit assignment without sacrificing the verifier-bounded ceiling.

AI.tldr: CrEST is a hierarchical credit assignment framework for multi-turn tool-use agents that combines RLVR's verifier-bounded ceiling with dense token-level signals from a privileged self-teacher, resolving credit at turn and token levels to outperform RL and distillation baselines.
AI.motivation: RLVR suffers from trajectory-level credit assignment that conflates heterogeneous per-turn outcomes into one reward signal, while on-policy distillation is either teacher-bounded or prone to gradient concentration collapse. The authors aim to retain RL's verifier-bounded ceiling while obtaining dense token-level supervision without sacrificing that ceiling.
AI.method: CrEST resolves credit hierarchically at two levels: (1) turn-segmented verified advantages to address inter-turn dilution, and (2) entropy-gated self-teacher modulation to refine intra-turn token contributions. A privileged self-teacher provides dense token-level signals, and the teacher's role is reduced to modulating update magnitudes rather than determining update directions.
AI.result: Experiments on BFCL V3 and WildToolBench show CrEST consistently outperforms both RL and distillation baselines across two model scales, with the largest gains on long-trajectory and strict session-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: CrEST demonstrates that a teacher's role in policy optimization can be reduced from determining update directions to modulating update magnitudes, enabling dense credit assignment without sacrificing the verifier-bounded ceiling.

title: It's How You Ask: Gender-Associated Linguistic Bias in LLMs
summary: Professional communication is increasingly mediated by LLMs - but do these models serve all users equally? We show that when prompts contain linguistic features more commonly used by women (hedges, tag questions, collective reference), they systematically elicit shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses across three document types and four models. These effects persist after controlling for prompt complexity and feature carry-over. Explicit gender cues like sign-off names are encoded in the same representational space as linguistic dialect - suggesting shared underlying mechanisms - yet linguistic register is far more influential, producing large, consistent effects where names produce none. Our results further reveal that post-hoc mitigation is challenging: because these patterns are culturally embedded and outside conscious control, users cannot easily avoid them through strategic self-presentation, and mechanistic analysis reveals that linguistic features are encoded in early transformer layers and entangled with other features. Our work calls for upstream consideration of the influences of linguistic variation to mitigate disparate impacts of LLM-mediated workplace communication.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether LLMs treat workplace communication prompts differently based on gendered linguistic features, finding that women-associated language patterns (hedges, tag questions, collective reference) systematically elicit shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal model outputs across four models and three document types, while explicit gender cues (names) have no effect; the authors show these effects are robust, embedded in early transformer layers, and difficult for users to avoid, arguing for upstream mitigation.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLMs serve all users equally in professional communication, given that workplace communication is increasingly mediated by these models, and to understand whether gendered linguistic variation produces disparate impacts.
AI.method: The authors generated prompts containing linguistic features more commonly used by women (hedges, tag questions, collective references) and measured responses across three document types and four LLMs. They controlled for prompt complexity and feature carry-over, compared linguistic dialect effects against explicit gender cues (sign-off names), and performed mechanistic (probing/representational) analysis of early transformer layers to examine how these features are encoded.
AI.result: Women-associated linguistic features systematically elicit shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses across all models and document types. Effects persist after controlling for complexity and carry-over. Explicit gender cues (names) and linguistic dialect occupy the same representational space, but linguistic register produces large consistent effects while names produce none. These features are encoded in early transformer layers and entangled with other features, making post-hoc mitigation and strategic self-presentation ineffective.
AI.conclusion: Because gendered linguistic patterns are culturally embedded and largely outside conscious control, users cannot easily avoid disparate treatment through self-presentation, and mechanistic entanglement makes downstream fixes hard. The work calls for upstream consideration of linguistic variation to mitigate disparate impacts in LLM-mediated workplace communication.

title: Beyond Simulated Benchmarks: Evaluating Motion Representations for Fall Detection Under Real-World Data Scarcity
summary: Falls are a major health concern for older adults, and wearable sensors have been widely explored for detecting falls and enabling timely intervention. However, real-world falls are extremely rare: collecting 100 of them requires an estimated 100,000 days of monitoring, resulting in severely limited labelled data for training machine learning models. Consequently, many approaches rely on simulated datasets, often reporting high laboratory performance but limited real-world generalisation. We present a systematic evaluation of motion representations for wearable fall detection under real-world data scarcity. Using accelerometer signals, we compare interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation model representations. As an interpretable baseline, we additionally investigate a lightweight symbolic representation that converts short motion segments into symbolic sentences augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Experiments use FallAllD, a simulated falls dataset, and FARSEEING, a clinically verified real-world falls dataset. Through cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer, we examine how representation choices affect robustness under realistic deployment. Our results reveal that highly parameterised kernel and foundation models excel on simulated data but degrade severely under both data scarcity and domain shift. Although the interval-based representation achieves the strongest absolute real-world performance, augmenting a symbolic representation with physically-grounded impact descriptors yields the smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme scarcity, albeit at lower precision. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating beyond simulated benchmarks and show that representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given the scarcity of real-world data.

AI.tldr: A systematic evaluation of motion representations for wearable fall detection shows that highly parameterised models (kernel-based, foundation models) excel on simulated data but degrade severely under real-world data scarcity and domain shift, while a physically-grounded symbolic representation is most robust to domain shift and scarcity.
AI.motivation: Real-world falls are extremely rare (collecting ~100 falls requires an estimated 100,000 days of monitoring), leaving severely limited labelled data. Most prior work relies on simulated datasets with high lab performance but poor real-world generalisation, motivating a focus on representation choice under realistic data scarcity and domain shift.
AI.method: Systematically compared interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation-model motion representations using accelerometer signals, plus a lightweight symbolic representation converting short motion segments into symbolic sentences augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Evaluated on FallAllD (simulated) and FARSEEING (clinically verified real-world faults) via cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer.
AI.result: Highly parameterised kernel and foundation models perform best on simulated data but degrade severely under data scarcity and domain shift. Interval-based representation achieves the strongest absolute real-world performance. The symbolic representation augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors shows the smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme scarcity, though at lower precision.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation beyond simulated benchmarks is essential; representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given the scarcity of real-world data, with physically-grounded symbolic representations offering robustness to domain shift and scarcity.

title: TsuGO: Probing Search Efficiency in LLM Reasoning via Go Life-and-Death Problems
summary: The evaluation of LLM reasoning is moving from final-answer accuracy to process-level assessment, yet existing methods still fail to capture how models plan reasoning paths and allocate reasoning resources--that is, how they organize search. Prior process-level methods focus on the coherence and redundancy of chain-of-thought (CoT), and most benchmark tasks have a single objective solvable by static capabilities such as derivation and tool use, leaving search organization unmeasured. We introduce TsuGO, a process-level reasoning benchmark for evaluating Search Efficiency in LLM reasoning through Go life-and-death problems. These problems provide closed and verifiable solution spaces with an inherent adversarial structure, making candidate generation, response checking, branch comparison, and backtracking necessary parts of reasoning rather than incidental trace patterns. By constraining the solution space, TsuGO disentangles domain knowledge from search organization, parses CoT into a structured search tree, and reports Search Efficiency together with Token Efficiency and other diagnostic metrics and visualizations. Experiments show that current LLMs remain far from stable tsumego solving: stronger models succeed by finding the correct candidate earlier and sustaining effort on productive branches, but most models still behave much closer to unguided search algorithms than to neural-guided KataGo. Longer CoT or higher Token Efficiency does not necessarily imply better search. Our results identify search organization and reasoning-resource allocation as missing dimensions in LLM reasoning evaluation.

AI.tldr: TsuGO is a process-level benchmark that evaluates how LLMs organize search during reasoning, using Go life-and-death (tsumego) problems to measure Search Efficiency via structured search trees derived from chain-of-thought, finding that current LLMs largely behave like unguided search rather than neural-guided solvers.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning evaluation is shifting from final-answer accuracy to process-level assessment, but existing methods still miss how models plan reasoning paths and allocate reasoning resources (search organization). Prior process-level methods only measure CoT coherence/redundancy, and most benchmark tasks have a single objective solvable by static capabilities (derivation, tool use), leaving search organization unmeasured.
AI.method: Introduce TsuGO, a process-level reasoning benchmark built on Go life-and-death problems. These provide closed, verifiable solution spaces with inherent adversarial structure, making candidate generation, response checking, branch comparison, and backtracking essential. TsuGO constrains the solution space to disentangle domain knowledge from search organization, parses chain-of-thought into a structured search tree, and reports Search Efficiency, Token Efficiency, and other diagnostic metrics and visualizations.
AI.result: Current LLMs remain far from stable tsumego solving. Stronger models succeed by finding the correct candidate earlier and sustaining effort on productive branches, but most models behave closer to unguided search algorithms than to neural-guided KataGo. Longer CoT or higher Token Efficiency does not necessarily imply better search.
AI.conclusion: Search organization and reasoning-resource allocation are missing dimensions in LLM reasoning evaluation, and TsuGO identifies them as necessary components for assessing process-level reasoning quality beyond final-answer accuracy.

title: RippleMem: From Isolated Retrieval to Associative Recollection for Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-horizon reasoning and interaction. However, the main bottleneck is not simply storing past experience, but recovering the right set of evidence when relevant information is distributed across many interactions. Existing approaches struggle with this access problem. Full-context methods require noisy long-context search, flat retrieval often returns isolated and incomplete records, and graph-based memory systems can be expensive to construct while compressing rich event context. We introduce RippleMem, a long-term memory system that replaces one-shot retrieval with adaptive associative recollection. Inspired by cue-dependent episodic retrieval and associative completion, RippleMem stores interaction history as cue-rich episodic memory units and organizes them in an event-centric memory graph. Given a query, it first recalls relevant memory anchors through hybrid cues, then expands from these anchors along semantic and structural associations to recover missing supporting evidence. In this way, initially recalled memories serve not only as answer context, but also as cues for completing the evidence needed to answer. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that RippleMem achieves the best overall performance across evaluated settings, improving LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy by 3.95% on LoCoMo and up to 11.87% on LongMemEval-S, while reducing graph construction cost by about 30x.

AI.tldr: RippleMem is a long-term memory system for LLM agents that replaces one-shot retrieval with adaptive associative recollection. It stores interactions as cue-rich episodic memory units in an event-centric graph and, given a query, recalls anchor memories via hybrid cues then expands along semantic/structural associations to complete missing evidence. It achieves the best overall performance on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S while cutting graph construction cost by ~30x.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents increasingly need external memory for long-horizon reasoning, but the core bottleneck is recovering the right evidence when relevant information is scattered across many interactions. Existing methods fail: full-context search is noisy and costly, flat retrieval returns isolated/incomplete records, and graph-based memory systems are expensive to build and can compress rich event context. A better access mechanism is needed.
AI.method: RippleMem introduces adaptive associative recollection inspired by cue-dependent episodic retrieval and associative completion. It stores interaction history as cue-rich episodic memory units organized in an event-centric memory graph. At query time it (1) recalls relevant memory anchors using hybrid cues, and (2) expands from those anchors along semantic and structural associations to recover supporting evidence. Recalled memories serve both as answer context and as cues for completing the evidence needed to answer.
AI.result: On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, RippleMem achieves the best overall performance across evaluated settings, improving LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy by 3.95% on LoCoMo and up to 11.87% on LongMemEval-S, while reducing graph construction cost by about 30x.
AI.conclusion: RippleMem effectively addresses the evidence-access bottleneck in long-term memory for LLM agents by replacing one-shot retrieval with associative recollection along a memory graph, yielding state-of-the-art accuracy at substantially lower graph construction cost.

title: TANGCO: Learning Topology-Aware Capacity Allocation for Overload-driven Cascading Failures
summary: Networked systems, from power grids to traffic networks and cloud clusters, carry loads across nodes with limited capacity. A node whose load exceeds its capacity fails and sheds its load onto its neighbors, which can trigger a system-wide cascade. We study how to allocate a fixed capacity budget across nodes to resist these cascades under local load redistribution. The problem is difficult because no optimal allocation is known, and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, so exact and gradient-based optimization methods do not directly apply. We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which uses a graph neural network policy trained through the cascade simulator with policy-gradient learning and a heuristic anchor. We evaluate TANGCO on five synthetic graph families and five real networks spanning power, road, air, and Internet topologies. The learned policy improves on the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains ranging from 1.6% to 246%. The learned policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies, and TANGCO$^{pre}$, pre-trained on synthetic graphs, matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO$^{pre}$ allocates on a new network with no per-target training, matching the deployment cost of a hand-designed heuristic. Free-vector variants without the GNN, stay close to the heuristics, so the graph representation carries the gain beyond numerical search. Finally, analysis of the learned allocations identifies when local risk is sufficient, leads to an improved closed-form heuristic, and reveals the regimes where a topology-aware learned policy remains necessary.

AI.tldr: TANGCO is a graph neural network policy trained via policy-gradient on a cascade simulator to allocate a fixed capacity budget across network nodes, improving robustness to load-shedding cascades over hand-designed heuristics.
AI.motivation: Networked systems (power grids, traffic, clouds) face cascade failures when overloaded nodes shed load to neighbors. Allocating a fixed capacity budget to resist cascades is hard: no optimal allocation is known and the fail/survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, making exact and gradient-based methods inapplicable.
AI.method: TANGCO uses a graph neural network (GNN) policy trained directly through the cascade simulator with policy-gradient reinforcement learning and a heuristic anchor. It is evaluated on five synthetic graph families and five real networks (power, road, air, Internet). A pre-trained variant, TANGCO^pre, is trained on synthetic graphs and applied to unseen real networks without per-target training. Free-vector variants (no GNN) serve as ablations.
AI.result: The learned policy beats the best of four hand-designed heuristics on all 450 synthetic instances and 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains from 1.6% to 246%. Policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies; TANGCO^pre matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO^pre allocates with no per-target training at heuristic-level cost. Free-vector variants stay close to heuristics, showing the graph representation drives the gain.
AI.conclusion: Local risk is sometimes sufficient, leading to an improved closed-form heuristic, but topology-aware learned policies remain necessary in other regimes. The GNN representation, not just numerical search, is the key source of improved robustness and transferability.

title: Capability Sheaves for Compositional Agent-Harness Repair: Controlled Quotients and a Real-Repository Stress Test
summary:
Agent harnesses combine retrieval, routing, state, provenance, and verification, but locally successful components may disagree on shared state. We model this failure with a finite \emph{capability sheaf}: stalks encode typed behavior signatures, restriction maps retain shared fields, and accepted runs are useful global sections. An exact finite constraint-satisfaction problem (CSP) defines acceptance, while a linearized relative cohomology class provides a diagnostic and search feature.
  A controlled experiment over 20 task clusters introduces hidden interior mediators whose raw states are nuisance variables. Quotienting their coboundaries reduces the candidate budget from 2,000 to 1,000 per cluster; aligning the hidden state removes the gap. Exact CSP matches the quotient, so the result demonstrates invariance to stale representatives, not superiority over exact reasoning.
  We then test the method on a discovery split from the SWE-bench Multilingual pool of PatchFuseBench: 160 issues from 20 repositories, 875 real candidate patches, 2,579 source-aware edit atoms, and 153 newly executed patches. A first pool-level construction is constant because $[b-Dx]=[b]$ in $\operatorname{coker}D$ and therefore cannot rank configurations. A candidate-indexed repair is nontrivial on 848/875 candidates and varies within 120/160 issues. It resolves 118 issues versus 116 for a matched noncohomological selector, but the difference is not supported across repositories (exact sign-flip $p=0.75$). A leave-one-repository-out abstention gate reaches 127/160, tying the strong anchor and exceeding its matched gate by one issue ($p=1.0$). The discovery gate therefore fails and the confirmatory split remains sealed. The study supports the controlled invariance mechanism and an identifiability correction, but not a real-world cohomological advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper models agent-harness component disagreement using a finite capability sheaf, where acceptable runs are global sections and acceptance is an exact CSP; a linearized relative cohomology class serves as a diagnostic/search feature. A controlled experiment validates an invariance-to-stale-representatives mechanism, but a SWE-bench Multilingual discovery split shows no statistically supported real-world advantage (sign-flip p=0.75), the discovery gate fails, and the confirmatory split remains sealed.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses combine retrieval, routing, state, provenance, and verification, but locally successful components can disagree on shared state; the authors aim to formalize this failure and determine whether cohomological diagnostics yield genuine gains or merely invariance to stale representatives.
AI.method: A finite capability sheaf encodes typed behavior signatures as stalks and shared fields as restriction maps; accepted runs are useful global sections defined by an exact finite CSP, with a linearized relative cohomology class as a diagnostic and search feature. A controlled experiment over 20 task clusters introduces hidden interior mediators and quotients their coboundaries, reducing the candidate budget from 2,000 to 1,000 per cluster. A discovery split from SWE-bench Multilingual (PatchFuseBench) tests 160 issues, 875 real candidate patches, 2,579 edit atoms, and 153 executed patches, comparing pool-level vs. candidate-indexed constructions against a matched noncohomological selector and a leave-one-repository-out abstention gate.
AI.result: Exact CSP matches the quotient, confirming invariance to stale representatives rather than superiority. A pool-level construction is constant (since [b-Dx]=[b] in coker D) and cannot rank configurations. The candidate-indexed repair is nontrivial on 848/875 candidates and varies within 120/160 issues, resolving 118 vs. 116 issues for the matched noncohomological selector (not supported, exact sign-flip p=0.75). The abstention gate reaches 127/160, tying the anchor and exceeding its matched gate by one issue (p=1.0). The discovery gate fails and the confirmatory split remains sealed.
AI.conclusion: The study supports a controlled invariance mechanism and an identifiability correction, but not a real-world cohomological advantage. The confirmatory split remains sealed pending the failed discovery gate.

title: CROP: Task Relevance via Counterfactuals for Selective On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises a student language model on trajectories sampled from its current policy, but assigns equal credit to response tokens with unequal supervision value. Selective OPD addresses this limitation by allocating supervision non-uniformly across response tokens according to their estimated training value. Most existing criteria, however, focus primarily on optimization need, such as uncertainty or teacher-student disagreement, while task relevance, namely whether the supervision is tied to the semantic content of the current input, remains less directly characterized as a complementary dimension. To address this gap, we introduce Counterfactual Relevance for On-Policy Distillation (CROP), which operationalizes task relevance through a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin. For each source prompt, CROP constructs a validated original-paraphrase-counterfactual triplet, holds the student rollout fixed, and measures each response position by its sensitivity to a task-relevant condition change calibrated by its sensitivity to a meaning-preserving rewrite. Matched selection controls show that CROP identifies more useful supervision positions than random or lowest-relevance selection, while component comparisons confirm the value of both counterfactual sensitivity and paraphrase calibration. Across two teacher-student settings, CROP improves aggregate performance by 1.92 and 2.96 points over the strongest non-CROP selector. These results support task relevance as a complementary criterion for selective OPD and establish CROP as a model-internal, contrast-specific method for allocating token-level supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CROP, a selective on-policy distillation method that allocates token-level supervision based on task relevance, measured via a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin, and shows it outperforms existing selectors.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) assigns equal credit to all response tokens despite unequal supervision value. Existing selective OPD criteria focus mainly on optimization need (uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement) while task relevance—whether supervision is tied to the semantic content of the current input—is not directly characterized as a complementary dimension. The work aims to fill this gap.
AI.method: CROP operationalizes task relevance via a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin. For each source prompt, it constructs a validated original-paraphrase-counterfactual triplet, holds the student rollout fixed, and scores each response position by its sensitivity to a task-relevant condition change, calibrated by its sensitivity to a meaning-preserving paraphrase rewrite.
AI.result: Matched selection controls show CROP identifies more useful supervision positions than random or lowest-relevance selection. Component comparisons confirm the value of both counterfactual sensitivity and paraphrase calibration. Across two teacher-student settings, CROP improves aggregate performance by 1.92 and 2.96 points over the strongest non-CROP selector.
AI.conclusion: Task relevance serves as a complementary criterion for selective OPD, and CROP establishes a model-internal, contrast-specific method for allocating token-level supervision.

title: History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the 9th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition and Computer Vision (PRCV 2026) as an oral paper
summary: Forecasting the long-horizon evolution of mechanical systems from position-only observations is a pivotal yet difficult task, as hidden velocities and trajectory-specific physical properties must be inferred simultaneously. Although physics-guided neural networks like Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) guarantee physical plausibility, they generally require complete state inputs and lack adaptability to changing system parameters. To break these limitations, we introduce History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks (HiLNN). Grounded in the insight that temporal position sequences implicitly encode underlying dynamics, HiLNN employs a recurrent encoder to extract a latent context from history. This context not only reconstructs the unobserved initial velocity but also adaptively modulates the mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients of a structured Lagrangian system. By leveraging a differentiable RK4 rollout scheme, the entire pipeline is optimized end-to-end under multi-step trajectory supervision and energy-consistency regularization. Empirical evaluations across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems show that HiLNN delivers superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/yingtian22/History-informed-LNN.

AI.tldr: HiLNN introduces a history-informed Lagrangian neural network that forecasts long-horizon mechanical system evolution from position-only data by using a recurrent encoder to infer latent context, reconstruct initial velocity, and adapt system parameters, trained end-to-end with differentiable RK4 rollouts and energy regularization.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon forecasting from position-only observations is difficult because hidden velocities and trajectory-specific physical properties must be inferred simultaneously. Existing Lagrangian Neural Networks require complete state inputs and cannot adapt to changing system parameters, limiting their applicability.
AI.method: HiLNN uses a recurrent encoder to extract a latent context from temporal position history. This context reconstructs the unobserved initial velocity and adaptively modulates the mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients of a structured Lagrangian system. A differentiable RK4 rollout scheme enables end-to-end optimization under multi-step trajectory supervision and energy-consistency regularization.
AI.result: Across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems, HiLNN achieves superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: HiLNN overcomes the state-completeness and parameter-adaptability limitations of conventional LNNs, enabling accurate and physically consistent long-horizon forecasting from position-only observations. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/yingtian22/History-informed-LNN.

title: vToken: Token-Level Virtualization for Reclaimable KV Caches
summary: Large language model serving faces a critical memory bottleneck: the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention uses fixed-size memory blocks to reduce allocator-level fragmentation, but recent KV eviction algorithms operate at a token granularity finer than block-level management. This mismatch causes intra-block fragmentation, leaving a large fraction of allocated KV memory unreclaimable. We present vToken, a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. vToken maintains a stable logical token view through token-table indirection and realizes physical reclamation by repacking live tokens asynchronously. The design preserves PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility. We implement vToken in vLLM and evaluate it with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands across models. Compared with a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2\%--72.3\% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37$\times$. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends the maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2$\times$, while reducing the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.

AI.tldr: vToken is a lightweight token-level virtualization layer for LLM serving that decouples logical token eviction from physical KV block placement, eliminating intra-block memory fragmentation and improving throughput/concurrency while preserving PagedAttention and CUDA Graph compatibility.
AI.motivation: LLM serving faces a KV cache memory bottleneck that grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention reduces allocator-level fragmentation using fixed-size blocks, but KV eviction algorithms (e.g., H2O, Random, Scissorhands) operate at fine token granularity. This token-vs-block granularity mismatch causes intra-block fragmentation, leaving a large fraction of allocated KV memory unreclaimable and thus undermining the benefits of eviction.
AI.method: vToken adds a token-level virtualization layer using token-table indirection to maintain a stable logical token view, plus asynchronous repacking of live tokens for physical reclamation. It decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement while keeping PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility intact. Implemented in vLLM and evaluated with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands against a paired Naive-Evict baseline.
AI.result: Compared to Naive-Evict, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2%–72.3% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37×. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2×, while shrinking the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.
AI.conclusion: Token-level virtualization via vToken resolves the granularity mismatch between token-level eviction and block-level physical management, reclaiming otherwise wasted KV memory and substantially improving serving efficiency with minimal integration overhead.

title: Motor, Cognitive, or Corpus? What Survives Cross-Lingual Transfer in Speech-Based Parkinsons Disease Detection
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech representations achieve strong performance for Parkinson's disease (PD) detection within individual corpora. However, it remains unclear whether these models capture disease-related characteristics or exploit dataset-specific confounds, particularly since most SSL backbones are pretrained exclusively on healthy speech. To investigate this question, we perform a layer-wise analysis of nine SSL speech backbones using a low-capacity logistic regression probe across three languages. We structure the evaluation as multiple scenarios that progressively introduce distribution shifts in participant identity, recording conditions, language, and pathology. Our results reveal two key findings. First, layer selection is highly corpus-dependent: the optimal representation layer is determined primarily by the source dataset rather than by the SSL architecture itself. Second, the transferred discriminative signal lacks pathological specificity: classifiers trained to detect PD assign similarly high probabilities to both PD and dementia speech in the target corpus. These results highlight critical limitations that must be addressed before speech-based pathology recognition models can be reliably deployed in clinical settings.

AI.tldr: A layer-wise analysis of nine self-supervised speech models using logistic regression probes shows that the optimal representation layer depends on the source corpus rather than the SSL architecture, and that transferred PD detection signal lacks pathological specificity (it also flags dementia speech).
AI.motivation: SSL speech representations perform well for Parkinson's disease detection within individual corpora, but it is unclear whether they capture true disease-related characteristics or merely exploit dataset-specific confounds—especially since most SSL backbones are pretrained exclusively on healthy speech.
AI.method: Layer-wise probing of nine SSL speech backbones with a low-capacity logistic regression probe across three languages, evaluated under multiple scenarios that progressively introduce distribution shifts in participant identity, recording conditions, language, and pathology.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) optimal layer selection is highly corpus-dependent, driven mainly by the source dataset rather than the SSL architecture; (2) the transferred discriminative signal is not pathologically specific—classifiers trained to detect PD assign similarly high probabilities to both PD and dementia speech in the target corpus.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal critical limitations that must be addressed before speech-based pathology recognition models can be reliably deployed in clinical settings.

title: Knowledge-guided Pattern Discovery via Coupled Tensor Factorizations
summary: In order to understand complex systems such as the human metabolome or human brain, different sensing technologies are used, generating complex data. These datasets are often multiway, i.e., with more than two axes of variation such as a subjects by metabolites by time array. While tensor factorizations have successfully revealed interpretable patterns from such complex data, they have so far been mainly data-driven. On the other hand, there is more to data -- there are computational models (of these systems), which are rich sources of prior information. In this paper, we introduce a knowledge-guided approach that brings together data and computational models by jointly analyzing real data and simulated data (generated using a computational model) using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling. Our experiments on real metabolomics measurements demonstrate that guiding the analysis of such noisy data with simulated data improves the pattern discovery performance while also revealing potential discrepancies between data and computational models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a knowledge-guided framework that couples real multiway data with data simulated from computational models via coupled tensor factorization with linear coupling, to improve pattern discovery in noisy datasets such as metabolomics measurements.
AI.motivation: Complex systems (e.g., human metabolome or brain) are measured by multiple sensing technologies, producing multiway data. Existing tensor factorizations are mostly data-driven and fail to exploit the rich prior information available in computational models of these systems. The work aims to bridge this gap by jointly leveraging real data and model-based simulated data.
AI.method: The authors propose a knowledge-guided approach using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling, jointly analyzing real data and simulated data generated from a computational model. Both datasets are coupled within the factorization framework so the model-derived information guides the decomposition of the noisy real observations.
AI.result: Experiments on real metabolomics measurements show that guiding the analysis of noisy data with simulated data improves pattern discovery performance, while also revealing potential discrepancies between the real data and the computational models.
AI.conclusion: Coupling real multiway data with model-generated simulated data through coupled tensor factorizations effectively improves interpretable pattern discovery and simultaneously exposes model–data inconsistencies, advancing beyond purely data-driven tensor analysis.

title: Are You Sure You're Sure? On the Impact of Instruction Tuning on Confidence and Lexical Diversity
summary: Instruction-tuned language models achieve strong performance across a range of generation tasks, but have also recently been shown to exhibit verbalized overconfidence. In question answering, verbalized model overconfidence may be associated with the consistency of the generated supporting rationales. In this paper, we study whether corresponding changes in the lexical diversity of generated answer rationales accompany changes in model confidence induced by instruction tuning. We evaluate three matched base and instruction-tuned models across question-answering benchmarks and find that instruction tuning consistently alters answer confidence, despite limited changes in predictive accuracy and decreases in likelihood-based calibration. Secondly, we observe a non-uniform effect of instruction tuning on rationale diversity: cross-rationale diversity consistently decreases, whereas surface-level lexical diversity varies in both direction and magnitude across models and benchmarks. Finally, we find that these differences persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length, confirming that confidence and rationale diversity capture distinct effects of instruction tuning.

AI.tldr: Instruction tuning consistently increases verbalized confidence in question answering without much accuracy gain, while reducing cross-rationale diversity; these effects are distinct from answer selection and rationale length.
AI.motivation: Recent work shows instruction-tuned language models exhibit verbalized overconfidence. The authors aim to investigate whether changes in model confidence induced by instruction tuning are accompanied by corresponding changes in the lexical diversity of generated answer rationales, probing the relationship between confidence and rationale consistency/diversity.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three matched pairs of base and instruction-tuned language models across question-answering benchmarks. They measure answer confidence, predictive accuracy, likelihood-based calibration, and two facets of rationale diversity: cross-rationale diversity (consistency across generated rationales for the same question) and surface-level lexical diversity. They also control for answer selection and rationale length to isolate the effects.
AI.result: Instruction tuning consistently alters (increases) answer confidence despite only limited changes in predictive accuracy and a decrease in likelihood-based calibration. Its effect on rationale diversity is non-uniform: cross-rationale diversity consistently decreases, while surface-level lexical diversity varies in both direction and magnitude across models and benchmarks. These differences persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length.
AI.conclusion: Confidence and rationale diversity capture distinct effects of instruction tuning: instruction tuning raises verbalized confidence and reduces cross-rationale diversity, but these are not explained by accuracy, answer choice, or rationale length, suggesting the overconfidence and rationale homogenization are separate consequences of instruction tuning.

title: Novel Knowledge-Guided Generative Methods for Synthetic Transcriptomic Data
summary: As biomedical research increasingly relies on data-intensive tools, the quality and utility of datasets are critical. Challenges such as imbalances, biases, and ethical or legal constraints often limit access to high-quality data. Synthetic data generation can help overcome these limitations. Here, we present a comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, investigating strategies to incorporate prior biological knowledge via gene graphs. This ensures that synthetic data capture real-world gene patterns, maintaining their usefulness for downstream tasks. In particular, we introduce and benchmark three variants of the Generative Adversarial Network. Among the alternatives, MK-TGAN - an innovative multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based model - stands out for its performance in terms of both the realism and utility of the generated data. Unlike other methods, MK-TGAN leverages prior knowledge graphs by exploiting graph neural networks. Our results show that prior knowledge integration strategies improve performance, and that MK-TGAN consistently produces synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks generative models for synthetic transcriptomic data and shows that incorporating prior biological knowledge via gene graphs improves realism and utility, with the proposed MK-TGAN (multi-kernel graph-neural-network GAN) performing best.
AI.motivation: Biomedical research increasingly depends on data-intensive tools, but datasets often suffer from imbalances, biases, and ethical/legal access constraints. Synthetic data generation is proposed as a way to overcome these limitations while preserving data utility.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, investigating strategies to inject prior biological knowledge through gene graphs. Three Generative Adversarial Network variants are introduced and benchmarked, including MK-TGAN, an innovative multi-kernel Graph Neural Network-based model that exploits prior knowledge graphs.
AI.result: Prior knowledge integration strategies improve performance. MK-TGAN consistently produces synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility compared to the alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging gene graphs via graph neural networks enhances synthetic transcriptomic data generation, and MK-TGAN stands out as the best model for producing realistic, biologically plausible data useful for downstream tasks.

title: Towards Context-Aware Clinical Motion Understanding in Daily Living at Home: Freezing of Gait Detection with Egocentric Vision
comment: Accepted to ECCV Workshop 2026 (Human Motion Challenges in Real-World and Clinical Settings)
summary: Understanding motion in daily living requires context beyond kinematics, because similar inertial patterns during activities of daily living (ADLs) can reflect intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological movement impairment. Egocentric vision provides task-related context that may help disambiguate these cases. We investigate this challenge through freezing of gait (FOG) detection in Parkinson's disease (PD), a symptom strongly influenced by contextual factors during ADLs. Using synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels collected from 13 PD participants in their homes, we evaluate frozen representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models, alongside an IMU-based TCN trained from scratch, under leave-one-subject-out evaluation. The IMU-based TCN achieved the strongest event-detection performance, reaching 42.3 F1 and 83.0 AUROC, compared with 32.6 F1 and 77.2 AUROC for V-JEPA2 ego-video features. Although ego-video alone did not outperform IMU-based sensing, it showed above-chance discrimination, and qualitative analyses suggest that egocentric vision may capture FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs. Together, these results support the use of pretrained ego-video representations to add contextual information to wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living.

AI.tldr: The paper explores whether egocentric vision can add contextual information to wearable IMU sensing for detecting freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease during daily living. Using synchronized ego-video and IMU data from 13 participants at home, frozen representations from pretrained video/time-series foundation models and an IMU-based TCN are evaluated. The IMU TCN performed best (42.3 F1, 83.0 AUROC), while the V-JEPA2 ego-video features showed above-chance but weaker discrimination (32.6 F1, 77.2 AUROC), with qualitative evidence that vision captures FOG-relevant information complementary to IMUs.
AI.motivation: Similar inertial patterns during activities of daily living can correspond to different underlying causes (intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological impairment), and kinematics alone cannot disambiguate them. FOG in Parkinson's disease is strongly context-dependent, motivating the use of egocentric vision to provide task-related context for better clinical motion understanding.
AI.method: Data were collected from 13 Parkinson's disease participants in their homes using synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels. Frozen representations from pretrained egocentric-video and time-series foundation models were evaluated, along with an IMU-based temporal convolutional network (TCN) trained from scratch. Evaluation used leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, assessed via F1 and AUROC, supplemented by qualitative analyses.
AI.result: The IMU-based TCN achieved the strongest event-detection performance (42.3 F1, 83.0 AUROC), outperforming the best ego-video representation V-JEPA2 (32.6 F1, 77.2 AUROC). Ego-video alone showed above-chance discrimination but did not surpass IMU sensing. Qualitative analyses suggest egocentric vision captures FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained ego-video representations are a promising means to add contextual information to wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living, even though IMU-based sensing remains the stronger standalone detector. The complementary nature of vision motivates future multimodal integration for improved FOG detection.

title: Toward a Gricean Retreat: Probing LLMs for Knowledge Boundaries and Referent Specificity
summary: When asked about entities outside their knowledge boundary, LLMs routinely fabricate plausible-sounding details rather than backing off to safer, more general claims. We frame this failure through a Gricean lens: a cooperative speaker who is uncertain about a referent retreats up the specificity hierarchy, trading informativeness for truthfulness. We ask whether LLMs have the ingredients to perform this retreat. Using a T-REx-based benchmark that varies entity familiarity and referent specificity, we probe models to answer two questions: (i) do their activations encode whether a referent falls inside the knowledge boundary, and (ii) do they anticipate the specificity of the referent they are about to generate? We find that the answer to both is yes, but the two signals are not reconciled in generation. Models overwhelmingly prefer specific referents even when the entity is unknown to them, and do so even when offered correct generic alternatives. The substrate for a Gricean retreat is present, but the policy that would act on it is not. We position our findings as a first step toward Gricean alignment, training or steering objectives that couple knowledge-boundary awareness to referent-specificity during generation.

AI.tldr: LLMs encode both knowledge-boundary awareness and referent-specificity signals, but do not use them to retreat to safer generic claims when uncertain, causing fabrication.
AI.motivation: LLMs fabricate specific details about entities beyond their knowledge boundary instead of retreating to safer, more general claims. The authors frame this as a violation of Gricean cooperative communication, where a rational speaker should trade informativeness for truthfulness when uncertain.
AI.method: Using a T-REx-based benchmark varying entity familiarity and referent specificity, the authors probe model activations to answer two questions: (i) whether activations encode whether a referent falls inside the knowledge boundary, and (ii) whether models anticipate the specificity of the referent they are about to generate. They then test whether models reconcile these signals during generation, including offering correct generic alternatives.
AI.result: Models' activations encode both knowledge-boundary status and anticipated referent specificity, but the two signals are not reconciled. Models overwhelmingly prefer specific referents even for unknown entities, and persist even when correct generic alternatives are offered.
AI.conclusion: The substrate for a Gricean retreat exists in model activations, but the generation policy that would act on it is absent. The authors position this as a first step toward "Gricean alignment"—training or steering objectives that couple knowledge-boundary awareness to referent-specificity during generation.

title: Virtual Temperature Sensors in Power Transformers Using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
summary: Accurate modeling and forecasting of power transformer thermal behavior are critical for reliability, asset lifetime, and optimized power system operation. Numerical approaches such as finite element methods (FEM) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) offer high fidelity but are computationally expensive, require complex mesh generation, and are often impractical for real-time or large-scale applications, particularly when transformer geometries are unknown. Lumped-parameter thermal models are more practical but depend on transformer-specific thermal constants and may fail to capture dynamic responses under varying operating and environmental conditions. Purely data-driven machine learning methods, including artificial neural networks, convolutional neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown success in forecasting transformer temperatures but typically require large volumes of high-quality training data and may produce physically inconsistent or uninterpretable results. This paper develops a physics-aware Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) framework for forecasting transformer thermal behavior from real-world time-series data. Neural ODEs model system dynamics in continuous time, providing smooth trajectory prediction and a natural representation of continuously evolving thermal dynamics. A key contribution is the integration of simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the Neural ODE formulation. The model is evaluated across datasets from fifteen transformers in different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms. The results demonstrate that the developed Neural ODE framework provides a standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting approach for heterogeneous transformer units.

AI.tldr: A physics-aware Neural ODE framework is developed to forecast power transformer thermal behavior from real-world time-series data, integrating simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the continuous-time dynamics model.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for transformer thermal modeling each have limitations: FEM/CFD are computationally expensive and impractical for real-time use; lumped-parameter models require transformer-specific constants and struggle with dynamic responses; purely data-driven ML models need large training datasets and may yield physically inconsistent results. A robust, standardized, real-time forecasting approach is needed that works across heterogeneous transformer units.
AI.method: A Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) framework models thermal dynamics in continuous time. Simplified heat-transfer equations are integrated directly into the Neural ODE formulation to enforce physics awareness. The model is evaluated on real-world time-series data from fifteen transformers across different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms.
AI.result: The Neural ODE framework provides smooth trajectory predictions and a natural representation of continuously evolving thermal dynamics, delivering a standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting approach across the fifteen heterogeneous transformer units.
AI.conclusion: Integrating simplified heat-transfer physics into a Neural ODE formulation yields a practical, robust, and standardized method for forecasting transformer thermal behavior across diverse designs and cooling mechanisms, overcoming limitations of purely numerical or data-driven approaches.

title: NAS-Driven Hardware Accelerator Exploration for Edge AI and Quantization Effects on the Pareto Space
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, accepted for presentation to the 39th IEEE International System-on-Chip Conference, Heidelberg, Germany, September 30 - October 2, 2026
summary: Edge AI deployment demands neural architectures that are simultaneously accurate, computationally efficient, and hardware-deployable - a challenge addressed by hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS). While recent works incorporate quantization directly into the NAS loop, these approaches expand search complexity and tightly couple architecture and quantization design. The simpler post-search quantization strategy has received little analytical attention: the effects of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) on the NAS-discovered Pareto structure remain uncharacterised, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration. This paper addresses both gaps. First, a three-stage pipeline is proposed: a hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201, a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control, and an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping.
