Second, an empirical study characterises how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space through formal stability metrics on ground-truth data for all 15,625 architectures, and demonstrates that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-stage pipeline combining hardware-agnostic NAS, a PTQ quantization bridge, and evolutionary hardware DSE, and empirically characterizes how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space, finding an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate.
AI.motivation: Edge AI requires architectures that are accurate, efficient, and deployable. Existing hardware-aware NAS methods integrate quantization into the search loop, which increases search complexity and entangles architecture and quantization design. The simpler post-search quantization (PTQ) strategy lacks analytical characterization of how it affects the NAS Pareto structure, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration. This paper addresses both gaps.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline is proposed: (1) a hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201; (2) a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control; and (3) an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. An empirical study characterizes how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space using formal stability metrics over ground-truth data for all 15,625 architectures, comparing FP32 zero-shot surrogates against dedicated INT4-trained surrogates across two standard search strategies.
AI.result: INT4 PTQ measurably perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space. An FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies, despite the quantization mismatch.
AI.conclusion: Post-search PTQ perturbs the NAS Pareto structure, and simple FP32 zero-shot surrogates can outperform INT4-trained surrogates for Pareto coverage, motivating the proposed pipeline that bridges NAS, quantization, and hardware mapping for edge deployment.

title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
summary: Measuring training data influence consistently across language model pretraining is challenging. It is difficult to select downstream tasks or validation sets representative of a model's general capabilities, and reliance on task performance at intermediate checkpoints complicates comparisons across training. We propose a measure of training data influence that does not require selecting a downstream task or validation set as the attribution target. Specifically, we define an example's influence by how much its gradient update reduces the squared distance to the final parameters of a given pretraining run, and estimate this quantity from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applying the method to 18 configurations from the Pythia and PolyPythia suites, we find systematic temporal changes in influential data. Early in training, literature-related data are more strongly aligned with the trajectory toward the final parameters, whereas STEM data become more strongly aligned in later stages. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across model configurations. Our results provide a tractable trajectory-level view of how influential data change throughout pretraining, complementing influence analyses defined with respect to specific downstream tasks or validation sets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a task-free measure of training data influence based on how much each example's gradient update reduces squared distance to the final pretraining parameters, then applies it across Pythia/PolyPythia to reveal a temporal shift in influential data.
AI.motivation: Existing influence analyses require choosing a downstream task or validation set as the attribution target, which is hard to make representative of general capabilities, and comparing across training is complicated by relying on task performance at intermediate checkpoints.
AI.method: Define an example's influence by the reduction in squared distance to the final parameters of a pretraining run caused by its gradient update, and estimate this quantity from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Apply to 18 configurations from the Pythia and PolyPythia suites.
AI.result: Influential data show systematic temporal changes: early in training, literature-related data align more strongly with the trajectory toward final parameters, while STEM data align more strongly in later stages. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across model configurations.
AI.conclusion: The method offers a tractable, trajectory-level view of how influential data change throughout pretraining, complementing influence analyses tied to specific downstream tasks or validation sets.

title: Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have advanced primarily through architectural innovation, while training regimes for large-scale heterogeneous corpora remain under-explored. As a result, pre-training distributions are often poorly controlled with respect to domain imbalance, context requirements, prediction horizons, and missingness. We introduce ORBIT (Omni-Range Bootstrap Incremental Training), a training paradigm that makes this distribution explicit and controllable. ORBIT combines Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling, which controls dataset exposure and samples records, target variables, context windows, and prediction horizons, with Omni-Range Incremental Training, which varies context lengths and prediction horizons throughout a single training stage. Under ORBIT, we train Falcon-2.0, a simple univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction. We further introduce Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment, a training objective that uses late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers for shallow layers without additional inference cost. Evaluations on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench demonstrate strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ORBIT, a controllable pre-training paradigm for time series foundation models, and Falcon-2.0, a univariate Transformer trained under it, achieving strong zero-shot forecasting.
AI.motivation: Time series foundation models have progressed mainly through architectural innovation, while training regimes for large heterogeneous corpora remain under-explored, leading to poorly controlled pre-training distributions with respect to domain imbalance, context requirements, prediction horizons, and missingness.
AI.method: ORBIT combines Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling (controlling dataset exposure and sampling records, target variables, context windows, and prediction horizons) with Omni-Range Incremental Training (varying context lengths and horizons within a single training stage). Falcon-2.0 is a univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction, further enhanced by Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment (late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers for shallow layers).
AI.result: Evaluations on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench show strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Controlling the pre-training distribution via ORBIT, combined with a simple encoder-only architecture and alignment training, yields competitive zero-shot forecasting without architectural complexity or extra inference cost.

title: StateBridge: Training-free Hidden-state Alignment for Latent Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables, accepted by COLM2026
summary: Large language model based multi-agent systems usually communicate in text, i.e., using discrete tokens. However, text introduces a discrete bottleneck. Converting the sender's continuous hidden states into discrete tokens discards information that token identities alone cannot capture. Recent work proposes latent communication as an alternative, where agents transmit hidden representations directly without converting them to text. However, existing latent methods either inject working memory layer by layer across the transformers, or require trained projectors that limit portability. We propose StateBridge, a training-free latent communication approach that aligns the sender's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input space via a closed-form orthogonal transformation. Lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring ensure compatibility with the pretrained input distribution. The aligned states are prepended to the input of the receiver agent as a continuous prefix. We evaluate StateBridge on math reasoning, code generation, and question answering with four models from two families. StateBridge achieves the best or tied-best score on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: StateBridge is a training-free latent communication method for LLM multi-agent systems that aligns sender hidden states to the receiver's input space using a closed-form orthogonal transformation, with norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring. It outperforms baselines on 22/26 model-task pairs.
AI.motivation: Text-based multi-agent communication suffers from a discrete bottleneck: converting continuous hidden states into tokens discards information. Existing latent communication methods either inject working memory layer-by-layer across transformers or rely on trained projectors, limiting portability. The paper aims to provide a training-free, portable latent communication approach.
AI.method: StateBridge aligns the sender's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input space via a closed-form orthogonal transformation (training-free). Lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring ensure compatibility with the pretrained input distribution. The aligned states are prepended to the receiver's input as a continuous prefix.
AI.result: Evaluated on math reasoning, code generation, and question answering using four models from two families, StateBridge achieves the best or tied-best score on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: StateBridge demonstrates that training-free, projection-free latent communication can transfer continuous information between LLM agents effectively, offering a portable alternative that avoids the discrete text bottleneck and outperforms existing latent methods.

title: DFM Mimir v1: An Open HRM Delivering Frontier Performance at 1B Parameters Using Only Permissible Post-Training Data
comment: Technical Report, 20 Pages, 1 Model, Hierarchical Reasoning Model
summary: Current large language model development relies on massive, often non-permissible datasets, creating a high barrier for researchers committed to open-source and ethically sourced data. We introduce Mimir v1, a 1-billion-parameter language model based on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) architecture, that is trained from scratch and delivers highly competitive performance for English and sets a new state of the art for Danish using only permissible post-training data. Trained on a mixture of 161 datasets, Mimir v1 outperforms the original HRM-Text 1B and competes with larger frontier models like Qwen 3.5 4B and Gemma 4 E2B, tested across 20 benchmarks for English, Math & Code and Danish. The model is available on the Hugging Face Hub: https://huggingface.co/danish-foundation-models/DFM-Mimir

AI.tldr: Mimir v1 is a 1B-parameter, from-scratch language model built on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) architecture. Trained exclusively on permissible post-training data (161 datasets), it achieves highly competitive English performance and state-of-the-art Danish results, outperforming HRM-Text 1B and competing with larger frontier models across 20 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM development relies on massive, often non-permissible datasets, which creates a high barrier for researchers committed to open-source and ethically sourced data. The work aims to demonstrate that competitive performance can be achieved using only permissible data.
AI.method: Mimir v1 is a 1-billion-parameter language model based on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) architecture, trained from scratch on a mixture of 161 permissible post-training datasets. It was evaluated across 20 benchmarks covering English, Math & Code, and Danish.
AI.result: Mimir v1 outperforms the original HRM-Text 1B model and competes with larger frontier models such as Qwen 3.5 4B and Gemma 4 E2B. It delivers highly competitive performance for English and sets a new state of the art for Danish.
AI.conclusion: A 1B-parameter model trained from scratch on permissible post-training data can deliver strong, competitive performance, including state-of-the-art Danish results, lowering the barrier for open-source and ethically sourced research. The model is publicly available on the Hugging Face Hub.

title: LLM-Guided Graph Generation for Structure-Based Local Improvement Methods
summary: Large neighborhood search normally selects a random subset of decision variables for iterative optimization. For efficiently solving different problems, researchers tend to design variable selection strategies by taking into account structural features from different domains. In this paper, we build an automatic pipeline that is problem-agnostic to all problems in the MiniZinc format. By prompting an LLM with our semantic guidelines, we guide the LLM to produce a graph generator that maps any instance of a problem type to a uniform weighted graph, where nodes represent decision variables and edges represent constraint relationships. These problem-agnostic graphs guide our structure-based local improvement framework (SLIM) in variable selection. Meanwhile, the weighted graph enables all problem instances to share the same generic graph representation, from which the same graph features can be extracted and used for configuration selection. We evaluated our pipeline on instances across 20 MiniZinc competition problems, finding that algorithm selection achieves a 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against a one-shot Gurobi baseline, more than doubling the best single configuration (19.3%). Configuration and feature ablation boost the performance further to 44.0%, demonstrating that LLM-based semantic generation enables effective automated structure extraction and feature extraction for constraint optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper automates structure extraction for MiniZinc constraint optimization problems by prompting an LLM to generate a graph generator mapping instances to weighted variable-dependency graphs, enabling structure-based variable selection and algorithm configuration selection, achieving a 39.5% problem-weighted win rate against Gurobi.
AI.motivation: Existing large neighborhood search variable selection strategies rely on hand-designed, domain-specific structural features, limiting generality. The authors aim to build an automatic, problem-agnostic pipeline that works across all MiniZinc-format problems without manual per-domain engineering.
AI.method: An LLM is prompted with semantic guidelines to produce a graph generator that maps any problem instance to a uniform weighted graph, with nodes as decision variables and edges as constraint relationships. This yields a structure-based local improvement framework (SLIM) for variable selection, plus a shared generic graph representation from which graph features are extracted for configuration (algorithm) selection.
AI.result: Across 20 MiniZinc competition problems, algorithm selection achieves a 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against a one-shot Gurobi baseline, more than doubling the best single configuration (19.3%). Configuration and feature ablation further improves performance to 44.0%.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based semantic generation enables effective automated structure and feature extraction for constraint optimization, showing strong generality and performance improvements over single-configuration and baseline solvers.

title: SAEVerbalizer: Generating Explanations for Sparse Autoencoder Features via Representation Verbalization
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are proposed to extract numerous features from large language model (LLM) representations, yet explaining these features still relies primarily on external observation. This reliance leads to superficial explanations inferred from observed model behavior and computational inefficiency from collecting such behavioral evidence at scale. We introduce SAEVerbalizer, a framework that injects SAE decoder directions into an LLM's representations and fine-tunes the LLM's downstream layers to generate natural-language explanations of the injected features. Once trained, the resulting verbalizer explains SAE features directly from decoder directions, addressing both limitations. Our experiments show that the learned verbalization capability generalizes to unseen features, transfers across separately trained SAE dictionaries, and, with a lightweight adapter, extends to SAE features from different LLMs. Intervention experiments show that injecting multiple directions yields an explanation combining their meanings, while reversing individual directions produces corresponding meaning shifts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SAEVerbalizer, a framework that turns sparse autoencoder (SAE) decoder directions into natural-language explanations by injecting them into an LLM and fine-tuning downstream layers, overcoming the need for external behavioral evidence.
AI.motivation: SAEs extract many features from LLM representations, but existing methods for explaining these features rely on passive external observation of model behavior. This yields superficial interpretations and is computationally inefficient when collecting behavioral evidence at scale.
AI.method: SAEVerbalizer injects SAE decoder directions into an LLM's representations and fine-tunes the downstream layers to generate natural-language explanations of the injected features. Once trained, it verbalizes features directly from the decoder directions. The approach is augmented with a lightweight adapter for cross-model transfer.
AI.result: The learned verbalization capability generalizes to unseen features, transfers across separately trained SAE dictionaries, and extends to SAE features from different LLMs via a lightweight adapter. Intervention experiments show that injecting multiple directions produces combined explanations, and reversing individual directions yields corresponding shifts in meaning.
AI.conclusion: SAEVerbalizer directly explains SAE features from decoder directions, addressing the limitations of superficial, behavior-based explanations and improving computational efficiency, while demonstrating strong generalization, transfer, and interpretability through direction manipulation.

title: Large-scale Testing Global Optimization Methods with Black-box Adversarial Attacks
summary: Existing global optimization benchmark suites are of a moderate size and are based on a small number of analytical functions that date back even to the 1970s. This causes a risk of biasing the development of global optimization methods. We argue that the tasks related to the black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) can serve as valuable global optimization benchmark in many-dimensional space. We demonstrate the efficiency of several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics in solving example BBAA problems. Thus, we take a step towards convergence of global optimization methods to the challenges and needs that arise in the modern machine learning field.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) problems can serve as modern, high-dimensional benchmarks for global optimization, and demonstrates that evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics perform well on such tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing global optimization benchmark suites are moderate in size and rely on a small set of analytical functions dating back to the 1970s, which risks biasing the development of optimization methods. There is a need for benchmarks aligned with modern machine learning challenges.
AI.method: The authors propose using black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) tasks as many-dimensional global optimization benchmarks and evaluate the efficiency of several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics on example BBAA problems.
AI.result: Various evolutionary algorithms and metaheuristics are shown to be efficient in solving the example BBAA problems, indicating their suitability for this modern benchmark context.
AI.conclusion: BBAA provides a valuable benchmark domain that brings global optimization research closer to the challenges and needs of modern machine learning, reducing reliance on outdated benchmark suites.

title: LongEarth-R1: Benchmarking and Aligning Vision-Language Models for Long-Horizon Earth Observation Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon Earth observation reasoning requires models to organize multi-stage geographic evolution, localize spatial changes, detect temporal anomalies, and infer future from extended image sequences. However, existing remote sensing vision-language models mainly focus on isolated images, image pairs, or short sequences, limiting reliable grounding in the relevant frames and regions. We introduce LongEarth-Bench, a benchmark containing approximately 120k question-answering samples derived from 117k unique images. Its sequences average 15.14 frames and extend to 30 frames, covering 12 tasks across evolution summarization, spatial reasoning, anomaly identification, and logical prediction. A 30k-sample subset further provides structured reasoning traces linking key frames and changed regions to final answers. We develop LongEarth through supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision. Building on LongEarth, LongEarth-R1 applies group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards. LongEarth-R1 achieves the best results on all 12 long-sequence tasks while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LongEarth-Bench (a ~120k QA benchmark from 117k images with 15.14-frame average sequences extending to 30 frames covering 12 long-horizon Earth observation tasks), LongEarth (an SFT model with sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought), and LongEarth-R1 (which applies group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards), achieving best results on all 12 tasks while staying competitive on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing vision-language models focus on isolated images, image pairs, or short sequences, limiting reliable grounding in relevant frames and regions for long-horizon Earth observation reasoning—which requires organizing multi-stage geographic evolution, localizing spatial changes, detecting temporal anomalies, and predicting the future from extended image sequences.
AI.method: The authors build LongEarth-Bench with ~120k QA samples from 117k unique images (average 15.14 frames, up to 30 frames) spanning 12 tasks across evolution summarization, spatial reasoning, anomaly identification, and logical prediction; a 30k subset provides structured reasoning traces linking key frames and changed regions to answers. They train LongEarth via supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision, then develop LongEarth-R1 using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with format, temporal, and spatial rewards.
AI.result: LongEarth-R1 achieves the best results on all 12 long-sequence tasks while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and models enable reliable long-horizon Earth observation reasoning, with LongEarth-R1 setting state-of-the-art performance across all long-sequence tasks while preserving strong performance on standard benchmarks.

title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure
summary: Modern language models are trained on heterogeneous web-scale text corpora. Consequently, studying knowledge and skill acquisition is difficult, as prior exposure to related content is hard to characterize. To address this challenge, we introduce LITTLECURRICULUM, a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material, explicitly excluding concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5. Training a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on LITTLECURRICULUM yields LITTLELEARNER, a model with sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation, yet with clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to interpretable curriculum guidelines. We release LITTLECURRICULUM and LITTLELEARNER as a developmentally restricted sandbox to study how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope. We illustrate the sandbox's utility in a first suite of experiments on injecting new knowledge through post-training and in-context learning. These methods let LITTLELEARNER better utilize existing knowledge, but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities. Our findings underscore the value of this controlled environment for future investigations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LITTLECURRICULUM, an 88B-token pretraining corpus restricted to U.S. elementary school (≤ Grade 5) content, used to train LITTLELEARNER (a 5B-parameter LLM) from scratch, creating a controlled sandbox with interpretable knowledge boundaries for studying model learning.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs are trained on heterogeneous web-scale corpora, making it hard to characterize prior exposure to related content and thus difficult to study knowledge/skill acquisition in a controlled way.
AI.method: Curate LITTLECURRICULUM, an 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material that explicitly excludes concepts, facts, and vocabulary above Grade 5; train a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on it to produce LITTLELEARNER; evaluate knowledge injection via post-training and in-context learning experiments.
AI.result: LITTLELEARNER has sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation while exhibiting clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to curriculum guidelines. Post-training and in-context learning improve utilization of existing knowledge but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The controlled environment provided by LITTLECURRICULUM and LITTLELEARNER is valuable for studying how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope, supporting future investigations.

title: The Time Value of Evolution
comment: Submitted to AAAI 2026, 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables
summary: In evolutionary search, a weak child can be a valuable ancestor that makes high-fitness regions reachable. Immediate-return control is blind to this delayed utility, penalizing mutations through their immediate offspring even when they open productive future lineages. We formalize this hidden dynamic as the time value of evolution within a finite-horizon Markov decision process. To exploit it, we introduce Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG), a long-horizon actor-critic framework for automated trading policy discovery. Our architecture decouples search control into specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone: a bootstrapped critic head estimates the value of finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, while an actor head dynamically modulates mutation intensity over the remaining search budget. We isolate the impact of long-horizon credit assignment against immediate-return optimization across 90 paired runs under matched operators, lineage supervision, folds, seeds, and budgets. Path-based credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, increasing validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units. LVPG also produces fewer temporary regressions than immediate-return optimization and recovers from them more often. Finite-horizon lineage value yields more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies within identical resource constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG), a long-horizon actor-critic framework that credits mutations for their delayed, multi-generational value rather than only their immediate offspring, and shows it accelerates finite-budget evolutionary search for trading policies.
AI.motivation: Immediate-return control in evolutionary search penalizes mutations based on their direct offspring's fitness, ignoring that a weak child can still open productive future lineages. The authors formalize this overlooked delayed utility as the time value of evolution and aim to exploit it through long-horizon credit assignment.
AI.method: They model the problem as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and design LVPG, which decouples search control into specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone: a bootstrapped critic head estimates finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, while an actor head dynamically modulates mutation intensity over the remaining search budget. Evaluation uses 90 paired runs with matched operators, lineage supervision, folds, seeds, and budgets to isolate long-horizon credit assignment against immediate-return optimization.
AI.result: Path-based credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, improving validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units. LVPG produces fewer temporary regressions than immediate-return optimization and recovers from them more often. Finite-horizon lineage value yields more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies under identical resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for the finite-horizon value of lineage (delayed utility across generations) rather than immediate offspring fitness enables more selective, non-monotonic evolutionary search that discovers stronger policies with fewer and more recoverable regressions under the same resource budget.

title: Rules or Character? Scaling Laws for AI Safety Design
comment: Accepted at AIES 2026 (9th AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society). 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) safety systems combine character shaping (e.g., Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback [RLHF], Constitutional AI), which modifies behavioral distributions at training time, with rule enforcement (e.g., output filters, safety classifiers), which blocks harmful outputs at inference time, yet little formal analysis exists on how their optimal balance should change as deployment scales increase. We introduce a stylized comparative-statics model that parameterizes safety design as a resource allocation alpha in [0,1] between these two approaches, incorporating scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and character fragility -- the risk that shaped behavior degrades or collapses under novel conditions. Under a multiplicative Pareto damage model, we derive closed-form expected harm and supplement it with tail-risk (CVaR) analysis via Monte Carlo simulation. Across three scenarios (optimistic, moderate, pessimistic), the optimal alpha* is interior or at the rules-only boundary and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows, from negligible (Delta alpha* = +0.01) to pronounced (Delta alpha* = +0.21) depending on scenario. The dominant parameter is the baseline character fragility rate p^(0)_frag, which shifts alpha* by 0.50 across its range -- far exceeding the effect of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large T. These results suggest that safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale per se than on the reliability of character shaping under distributional shift.

AI.tldr: A comparative-statics model shows the optimal allocation between AI character shaping and rule enforcement depends mainly on character-shaping reliability under distributional shift, not deployment scale.
AI.motivation: AI safety systems combine training-time character shaping (e.g., RLHF, Constitutional AI) with inference-time rule enforcement (e.g., output filters, safety classifiers), but little formal analysis exists on how their optimal balance should change as deployment scale increases.
AI.method: Introduces a stylized comparative-statics model parameterizing safety design as a resource allocation α ∈ [0,1] between character shaping and rule enforcement, incorporating scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and character fragility. Uses a multiplicative Pareto damage model to derive closed-form expected harm, supplemented with tail-risk (CVaR) analysis via Monte Carlo simulation across optimistic, moderate, and pessimistic scenarios.
AI.result: The optimal α* is interior or at the rules-only boundary and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows (Δα* from +0.01 to +0.21 by scenario). The dominant parameter is baseline character fragility rate p^(0)_frag, shifting α* by 0.50 across its range, far exceeding effects of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large T.
AI.conclusion: Safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale per se than on the reliability of character shaping under distributional shift, suggesting efforts should focus on robustness of character shaping rather than scale-dependent rebalancing.

title: A Probe Direction Is a Property of Its Prompt
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 13 appendices. Code, data manifests and results: https://github.com/vcnoel/probe-direction
summary: A model that behaves differently when it senses it is being tested would undermine the evaluations we rely on, so recent work has sought to read that sense directly from a model's activations. The standard instrument contrasts activations on prompts that announce an evaluation against prompts that do not, and reports how well the resulting direction separates held-out cases. That number is then compared across models and correlated with scale. We observe that the instrument has a free parameter its readings do not disclose: "a prompt that announces an evaluation" is not a prompt but a choice among many, and nothing in the method fixes which. Holding the task text fixed and varying only that choice, we find that the reported score, and even the direction in which it trends with model size, follows the prompt rather than the model; two published studies that disagree about the sign of that trend are both reproducible from a single design, by choice of prompt alone. Treating the prompt as a facet of a measurement design rather than an implementation detail, we find the model under study accounts for a small share of the variance in the number reported about it, and most of the rest lies in how each model responds to each prompt: collecting more evaluation items cannot repair the measurement, while varying prompts can. A further check finds that the split these probes are scored on is largely separable from surface form alone, so a direction carrying no information about evaluation at all still reproduces a substantial fraction of each published score. We conclude that a single-prompt design cannot support comparison between models, and we give the number of prompts a defensible comparison requires.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques the standard method for measuring a model's "situational awareness" of being evaluated, showing that choosing just one "evaluation-announcing" prompt makes results arbitrary: reported scores and even their sign versus model scale depend on prompt choice, not the model, and most measured variance comes from model–prompt interaction rather than the model itself.
AI.motivation: Recent work reads a model's sense of being tested from activations via a contrast between prompts that announce evaluation and prompts that do not. Because that contrast instrument has an undisclosed free parameter—which specific prompt is used—the resulting single number may not actually characterize the model, undermining cross-model comparisons and scale correlations.
AI.method: They hold task text fixed and vary only the choice of the "evaluation-announcing" prompt, then measure how reported scores and their trend with model size change. They model the measurement using variance decomposition (treating prompt as a design facet), test surface-form separability by constructing directions carrying no evaluation information, and compute how many prompts a defensible comparison requires.
AI.result: The reported score and the direction of its scale trend follow the prompt rather than the model; two published studies with opposite signs are both reproducible from one design by prompt choice alone. Model identity accounts for only a small share of variance, with most lying in model–prompt interaction. Adding evaluation items does not fix the measurement, while varying prompts does. Surface form alone explains a substantial fraction of each published score.
AI.conclusion: A single-prompt design cannot support comparison between models, and the paper specifies the number of prompts required for a defensible comparison.

title: Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research
summary: The replicability of papers is a cornerstone of scientific knowledge, ensuring the reliability of existing results and providing a base for further experiments. The act of replication typically illuminates details that were previously underspecified, and thus requires similar hypothesis-driven exploration to open-ended research. In this work, we develop Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication. To provide reward signal, we introduce an auto-generated rubric-based judge that has low noise and agrees with human assessment of replication quality. We post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter "AI Scientist" agent that leverages coding agents as tools, surpassing the performance of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis of individual rollouts reveals that Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach. We believe that our results provide a stepping stone towards AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without requiring complex harnesses.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication, an auto-generated rubric-based judge for rewards, and Faraday, a 27B-parameter AI Scientist agent that outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks.
AI.motivation: Paper replicability is a cornerstone of scientific knowledge, but replication is open-ended and hypothesis-driven, illuminating underspecified details. The authors aim to build AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without complex harnesses, using replication as a stepping stone.
AI.method: Develop Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication. Introduce an auto-generated rubric-based judge that provides low-noise reward signals agreeing with human assessment of replication quality. Post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter AI Scientist agent that uses coding agents as tools.
AI.result: Faraday surpasses the performance of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis of rollouts shows Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a stepping stone toward AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without requiring complex harnesses.

title: Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model
summary: Existing predictive models in learning analytics often treat student academic history as a simple sequence, overlooking the concurrent nature of courses taken within a semester. This simplification can lead to inaccurate performance predictions, particularly for students with heavy or challenging course loads. This paper introduces a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation (TRACE) that addresses this limitation by jointly predicting both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for an upcoming semester. Our approach encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture the effects of course concurrency and utilizes a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction. We demonstrate that predicting courses taken in addition to the grades in those courses leads to significant improvements in prediction quality. Trained on ten years of institutional data, our joint prediction model reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture that predicts grades alone. The model also outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models, as well as graph neural network-based approaches, and offers natural ways to incorporate student attribute data. This work demonstrates the utility of modern neural architectures for creating interpretable models that can be adapted to new institutions via retraining and recalibration, as well as the importance of key techniques, such as predicting courses taken during training. We discuss how this model could be incorporated into early detection systems at institutions of higher education.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a Transformer-based model that jointly predicts the set of courses and the grades a student will receive next semester, capturing concurrent course loads rather than treating academic history as a simple sequence. Joint prediction nearly halves grade prediction error compared to a grade-only architecture and outperforms LSTM and GNN baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-analytics predictive models treat a student's academic history as a simple sequence, ignoring that multiple courses are taken concurrently within a semester. This simplification causes inaccurate grade predictions, especially for students with heavy or difficult course loads. The authors aim to address this limitation by explicitly modeling course concurrency and the co-prediction of course selection and grades.
AI.method: The paper proposes TRACE (TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation), which encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture concurrency effects. It uses a novel loss function that combines course-set prediction with grade prediction, allowing the model to jointly estimate both which courses a student will take and their grades in an upcoming semester. The model was trained on ten years of institutional data and can incorporate student attribute data. It is compared against a grade-only version of the same architecture, LSTM-based sequential models, and graph neural network approaches.
AI.result: Jointly predicting course enrollment alongside grades reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture predicting grades alone. TRACE also outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models and graph neural network-based methods, and naturally accommodates student attribute data.
AI.conclusion: Modern neural architectures such as Transformers are effective for interpretable student performance prediction when they model course concurrency and jointly predict course selection. Key techniques, notably predicting courses taken during training, substantially improve accuracy. The model can be adapted to new institutions through retraining and recalibration and is suitable for integration into early detection systems in higher education.

title: Neural Quadratic Forms: A Unified Minimal Model for Sudden Learning and Scaling Laws
summary: Neural networks trained by gradient descent on a smooth cost function can nevertheless learn in steps: the cost holds on long plateaus and then drops abruptly. Meanwhile, training losses instead follow smooth power laws. Variants of both behaviors occur in architectures with very different microscopic structures, which is the signature of a few relevant collective variables. We show that a symmetry fixes what those variables are: a network layer is a sum over interchangeable units, so relabeling the units leaves it unchanged; given smoothness and the condition that a unit's gradient vanish at the origin, symmetry then enforces a universal leading form for the expansion about the near-zero weights present at the start of training, the quadratic $\Tr[WW^{\top}A(x)]$, in which every architectural detail is confined to a single ``structure matrix" $A(x)$ that we compute for each architecture. Perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, and convolutions become one model at different $A$. Its training dynamics then close on the ``order parameter" $M=WW^{\top}$ and, whenever the data matrices share an eigenbasis, reduce to a Lotka--Volterra equation whose modes switch on one after another. The smaller the initial weights, the further apart the switch-on times, and the plateaus appear as a singular limit of a smooth flow; when many modes are unresolved the same events merge into a power law in training time whose exponent the theory predicts. We confirm both numerically across training methods and architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that despite smooth loss functions, neural networks trained by gradient descent can learn in discrete steps (long plateaus followed by abrupt drops). A symmetry argument (permutation of interchangeable units in a layer) fixes the universal leading-order form of the dynamics — a quadratic involving a per-architecture "structure matrix" — reducing training dynamics to a Lotka–Volterra equation on an order parameter, which explains both stepwise learning and power-law training curves.
AI.motivation: Neural networks trained with gradient descent exhibit two seemingly contradictory empirical behaviors: abrupt, stepwise drops in test/performance cost versus smooth power-law decay of training loss. These behaviors recur across architectures with very different microscopic details, suggesting a description in terms of a few relevant collective variables. The paper aims to identify those collective variables and unify stepwise and smooth learning within a single theory.
AI.method: The authors exploit the permutation symmetry of a layer (a sum over interchangeable units, invariant under relabeling). Assuming smoothness and that each unit's gradient vanishes at the origin, symmetry forces the cost's leading expansion near the small initial weights to be the quadratic Tr[WW^T A(x)], where all architecture-specific detail is confined to a computable "structure matrix" A(x). This unifies perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, and convolutions as one model with different A. The training dynamics close on the order parameter M = WW^T and, when data matrices share an eigenbasis, reduce to a Lotka–Volterra system whose modes activate sequentially. Plateaus emerge as a singular limit of this smooth flow as initial weights shrink, while unresolved modes merge into a power law in training time whose exponent the theory predicts. Predictions are verified numerically across training methods and architectures.
AI.result: The theory predicts that the smaller the initial weights, the further apart the mode switch-on times, yielding plateaus as a singular limit of a smooth flow; when many modes are unresolved, these events merge into a power law in training time with a predicted exponent. Both stepwise plateaus and smooth power-law training curves are confirmed numerically across multiple training methods and architectures (perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, convolutions).
AI.conclusion: A symmetry-based (permutation invariance) argument identifies the universal leading-order form of cost dynamics near initialization, collapsing disparate architectures into a single model characterized by a structure matrix A(x). The resulting Lotka–Volterra reduction explains both abrupt stepwise learning and smooth power-law losses as aspects of one underlying flow, unifying previously separate observations.

title: Who Speaks Matters: Authority-Aware Multi-View RAG over Italian Parliamentary Proceedings
comment: Accepted at ISWC 2026 In-Use Track. Please cite the ISWC version
summary: Parliamentary proceedings are a primary record of democratic deliberation, yet their volume and fragmentation make multi-perspective access difficult for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to parliamentary transcripts introduces three specific risks: dominance of the most frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers according to topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text. We present ParliamentRAG, a RAG system for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that addresses these risks jointly. Its core contribution is a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority as a function of the current query, combining interpretable components such as profession, education, and previous interventions. Given a user query, the system retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a summary synthesizing their perspectives, accompanied by supporting quotations. ParliamentRAG is evaluated against Google NotebookLM on 15 policy topics via a two-level protocol combining automated metrics and blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts. The system achieves higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose-oriented dimensions.

AI.tldr: ParliamentRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation system for Italian parliamentary transcripts that uses topic-dependent speaker authority weighting to produce multi-perspective summaries with faithful citations, outperforming Google NotebookLM on coverage, citation faithfulness, and source-related expert preferences.
AI.motivation: Parliamentary proceedings form the primary record of democratic deliberation, but their volume and fragmentation hinder multi-perspective access for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Applying RAG to parliamentary transcripts introduces three specific risks: dominance of the most frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers by topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text. The paper seeks a system that jointly mitigates these risks.
AI.method: ParliamentRAG proposes a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority as a function of the current query, combining interpretable components such as profession, education, and previous interventions. Given a user query, it retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a summary synthesizing their perspectives with supporting quotations. Evaluation uses a two-level protocol on 15 policy topics combining automated metrics and blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts, benchmarked against Google NotebookLM.
AI.result: ParliamentRAG achieves higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose-oriented dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The topic-dependent authority model effectively addresses the three identified RAG risks for parliamentary transcripts, yielding balanced multi-perspective coverage and fully faithful citations, though prose quality remains a relative weakness compared to NotebookLM.

title: Where You Measure Decides What You Measure: Position Selection in Ablation-Based SAE Evaluation
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/vcnoel/sae-artifact
summary: Sparse autoencoders are meant to name the things a language model computes, and the usual way to check that a latent matters is to switch it off and see what changes. But a latent fires at many tokens, and the effect has to be measured at one of them. The convention is to measure where the latent fires hardest. That choice is almost never reported, and it is not made by the experimenter: it is made by the dictionary under evaluation. Change the dictionary and the measurement moves to a different token. We show this is not a detail. Take two sparse autoencoders released by Google for the same model and match their latents by decoder similarity: even among the pairs the two dictionaries encode almost identically, they pick different tokens for a large share of them. Two dictionaries compared under the usual protocol are therefore very often compared at different places. To separate the convention from the dictionaries we train six autoencoders from one initialisation, differing only in fitting choices, so that a latent means the same thing in each. Most of the variance such a comparison reads as "these dictionaries disagree about this latent" turns out to be the position instead: it falls from 7.6% and 11.9% of variance to near zero once every dictionary is measured at the same token. More evaluation data does not rescue it. Across a sixteenfold range of corpus sizes the dictionaries agree less about where to measure, not more, so the problem grows with scale. The correction is one line of evaluation code. We give the protocol an ablation-based causal number must report to be comparable across papers, and an audit of five published papers against it. In short: a causal number reported without its position describes the token it was taken at as much as the latent it was taken from.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the convention of measuring a sparse autoencoder latent's causal effect at the token where it fires hardest is dictionary-dependent, making cross-dictionary comparisons misleading; the authors propose a one-line evaluation correction and audit prior work against it.
AI.motivation: Sparse autoencoders aim to name what a language model computes, and the standard way to verify a latent's importance is ablating it and measuring the effect. However, the measurement position (where the latent fires hardest) is chosen by the dictionary under evaluation, not the experimenter, so different dictionaries effectively measure effects at different tokens. This threatens the validity of comparing dictionaries or interpreting causal effect sizes.
AI.method: The authors (1) take two Google-released sparse autoencoders for the same model, match latents by decoder similarity, and check whether matched pairs select the same measurement token; (2) train six autoencoders from one initialization differing only in fitting choices so latents mean the same thing across dictionaries; (3) decompose variance in latent "agreement" into position-dependent vs. dictionary-dependent components; (4) sweep a sixteenfold range of evaluation corpus sizes; and (5) propose a reporting protocol requiring an ablation-based causal number to include its measurement position, then audit five published papers.
AI.result: Even among latent pairs with nearly identical decoders, the two dictionaries pick different measurement tokens for a large share. Across the six same-initialization autoencoders, variance read as dictionary disagreement falls from 7.6% and 11.9% to near zero once all dictionaries are measured at the same token, showing most disagreement is positional. More evaluation data does not help: across a sixteenfold range of corpus sizes, dictionaries agree less about where to measure, so the problem grows with scale.
AI.conclusion: A causal/ablation number reported without its measurement position describes the token it was taken at as much as the latent it was taken from. The measurement-position convention must be made explicit and shared across dictionaries for comparisons to be meaningful, which can be fixed with a one-line change to evaluation code.

title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of improving models, systems, and other technical artifacts through long-horizon experimentation. To understand the current state of this capability, however, evaluation must go beyond final scores, which neither reveal where progress is gained or lost nor indicate whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. We therefore present a systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks based on a new framework that uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior through Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control and controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse within and across tasks. The results show that current agents operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but their performance varies substantially across runs, their strongest solutions mainly adapt or combine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty remains rare. Detailed analysis reveals that observed performance is shaped by multiple factors, including distinct process bottlenecks behind similar final outcomes, experience reuse that can help or mislead subsequent decisions, and harness designs that affect performance stability. These findings suggest concrete directions for improving model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon autonomous experimentation tasks, introducing a framework that characterizes within-run behavior (Solution Framing, Execution, Feedback Control) and measures experience reuse. It finds current agents behave more like engineering optimizers than autonomous researchers: they implement solutions but vary across runs, mostly adapt established techniques, and rarely produce genuine methodological novelty.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluations of autonomous agents rely on final scores, which fail to reveal where progress is gained or lost during long-horizon experimentation, and do not indicate whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. The authors aim to move beyond aggregate outcomes to understand how agents actually behave and learn within and across runs.
AI.method: The authors present a systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks. The framework uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior across three dimensions—Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control—and uses controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse both within and across tasks.
AI.result: Current agents operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but performance varies substantially across runs, their strongest solutions mainly adapt or combine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty remains rare. Analysis also reveals distinct process bottlenecks behind similar final outcomes, experience reuse that can help or mislead subsequent decisions, and harness designs that affect performance stability.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest concrete directions for improving model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design, indicating that evaluation should capture process-level behavior and experience reuse rather than final scores alone.

title: Simulation-to-real transfer learning for infrared spectroscopic chemical sensing and analysis from molecules to complex samples
summary: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is widely used for chemical sensing, but extracting reliable chemical information from spectra remains challenging. Conventional interpretation is labor-intensive, relies on prior knowledge and reference spectra, and is difficult to scale, whereas most machine-learning methods are tailored to individual tasks or datasets, require large labeled training sets, and transfer poorly across analytical objectives and experimental datasets. Here we introduce UltraIR, a foundation model for IR spectroscopy with more than 100 million parameters that enables simulation-to-real transfer learning for chemical sensing and analysis from molecules to complex samples. UltraIR is pretrained on approximately 60 million simulated IR spectra using spectral reconstruction, molecular fingerprint similarity alignment, and functional-group prediction, then adapted to downstream objectives with task-specific labels or targets. Across functional-group prediction, molecular structure elucidation, physicochemical property prediction, mixture-component identification and quantification, bacterial classification, medicinal-herb geographic origin traceability and constituent quantification, microplastics classification, and soil property prediction, UltraIR outperforms conventional machine-learning and task-specific deep-learning baselines. It performs strongly with limited labeled experimental spectra and in zero-shot inference for the same analytical task across Fourier-transform infrared spectrometers and laboratories, providing a route to adaptable, data-efficient chemical sensing from complex real-world samples.

AI.tldr: UltraIR is a >100M-parameter foundation model for infrared spectroscopy, pretrained on ~60M simulated spectra, that transfers to diverse chemical-sensing tasks and beats conventional ML and task-specific deep-learning baselines, including under low-data and zero-shot cross-instrument settings.
AI.motivation: IR spectroscopy is widely used but extracting reliable chemical information is hard: manual interpretation is slow and knowledge-dependent, while current ML approaches are task/dataset-specific, data-hungry, and generalize poorly across objectives and instruments. A general, transferable model is needed.
AI.method: UltraIR is a foundation model with >100M parameters pretrained on ~60M simulated IR spectra using three objectives: spectral reconstruction, molecular fingerprint similarity alignment, and functional-group prediction. It is then adapted to downstream tasks with task-specific labels/targets, enabling simulation-to-real transfer across molecules and complex samples.
AI.result: UltraIR outperforms conventional ML and task-specific deep-learning baselines across functional-group prediction, molecular structure elucidation, physicochemical property prediction, mixture identification/quantification, bacterial classification, medicinal-herb origin traceability and quantification, microplastics classification, and soil property prediction. It performs strongly with limited labeled experimental spectra and in zero-shot inference across FTIR spectrometers and laboratories.
AI.conclusion: UltraIR provides a route to adaptable, data-efficient chemical sensing from complex real-world samples, enabling simulation-to-real transfer and strong cross-instrument/laboratory zero-shot generalization for IR spectroscopy.

title: Enhancing Virtual Agents through SLMs and Edge-Computing: An Exploratory Evaluation of Think and Memory Processes
summary: Embodied intelligent virtual agents are expected to operate as persistent, adaptive, and context-aware entities within complex virtual and Metaverse worlds. However, implementing cognitively capable agents in such environments is conceptually and technologically challenging. Among a range of blueprints and development approaches, the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) has been developed as an implementation-oriented framework for architecting components of perception, memory, reasoning, planning, and embodied action. Considering the recent advances in edge computing and generative AI language models, this paper explores the use of Small Language Models (SLMs) to support edge-based operation of selected CEAA components, focusing on "Think" and "Memory" as processes central to cognitive orchestration and persistence of virtual agents in interactive virtual worlds. An edge-based virtual agent gateway system was developed and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX using Qwen2.5 models of different sizes, exploring the system's capability to process service requests and handle memory-driven conversations. A series of simulation experiments evaluated routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, demonstrating an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes to support the development of embodied agents whose cognitive "brain" can operate efficiently and contextually for interactive experiences in immersive virtual worlds.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates an edge-based virtual agent gateway using Small Language Models (Qwen2.5 on NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX) to implement selected CEAA "Think" and "Memory" processes, measuring routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency.
AI.motivation: Embodied intelligent virtual agents need to act as persistent, adaptive, context-aware entities in complex virtual/Metaverse worlds, but implementing cognitively capable agents is conceptually and technologically challenging. Edge computing and generative AI advances create an opportunity to run cognitive components efficiently on-device.
AI.method: Uses the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) implementation framework, focusing on "Think" and "Memory" processes. Deploys an edge-based virtual agent gateway system on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX using Qwen2.5 Small Language Models of varying sizes, and runs simulation experiments.
AI.result: Experiments evaluated routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, demonstrating an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes.
AI.conclusion: SLMs can feasibly support edge-based operation of key CEAA cognitive components, enabling embodied agents whose cognitive "brain" operates efficiently and contextually for interactive immersive virtual world experiences.

title: When Local Variance Optimality Is Not Enough: RoPE-Aligned Q/K Rotations for Dynamic 4-Bit Quantisation
summary: Rotation-based post-training quantisation commonly applies an orthogonal transform across an entire attention head to reduce outlier-induced error. RoPE instead partitions each head into two-dimensional frequency pairs, raising the question of whether a transform respecting this decomposition can improve on full-head mixing. Prior work has established the per-pair rotations that commute with RoPE. We state the converse result that, for distinct frequencies, no other single-head orthogonal map commutes with RoPE. For the head-shared parameterisation used in our experiments, we then derive the rotation angle that minimises the larger channel variance under a pooled-covariance, position-averaged surrogate and verify that the implementation attains its analytic minimum. The evaluated head-shared pairwise configuration does not improve accuracy in the tested dynamic W4A4KV4 setting. Across four checkpoints, replacing the full-head Hadamard with this configuration increases perplexity at both short and long context lengths. Composing the pairwise rotation with the Hadamard satisfies the selected $\pm0.05$-PPL interval criterion under the default estimator. Estimating the shared angle from K alone improves pairwise-only on every checkpoint but does not close its gap to full-head mixing. The analytic objective controls a position-averaged second moment of a pooled calibration covariance, whereas the dynamic quantiser sets its step from a tokenwise group range. The pairwise transform also has only two-channel mixing support. Along a controlled interpolation from two-channel to full-head mixing, K range, relative quantisation error, and perplexity degradation decrease as support increases. These results show that optimality for a structured surrogate need not reduce quantisation error when the surrogate and mixing support are misaligned with the quantiser's scale-setting statistic.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether a rotation respecting RoPE's two-dimensional frequency-pair decomposition can outperform standard full-head orthogonal transforms in post-training quantisation. It proves a converse uniqueness result, derives an optimal shared rotation angle under a pooled-covariance surrogate, and shows empirically that the pairwise configuration degrades accuracy relative to full-head Hadamard mixing, attributing the failure to misalignment between the analytic surrogate, limited mixing support, and the quantiser's tokenwise scale-setting statistic.
AI.motivation: Rotation-based post-training quantisation typically applies an orthogonal transform across an entire attention head to reduce outlier-induced error, whereas RoPE partitions each head into two-dimensional frequency pairs. The paper asks whether a transform respecting this RoPE decomposition can improve on full-head mixing.
AI.method: The authors state the converse result that, for distinct frequencies, no other single-head orthogonal map commutes with RoPE beyond the known per-pair rotations. They derive the rotation angle minimising the larger channel variance under a pooled-covariance, position-averaged surrogate for a head-shared parameterisation. Experiments evaluate this pairwise configuration and a pairwise-plus-Hadamard composition in a dynamic W4A4KV4 setting across four checkpoints, measuring perplexity at short and long contexts, comparing angle estimation from K alone versus K&V, and performing a controlled interpolation from two-channel to full-head mixing support.
AI.result: The implementation attains the analytic minimum of the surrogate objective. The head-shared pairwise configuration does not improve accuracy: replacing the full-head Hadamard increases perplexity at both short and long contexts across all four checkpoints. Composing pairwise rotation with Hadamard satisfies the ±0.05-PPL interval criterion under the default estimator. Estimating the shared angle from K alone improves pairwise-only results on every checkpoint but still underperforms full-head mixing. Along the interpolation, K range, relative quantisation error, and perplexity degradation decrease as mixing support increases.
AI.conclusion: Optimality for a structured surrogate need not reduce quantisation error when the surrogate and mixing support are misaligned with the quantiser's scale-setting statistic. The analytic objective controls a position-averaged second moment of a pooled calibration covariance, whereas the dynamic quantiser sets its step from a tokenwise group range, and the pairwise transform has only two-channel mixing support—so the derived optimum fails to transfer to actual quantisation error reduction.

title: RAIL: An Automatic Classifier of the Artificial Intelligence Readiness Level
summary: Assessing the maturity of artificial intelligence technologies is essential for investment decisions, project management, and policy monitoring, yet the available readiness frameworks are heterogeneous and difficult to apply automatically: the adaptation of Technology Readiness Levels to AI lacks AI-specific gating criteria, the Machine Learning Technology Readiness Levels presuppose access to internal process artifacts, and AI/data readiness dimension models employ scales that resist direct comparison. This paper makes two contributions. First, we unify these three frameworks into the Unified AI Readiness Level (AIRL), a nine-level ordinal scale built on an environmental evidence ladder and complemented by dimensional caps (covering specification, data existence, data quality, data legality, expert knowledge, and algorithmic maturity) together with a generality-anchoring rule and explicit assignment disciplines, so that a readiness level becomes decidable from a natural-language description of the work alone. Second, we propose RAIL (Readiness Assessment via Independent LLM-experts), a panel-of-experts classifier that operationalizes the scale: one evidence agent and six independent dimension agents, each a large language model with a narrowly scoped mandate, deliver verdicts that a deterministic minimum rule aggregates and a chief expert reviews under asymmetric authority, confirming or lowering the panel's recommendation but never raising it above the caps. The method was tested in the analysis of several research works showing consistency and avoiding overestimation from monolithic LLM classifiers.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies three heterogeneous AI readiness frameworks into a single nine-level Unified AI Readiness Level (AIRL) that is decidable from natural-language descriptions alone, and operationalizes it via RAIL, a panel-of-experts LLM classifier whose deterministic aggregation and asymmetric chief-expert review prevent overestimation.
AI.motivation: Existing AI readiness frameworks are heterogeneous and hard to apply automatically: Technology Readiness Levels lack AI-specific gating criteria, Machine Learning Technology Readiness Levels require access to internal process artifacts, and AI/data readiness dimension models use scales that resist direct comparison. This hinders investment decisions, project management, and policy monitoring.
AI.method: The authors construct AIRL, a nine-level ordinal scale grounded in an environmental evidence ladder with dimensional caps spanning specification, data existence, data quality, data legality, expert knowledge, and algorithmic maturity, plus a generality-anchoring rule and explicit assignment disciplines. They then build RAIL, a panel-of-experts classifier with one evidence agent and six independent dimension agents (each an LLM with a narrowly scoped mandate), aggregated by a deterministic minimum rule and reviewed by a chief expert with asymmetric authority that can only confirm or lower, never raise, the panel's recommendation above the caps.
AI.result: Testing on several research works showed the method is consistent and avoids the overestimation typical of monolithic LLM classifiers.
AI.conclusion: The AIRL scale and RAIL classifier together provide a unified, automatically applicable, and conservative AI readiness assessment that remains decidable from natural-language descriptions and resists overestimation.

title: Reduced Matrix Multiplication: Input-Adaptive Matrix-Product Reduction for LLM Inference
summary: Transformer-based language models achieve strong performance but incur substantial inference cost due to repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications. We propose Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM), a training-free, input-adaptive inference method that reduces Transformer matrix products by selecting informative slices along their contraction dimensions, without modifying model weights. Under a simple retention-ratio control, RMM provides a smooth and predictable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Across language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, we find that reduction tolerance depends on the model family, task, component, and retention ratio, although it often improves with model scale. Under moderate reduction, RMM remains robust across the evaluated discriminative, autoregressive generation, and long-context settings. We further show that the same principle extends to multimodal vision-language inference. Mechanistic ablations reveal a structural asymmetry within Transformers: attention-side computations are substantially more reducible than MLP components. Finally, wall-clock benchmarks with custom kernels on an NVIDIA A100 show that these computational savings can translate into practical runtime gains, especially at longer sequence lengths. Together, these results position RMM as a scalable direction for input-adaptive inference-time optimization.

AI.tldr: RMM is a training-free, input-adaptive inference method that reduces Transformer matrix multiplications by selecting informative slices along contraction dimensions, offering a smooth accuracy-efficiency trade-off without altering model weights.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based language models achieve strong performance but incur substantial inference cost due to repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications, motivating cheaper input-adaptive inference without retraining.
AI.method: Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM) selects informative slices along the contraction dimensions of Transformer matrix products under a retention-ratio control; it requires no weight modification and is applied at inference time, with custom kernels benchmarked on an NVIDIA A100.
AI.result: Across 1B-70B models, reduction tolerance depends on model family, task, component, and retention ratio, and often improves with model scale. RMM is robust under moderate reduction in discriminative, autoregressive generation, and long-context settings, and extends to multimodal vision-language inference. Ablations show attention-side computations are substantially more reducible than MLP components, and custom kernels yield practical runtime gains, especially at longer sequence lengths.
AI.conclusion: RMM is a scalable direction for input-adaptive inference-time optimization, offering predictable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs with practical wall-clock speedups.

title: Academic League of Artificial Intelligence - An Integrative Perspective of Teaching, Research, and Extension
summary: Academic leagues have become important mechanisms for promoting extracurricular education and strengthening the integration between universities and society. This paper presents the organizational framework adopted by the Academic League of Artificial Intelligence (LIA) at the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC), designed to integrate teaching, research, and university extension through a student-centered, project-based approach. The framework combines democratic governance, collaborative learning, and dynamic project organization to foster both technical and transversal competencies. The framework is illustrated through representative initiatives, including competition teams, study groups, open lectures, knowledge repositories, and AI-powered applications with social impact. These projects demonstrate how diverse educational, scientific, and extension activities can be developed within a common organizational structure while promoting leadership, scientific production, community engagement, and knowledge preservation. The reported experience indicates that the proposed framework provides a flexible and replicable model for integrating the three university pillars into engineering and computing education, offering practical guidance for academic leagues and similar student organizations.

AI.tldr: The paper describes the organizational framework of the Academic League of Artificial Intelligence (LIA) at UFSC, showing how a student-centered, project-based structure integrates teaching, research, and university extension within a single academic organization.
AI.motivation: Academic leagues are increasingly important for extracurricular education and university-society integration, but there is a need for a clear, replicable organizational framework that unifies teaching, research, and extension while developing both technical and transversal student competencies.
