AI.method: The authors present LIA's organizational framework, which combines democratic governance, collaborative learning, and dynamic project organization under a student-centered, project-based model. The framework is illustrated through representative initiatives including competition teams, study groups, open lectures, knowledge repositories, and AI-powered applications with social impact.
AI.result: The initiatives demonstrate that diverse educational, scientific, and extension activities can operate within one common organizational structure while promoting leadership, scientific production, community engagement, and knowledge preservation. The reported experience indicates the framework is flexible and replicable.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a flexible and replicable model for integrating the three university pillars (teaching, research, and extension) into engineering and computing education, providing practical guidance for academic leagues and similar student organizations.

title: Symmetry-Breaking De Novo Crystal Generation via Markovian Jump Diffusion
summary: Generating crystals has recently attracted significant interest due to their broad applications in materials science. However, existing generative models struggle to produce complete crystallographic specifications, limiting their ability to capture global symmetry and structural dependencies. In particular, current state-of-the-art approaches generate crystals only up to site symmetries and rely on sampling space groups from empirical distributions during generation. Inspired by \emph{spontaneous symmetry breaking} in physics, where crystals break symmetries under external conditions, we propose a novel diffusion-based framework that generates full structure specifications by reversing from the lowest-symmetry priors. Our method leverages a Markovian jump-diffusion process to model these symmetry-breaking dynamics, enabling it to traverse different space groups in a physically motivated manner. Our model, dubbed \emph{Symmetry-breaking Crystal Diffusion} (SbCD), introduces a principled approach to explicitly incorporate inter-space-group transitions into the generative process. In de novo generation experiments on MP20 and MPTS-52, SbCD outperforms its symmetry-preserving counterpart by a substantial margin, offering a promising perspective for generative modeling of crystalline materials.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Symmetry-breaking Crystal Diffusion (SbCD), a diffusion-based generative model that generates full crystal structure specifications by reversing from lowest-symmetry priors, leveraging a Markovian jump-diffusion process to model inter-space-group transitions inspired by spontaneous symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: Existing crystal generative models fail to produce complete crystallographic specifications, generating only up to site symmetries and sampling space groups from empirical distributions. This limits their ability to capture global symmetry and structural dependencies in crystalline materials.
AI.method: SbCD models symmetry-breaking dynamics using a Markovian jump-diffusion process, reversing from lowest-symmetry priors to traverse different space groups in a physically motivated way, explicitly incorporating inter-space-group transitions into the generative process.
AI.result: In de novo generation experiments on MP20 and MPTS-52 benchmarks, SbCD outperforms its symmetry-preserving counterpart by a substantial margin.
AI.conclusion: SbCD provides a principled framework for incorporating inter-space-group transitions into generative crystal modeling, offering a promising new perspective for generating crystalline materials by reversing spontaneous symmetry breaking.

title: A Unifying Perspective on Causal World Models: From Observations to Representations to Structure
summary: World Models (WM) are increasingly seen as a foundation for intelligent agents that can predict, plan, and act beyond their training distribution. In this paper, we study WMs from a causal perspective across multiple levels of abstraction, ranging from perceptual observations to building a conceptual representation of the structure governing the environment dynamics. We argue that useful WMs must go beyond generative capabilities alone: they should also capture entity properties, entity-to-entity interactions, and entity-to-environment interactions that determine and explain the dynamics of a system. We provide a formal definition of Causal WMs (CWMs) grounded in the tasks they are intended to support, connecting world modelling with existing work in causal representation learning, object-centric learning, causal discovery, structural causal models, and model-based decision-making. Finally, we relate CWMs to the literature on identifiability, clarifying when the components of a WM can be recovered from data and up to which equivalence. With this, we ground WMs in representations and structures that support causal reasoning and informed decision-making.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Causal World Models (CWMs), arguing that useful world models must go beyond generation to capture entity properties, entity-entity interactions, and entity-environment interactions, and grounds them formally in causal representation learning, object-centric learning, causal discovery, structural causal models, and model-based decision-making, while analyzing identifiability.
AI.motivation: World Models are increasingly viewed as foundations for intelligent agents that can predict, plan, and act out-of-distribution. The authors argue that current generative capabilities alone are insufficient; useful WMs must also capture the causal structure governing environment dynamics (entity properties and interactions), so they formalize CWMs to support causal reasoning and informed decision-making.
AI.method: The authors take a causal perspective on WMs across multiple levels of abstraction (from perceptual observations to conceptual representations of environment dynamics). They provide a formal definition of Causal World Models (CWMs) grounded in the tasks they support, connecting world modelling to causal representation learning, object-centric learning, causal discovery, structural causal models, and model-based decision-making, and relate CWMs to identifiability results.
AI.result: The paper delivers a formal grounding of Causal World Models that spans multiple abstraction levels and connects them to several established causal/Object-centric frameworks, and clarifies under which conditions and up to which equivalence the components of a World Model can be recovered from data (identifiability).
AI.conclusion: Useful World Models must capture entity properties, entity-to-entity interactions, and entity-to-environment interactions that determine system dynamics, not just generative ability. By grounding WMs in causal representations and structures, the work supports causal reasoning and informed decision-making, and clarifies identifiability of WM components from data.

title: Doubly Robust Estimation of Causal Effect on CVR with Targeted Regularization
summary:
Post-click conversion rate (CVR) is a key metric in various scenarios including e-commerce and advertising, reflecting the efficiency and user experience in the second stage of the conversion process. Estimating the causal effect on CVR is therefore of great practical importance. However, directly applying existing causal inference methods to clicked samples introduces sample selection bias and increased variance due to the exclusion of non-click data. Recent studies on CVR prediction introduce "ideal loss", which optimizes model parameters using an unbiased estimate of the loss over the full sample. Nevertheless, there is no guarantee that unbiasedness of the loss implies unbiasedness of the final estimator.
  We revisit this challenge from the perspective of semiparametric theory. Specifically, we develop a new doubly robust causal effect estimator for chain-structured outcomes such as CVR, and derive its theoretical properties in detail. It achieves a faster convergence rate compared to nuisance parameters estimation and is therefore more robust when using flexible nonparametric estimators, including neural networks. Based on these theoretical findings, we further design a framework based on targeted regularization to improve numerical stability and practical applicability.
  Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method. In addition, we find that naively combining loss debiasing with standard causal estimators underperforms our method, highlighting the necessity of developing the new estimator tailored to this CVR-style objective with solid theoretical guarantees.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a new doubly robust causal effect estimator for chain-structured outcomes like post-click conversion rate (CVR), avoiding selection bias and variance issues from click-only samples, and pairs it with targeted regularization. Experiments show it outperforms naive combinations of loss debiasing with standard causal estimators.
AI.motivation: Estimating the causal effect on CVR is practically important, but applying existing causal inference methods only to clicked (selected) samples causes sample selection bias and increased variance. Prior "ideal loss" work in CVR prediction debiases the loss over the full sample, yet unbiasedness of the loss does not guarantee unbiasedness of the final estimator.
AI.method: The authors approach the problem using semiparametric theory and construct a doubly robust causal effect estimator tailored to chain-structured outcomes (e.g., click→conversion). They derive its theoretical properties, proving it achieves a faster convergence rate than nuisance parameter estimation, making it robust to flexible nonparametric estimators such as neural networks. They further design a targeted-regularization framework to improve numerical stability and practical applicability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method. Additionally, naively combining loss debiasing with standard causal estimators underperforms the proposed method, confirming the need for an estimator specifically designed for the CVR-style objective with solid theoretical guarantees.
AI.conclusion: A dedicated doubly robust estimator with targeted regularization is necessary and effective for causal CVR estimation, providing faster convergence and better practical performance than existing debiased-loss or standard causal estimators.

title: MARC v1: An Open-Source Multi-Agent Framework for Clinical AI Reasoning and Coordination
summary: We present Multi-Agent Reasoning and Coordination (MARC), an open-source framework that replaces monolithic LLM prompting with deterministic multi-agent orchestration for clinical reasoning. MARC coordinates role-specialized agents for extraction, reasoning, answer generation, and evaluation, with explicit context passing and traceable intermediate outputs, enabling stage-wise failure attribution. We additionally introduce a Decomposer module that generates task-specific agent prompts from a plain-language description, eliminating manual prompt engineering. The framework supports both API-based and local CPU-compatible deployments and is entirely configurable via YAML, without code modifications. MARC is designed to be model-agnostic, interpretable, and accessible to clinical domain experts without programming expertise. The full framework is available at https://github.com/Penn-RAIL/MARC-v1.

AI.tldr: MARC is an open-source multi-agent framework that replaces monolithic LLM prompting with deterministic, role-specialized agent orchestration for clinical reasoning, featuring a Decomposer for automatic prompt generation and YAML-based configuration for non-programmers.
AI.motivation: Replace opaque, monolithic LLM prompting in clinical reasoning with a transparent, interpretable system that enables stage-wise failure attribution and eliminates the need for manual prompt engineering, while remaining accessible to clinical domain experts without programming skills.
AI.method: Deterministic multi-agent orchestration coordinating role-specialized agents for extraction, reasoning, answer generation, and evaluation, with explicit context passing and traceable intermediate outputs. A Decomposer module generates task-specific agent prompts from plain-language descriptions. The framework is configured entirely via YAML (no code changes), is model-agnostic, and supports both API-based and local CPU-compatible deployments.
AI.result: The paper presents the MARC framework as an open-source artifact (available at https://github.com/Penn-RAIL/MARC-v1), demonstrating a configurable, model-agnostic, interpretable clinical reasoning system; the abstract does not report quantitative evaluation results.
AI.conclusion: MARC provides an interpretable, model-agnostic, and non-programmer-accessible alternative to monolithic LLM prompting for clinical reasoning, with stage-wise traceability and automated prompt generation enabling domain experts to configure multi-agent workflows without code modifications.

title: AlayaWorld: Interactive Long-Horizon World Modeling - Full Technical Report (v1.1)
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by the first name and their role. See the contribution section for details
summary: This report presents an improved version of AlayaWorld. While the backbone architecture, chunk-wise autoregressive generation scheme, and training data remain unchanged from the previous release, we substantially revise how conditioning signals are represented and integrated into the model. The new design is guided by a simple principle: conditioning signals should match the generated content as closely as possible in both latent representation and temporal structure. To this end, we make two major changes. First, we replace the previous depth-warping-based spatial memory with a streaming 3D point-cache renderer. Second, we redesign the conditioning pipeline so that visual conditions are encoded in the same causal-VAE latent space, with temporal statistics consistent with those of the generated video. Concretely, the new version introduces six modifications: (1) replacing static-frame image conditioning with motion-aware latent conditioning; (2) causally encoding re-rendered spatial memory as a continuous sequence; (3) aligning the temporal-memory window in pixel space; (4) adopting hard memory dropout that removes memory tokens rather than zeroing them; (5) unifying the VAE encoding and decoding protocol across training and inference; and (6) removing the camera AdaLN branch, such that viewpoint control is provided entirely through the re-rendered spatial condition.

AI.tldr: An improved version of the AlayaWorld video-generation model that revises how conditioning signals are represented and integrated, while keeping the backbone, autoregressive generation scheme, and training data unchanged. The core principle is making conditioning match generated content in both latent representation and temporal structure.
AI.motivation: To improve AlayaWorld by ensuring conditioning signals align as closely as possible with the generated content in both latent representation and temporal structure, addressing mismatches in the previous conditioning design.
AI.method: Two major changes: (1) replace the depth-warping-based spatial memory with a streaming 3D point-cache renderer; (2) redesign the conditioning pipeline to encode visual conditions in the same causal-VAE latent space with temporally consistent statistics. Concretely, six modifications: (1) static-frame image conditioning replaced by motion-aware latent conditioning; (2) causally encoding re-rendered spatial memory as a continuous sequence; (3) aligning the temporal-memory window in pixel space; (4) adopting hard memory dropout that removes memory tokens instead of zeroing them; (5) unifying the VAE encoding/decoding protocol across training and inference; (6) removing the camera AdaLN branch so viewpoint control comes entirely from the re-rendered spatial condition.
AI.result: The report describes the design changes but does not provide quantitative benchmark results in the abstract; results are architectural/design improvements rather than measured performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: The revised conditioning strategy—matching conditioning to generated content in latent space and temporal structure—represents the key improvement, with viewpoint control consolidated into the re-rendered spatial condition and a fully unified VAE protocol across training and inference.

title: Active-Trace Complexity Bounds for Moreau--Yosida Unadjusted Langevin Sampling
summary: We study the Moreau--Yosida unadjusted Langevin algorithm (MYULA) for the nonsmooth composite target \[ π(dx)\propto \exp\{-f(x)-g(x)\}\,dx, \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d, \] where \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_f\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is convex and \(G\)-Lipschitz. Let \(g_λ\) be the Moreau envelope of \(g\), \(π_λ\) the corresponding smoothed target, and \(a_λ=\operatorname{tr}H_λ\), where \(H_λ\) is the a.e./weak Hessian of \(g_λ\). We show that the leading MYULA discretization error is controlled by the reference active trace \(B_{\mathrm{ref}}\), the average of \(a_λ\) along the heat substep of one MYULA update started from \(π_λ\), rather than by the global curvature bound \(d/λ\). If \(M_λ\) is an a.e. upper bound for \(a_λ\), then, up to logarithmic factors, \[ N \lesssim \frac{1}{m} \left[ L_f + \frac{ τ_f+G^2+B_{\mathrm{ref}} }{ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{alg}}^2 } + \frac{M_λ}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{alg}}} \right], \qquad τ_f:= \sup_x\operatorname{tr}\nabla^2 f(x), \] iterations suffice to ensure \(\sqrt m\,W_2(μ_N,π_λ)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{alg}}\), where \(μ_N\) is the law of the \(N\)-th iterate and \(W_2\) is the quadratic Wasserstein distance. We also prove the Moreau-bias bound \[ \sqrt m\,W_2(π_λ,π) \leq \frac{G^2λ}{4}. \] Thus, choosing \(λ\asymp\varepsilon/G^2\) gives an end-to-end guarantee for \(π\). The universal estimate \(B_{\mathrm{ref}}\leq d/λ\) yields \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) accuracy dependence. For the structured piecewise-linear, lasso-type, group, and total-variation penalties considered here, curvature--tube estimates make \(B_{\mathrm{ref}}\) independent of \(λ\), yielding \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) for the same classical MYULA kernel.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes MYULA for composite sampling where the nonsmooth part is Lipschitz (weakly convex) rather than handled by standard prox conditions. It refines the discretization error bound using a "reference active trace" B_ref — the average of the Moreau-envelope Hessian trace along the heat substep — instead of the crude d/λ bound, achieving near-quadratic (Õ(ε⁻²)) complexity for structured penalties (lasso, group, TV) versus Õ(ε⁻³) in general.
AI.motivation: Standard MYULA analyses bound the Moreau-envelope Hessian trace by the global curvature d/λ, which is loose for non-strongly-convex or weakly convex g (e.g., lasso, group, TV penalties). This yields pessimistic Õ(ε⁻³) mixing guarantees. The authors seek sharp, structure-aware complexity that reflects the actual low-dimensional or sparsely active curvature of g rather than a uniform worst-case bound.
AI.method: Consider target π(dx) ∝ exp(−f(x)−g(x))dx with f m-strongly convex and L_f-Lipschitz gradient, and g convex and G-Lipschitz. Smooth g via its Moreau envelope g_λ, giving smoothed target π_λ, and define a_λ = tr H_λ where H_λ is the a.e./weak Hessian of g_λ. Run MYULA on π_λ. The key quantity is B_ref, the average of a_λ along the heat substep of one MYULA update initialized at π_λ. The analysis shows the leading discretization error is controlled by B_ref rather than d/λ, with M_λ an a.e. upper bound on a_λ. A Moreau-bias bound √m W₂(π_λ,π) ≤ G²λ/4 links the smoothed to the original target. Curvature–tube estimates are used to make B_ref λ-independent for structured penalties.
AI.result: Up to log factors, N ≲ (1/m)[L_f + (τ_f + G² + B_ref)/ε²_alg + M_λ/ε_alg] MYULA iterations suffice for √m W₂(μ_N, π_λ) ≤ ε_alg, with τ_f = sup_x tr ∇²f(x). The Moreau-bias bound gives √m W₂(π_λ,π) ≤ G²λ/4, so choosing λ ≍ ε/G² yields an end-to-end guarantee for π. The universal estimate B_ref ≤ d/λ recovers Õ(ε⁻³). For piecewise-linear, lasso, group, and TV penalties, curvature–tube estimates make B_ref independent of λ, giving Õ(ε⁻²) for the same classical MYULA kernel.
AI.conclusion: The complexity of the classical MYULA kernel can be improved from Õ(ε⁻³) to Õ(ε⁻²) for structured nonsmooth penalties by replacing the blanket d/λ curvature bound with the structure-sensitive reference active trace B_ref. This provides sharper, near-optimal nonasymptotic guarantees and clarifies the role of the penalty's active curvature in MYULA convergence.

title: Synthetic Persona Pretraining: Alignment from Token Zero
summary: As language-model-based AI is increasingly deployed in autonomous settings, aligning its goals and values with those of humans becomes critical. Today, alignment, and the assistant identity itself, are typically introduced only after pretraining, once behavioral priors are already established. This can make values a thin overlay, rather than deeply rooted, and facilitate subsequent misalignment. Pursuing a different paradigm, we introduce Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP), which installs the desired assistant persona from token zero in pretraining. First, we annotate pretraining documents with value-aligned first-person reflections derived from a normative value constitution. Second, we pretrain via the standard cross-entropy loss on standard pretraining documents as well as their reflections, which installs the desired persona among a multitude of other personas. Finally, we post-train on user-assistant dialogue data, which binds this desired persona to the assistant identity, a process we call persona binding. By pretraining models up to 3B parameters on 500B tokens, we show that SPP improves constitution following and jailbreak robustness, and reduces the misalignment rate in out-of-distribution moral dilemmas, while preserving capabilities. Early intervention matters: compared with alignment from token zero, introducing SPP only at the end of pretraining yields weaker constitution adherence, does not shift value priorities, and leads to less aligned choices in dilemmas. This advantage depends on persona binding and, importantly, increases with pretraining budget. Overall, our results show that shaping values early is critical for alignment and establish pretraining-time persona interventions as an effective approach to do so.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP), which embeds a desired value-aligned assistant persona into language models from the very first token of pretraining. Testing models up to 3B parameters on 500B tokens, SPP improves constitutional adherence, jailbreak robustness, and alignment in moral dilemmas while preserving capabilities. The authors find that early intervention matters and that the benefits grow with pretraining budget.
AI.motivation: Current alignment methods introduce values and the assistant identity only after pretraining, when behavioral priors are already set, making values a thin overlay that is vulnerable to later misalignment. The authors argue for a fundamentally different paradigm: installing the desired persona during pretraining itself so values are deeply rooted rather than bolted on.
AI.method: Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP) consists of three stages: (1) annotate pretraining documents with value-aligned first-person reflections synthesized from a normative value constitution; (2) pretrain with standard cross-entropy loss on both normal documents and their reflections, installing the desired persona among many others; (3) post-train on user-assistant dialogue data to bind this persona to the assistant identity, a step called "persona binding." Ablations compare alignment from token zero versus introducing SPP only at the end of pretraining.
AI.result: SPP improves constitution following and jailbreak robustness, reduces the misalignment rate on out-of-distribution moral dilemmas, and preserves capabilities. Introducing SPP only at the end of pretraining yields weaker constitution adherence, no shift in value priorities, and less aligned dilemma choices, demonstrating that early intervention matters. The advantage depends on persona binding and increases with pretraining budget.
AI.conclusion: Shaping values early is critical for alignment. Pretraining-time persona interventions such as SPP are an effective approach to deeply root desired values in language models, and their benefits scale with pretraining budget.

title: OmniScientist: An Omni-Modal Omni-Discipline AI Scientist
comment: 30 pages, 13 figures, 19 tables. Project page: https://omni-scientist.github.io/
summary: Recent advances in foundation models have enabled AI scientists to automate increasingly complete research workflows, from hypothesis generation and code execution to manuscript preparation. Yet workflow coverage alone does not provide access to the full evidence on which scientific discovery depends. Existing systems typically reason over text, code, labels, or precomputed summaries, leaving scientifically decisive spatial, temporal, cross-channel, and procedural relations unavailable to the agent. We introduce OmniScientist, an end-to-end, omni-modal AI scientist that conducts multidisciplinary research directly from heterogeneous raw evidence. A perception layer and 3 autonomous agents for ideation, experiment, and writeup operate within a deterministic pipeline, allowing observations to shape research questions, experimental decisions, and final claims throughout the research lifecycle. By running idea, rigour, and claim checks in code, the system enforces novelty screening, statistical validity, execution provenance, and numerical traceability. We evaluate OmniScientist on 36 real-data cases spanning 5 discipline families, 4 families of scientific evidence, and modalities including images, signals, audio, video, 3-D structures, trajectories, tables, formulae, and graphs. The system completes the full path from raw data to a compiled manuscript in all 36 cases and achieves a mean overall paper score of 6.3 with the reference reasoning backbone. In paired comparisons against a blind variant that receives only precomputed scalar features, direct perception improves all 7 evaluation dimensions and wins 85% of head-to-head judgments. These results show that lifecycle-wide perception is essential for evidence-grounded scientific discovery and provides a practical path toward broadly capable AI scientists.

AI.tldr: OmniScientist is an end-to-end, omni-modal AI scientist that conducts research directly from heterogeneous raw evidence, using a perception layer and three autonomous agents (ideation, experiment, writeup) within a deterministic pipeline that enforces novelty, statistical validity, provenance, and traceability via in-code checks.
AI.motivation: Existing AI scientist systems reason only over text, code, labels, or precomputed summaries, leaving scientifically decisive spatial, temporal, cross-channel, and procedural relations unavailable. The authors argue that workflow coverage alone is insufficient and that lifecycle-wide perception of raw evidence is essential for evidence-grounded discovery.
AI.method: OmniScientist combines a perception layer with three autonomous agents (ideation, experiment, writeup) in a deterministic pipeline so that observations shape research questions, experimental decisions, and final claims. Novelty screening, statistical validity, execution provenance, and numerical traceability are enforced through idea, rigour, and claim checks implemented in code.
AI.result: Evaluated on 36 real-data cases spanning 5 discipline families, 4 families of scientific evidence, and 9 modalities (images, signals, audio, video, 3-D structures, trajectories, tables, formulae, graphs), the system completed the full raw-data-to-manuscript path in all 36 cases, achieving a mean overall paper score of 6.3. Direct perception improved all 7 evaluation dimensions and won 85% of head-to-head judgments compared to a blind variant receiving only precomputed scalar features.
AI.conclusion: Lifecycle-wide perception is essential for evidence-grounded scientific discovery, and OmniScientist provides a practical path toward broadly capable AI scientists that reason directly over heterogeneous raw evidence.

title: Sparse Orthogonal Regression Technique: A Spectral Framework for Equation Discovery, Approximation, and Integration
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for oral presentation at the 29th International Conference on Discovery Science (DS 2026), Mainz, Germany, October 5-9, 2026. To appear in Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS)
summary: We develop the Sparse Orthogonal Regression Technique (SORT), a sparse spectral framework for learning orthonormal-basis expansions from noisy and irregularly sampled data. SORT estimates expansion coefficients directly from observations using L1-regularized regression, avoiding explicit quadrature or analytic inner-product evaluation. The central application is data-driven discovery of ordinary differential equations: vector fields are represented in chosen orthogonal bases and learned as sparse coefficient expansions. This provides a complementary route to symbolic regression, grammar-based discovery, and SINDy-style sparse identification by first recovering a compact spectral representation, which can later guide searches for simpler analytic forms. Across the dynamical-system experiments, SORT matches or improves upon library-based sparse-regression baselines when the basis is well adapted to the problem, and shows more stable degradation under sparse sampling, noisy derivative estimates, and representation mismatch. Specific examples illustrate why this representation is useful: if a finite library misses the problem-specific nonlinearity, the resulting model can fail. SORT is not immune to mismatch, but it shifts the problem away from brittle selection among generic terms to basis design adapted to the problem domain. The experiments also show that dominant low-order coefficients persist as model order increases, supporting order-consistent model growth. Beyond equation discovery, the same learned expansion supports nonlinear approximation and estimation of complex, high-dimensional integrals by coefficient readout. Overall, SORT provides a reusable intermediate representation for system identification, approximation, and integration, while making basis design an explicit part of the scientific modeling problem.

AI.tldr: SORT is a sparse spectral framework that learns orthonormal-basis expansions directly from noisy, irregularly sampled data via L1-regularized regression, avoiding quadrature or analytic inner products. Its main use is data-driven discovery of ODEs, where vector fields are learned as sparse coefficient expansions in chosen orthogonal bases, offering a complementary alternative to SINDy-style and symbolic approaches and extending to approximation and high-dimensional integration.
AI.motivation: Library-based sparse regression (e.g., SINDy) and symbolic/grammar approaches can fail brittly when the finite library misses the problem-specific nonlinearity, and they rely on generic term selection. The authors seek a more stable route that recovers a compact spectral representation first, and explicitly turns basis design into part of the modeling problem rather than brittle selection among generic candidate terms.
AI.method: SORT learns expansion coefficients directly from observations using L1-regularized regression in an orthogonal-basis spectral representation, without explicit quadrature or analytic inner products. Vector fields are represented in chosen orthogonal bases and learned as sparse coefficient expansions. The framework supports data-driven ODE discovery, nonlinear approximation, and estimation of complex high-dimensional integrals via coefficient readout, with basis design adapted to the problem domain.
AI.result: Across dynamical-system experiments, SORT matches or improves upon library-based sparse-regression baselines when the basis is well adapted, and degrades more stably under sparse sampling, noisy derivative estimates, and representation mismatch. Experiments show dominant low-order coefficients persist as model order increases, supporting order-consistent model growth. Specific examples illustrate that a finite library missing the problem-specific nonlinearity can fail, whereas SORT shifts the difficulty from brittle term selection to basis design.
AI.conclusion: SORT provides a reusable intermediate representation for system identification, approximation, and integration, making basis design an explicit part of scientific modeling. It complements symbolic regression, grammar-based discovery, and SINDy-style sparse identification by first recovering a compact spectral representation that can later guide searches for simpler analytic forms.

title: Intern-S2-Preview: Scientific Agentic Foundation Model
summary: Scientific discovery increasingly requires AI systems that can reason over scientific evidence of heterogeneous modalities, interact with scientific tools and environments, and sustain progress across long task horizons. We present Intern-S2-Preview, a series of scientific agentic foundation models designed to support multimodal scientific understanding, reasoning, generation, and long-horizon tasks. The training pipeline begins with scientific multimodal pre-training over rendered scientific documents, interleaved image-text data, and diverse scientific corpora. Starting from the pretrained checkpoint, we apply a unified post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning, scalable multi-task reinforcement learning (RL), black- and white-box agentic RL, and on-policy distillation. This pipeline is supported by practical techniques that improve rollout and training stability and efficiency, including partial rollout with off-policy correction, adaptive length regularization, online speculative decoding, robust multi-task optimization, and trace-aware experience assembly for agentic tasks. At the architecture level, Intern-S2-Preview-397B extends time series modelling from efficient long-sequence understanding to numerical forecasting, while Memory Decoder is studied as a separate memory-augmented path for rapid scientific specialization without modifying the frozen 397B backbone. Evaluations across scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general-purpose benchmarks show that Intern-S2-Preview-397B achieves competitive or leading results in multiple settings. The time series modules improve scientific signal understanding and forecasting on SciTS, while the separate Intern-MemDec-4B extension improves the Biology-Instructions average score from 56.92 to 60.32 without modifying the frozen 397B backbone.

AI.tldr: Intern-S2-Preview is a family of scientific agentic foundation models (up to 397B parameters) trained via scientific multimodal pretraining followed by a unified post-training pipeline (SFT, multi-task RL, black/white-box agentic RL, on-policy distillation). It extends time series modeling to numerical forecasting and studies a Memory Decoder path for rapid scientific specialization without modifying the frozen backbone.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery requires AI systems that can reason over heterogeneous, multimodal scientific evidence, interact with scientific tools and environments, and sustain progress over long task horizons—capabilities not adequately supported by existing models.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) scientific multimodal pre-training over rendered scientific documents, interleaved image-text data, and diverse scientific corpora; (2) a unified post-training pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, scalable multi-task reinforcement learning, black-box and white-box agentic RL, and on-policy distillation. Training stability/efficiency techniques include partial rollout with off-policy correction, adaptive length regularization, online speculative decoding, robust multi-task optimization, and trace-aware experience assembly. Architecturally, Intern-S2-Preview-397B extends time series modeling to numerical forecasting, and Memory Decoder (Intern-MemDec-4B) is studied as a memory-augmented path for rapid specialization on a frozen 397B backbone.
AI.result: Intern-S2-Preview-397B achieves competitive or leading results across scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general-purpose benchmarks. Time series modules improve scientific signal understanding and forecasting on SciTS. The separate Intern-MemDec-4B extension raises the Biology-Instructions average score from 56.92 to 60.32 without modifying the frozen 397B backbone.
AI.conclusion: The unified post-training pipeline with stability/efficiency techniques enables Intern-S2-Preview models to reach competitive or leading performance across diverse tasks, while time series forecasting and the Memory Decoder offer effective, low-cost routes for scientific specialization.

title: Intervention-Aware Clinical World Model for Post-Op Outcome Forecasting in Cardiology
comment: Medical World Models (MWM) Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Many clinical prediction models treat post-intervention outcomes as a one-step mapping from baseline measurements to a future endpoint. However, recovery after a procedure often unfolds as an irregular trajectory: clinical observations, medication changes, repeat interventions, and physiological measurements are recorded asynchronously and can change risk assessment over time. We propose an intervention-aware clinical world model that represents each patient with a structured latent state and evolves it through time-ordered post-intervention events. The model first encodes baseline imaging into a 3D spatial latent state. It then updates this state using procedural context, static covariates, elapsed time, and peri-event physiological embeddings. Follow-up imaging provides training-only supervision through a latent forecasting objective. We apply the framework to atrial fibrillation ablation. During the 90-day recovery window, irregular post-procedure records provide clinically meaningful evidence for long-term recurrence risk. In repeated internal cross-validation on DECAAF-II, our model achieves AUROC 0.756 and AUPRC 0.777 for recurrence prediction. It also achieves a scar-extent MAE of 2.971 percentage points without requiring follow-up MRI intensities at inference. The learned state supports recurrence-risk queries at different horizons and retrospective input editing of blanking-period records.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an intervention-aware clinical world model that evolves a structured latent state through irregular, time-ordered post-intervention events. Applied to atrial fibrillation ablation, it predicts recurrence from asynchronous post-procedure records, achieving AUROC 0.756 and AUPRC 0.777, and estimates scar extent with MAE 2.971 without follow-up MRI at inference.
AI.motivation: Standard clinical prediction models map baseline measurements directly to a future endpoint, ignoring that recovery after a procedure is an irregular trajectory with asynchronous clinical observations, medication changes, repeat interventions, and physiological measurements that can update risk over time.
AI.method: An intervention-aware clinical world model encodes baseline imaging into a 3D spatial latent state, then updates it sequentially using procedural context, static covariates, elapsed time, and peri-event physiological embeddings. Follow-up imaging provides training-only supervision via a latent forecasting objective. The framework is applied to atrial fibrillation ablation over a 90-day recovery window, and supports recurrence-risk queries at multiple horizons plus retrospective editing of blanking-period records.
AI.result: In repeated internal cross-validation on DECAAF-II, the model achieves AUROC 0.756 and AUPRC 0.777 for recurrence prediction, and a scar-extent MAE of 2.971 percentage points without requiring follow-up MRI intensities at inference time.
AI.conclusion: Modeling post-intervention recovery as an evolving latent state over time-ordered irregular events provides clinically meaningful evidence for long-term recurrence risk and enables flexible risk queries and input editing, outperforming one-step baseline-to-outcome approaches.

title: The data geometry of masking diffusion: Certified-optimal schedules via unmasking growth complexity
summary: We study masking diffusion for discrete sampling and introduce a path-resolved measure of data geometry called the \emph{unmasking growth complexity} ({\textsf{UGC}\xspace}). Its local increments directly control Kullback--Leibler (KL) discretization error, yielding a unified analysis of Bernoulli-subset and fixed-cardinality unmasking schemes. In log-reveal-odds coordinates, this structure yields optimized single-block and multi-block schedules, and quantifies the gains from adapting computational effort to data geometry. Crucially, we show how {\textsf{UGC}\xspace} increments can be estimated from samples via KL increments along coupled reveal trajectories. This leads to \emph{certified-optimal} samplers that achieve a prescribed KL error with high probability and iteration complexity within a constant factor of the corresponding oracle procedure. Collapsing the \ugc path yields the aggregate {\textsf{UGC}\xspace} mass, which connects to classical multivariate dependence measures and complexity measures from previous analyses of discrete diffusion. In the fine-partition limit, the squared integral of the square-root {\textsf{UGC}\xspace} density determines the sharp leading-order optimal Euler discretization error. Examples exhibit substantial dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules, including $\widetildeΩ(\sqrt{d})$ improvements achievable with a constant number of adaptively placed blocks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "unmasking growth complexity" (UGC), a path-resolved measure of data geometry for masking diffusion in discrete sampling. UGC increments control KL discretization error, enabling unified analysis of unmasking schemes, optimized schedules, and certified-optimal samplers whose complexity is within a constant factor of an oracle, with dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules.
AI.motivation: Masking diffusion is a powerful tool for discrete sampling, but existing analyses provide only coarse or aggregate guarantees and do not explain how per-step discretization error depends on local data geometry. The goal is to develop a path-resolved complexity measure that (a) unifies different unmasking schemes, (b) enables optimized schedules and adaptive computational effort, and (c) yields sample-efficient certified-optimal samplers with oracle-competitive iteration complexity.
AI.method: The authors define the unmasking growth complexity (UGC) and analyze its local increments in log-reveal-odds coordinates, where they directly bound Kullback–Leibler discretization error. They design optimized single-block and multi-block unmasking schedules, and estimate UGC increments from samples via KL increments along coupled reveal trajectories. They also study the aggregate UGC mass (linking to multivariate dependence measures) and the fine-partition limit, where the squared integral of the square-root UGC density yields the sharp leading-order optimal Euler discretization error.
AI.result: The framework yields a unified analysis of Bernoulli-subset and fixed-cardinality unmasking schemes, certified-optimal samplers achieving prescribed KL error with high probability and iteration complexity within a constant factor of the oracle procedure, and examples showing substantial dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules, including a roughly Omega(sqrt(d)) improvement achievable with a constant number of adaptively placed blocks.
AI.conclusion: Path-resolved UGC provides a principled, unified lens for analyzing and optimizing discrete masking diffusion. It connects local error control to aggregate complexity measures, enables certified-optimal adaptive sampling with oracle-level efficiency, and demonstrates significant dimension-dependent improvements over coarse schedules.

title: DARTree: Speculative Diffusion Decoding with Autoregressive Draft Trees
summary: Speculative decoding losslessly accelerates autoregressive language models by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel. Diffusion-based drafters further reduce proposal latency by predicting an entire token block in parallel, but their position-wise distributions are marginal rather than conditioned on tokens selected along each draft path. Existing recurrent correction incorporates causal information along a single draft chain, whereas diffusion-based tree construction broadens candidate coverage without carrying this correction along individual branches. We introduce DARTree, a training-free speculative decoding method that extends a pretrained AR correction head from chains to trees. DARTree first constructs a fixed-width candidate tree by expanding and scoring all nodes at each depth in a single batch, and then only applies best-first pruning to select the verification tree, decoupling AR-head inference from sequential heap operations. Across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, DARTree achieves the highest average acceptance length and speedup in all four model--temperature configurations, accepting up to 12.97 tokens per verification round, 98.6\% more than DFlash and 27.9\% more than Domino in the same setting, and reaching up to 9.73$\times$ lossless speedup over locally measured autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: DARTree is a training-free speculative decoding method that extends a pretrained autoregressive (AR) correction head from chains to trees, using fixed-width candidate tree expansion with best-first pruning to achieve state-of-the-art acceptance length and speedup.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding accelerates AR language models by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel. Diffusion-based drafters predict whole token blocks in parallel, but their distributions are marginal (position-wise) rather than conditioned on tokens along each draft path. Existing recurrent correction only carries causal information along a single chain, while diffusion-based tree construction broadens candidate coverage without propagating this correction along individual branches. The gap motivates combining causal correction with tree-structured drafting.
AI.method: DARTree extends a pretrained AR correction head from chains to trees in a training-free manner. It constructs a fixed-width candidate tree by expanding and scoring all nodes at each depth in a single batch, then applies best-first pruning to select the verification tree. This decouples AR-head inference from sequential heap operations, avoiding the latency of per-node sequential processing.
AI.result: Across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, DARTree achieves the highest average acceptance length and speedup in all four model-temperature configurations, accepting up to 12.97 tokens per verification round (98.6% more than DFlash and 27.9% more than Domino in the same setting), and reaching up to 9.73x lossless speedup over locally measured autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: DARTree demonstrates that combining tree-structured candidate expansion from diffusion with chain-style causal correction yields a training-free speculative decoding approach with superior acceptance length and lossless decoding speedup across diverse benchmarks.

title: Exponential Convex Calibration Dimension for the Multi-Label Jaccard Measure
summary: The per-instance Jaccard score, or intersection over union (IoU), is standard in multi-label classification and binary segmentation. With $s$ labels, its loss matrix has $2^s$ outcomes and reports. Under the convention $\mathrm{Jac}(\varnothing,\varnothing)=1$, we prove that the Jaccard score, shifted-loss, and ordinary loss matrices are nonsingular and that the loss columns have affine dimension $2^s-1$. The proof combines a finite MinHash Gram representation with Boolean Möbius inversion. For exact calibration, we prove $2^{s-1} \leq \mathrm{CCdim}(L^{\mathrm{Jac}}) \leq 2^s-1$. The lower bound uses a factorially weighted distribution with $2^{s-1}+1$ supported outcomes and Bayes-optimal reports. Consequently, every exactly calibrated convex surrogate requires exponentially many prediction coordinates. We also give two polynomial-dimensional approximation guarantees with explicit regret transfers. A new $F_1$-to-Jaccard transfer turns an existing $(s^2+1)$-dimensional $F_1$ surrogate into a polynomial-time rule with asymptotic Jaccard regret at most $3-2\sqrt{2}$. For any $α>0$ and $0<ρ<1$, a MinHash square-loss surrogate attains Jaccard-regret floor $α$ uniformly over arbitrary conditional label distributions. With probability at least $1-ρ$, the direct construction has dimension $O((s^2+s\log(1/ρ))/α^2)$, while a signed variant has dimension $O((s+\log(1/ρ))/α^2)$. Thus zero-regret calibration requires exponential dimension, whereas every fixed additive regret tolerance admits polynomial prediction dimension.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the per-instance Jaccard score (IoU) in multi-label classification and binary segmentation. It proves the Jaccard, shifted-loss, and ordinary loss matrices are nonsingular with loss columns of affine dimension 2^s - 1, bounds the calibration dimension as 2^(s-1) ≤ CCdim ≤ 2^s - 1, and shows zero-regret exact calibration requires exponential prediction coordinates. It then gives two polynomial-dimensional approximation guarantees, including an F1-to-Jaccard regret transfer and a MinHash square-loss surrogate achieving any fixed additive regret with polynomial dimension.
AI.motivation: The Jaccard score (IoU) is the standard evaluation metric in multi-label classification and binary segmentation, but its loss matrix has 2^s outcomes, raising the question of how many prediction coordinates (calibration dimension) are needed to calibrate or optimize it. The paper aims to characterize the intrinsic complexity of Jaccard loss and determine whether polynomial-dimensional surrogates can achieve low Jaccard regret.
AI.method: Using the convention Jac(∅,∅)=1, the authors combine a finite MinHash Gram representation with Boolean Möbius inversion to prove nonsingularity of the Jaccard, shifted-loss, and ordinary loss matrices and that loss columns have affine dimension 2^s - 1. They establish the lower bound CCdim ≥ 2^(s-1) using a factorially weighted distribution supported on 2^(s-1)+1 outcomes together with Bayes-optimal reports, and the upper bound CCdim ≤ 2^s - 1. For polynomial approximations, they introduce an F1-to-Jaccard regret transfer yielding a polynomial-time rule with asymptotic Jaccard regret ≤ 3 - 2√2, and a MinHash square-loss surrogate attaining arbitrary fixed regret floor α uniformly over conditional label distributions, constructed directly or in a signed variant with controlled dimension.
AI.result: It is shown that exact zero-regret calibration requires exponentially many prediction coordinates, with 2^(s-1) ≤ CCdim ≤ 2^s - 1. In contrast, any fixed additive regret tolerance α > 0 admits polynomial prediction dimension: the direct MinHash construction has dimension O((s^2 + s log(1/ρ))/α^2) and the signed variant O((s + log(1/ρ))/α^2), each with probability at least 1 - ρ. The F1-to-Jaccard transfer converts an (s^2+1)-dimensional F1 surrogate into a polynomial-time rule with asymptotic Jaccard regret at most 3 - 2√2.
AI.conclusion: Zero-regret calibration for the Jaccard score is intractable, requiring exponential prediction dimension, so no polynomial-dimensional convex surrogate can be exactly calibrated. However, the problem becomes tractable for any fixed positive regret tolerance: polynomial-dimensional surrogates (MinHash square-loss, signed variants) achieve arbitrary additive regret, and an F1 surrogate yields a polynomial-time rule with bounded asymptotic Jaccard regret. This separates exact calibration (exponential) from ε-approximate calibration (polynomial).

title: Defensive Boosting for Online Probabilistic Forecasting
summary:
We study online probabilistic forecasting of binary outcomes chosen by an adaptive adversary. Given an online learning algorithm for a weak hypothesis class $H$, we would like to efficiently obtain two incomparable guarantees that existing online boosting techniques provide separately. Online gradient boosting competes in Brier score with the best predictor induced by the span of $H$ on every sequence, but promises nothing when the span does not contain an accurate predictor. Online weak-to-strong boosting drives classification error to zero under a weak-learning condition, but promises little when that condition fails.
  We give a simple defensive forecasting algorithm, the Defensive Booster, that obtains both guarantees. On every adaptive sequence, its Brier score is competitive with the best prediction induced by the span of $H$ at the same rate as online gradient boosting; simultaneously, whenever the realized transcript satisfies the smooth weak-learning condition, its Brier score and randomized classification error satisfy the same rate guarantee as online classification boosting. This is achieved by operationalizing the "dual view" of boosting: When the algorithm's randomized classification error is persistently high, its mistake weights form a smooth reweighting on which every weak hypothesis has low edge, yielding an ex-post hard-core certificate that the weak-learning condition fails. We also develop a strongly adaptive variant, which satisfies both guarantees on every time interval. The Defensive Booster is very efficient: it accesses just one weak-class learner, whereas the prior online boosting methods we compare against maintain large weak-learner ensembles. Experiments on synthetic and real data streams demonstrate its strong predictive performance (sometimes substantially improving over all prior baselines) coupled with orders-of-magnitude faster runtime.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Defensive Booster, an efficient online forecasting algorithm that simultaneously achieves two guarantees previously only available separately: competitiveness in Brier score with the best predictor in the span of a weak hypothesis class (like online gradient boosting), and driving error to zero under the smooth weak-learning condition (like online weak-to-strong boosting). It does so using a single weak-class learner rather than large ensembles, with strong empirical performance and much faster runtime.
AI.motivation: Existing online boosting techniques provide two incomparable guarantees that no single prior method achieves together. Online gradient boosting competes in Brier score with the best predictor in the span of H on every sequence but fails when the span lacks an accurate predictor. Online weak-to-strong boosting drives classification error to zero under a smooth weak-learning condition but offers little when that condition fails. The gap motivates an algorithm that secures both guarantees simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors propose a defensive forecasting algorithm called the Defensive Booster, operationalizing the "dual view" of boosting. It maintains randomized classification; when error is persistently high, the mistake weights form a smooth reweighting on which every weak hypothesis has low edge, producing an ex-post hard-core certificate that the weak-learning condition fails. A strongly adaptive variant is also developed to satisfy both guarantees on every time interval. The algorithm accesses only one weak-class learner.
AI.result: The Defensive Booster achieves Brier score competitive with the best prediction induced by the span of H at the same rate as online gradient boosting on every adaptive sequence, while simultaneously matching the rate guarantee of online classification boosting in Brier score and randomized classification error whenever the smooth weak-learning condition holds. Experiments on synthetic and real data streams show strong predictive performance, sometimes substantially improving over all prior baselines, with orders-of-magnitude faster runtime.
AI.conclusion: The Defensive Booster resolves the gap between the two incomparable online boosting guarantees within a single, highly efficient algorithm requiring only one weak-class learner, and its strongly adaptive variant extends the guarantees to every time interval. Empirical results confirm its predictive advantages and dramatically reduced runtime compared to prior ensemble-based methods.
